Signal Integrity & Noise Load: Each transmission drifts—small errors compound across generations; no verification mechanism; signal degrades slowly but inevitably, occasionally corrected when a variant proves more effective.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Reciprocity and kin loyalty anchor the implicit code; free-riding punished by exclusion; fairness intuitive, not articulated.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: No codified law; conduct regulated by custom internalized through imitation and social consequence.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: Disputes resolved by dominance contest, avoidance, or fission; sanction ranges from social coldness to expulsion; no third-party adjudication.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: No formal rights; protection comes from band membership; compliance burden is behavioral conformity to group norms.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: Wrongs unredressed accumulate as grudge or lead to fission; no institutional redress.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: No formal inquiry; understanding is procedural—embodied know-how without propositional theory.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: The Acheulean reduction sequence—platform preparation, bifacial thinning, edge refinement—represents the leading technical method; transmission requires extended observation and practice, and error correction is mimetic, not verbal.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: Knowledge stock is thin but sufficient; skill concentrates in practiced adults; distribution widens as juveniles mature into knapping competence; no formal schooling.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: Mode 1 techniques persist alongside Acheulean; older methods not actively shed, but drift into disuse as bifacial tools prove superior; knowledge decays at death and is rebuilt by each learner.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: No recoverable mythos; identity is the band itself—those one eats with, sleeps beside, and follows.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: None articulated; legitimacy is presence and shared practice.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: The handaxe is the signature artifact—symmetrical, often exceeding functional necessity, suggesting aesthetic attention or display; no decoration, pigment, or ornament yet evident.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: Forms remain fresh because transmission is slow and variable; no exhaustion within this window.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: No recoverable cosmology; orientation to the world is practical and immediate; existential outlook unknowable but likely unreflective.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: No clear ritual evidence in this window; if present, it leaves no archaeological trace.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: None.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: Not applicable; no system to diffuse.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: No prior enchantment to lose; dimension inert.

docs.title: 50,000 BCE – 42,000 BCE — Final Neanderthal Populations in Southern Iberia
docs.text: Summary: The last Neanderthal populations in Europe contracted into the southern Iberian refugium as climate deteriorated and, possibly, anatomically modern humans expanded from the east; the binding constraint was demographic fragility — small, isolated bands whose knowledge base and reproductive viability eroded with each generation lost, until imitative transmission itself could no longer sustain continuity.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: The Gibraltar corridor and southern coastal strip formed a cul-de-sac bounded by the Mediterranean to the south and east, the Atlantic to the west, and increasingly inhospitable interior plateaus to the north; caves such as Gorham's Cave, Vanguard Cave, and the Gibraltar complex offered sheltered occupation points along limestone cliffs overlooking the strait, where the African coast lay visible on clear days; the terrain compressed remaining populations into a narrow littoral band with limited dispersal options.

Climate Regime & Volatility: Marine Isotope Stage 3 conditions brought fluctuating but generally cooling climate; the southern Iberian coast retained Mediterranean woodland refugium conditions — milder winters and more stable moisture than the glacial steppe expanding across central Europe — yet even this refuge experienced periodic cold spikes that thinned plant cover and reduced prey density; interannual volatility exceeded the buffering capacity of small bands.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: Acute hazards remained moderate — seismic activity along the Gibraltar arc posed occasional risk, and storm surges threatened low-lying coastal camps — but the chronic hazard of climatic deterioration outweighed episodic shocks; each cold oscillation that killed off a hunting band or forced abandonment of a site erased decades of accumulated technique.

Resource & Energy Endowment: The coastal zone offered diversified resources: shellfish beds in the intertidal zone, marine mammals, terrestrial ungulates including ibex and red deer in the hinterland, and plant foods in the littoral scrub; yet total biomass productivity declined as glacial conditions intensified, and the carrying capacity of the refugium shrank even as populations concentrated within it.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Low population density and mobile lifeways left negligible cumulative waste load; shell middens at Gorham's Cave accumulated slowly over millennia without saturating local sinks; environmental degradation derived from climate-driven vegetation loss, not anthropogenic pressure.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: Endemic pathogen pressure remained low in the small, dispersed population, though novel diseases introduced through contact with expanding modern human groups — if such contact occurred — may have contributed to attrition; baseline mortality from injury, childbirth, and exposure ran high in the absence of surplus population to absorb losses.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: Isotopic evidence from late Neanderthal remains indicates continued reliance on large terrestrial herbivores supplemented by marine resources at coastal sites; physiological robustness persisted but population-level nutritional stress increased as prey availability contracted; skeletal pathologies suggest hard use and frequent injury.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Evidence of healed fractures and dental lesions indicates ongoing care within kin groups; healing capacity depended entirely on kin-based nursing and accumulated herbal knowledge passed by demonstration; the loss of experienced individuals severed chains of healing technique irretrievably.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Small, isolated bands faced demographic collapse thresholds: genetic evidence from El Sidron shows very low genetic diversity and close kinship within groups; viable mate-finding required inter-band contact that became increasingly difficult as populations contracted and intervening territories emptied.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Population estimates for late Iberian Neanderthals run in the low thousands at most, scattered across the southern tier; birth rates could not offset elevated mortality once band sizes fell below the threshold at which enough adults remained to provision children and transmit technique; the demographic spiral accelerated as each death removed both a producer and a repository of knowledge.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: The proportion of dependents — children, injured, elderly — could not exceed what a shrinking productive cohort could carry; bands that lost key adults dissolved, their dependents dying or dispersing into other failing groups; the attrition load compounded rather than cleared.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: Subsistence rested on hunting and gathering within a coastal-littoral niche: shellfish collection required only simple techniques, but large-game hunting demanded coordinated drives and butchery knowledge that degraded as experienced hunters died; the provisioning floor rose as technique eroded.

Energy Capture & Conversion: All energy derived from human muscle, fire, and direct consumption of animal and plant calories; fire maintenance and hearth construction persisted at Gorham's Cave through the final occupation levels, indicating continued capacity to convert fuel into warmth and cooking, but no intensification occurred.

Labor Organization & Coercion: Labor organization remained kin-based and task-flexible: individuals shifted between foraging, hunting, tool-making, and childcare as immediate need dictated; no coercion existed beyond the demands of group survival; cooperation was the condition of existence, not a choice.

Production & Surplus Capacity: No surplus accumulated beyond immediate consumption and short-term caching; stone tool production continued in local Mousterian traditions, but innovation ceased and assemblages simplified as knowledgeable knappers died without fully training successors; the technique ceiling lowered.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: Storage was negligible: smoked or dried meat, cached nuts, and shellfish could buffer days to weeks, not seasons; no institutional reserves existed; each failed hunt or bad winter drew directly on bodies rather than stores.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: Inter-band exchange — of mates, raw materials, and technique — collapsed as bands became more isolated; lithic raw material sourcing contracted to immediately local stone, indicating reduced mobility and severed contact networks; the logistics of knowledge transfer, dependent on physical co-presence, failed.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: No medium of deferred exchange existed; reciprocal obligations within bands persisted, but the network of obligations between bands — the slow-moving credit system of kinship and alliance — dissolved as partners disappeared.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: No extraction apparatus existed; redistribution occurred through immediate sharing within the band, a practice that functioned only while the band itself persisted.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: No accumulated wealth existed to distribute or defend; individuals held personal tools and ornaments, but these conferred no lasting advantage and were abandoned or buried with the dead.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Butchery waste, ash, and shell accumulated in occupation layers but posed no systemic burden; the economic residue was the inability to accumulate — each generation started near the subsistence floor, and the floor rose as technique degraded.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Small bands organized around close kin: genetic evidence from El Sidron shows patrilocal residence with females dispersing between groups; inheritance meant nothing beyond the passing of technique from parent to child through demonstration — and this transmission failed when the chain broke.

Association & Mutual Aid: Mutual aid was total within the band and attenuated between bands as contact ceased; the pooling of risk that inter-band networks once provided — refuge in bad years, mates in good ones — collapsed as the network itself dissolved.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: Evidence of symbolic behavior — the engraved Gorham's Cave crosshatch, possible feather ornaments, pigment use — suggests continued expressive and social activity, but the audience shrank with the population; sociability contracted to the immediate kin circle.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: No formal stratification existed; status derived from skill, experience, and demonstrated competence in hunting and healing; the loss of high-status individuals through death removed both leadership and the knowledge that conferred status.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: No administrative apparatus existed; decision-making was face-to-face, immediate, and consensual; institutional memory resided in living heads alone.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: No coercive apparatus existed; force was personal and situational — the capacity to defend against predators, to drive prey, to deter encroachment by other hominins if any were encountered.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: The social residue was extinction itself: no channel existed to discharge the accumulated loss; each death of an experienced adult represented an unrecoverable subtraction from the group's capacity to persist; disorder was not riot or rebellion but dissolution — bands falling below viability and winking out.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: Leadership was personal and situational: the best hunter led the hunt, the most experienced healer tended the sick; authority derived from demonstrated competence and could not be transferred except by demonstration.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: Legitimacy questions did not arise in bands where cooperation was the condition of survival; allegiance was to kin and band, not to an abstract order.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: Collective resolve persisted — the continued occupation of Gorham's Cave through multiple millennia indicates sustained will to survive — but the will to act required bodies to act with, and bodies were what the demographic spiral removed.

External Relations & Posture: Relations with anatomically modern humans, if any occurred, are archaeologically invisible in the Gibraltar region during this window; whether displacement, avoidance, competition, or occasional interbreeding occurred remains contested; the posture of final Neanderthal populations may have been one of contraction and avoidance rather than confrontation.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: The emotional register of final Neanderthal populations is irrecoverable, but the archaeological evidence — continued hearth maintenance, careful tool production, symbolic marking — suggests persistence of collective will and mutual attachment rather than despair; yet the contraction of the social world must have registered as loss.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: The emotional residue was not disaffection but bereavement compounded — the accumulating loss of kin, of knowledge-holders, of the social world itself; whether this settled as despair or simply as diminished capacity is unknowable.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Communication remained gestural, demonstrative, and possibly proto-linguistic; whatever vocal capacity Neanderthals possessed, the code was fully shared within the band and did not require external media; mutual legibility was total among the living and ended with death.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Information moved at the speed of face-to-face contact; there was no transmission ahead, no message that could precede or outlast the messenger; knowledge traveled only as far as bodies traveled together.

Record, Storage & Persistence: No durable record existed; all knowledge resided in living memory and living hands; the engraved crosshatch at Gorham's Cave may represent a mark, but it could not encode technique or transmit it to those who had not already learned by watching.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: No formal censorship or framing existed; what could be shown could be learned; what could not be shown was lost.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: Reception was immediate and attentive — survival depended on watching and learning — but amplification did not exist; a technique demonstrated once to one learner reached only that learner.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: Each transmission introduced drift: the learner's hand did not move exactly as the teacher's, and the learner who became a teacher passed on the drifted version; across generations, technique degraded unless reinforced by contact with other practitioners — and that contact had ceased.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: The moral sense of Neanderthal populations is irrecoverable but can be inferred from behavior: care for the injured and elderly, sharing of food, burial or deliberate deposition of the dead all suggest a sense of obligation extending beyond immediate self-interest; justice was personal and relational, not codified.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: No codified law existed; norms were customary, learned by observation, and enforced by immediate social pressure within the band.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: Disputes were resolved face-to-face; sanction ranged from disapproval to exclusion; the small scale of the group made formal adjudication unnecessary and exclusion nearly fatal.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: No formal rights existed; protection derived from membership in the kin group; compliance with norms was the price of belonging.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: The moral residue was not impunity but irrelevance: with no institution to carry grievance forward, wrongs were redressed immediately or not at all; the accumulating wrong was extinction itself, and there was no one to redress it.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: No formal inquiry existed; understanding of the world was practical, embedded in technique, and transmitted by demonstration; the explanatory paradigm was the accumulated pattern-recognition of experienced individuals, lost when they died.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Mousterian stone-tool technology persisted — Levallois and discoid reduction, hafting, the production of points and scrapers — but assemblages at late sites show simplification and reduced diversity; the full repertoire of technique was not being transmitted; fire use, hide-working, and wooden tool production continued but did not intensify.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: Education was apprenticeship: children watched adults, imitated, were corrected by hand guidance; the knowledge stock resided entirely in living practitioners; skill distribution narrowed as the population shrank and specialists died without successors.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: The intellectual residue was catastrophic knowledge decay: techniques that took generations to develop were lost in a single death; the full Mousterian repertoire, fire-starting methods, medicinal plant knowledge, hunting strategies — all eroded as the population fell below the threshold at which chains of transmission could be maintained; this was the binding constraint of the imitative stage made lethal.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: Whatever origin narratives or identity-markers Neanderthal populations carried were held in living memory alone; the engraved crosshatch at Gorham's Cave, the possible collection of raptor feathers and eagle talons, suggest symbolic marking and perhaps shared identity, but the content is irrecoverable.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: No legitimating narrative for a political order existed; the band was the world, and its persistence was its own justification.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: Material culture included carefully made stone tools, possible pigment use, perforated shells that may have served as ornaments, and the engraved geometric figure at Gorham's Cave; the aesthetic was one of functional elegance in stone-working and modest personal adornment; whether this constituted art in any modern sense is contested.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: The cultural residue was not exhaustion of forms but loss of practitioners: the symbols and practices persisted as long as anyone remained to enact them, then ceased; meaning did not hollow out — it was severed.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: The cosmology of Neanderthal populations is inaccessible; deliberate treatment of the dead at other sites and the possible mortuary use of Sima de los Huesos suggest some orientation toward death and the beyond, but whether late Iberian Neanderthals carried such beliefs is unknown.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: If ritual practices existed, they were enacted bodily and left few traces; the repeated use of specific sites over millennia may indicate place-attachment with sacred overtones, but this is inference.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: No religious institutions existed; whatever spiritual authority individuals held derived from personal experience and reputation, not office.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: No diffusion or syncretism is visible; the spiritual life of final Neanderthal populations, if any, was local and self-contained.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: The spiritual residue was not disenchantment but termination: whatever sacred orientation existed ended with the last practitioners; the void left was not existential but literal — the absence of anyone to experience it.

docs.title: 900,000 BCE – 780,000 BCE — Gran Dolina TD6 and Homo antecessor
docs.text: Summary: Gran Dolina level TD6 in the Sierra de Atapuerca preserves the type specimens of Homo antecessor — a hominin species combining archaic and modern facial features, with cranial capacity around 1000 cc — alongside abundant Mode 1 tools and faunal remains. The defining feature of this assemblage is evidence of cannibalism: cut-marks and percussion damage on hominin bones indistinguishable from those on animal prey, indicating that these hominins processed and consumed their own kind. The binding constraint remains the imitative substrate — all knowledge held in living heads, passed by demonstration, lost at death — which here extends even to the treatment of the dead as food, a practice transmitted without moral codification or prohibition.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: Gran Dolina is a cave site in the Sierra de Atapuerca, a limestone massif in the northern Meseta of Iberia. The cave system sits at a junction of ecological zones — the Duero basin to the south, the Cantabrian foothills to the north — providing access to diverse habitats within walking range. The Pyrenees still blocked easy passage from Europe; Iberian populations remained semi-isolated, connected to the wider hominin world only through the Gibraltar corridor or difficult mountain routes.

Climate Regime & Volatility: The period 900–780 ka spans the transition from the Early to Middle Pleistocene, including the major climatic shift around 900 ka when glacial-interglacial cycles intensified. Gran Dolina TD6 accumulated during an interglacial phase — warm, relatively moist — supporting mixed woodland and open grassland. Seasonal variation was marked, with cold winters requiring shelter and fire or fat reserves to survive.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: The cave provided shelter from weather and predators. Seismic risk was low. The principal hazards were climatic deterioration during glacial advances and competition with large carnivores — hyenas, large cats, wolves — that also used cave sites.

Resource & Energy Endowment: The surrounding landscape supported abundant large fauna — deer, horse, bison, rhinoceros — as evidenced by the faunal assemblage at TD6. Flint and quartzite were available in local river gravels. Water came from springs and streams. The cave itself was a resource — defensible, dry, preserving heat.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Bone and lithic refuse accumulated on the cave floor, later buried by sediment. Population density was far too low to stress any environmental sink. The waste simply preserved, becoming the archaeological record.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: Interglacial warmth supported higher pathogen and parasite loads than glacial conditions. Mortality was high — from infection, injury, predation, and violence. The age profile of the TD6 hominin remains skews young, suggesting high juvenile and young-adult mortality.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: Homo antecessor was robust, medium-statured, with heavy brow ridges and large teeth. Cranial capacity averaged around 1000 cc — smaller than later Homo but larger than Homo erectus sensu stricto. The cut-marked bones show access to meat, including marrow; nutrition was adequate to support growth and reproduction, at least in favorable seasons.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: No direct evidence of healing practice. The presence of some older individuals among the remains suggests that some injured or ill individuals survived long enough to be supported, but this may reflect tolerance rather than active care. Without stored medical knowledge, recovery depended on rest and natural healing.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Reproductive biology followed the hominin pattern — extended juvenile dependency, slow maturation, pair-bonding within groups. The genetic evidence (from later Atapuerca sites) suggests small, inbred populations with limited gene flow — consistent with isolated bands occasionally meeting for mating.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Population density was extremely low. The TD6 assemblage represents accumulation over centuries or millennia, not a single event. Replacement rates were marginal; the population was vulnerable to local extinction from climatic shift, disease, or simple demographic stochasticity.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: The age profile suggests most individuals died before reaching old age. Dependency consisted mainly of immatures. The loss of adults erased whatever knowledge they carried; there was no mechanism to preserve expertise beyond the living.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: Subsistence combined hunting, scavenging, and gathering. The TD6 fauna shows primary access to carcasses — not just scavenging from carnivore kills but active hunting or early arrival at death sites. The hominin bones with processing marks indicate that human bodies were also part of the subsistence economy, whether from violence, opportunistic consumption of the dead, or deliberate killing.

Energy Capture & Conversion: Energy capture was muscular — human locomotion and hand-held tools. Fire use is attested at some Early Pleistocene sites but remains uncertain at TD6. If fire was available, it would have extended the edible range of foods and provided warmth and protection.

Labor Organization & Coercion: Division of labor followed age and sex gradients. Cooperative hunting, if practiced, required coordination by imitation and joint attention. Coercion within groups was interpersonal, not institutionalized.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Mode 1 tools — cores and flakes — were the only manufactured goods. Production was expedient: make, use, discard. No surplus accumulated beyond what bodies stored as fat.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: No material storage. The fat and marrow from prey, including the cannibalized dead, served as the immediate reserve. Buffering depended on group mobility and the ability to relocate when local resources failed.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: No evidence of exchange beyond immediate sharing. Raw materials were procured locally. Movement was on foot, carrying only what the body could bear.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: No material medium of value. Reciprocity was maintained in living memory and erased by death or dispersal.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: No surplus existed to extract. Distribution was immediate and governed by face-to-face negotiation and kin obligation.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: No durable assets to concentrate or defend. Inequality was situational and dissolved with each consumption event.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Lithic debitage, bone fragments, and butchery refuse accumulated on the cave floor. Disposal was abandonment; the cave's sedimentary regime buried and preserved the discard.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Bands were organized around kin — mothers with offspring, associated males. The genetic evidence from later Atapuerca (Sima de los Huesos) suggests small, inbred populations; TD6 likely followed a similar pattern. Inheritance was biological only; there was no property to pass.

Association & Mutual Aid: The band was the unit of mutual aid — food sharing, collective vigilance, assistance in childcare. The cannibalism evidence complicates this picture: mutual aid coexisted with the processing of group members as food, whether after death or through violence.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: Play and grooming would have reinforced bonds within the group. These activities left no archaeological trace but are inferred from primate baselines.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: Status differences were informal — dominance in specific contexts, deference to skilled foragers. There was no fixed hierarchy, no inherited rank.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: No administration. Decision-making was collective and immediate.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: Coercion was interpersonal. The same tools used for butchery could be used for violence. The cannibalism evidence suggests that lethal violence within or between groups was not taboo — or rather, that no taboo against it had been codified and transmitted.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: Social friction was discharged through fission, avoidance, or violence. The small scale of groups prevented grievance from accumulating into organized conflict; it either resolved, the group split, or someone died.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: Leadership was situational. Authority dissolved when the situation passed. There was no office, no stable role of leader.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: Allegiance was personal, owed to kin and familiar band members. There was no formal authority to legitimate.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: Collective action was coordinated by imitation and joint attention. Resolve formed around immediate goals — a hunt, a defense, a move — and dissolved when the action ended.

External Relations & Posture: Relations with other bands, if encountered, were probably cautious — avoidance, occasional violence, possible interbreeding. The cannibalism may have included intergroup violence, with the eaten being enemies rather than kin.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: Emotional life included fear, anger, affection, and grief, expressed through gesture and vocalization. The processing of human bodies as food suggests either emotional compartmentalization — treating dead or enemy humans as prey — or practices so normalized that they required no special emotional framing.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: Loss and exhaustion would have produced grief and apathy. Without ritual or narrative to process loss, emotional recovery depended on time and the demands of survival.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Communication relied on gesture, vocalization, and demonstration. There was no speech in the full linguistic sense — no syntax, no arbitrary symbols, no recursive structure. Meaning was conveyed by showing, not telling. Mutual legibility was limited to those who had learned together.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Information traveled at the speed of walking and the range of hearing. There was no way to send a message ahead or store one for later retrieval.

Record, Storage & Persistence: There was no record. The Mode 1 toolkit was simple enough to reinvent, but any refinement — a better knapping angle, a preferred raw material source — died with its discoverer unless demonstrated and copied in time.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: There was no discourse to frame or censor. Behavioral norms — who could approach whom, how to signal intent — were learned by observation and enforced by reaction.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: Attention was face-to-face. What was not witnessed was not known. There was no amplification, no way to reach beyond the immediate audience.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: Each transmission of technique or knowledge introduced drift. Without correction mechanisms, the signal degraded generationally. The stability of Mode 1 technology across hundreds of thousands of years may reflect this constraint — not stasis by choice but the floor below which accumulated noise erased improvement.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Moral intuitions — fairness, resentment of cheating, protection of kin — are inferred from primate baselines. The cannibalism evidence suggests that these intuitions did not extend to prohibiting the consumption of human flesh, at least not in all circumstances. There was no codified ethic, only felt reactions to behavior.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: There was no law. Norms were behavioral, learned by observation, enforced by immediate reaction. The absence of a taboo against cannibalism — or its presence but non-enforcement — illustrates the limits of uncodified norms.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: Disputes were resolved by dominance, negotiation, or fission. There was no third-party judgment, no formal sanction beyond immediate retaliation.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: There were no rights in the formal sense. Protection came from kin, allies, and one's own capacity for violence. Compliance was to immediate social pressure.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: Wrongs were redressed immediately or not at all. There was no accumulated grievance beyond living memory, no persistent record of transgression. The eaten left no descendants to demand justice; the eaters faced no judgment beyond their contemporaries.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: There was no inquiry in the reflective sense. Understanding was procedural — knowing where to find game, how to knap a flake, which plants were edible. There was no theory, no why, only how.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Mode 1 technology — simple cores and flakes — was the sole technical method. The TD6 assemblage shows competent knapping but no elaboration beyond the Early Pleistocene baseline. Technique was learned by observation and imitation, without verbal instruction.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: Education was demonstration. The knowledge stock was what living adults could show. Skill distribution depended on who was present during teaching and who survived to practice. There was no cumulative improvement across generations, only maintenance of the baseline.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: Knowledge decayed with each death. There was no obsolescence — no replacement of old by new — only loss. Whatever improvements arose were tested against the filter of transmission and mostly failed to persist.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: There was no mythos that survives. Identity was immediate — recognition of kin, familiarity with band members. There was no transmitted narrative of origin or history.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: There was no narrative to legitimate any practice. Cannibalism required no justification because there was no authority to question it, no code to violate, no story to explain or excuse.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: Material culture consisted of Mode 1 tools — functional, undecorated, varying by raw material and immediate need. There was no art, no ornament, no symbolic marking. The tools were purely utilitarian.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: There was no accumulated form to exhaust. Style did not exist because meaning was not stored. Each tool was made for immediate use, not for display or identity.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: There is no evidence of cosmology. The world was encountered, not explained. Existence was immediate, without speculation about its nature or purpose.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: There is no evidence of ritual in the TD6 assemblage. The processing of human bodies shows no special treatment distinguishing them from animal prey — no careful placement, no association with unusual objects, no pattern suggesting ceremony.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: There were no institutions and no doctrine. The spiritual dimension, as far as evidence shows, was not yet occupied.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: There was nothing to diffuse. Each group's orientation to the world was self-generated and died with it.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: There was no enchantment to lose. The sacred had not yet emerged as a category. The dead were food, not ancestors; the world was resource, not cosmos. The void that later disenchantment would leave had not yet been filled by what it would empty.

docs.title: 200,000 BCE – 100,000 BCE — Iberian Neanderthal Establishment
docs.text: Summary: Classic Neanderthals establish themselves across the Iberian Peninsula during a window spanning interglacial warmth and early glacial cooling, developing regional Mousterian variants and occupying diverse ecological niches from the Cantabrian coast to the Mediterranean littoral. The binding constraint is the imitative transmission ceiling: all technological knowledge passes hand-to-hand, limiting the complexity of coordinated action and ensuring that each group's repertoire drifts with the deaths and births of its members.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: The Iberian Peninsula provides a topographically varied arena bounded by the Pyrenees, the Cantabrian Cordillera, the central Meseta, and coastal margins on three sides. River valleys — the Ebro, Tagus, Guadiana, Guadalquivir — channelize movement and concentrate resources, while limestone massifs punctuated by caves and rockshelters offer defensible occupation sites. The Gibraltar corridor connects to North Africa across a strait narrow enough to sight land but too wide for crossing by available means.

Climate Regime & Volatility: The window opens in MIS 6 glacial conditions, passes through the Eemian interglacial (MIS 5e, ~130–115 ka) with temperatures warmer than present, then cools into early MIS 5 substages. Forest cover expands during the interglacial — oak, pine, and Mediterranean sclerophyll — then contracts and gives way to steppe-woodland as cooling resumes. Seasonality intensifies, with colder winters at altitude and along the northern coast.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: Drought cycles and cold snaps during stadial intervals impose periodic stress on prey populations and plant resources. Seismic activity along the Betic margin poses localized risk. Flooding in valley floors seasonally displaces occupation to higher terraces.

Resource & Energy Endowment: Abundant flint, quartzite, and chert outcrops supply lithic raw material; quality varies by region, with fine-grained sources concentrated in the Cantabrian and eastern coastal zones. Fuel wood is plentiful during interglacial forest phases but scarcer on glacial steppes. Game biomass fluctuates with vegetation regime.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: At band-level occupation densities, the landscape absorbs all organic and lithic discard without saturation. Fire-altered soils accumulate at hearth sites but disperse over generational timescales. No feedback from waste accumulation constrains settlement.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: Endemic parasites and zoonotic exposure from prey processing impose a background mortality load. No epidemic disease signatures appear in the skeletal record; wound infection and sepsis from trauma contribute to premature death. Life expectancy at birth likely sits below 35 years, with high juvenile mortality.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: Neanderthal bodies are stocky, cold-adapted, and heavily muscled, requiring elevated caloric intake — estimated at 3,500–5,000 kcal daily. Isotopic evidence from later Iberian Neanderthals indicates heavy reliance on large herbivores. Dental wear and skeletal stress markers suggest episodic nutritional shortfall.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Healed fractures on Neanderthal remains across Europe demonstrate that injured individuals survive significant trauma with group support. No specialized healing knowledge exists; wound tending and convalescent provisioning are imitated behaviors constrained by what watching and copying can transmit.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Small effective population sizes inferred from later genetic evidence suggest frequent inbreeding and low genetic diversity. Pair-bonding patterns are unknown; extended juvenile dependency implies sustained parental investment.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Population density remains low — perhaps one individual per 10–50 square kilometers in favorable zones. Groups number 15–30 individuals. Replacement rates are slow; a single failed cohort can extinguish a local population, and recolonization depends on neighboring bands.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: The elderly rarely survive past 40; the dependent load consists primarily of juveniles and the recently injured. The productive adult cohort absorbs this load through sharing, but any spike in dependency strains the group's capacity.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: Subsistence centers on hunting large and medium herbivores — red deer, horse, aurochs, and wild boar during interglacials; ibex and reindeer during colder phases. Plant foods supplement the diet seasonally but leave scant archaeological trace. Coastal groups exploit shellfish and occasional marine mammals.

Energy Capture & Conversion: All energy conversion relies on human muscle and controlled fire. Hearth structures concentrate heat for warmth, cooking, and possibly hafting adhesive preparation. No evidence of hafted spears in this window; thrusting spears require close-range hunting with high injury risk.

Labor Organization & Coercion: Labor is organized by task visibility and demonstrated competence. No coercion apparatus exists beyond social sanction. Division by age and sex is plausible but undocumented; imitation channels task assignment toward those who have seen the task performed.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Production barely exceeds immediate consumption. A successful kill generates a temporary surplus that must be consumed within days before spoilage. No storage technology extends this window.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: Fat reserves in bodies constitute the only buffer against lean periods. Cached carcass parts freeze in winter at altitude but rot rapidly in Mediterranean zones. Risk pooling occurs through sharing within the band; no inter-group pooling is attested.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: Raw material sourcing indicates movement ranges of 30–100 km, accomplished through group mobility rather than exchange networks. No evidence of inter-group trade; exotic materials are absent from assemblages.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: No medium of deferred exchange exists. Reciprocity operates within the band on immediate or short-term cycles; obligations are remembered in living minds and cannot outlast the parties.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: Redistribution is informal and immediate: large carcasses are shared at the kill site or at camp. No extraction apparatus or tribute system exists.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Portable wealth is negligible — personal tool kits and ornaments if any. No stratification by accumulation is possible when nothing stores.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Bone refuse, lithic debitage, and ash accumulate at occupation sites, forming middens that attract scavengers. Discard is spatially organized — knapping areas separated from sleeping zones — but no formal waste management exists.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Kinship structures are reconstructed only by analogy; genetic evidence from later Neanderthals suggests patrilocal residence with female dispersal. Inheritance is meaningless where nothing durable is owned; knowledge passes by imitation, not bequest.

Association & Mutual Aid: The band is the sole unit of association. Mutual aid is universal within it — obligatory sharing of food and cooperative defense. Inter-group relations are unknown; territorial boundaries may exist but cannot be codified or negotiated in the absence of language.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: Non-work time is spent at camp in proximity to others. Juvenile play likely rehearses adult tasks. Grooming and physical contact maintain social bonds. No structured leisure activity leaves archaeological trace.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: Status differentiation is minimal and situational — the skilled knapper, the successful hunter — but cannot be formalized or inherited. No stratification apparatus exists.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: No administration exists. Coordination is face-to-face, limited to what can be gestured and demonstrated. Decision-making is consensus-based or dominance-based within small groups; no institutional memory carries decisions across generations.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: Coercion is personal — physical dominance, ostracism, violence. Weapons are hunting tools repurposed. No organized means of force exists; inter-group conflict, if it occurs, is raid-level and undocumented.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: Social friction is absorbed by fission — dissatisfied individuals leave to join other bands or found new ones. Disorder at the group level means dissolution, not reform. No apparatus decays because none exists.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: Leadership is situational and personal — the individual who knows where prey congregates, who has knapped the best tool. Authority cannot be abstracted from the person or transmitted beyond their presence.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: Allegiance is to persons, not positions. Legitimacy is demonstrated competence and generosity. Disaffection leads to departure, not reform.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: Collective action is limited to what can be coordinated by gesture and example in real time. Sustained campaigns are impossible; resolve lasts only as long as participants remain co-present and motivated.

External Relations & Posture: Relations with other bands are episodic and undocumented. Encounters may be hostile, neutral, or affiliative depending on kin ties and resource competition. No posture can be maintained across distance or time.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: Affect is immediate and interpersonal. Trust extends to band members and no further. Behavioral temper is shaped by recent success or failure in provisioning; mood shifts are unmediated by narrative or ideology.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: Spent will results in individual withdrawal or group fission. No collective apathy accumulates because no collective enterprise persists long enough to exhaust commitment.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Communication relies on gesture, facial expression, vocalization, and demonstrated action. No symbolic language is attested; mutual intelligibility is limited to what can be shown. Strangers are unintelligible until they have been observed long enough to learn local conventions.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Information travels at the speed of human movement — no faster than a person can walk to deliver it. Transmission range is limited to face-to-face contact; no relay or broadcast mechanism exists.

Record, Storage & Persistence: All information resides in living memory. When the knower dies, the knowledge dies. No external record — no mark, no mnemonic device, no notation — preserves information beyond a lifespan. Each generation rebuilds its repertoire from observation.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: Without language, framing is limited to what demonstration emphasizes. No censorship is possible because no propositional content circulates. Norms govern action, not speech.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: Attention is held by proximity and salience — the dramatic kill, the new technique. No amplification mechanism exists; information reaches only those present to witness it.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: Imitation introduces drift with each transmission. No verification mechanism corrects accumulated error. Signal integrity degrades across generations; techniques simplify or shift without correction.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Justice is retributive and immediate — wrongs are avenged or forgiven in person. Fairness in sharing is enforced by social sanction. No abstract principle underlies conduct; rightness is what the group tolerates.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: No codification exists. Conduct is regulated by custom transmitted through imitation and social pressure. Rules cannot be articulated, debated, or reformed; they drift with practice.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: Disputes are resolved by dominance, mediation by respected individuals, or fission. Sanction is personal — shaming, beating, expulsion. No formal adjudication process exists.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Rights are not conceptualized. Protection derives from group membership and personal ties. Compliance is to group norms, enforced by the cost of transgression — loss of sharing, ostracism, violence.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: Wrongs against the weak or marginal may go unredressed if no advocate presses the claim. Impunity accrues to the strong. No institutional mechanism accumulates or clears grievance.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: No inquiry exists in the propositional sense. Understanding is practical — the recognition of patterns in prey behavior, raw material quality, fire management — never articulated as theory.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Mousterian technology represents the applied knowledge ceiling: Levallois and discoid core reduction, prepared platforms, retouched flake tools. Regional variants — Quina, Ferrassie facies — indicate local traditions transmitted by imitation. Techniques are robust but not innovative within the window.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: Knowledge is transmitted by observation and guided practice. Skill distribution is uneven; not every individual masters every technique. The knowledge stock is limited to what the current generation can demonstrate.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: Techniques are lost when no practitioner survives to demonstrate them. Innovation is accidental and rare; most change is drift or loss. No mechanism recovers abandoned knowledge.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: No mythos can be articulated or transmitted without language. Identity is group membership, demonstrated by familiarity and shared practice. Memory is personal and dies with the rememberer.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: No narrative legitimates the order because no narrative exists. Authority rests on demonstrated competence and presence, not story.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: Material culture is functional: stone tools, possibly wooden spears, fire-hardened points. No unambiguous symbolic expression — no figurative art, no ornament — is attested for Iberian Neanderthals in this window. Pigment use, if present, may serve functional or aesthetic purposes undistinguished from utility.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: Without symbolic forms, exhaustion is meaningless. Techniques may become rote, but no meaning attaches to them that could hollow out.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: No cosmology can be reconstructed. Whether Neanderthals conceptualized death, an afterlife, or forces beyond the visible is unknown. Deliberate burial at some European sites suggests awareness of death; Iberian evidence in this window is sparse.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: No ritual is attested. Repeated behaviors — hearth placement, discard patterns — are practical, not demonstrably sacred. The boundary between routine and rite cannot be drawn without symbolic evidence.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: No institutions or doctrine exist. Whatever spiritual intuitions individuals hold remain private and untransmitted.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: Without transmissible belief, no diffusion or displacement occurs. Each individual's orientation is idiosyncratic and dies with them.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: Disenchantment presupposes enchantment that can be lost. If Neanderthals hold sacred orientations, they cannot accumulate or erode collectively; each generation starts fresh, shaped only by what it can observe and infer.

docs.title: 350,000 BCE – 200,000 BCE — Late Acheulean to Mousterian Transition
docs.text: Summary: A gradual technological shift across the Iberian Peninsula during which the Acheulean handaxe tradition gave way to prepared-core flaking techniques, culminating in the Mousterian industries associated with Neanderthals. The single most causal factor is the emergence and spread of the Levallois method — a technique for predetermining flake shape before detachment — which offered greater efficiency in raw material use and more standardized tool blanks, but required more complex mental planning and more precise motor control, both of which had to be transmitted through imitation alone.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: The Iberian Peninsula remained bounded by the Pyrenees and surrounded by sea, with the Gibraltar Strait narrowing to fourteen kilometers at its closest point. Internal movement followed major river valleys — the Ebro, Tagus, Guadiana, and Guadalquivir — while the Meseta central plateau imposed its own barriers of elevation and aridity. The Cantabrian coast offered Atlantic-facing habitats distinct from the Mediterranean littoral. This geography channeled population movement and created semi-isolated regional pockets where technological variants could develop independently.

Climate Regime & Volatility: The window spans multiple glacial-interglacial cycles, including Marine Isotope Stages 10 through 7. Glacial phases brought steppe-tundra conditions to northern Iberia and expanded arid zones in the interior, while interglacials restored Mediterranean woodland and deciduous forest. The southern coast and Gibraltar corridor remained relatively buffered, serving as refugia during cold phases. This climatic oscillation drove repeated expansion and contraction of habitable zones, fragmenting and reuniting populations.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: No evidence of catastrophic volcanic or seismic events affecting Iberian populations during this window. Drought and cold posed the primary hazards, forcing movement to better-watered or warmer refugia. Coastal populations faced rising and falling sea levels, which periodically exposed and drowned coastal plains.

Resource & Energy Endowment: Flint remained the preferred raw material where available, with outcrops in the Ebro valley, parts of the Meseta, and the Mediterranean coast. Quartzite and quartz were used where flint was scarce. Large herbivore populations — horses, aurochs, red deer, and during cold phases, reindeer — provided the primary protein source. Wood for spears and fuel was available in most contexts.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Population densities remained low enough that no cumulative environmental impact is detectable. Occupation sites show refuse accumulation, but abandonment and natural decay cleared the record between occupations.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: Skeletal evidence is sparse for this transitional period. General Middle Pleistocene mortality patterns apply: high infant mortality, significant attrition from trauma and infection, and few individuals surviving past forty. Endemic disease load was likely lower than in later agricultural populations, but episodic epidemic exposure from animal contact remained possible.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: The populations of this window — late Homo heidelbergensis transitioning toward Neanderthal morphology — were robustly built, with heavy musculature and large brains (1,200-1,400 cc). Dental wear indicates mixed diets with substantial meat consumption. Nutritional stress episodes are recorded in enamel hypoplasia, but overall physiological condition appears adequate for survival and reproduction.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Continuity with earlier periods: injured individuals sometimes survived, implying tolerance or active care. No specialized healing practices can be inferred beyond wound tending and rest. The transition period shows no change in this capacity.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Pronounced sexual dimorphism continued. Genetic evidence from later Neanderthal populations shows low diversity, suggesting small effective population sizes and possibly inbreeding, a pattern likely extending back into this transitional period. Pair bonding and family structure remain invisible in the archaeological record.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Population density across Iberia was low — perhaps a few thousand individuals in the entire peninsula at any time, organized in bands of fifteen to thirty. The glacial-interglacial oscillations drove cycles of population expansion into newly habitable areas during warm phases and contraction to refugia during cold phases. The southern coast and Gibraltar corridor maintained population continuity through cold intervals.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: The demographic profile skewed young, with few elderly. The productive cohort carried the burden of dependent young and incapacitated injured; the elderly were rare enough that their dependency was minimal. Overall, the population replaced itself, but with little margin for sustained growth.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: Hunting of large and medium game remained the subsistence base. Site assemblages show processing of horses, deer, aurochs, and rhinoceros. Plant foods were certainly consumed but leave minimal archaeological trace. Coastal sites (e.g., Gibraltar area) show early shellfish exploitation. The provisioning floor was set by hunting success, which was seasonal and variable.

Energy Capture & Conversion: Human muscle remained the sole motive power. Fire use was established, providing warmth, protection, and cooking capacity. The energetic budget centered on the hunt: the caloric investment in pursuit and kill had to be recovered in meat returns. The Levallois technique may have improved this balance by producing more usable cutting edge per unit of raw material transported.

Labor Organization & Coercion: Cooperative hunting required coordination, achieved through imitation and situational leadership rather than formal organization. Division of labor by sex and age is inferred from sexual dimorphism and the demands of child-rearing but cannot be directly observed. Coercion, if any, was personal and immediate, not institutionalized.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Production was limited to stone tools, wooden spears, and perishable equipment. The Levallois technique represented a production innovation: by preparing a core in advance, the knapper could produce multiple flakes of predictable shape, reducing waste and transport cost. No surplus accumulation beyond immediate consumption; meat spoiled quickly without preservation technology.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: No storage capacity. The body's fat reserves and the ability to move to better-provisioned areas were the only buffers against scarcity. Hunting success in autumn, when animals were fattest, provided a seasonal peak that had to carry populations through winter.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: No evidence of inter-group exchange. Raw material sourcing shows transport distances of tens of kilometers, consistent with band-range mobility rather than trade. Each group was self-sufficient within its territory.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: Absent. Reciprocity was immediate and personal, held in memory and discharged within the group. No medium of deferred exchange existed.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: Redistribution occurred through sharing of kills. Ethnographic analogy suggests strong norms of sharing, enforced by immediate social pressure. No extraction by dominant individuals beyond what sharing norms permitted.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: No material wealth beyond personal tools. Tools were made, used, and discarded; no accumulation or defense of holdings is evident.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Lithic debris accumulated at knapping sites; butchery waste at processing locations. Abandonment cleared these sites, and natural processes buried or dispersed the debris. No managed waste disposal.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Bands were kin-based, with genetic evidence from later Neanderthal sites showing close relatedness within groups. Inheritance of territory and technique passed through demonstration within family lines. Marriage or mating patterns are unknown but presumably involved some exchange between groups to maintain genetic diversity, however limited.

Association & Mutual Aid: Mutual aid within the band was essential for survival. Hunting, child-rearing, and care of the injured required cooperation. The band itself was the unit of association; no broader structures existed.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: No dedicated leisure is observable. Sociability was embedded in daily activity — the hunt, the hearth, the camp. Play among juveniles likely served learning functions, but leaves no trace.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: No evidence of ranked status. Leadership was situational — the skilled hunter, the experienced elder — not institutionalized. Sexual dimorphism implies role differentiation but not hierarchy. The band was small enough that all members knew each other personally.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: Absent. No administration; no institutions beyond the band itself.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: Weapons were hunting tools: wooden spears, stone-tipped spears toward the end of the window, handaxes, and flake tools. Interpersonal violence occurred — cranial trauma is attested in skeletal remains — but no organized coercive apparatus existed. Conflict with other groups was probably rare given low population density and large territories.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: Grievance was resolved immediately through dominance, submission, or departure. The small scale of the group meant that persistent conflict was unsustainable; resolution or fission followed quickly. No accumulated grievance; no disorder beyond the interpersonal.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: Leadership was personal and situational — the skilled hunter led the hunt, the experienced knapper demonstrated technique. No permanent leadership; authority was earned and lost with demonstrated competence.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: Allegiance was to the band, held through face-to-face bonds. No abstract legitimacy; the group simply was, and membership was identity.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: Collective action for hunting required coordinated will, achieved through shared attention and imitation rather than command. The adoption and spread of Levallois technique across the peninsula implies a diffuse collective will to learn and improve, though this was not articulated or directed.

External Relations & Posture: Other bands were distant and rarely encountered. Relations were probably cautious — neither hostile nor allied, simply other. Mating exchanges may have occurred during chance encounters, but no sustained inter-group relations are evident.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: Unknowable directly. The continuation of band life over this long window implies sufficient internal cohesion and trust to maintain cooperation. The demands of imitative learning and cooperative hunting required tolerance and patience.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: No evidence. The long continuity of the transition implies sustained engagement with the demands of survival. Exhaustion and despair were individual, not collective, and left no mark.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Communication remained gestural, postural, and vocal but pre-linguistic. The Levallois technique required transmission of a more complex operational sequence than Acheulean handaxe manufacture — the core had to be prepared in multiple stages before the final flake was struck — and this increased the informational demands on imitative learning. Whether this pressure contributed to the evolution of enhanced communication is debated but cannot be resolved from the evidence.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Face-to-face and immediate. Information traveled at walking pace and could not be sent ahead. The spread of Levallois technique across the peninsula took thousands of years, consistent with slow diffusion through population contact rather than rapid transmission.

Record, Storage & Persistence: No external record. The technique itself was the only "storage" — embodied in the knapper's skill and the tools produced. When practitioners died, their knowledge died unless already transmitted by imitation.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: Absent. What could be shown could be learned; nothing could be forbidden except by preventing demonstration.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: Attention was local and immediate. The learner watched the master; no amplification beyond the circle of observers was possible.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: Each imitative transmission introduced error. The Levallois technique's greater complexity may have increased transmission fidelity — failure to execute the sequence correctly produced unusable results, creating selection pressure for accurate learning — but drift remained inevitable. Regional variants in technique reflect accumulated transmission differences.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Norms were enacted in practice, not articulated. Sharing of meat, care of the injured, and treatment of the dead implied standards of conduct, but these were felt obligations, not stated rules.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: No codification. Custom was behavior, not text or doctrine.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: Disputes were resolved immediately by the parties involved. No third-party adjudication; no formal sanction beyond social pressure and personal retaliation.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Absent. Individuals had no rights beyond what group membership and personal relationships secured.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: Wrongs were either avenged or absorbed. Memory of grievance was personal and died with the aggrieved. No backlog accumulated.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: No formal inquiry. The world was navigated through embedded practical knowledge, not theorized. Understanding of stone fracture mechanics, animal behavior, and landscape was profound but implicit, never abstracted into theory.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: The central intellectual development of the window is the emergence of prepared-core techniques, culminating in the Levallois method. This required a mental template of the desired flake, a multi-stage reduction sequence to prepare the core, and precise motor control to execute the final strike. The technique represented a genuine advance in cognitive planning — holding a future state in mind through multiple intermediate steps — though it remained within the bounds of imitative transmission. Hafting of stone points to wooden shafts also emerged during this window, requiring adhesives (birch pitch) and binding, adding further complexity to the technical repertoire.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: Learning remained imitative. The knowledge stock was the sum of living practitioners; skill distribution was uneven, with some individuals more adept than others, but no formal differentiation. The Levallois technique may have been more demanding to learn, narrowing the pool of fully competent practitioners.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: Acheulean handaxe manufacture did not disappear instantly; it persisted alongside prepared-core techniques for millennia before fading. This gradual obsolescence reflects the slow pace of transmission-by-imitation: no one declared the old technique obsolete; it simply produced fewer practitioners as learners chose to copy the newer method. Knowledge decayed continuously through transmission error and practitioner death.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: No evidence of narrative identity. The band was identity; membership was belonging. No origin stories could survive the generation that held them.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: Absent. The order required no justification because it was not conceived as contingent or alterable.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: No clear evidence of symbolic art or ornament during this window. Material culture was functional: tools for hunting and processing, hearths for warmth and cooking. Some handaxes show symmetry beyond strict functional requirement, but whether this reflects aesthetic intention or simply skilled manufacture remains debated. The transition to Levallois involved a change in tool morphology — from large bifacial handaxes to smaller, thinner flakes — which represents a material-culture shift even if not a symbolic one.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: Forms could not exhaust because they were not fixed. The gradual replacement of Acheulean by Mousterian was not a rejection of exhausted forms but a functional displacement: the newer technique worked better, and learners chose to copy it.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: Unknowable. The continuation of body-disposal practices (suggested by occasional deliberate burials in later Mousterian contexts) implies some orientation toward death, but the content of any cosmology is beyond recovery.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: No clear evidence of ritual during this transitional window. The Sima de los Huesos practice, if it continued, left no comparable accumulation. Occasional possible burials in later Mousterian sites (Sima de las Palomas, Kebara) suggest the practice persisted or emerged independently, but remains contested.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: Absent. No institution; no doctrine; no authority.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: Not applicable at this scale. If spiritual orientations existed, they were local to each band and could not spread except through population contact and imitation.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: Not applicable. The sacred, if present, was not differentiated from daily life and could not be lost.

docs.title: 100,000 BCE – 50,000 BCE — Late Neanderthal Iberian Refugium
docs.text: Summary: During a fifty-thousand-year span dominated by glacial conditions (MIS 5d–3), the Iberian Peninsula functions as a refugium for Neanderthal populations, with southern and coastal zones sustaining occupation while northern and interior regions become seasonally or permanently uninhabitable. The binding constraint remains the imitative transmission ceiling: technical knowledge and adaptive responses cannot be pooled, codified, or transmitted faster than hand-to-hand copying permits, leaving each isolated group to rediscover or lose solutions independently.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: The peninsula's topographic diversity becomes selectively important as climate deteriorates. The southern coastal strip, the Guadalquivir lowlands, and the eastern Mediterranean littoral retain habitable conditions; the Cantabrian coast offers sheltered valleys and marine resources. The central Meseta and Pyrenean uplands become seasonally harsh or abandoned. Caves and rockshelters — El Sidrón, Bolomor, Bajondillo — concentrate occupation evidence. The Gibraltar corridor remains a theoretical link to Africa but no crossing evidence exists.

Climate Regime & Volatility: The window spans MIS 5d through early MIS 3, including the pronounced cold of MIS 4 (71–57 ka). Glacial conditions push tree lines downslope, replace forest with steppe and scrubland in the interior, and shift fauna toward cold-adapted assemblages. Southern Iberia maintains warmer, more stable conditions, creating a refugium effect. Interannual volatility is high; short warm episodes interrupt stadial cold.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: Drought during cold-dry phases stresses water sources and concentrates fauna at remaining springs and river courses. Cold snaps at altitude can trap or kill exposed groups. Coastal storm surge affects littoral camps. Fire risk increases in dry scrubland.

Resource & Energy Endowment: Lithic raw material availability remains stable; flint and quartzite outcrops continue to supply tools. Fuel wood becomes scarcer in deforested interiors, concentrating occupation near remaining woodland. Prey biomass shifts: red deer decline in interior zones while horse, ibex, and cold-adapted species increase.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Occupation densities remain too low to saturate any sink. Ash and bone accumulate at long-occupied caves, forming stratified deposits valuable to archaeology but negligible as environmental burden.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: Endemic parasite loads persist. Nutritional stress during MIS 4 may elevate mortality; skeletal evidence from El Sidrón shows dietary stress markers. Wound infection and hunting trauma continue to claim lives. Life expectancy remains short; few individuals survive past 40.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: Isotopic analysis from El Sidrón (~49 ka, near the window's end) indicates heavy reliance on terrestrial herbivores with minimal plant or marine input. Caloric requirements remain high due to cold-adapted body plans. Nutritional shortfalls during harsh phases leave enamel hypoplasia and growth disruption in dental remains.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Healed injuries on Neanderthal skeletons demonstrate continued group support for the wounded. At El Sidrón, individuals with debilitating conditions survived long enough to leave skeletal evidence, indicating sustained care. Knowledge of wound treatment remains imitative — no cumulative medical tradition.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Genetic analysis from El Sidrón reveals a small group with low diversity and evidence of inbreeding, likely a single extended family. Population isolation during glacial conditions restricts mate exchange. Effective population size is critically low.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Population density drops as habitable area contracts. Estimates for late Neanderthal Iberia suggest total populations in the low thousands. Replacement rates are barely positive; local extinctions are common, recolonization slow. The demographic margin against extinction is thin.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: Dependent load consists of juveniles and the injured. The small size of the productive cohort means any additional dependency — a disabled adult, multiple children — strains provisioning. The elderly rarely survive to impose significant load.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: Hunting of medium and large herbivores remains the subsistence base: red deer, horse, ibex, aurochs depending on local fauna. Coastal groups exploit shellfish, as evidenced at Bajondillo and later at Gorham's Cave. Plant foods contribute seasonally but are archaeologically invisible.

Energy Capture & Conversion: Fire management is essential for survival during cold phases. Hearths are structured and repeatedly used. No evidence of hafted projectile weapons in this window — hunting remains close-range with thrusting spears, maintaining high injury risk.

Labor Organization & Coercion: Labor organization remains imitative and informal. Genetic evidence from El Sidrón suggests task division by sex: adult males show heavier wear patterns consistent with hunting, females with hide processing. This division is inferred, not observed; enforcement is social, not coercive.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Production remains hand-to-mouth. A successful hunt generates temporary surplus consumed before spoilage. No technology extends preservation beyond natural cold storage during winter.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: Body fat is the primary reserve. Cached meat may freeze at altitude during winter. No evidence of systematic food storage or caching. Inter-group buffering is unlikely given population isolation.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: Raw material sourcing continues to indicate mobility ranges of 30–100 km. Some longer-distance transport of high-quality flint occurs, but mechanisms are unclear — group mobility or occasional inter-group contact. No sustained exchange networks are attested.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: No medium of stored value or deferred obligation exists beyond remembered reciprocity within the band. Credit has no meaning when nothing stores.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: Redistribution remains immediate sharing of kills. No extraction apparatus, tribute, or taxation exists.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Portable wealth is negligible. Personal tool kits may vary in quality, but accumulation is impossible. No stratification by wealth occurs.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Organic waste, bone, and lithic debitage accumulate at occupation sites. Spatial organization within caves separates activity zones, but waste routing is informal — discard rather than management.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: El Sidrón's genetic evidence reveals a patrilocal residence pattern: related males stayed together while females came from outside groups. This implies inter-group contact for mate exchange despite population isolation. Inheritance remains meaningless where knowledge transmits by imitation.

Association & Mutual Aid: The band remains the sole unit of sustained association. Mutual aid is obligatory within it. Inter-group relations are episodic — mate exchange implies contact, but no evidence of alliance, conflict, or regular interaction survives.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: Non-work time is spent in proximity within shelter. Juvenile play, grooming, and physical contact maintain bonds. No structured leisure activities leave trace.
