Demographic Renewal & Density: Population remains stable or grows slowly after Timurid-era recovery. Bukhara and Khiva sustain urban density; rural populations fill irrigated valleys. No major migration reshapes the demographic landscape until Russian incursion.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: Succession wars and Safavid-Uzbek conflicts produce casualties and displacement; waqf endowments and communal networks absorb dependency loads within traditional capacities.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: Irrigated agriculture (grain, cotton, fruits, silk) sustains oasis populations; pastoralism supports steppe margins. The provisioning floor remains adequate but does not rise significantly above Timurid-era levels.

Energy Capture & Conversion: Human and animal muscle remain the sole energy sources. No technological change expands the work ceiling. Irrigation systems are maintained but not substantially extended.

Labor Organization & Coercion: Peasant agriculture, artisan guilds, and pastoral herding continue established patterns. Slavery persists, including captive-raiding from Persian borderlands. Corvee labor maintains irrigation and fortifications.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Agricultural and artisan production meets local needs; surplus is modest. Decline in Silk Road transit trade reduces external revenue. Manuscript production continues within madrasa and court scriptoria but without Timurid-scale royal investment.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: Granaries and treasuries operate at reduced scales compared to Timurid heights. Succession conflicts drain reserves periodically. Buffering capacity is adequate for ordinary fluctuations, strained by war.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: Overland trade contracts as maritime routes via the Cape of Good Hope and later the Indian Ocean littoral capture East-West commerce. Regional trade in horses, slaves, textiles, and grain continues. Bukhara and Khiva remain trading centers for Inner Asia, but global significance fades.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: Silver coinage circulates; credit networks persist among merchants. Waqf endowments continue to institutionalize wealth transfer. No monetary innovation occurs.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: Land tax, trade duties, and tribute fund khanate administrations. Extraction is adequate for reduced state functions; no expansion of fiscal capacity occurs.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Tribal aristocracy and religious scholars hold significant assets; waqf protects some holdings from confiscation. Wealth concentration is moderate by premodern standards.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Production waste remains within traditional absorption capacities; no accumulating residue.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Uzbek tribal structure overlays Islamic family norms. Tribal affiliation (Shaybanid, then Ashtarkhanid/Janid lineages) determines elite status. Appanage inheritance generates recurring fragmentation.

Association & Mutual Aid: Sufi orders (Naqshbandiyya remains prominent) continue to knit social fabric. Craft guilds organize urban production; neighborhood communities provide local solidarity. Charitable waqf sustains welfare functions.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: Poetry gatherings, musical performances, and hunting continue elite leisure. Public festivals mark religious holidays and Nowruz. Gardens and teahouses serve as sociability spaces.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: Uzbek tribal aristocracy forms the military-political apex; Persian-speaking bureaucrats and scholars staff administration and madrasas; merchants and artisans occupy middle tiers; peasants and slaves form the base. Boundaries are relatively stable; mobility occurs through scholarship, military service, or commerce.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: Persian bureaucratic tradition persists in chancelleries. Administrative capacity is adequate for reduced state functions but does not match Timurid efficiency. Corruption is endemic; capacity is localized.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: Uzbek cavalry armies, recruited from tribal levies, maintain khanate authority. Fortifications secure cities. Military technology does not advance; firearms are adopted slowly and incompletely. The balance against external powers (Safavids, Mughals, later Russia) trends unfavorably over the period.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: Succession disputes, tribal rivalries, and Safavid-Uzbek wars generate periodic disorder. Urban unrest follows contested transitions. The apparatus stabilizes under strong khans and fragments under weak ones; no terminal collapse occurs within the period.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: Khans derive authority from tribal leadership, military prowess, and Islamic legitimacy. Strong rulers (Abdullah Khan II, r. 1583–1598) concentrate power; weak successors fragment it. Personal charisma matters but cannot substitute for tribal and military backing.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: Uzbek khans claim Chinggisid descent through female lines and Islamic credentials. Patronage of madrasas and scholars reinforces legitimacy among the learned; tribal loyalty binds warriors. Popular allegiance varies with taxation and security.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: Will concentrates in the khan and his tribal coalition; collective resolve is fragmented among competing amirs. Capacity for sustained unified action is lower than under Timurids; campaigns are episodic rather than systematic.

External Relations & Posture: Uzbek khanates contest the Safavids for Khurasan; neither achieves lasting dominance. Relations with Mughals are diplomatic and commercial. Russia remains distant until the eighteenth century. Posture is defensive and regional; no expansive ambition succeeds.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: Sentiment fluctuates with security and prosperity. Under stable rule, public confidence is adequate; succession crises and external threats darken mood. Trust networks remain localized within tribal, religious, or neighborhood bounds.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: Chronic fragmentation and inconclusive wars erode elite cohesion. By 1700, the khanates are politically diminished, though culturally persistent. Apathy accumulates as external relevance fades.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Persian remains the primary language of administration, scholarship, and literature. Chagatai Turkish rises as a literary language (Nava'i's legacy institutionalized); Arabic persists for religious texts. Literacy remains confined to scholars, bureaucrats, and merchants but is maintained rather than expanded.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Couriers and caravans carry correspondence; news travels in weeks. Oral proclamation reaches the illiterate. Channels contract with reduced trade and political fragmentation.

Record, Storage & Persistence: Manuscript production continues in madrasa scriptoria and occasional court workshops. Libraries preserve Timurid-era collections; copying maintains texts in circulation. Baysunghur's calligraphic standards persist as models. Storage is adequate but not expanding.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: Religious orthodoxy constrains expression; Sufi mysticism retains latitude. No systematic censorship apparatus exists; patronage and social pressure shape what is written. Conservative norms narrow innovation.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: Manuscripts circulate among elites through copying, gift, and purchase. Poetry recitations and public readings persist. Canonical texts (Shahnameh, Khamsa, Nava'i's works) are repeatedly copied; new composition is more limited.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: Scribal copying maintains textual tradition with typical variant accumulation. Libraries preserve against loss; no catastrophic destruction occurs. Information regime is stable but stagnant; external information (European developments, maritime discoveries) barely penetrates.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Sunni Islamic shari'a provides the moral framework. Justice from rulers is expected and judged. Generosity, piety, and hospitality are cardinal virtues.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: Shari'a governs personal status, commercial, and criminal law. Customary law (urf) handles local matters. No significant legal codification or evolution occurs; the system is conservative and stable.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: Qadis adjudicate in urban courts; tribal leaders exercise jurisdiction in pastoral zones. Royal justice remains appellate. Sanctions are traditional: fines, corporal punishment, execution.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Dhimmi protections apply to diminishing non-Muslim minorities. Property rights depend on waqf status and power relations. Compliance burdens are moderate within the system; outsiders and the weak face arbitrary exactions.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: Powerful amirs and tribal leaders often escape accountability. The gap between proclaimed justice and delivery is typical; no mechanism closes it.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: Inquiry continues within established Islamic-Hellenistic paradigms; no new paradigm emerges. Ulugh Beg's astronomical tables remain authoritative. Scholarship is preservative and commentarial rather than innovative.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Calligraphy, illumination, and miniature painting continue at high but not advancing levels. Architectural practice maintains established techniques. No technical breakthroughs occur; firearms adoption lags.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: Madrasas remain the primary educational institutions; Bukhara hosts numerous establishments. Curriculum is traditional: Quran, hadith, fiqh, Arabic grammar, logic. The knowledge stock is maintained through manuscript transmission; distribution remains narrow.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: No paradigm shift renders knowledge obsolete; the system transmits received tradition. Some skills (Timurid-level miniature painting) decline for lack of patronage. External developments (European science, print technology) are unknown or ignored; relative obsolescence accumulates unrecognized.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: Uzbek identity combines Chinggisid-Turkic heritage with Persianate high culture and Sunni Islam. Timurid cultural legacy is appropriated rather than rejected; Nava'i becomes a foundational figure for Chagatai Turkish literature.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: Khans legitimate through genealogy (Chinggisid descent), military prowess, and Islamic piety. Patronage of madrasas and scholars demonstrates civilized rulership. The narrative is conservative, linking present to past legitimacy.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: Persian and Chagatai poetry continues to be composed and copied. Miniature painting persists at reduced scale; calligraphy maintains Timurid standards. Architecture produces notable works (Bukhara's seventeenth-century madrasas) within established idioms. Material culture is refined but not innovating.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: Classical forms are repeated rather than renewed; some hollowing occurs as innovation slows. Regional isolation prevents influx of new influences. The tradition is vital enough to persist but increasingly retrospective.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: Sunni Islam provides the cosmological frame; Sufi mysticism offers experiential depth. The world is divinely ordered; human action unfolds within divine will. No secularizing drift occurs.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: Daily prayer, fasting, pilgrimage, and zakat structure Muslim life. Sufi dhikr and shrine visitation remain widespread. Ritual practice is robust and unchanged.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: Ulama staff madrasas and serve as qadis; Sufi orders (Naqshbandiyya, Kubrawiyya) wield social influence. Doctrinal authority is diffuse; orthodoxy is enforced through social pressure and patronage rather than inquisition. Shi'ism is excluded; Sunni identity hardens against Safavid Persia.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: Sunni Islam consolidates; no significant diffusion or syncretism occurs within the Muslim population. Conversion pressure on remaining non-Muslims continues; minority communities shrink.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: No disenchantment is evident; the sacred suffuses public and private life. Manuscript production of religious and mystical texts reinforces spiritual engagement. The period ends with cosmology intact and unquestioned.

docs.title: Manuscript Stage in The Andean Cordillera and Pacific Coast — 600 CE – 1,810 CE
- 600 CE – 1,000 CE — Middle Horizon Empires and the Origins of Quipu Administration
- 1,000 CE – 1,400 CE — Late Intermediate Period and Regional Record Systems
- 1,400 CE – 1,532 CE — Inca Imperial Administration and Quipu Statecraft
- 1,532 CE – 1,570 CE — Spanish Conquest and the Introduction of Alphabetic Writing
- 1,570 CE – 1,650 CE — Toledan Reforms and Colonial Manuscript Infrastructure
- 1,650 CE – 1,700 CE — Mature Colonial Society and Creole Literary Culture
- 1,700 CE – 1,780 CE — Bourbon Reforms and Administrative Manuscript Expansion
- 1,780 CE – 1,810 CE — Late Colonial Crisis and Revolutionary Manuscript Culture
1700 CE – 1780 CE — Bourbon Reforms and Administrative Manuscript Expansion
docs.text: Summary: The Viceroyalty of Peru under Bourbon rule, where dynastic reformism drives an eightfold expansion of administrative manuscript production as the new intendancy system, scientific expeditions, and Enlightenment-influenced regulation generate unprecedented documentary flows, binding constraint remaining the Manuscript Stage infrastructure that enables systematic state legibility but still excludes the illiterate majority from direct participation in public records.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: The viceregal territory spans coastal desert from Guayaquil to Atacama, the central sierra from Quito to Potosi, and the altiplano basin, with Lima the administrative node linked by mule tracks requiring weeks to reach highland centers; the 1717 and 1739 partitions create the Viceroyalty of New Granada (northern Andes) and anticipate the 1776 creation of the Rio de la Plata viceroyalty, shrinking Peru's jurisdiction but concentrating administrative attention on the remaining core.

Climate Regime & Volatility: The Little Ice Age persists with moderate cooling; ENSO cycles produce periodic coastal flooding and highland drought, but irrigation infrastructure and vertical archipelago exploitation buffer shocks; no catastrophic climate event disrupts the period's administrative expansion.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: The 1746 Lima-Callao earthquake and tsunami kill approximately 5,000 and destroy much of the capital, prompting extensive reconstruction and generating massive documentary records of damage assessment, rebuilding contracts, and insurance claims; seismic risk remains constant along the Pacific margin.

Resource & Energy Endowment: Potosi silver production declines from its 17th-century peak but remains substantial; mercury from Huancavelica supplies amalgamation; guano deposits along the coast are not yet commercially exploited; timber for paper pulp remains imported from Europe via Spain, constraining local manuscript substrate production.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Mining effluent continues to contaminate highland watersheds around Potosi and Huancavelica; mercury pollution accumulates in soils and workers; urban waste in Lima and highland cities remains locally absorbed without reaching critical thresholds; the physical sink is adequate for period loads.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: Endemic typhus, dysentery, and respiratory illness persist; periodic smallpox outbreaks strike indigenous communities despite earlier demographic catastrophe having selected for survivors; Huancavelica mercury miners suffer chronic poisoning with shortened lifespans; baseline mortality remains elevated by European standards but stable.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: Highland populations maintain adequate nutrition through potato, maize, and quinoa cultivation with llama and alpaca pastoralism; coastal populations access marine protein; mining communities suffer nutritional stress from labor demands and mercury exposure; creole urban populations enjoy adequate provisioning.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Colonial hospitals (Hospital de Santa Ana, Hospital de San Andres in Lima) serve urban populations; indigenous communities rely on traditional healers and herbal remedies; Jesuit pharmacies disperse before the 1767 expulsion; healing capacity is uneven, concentrated in urban centers, inadequate for mining camps.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Complex casta system regulates intermarriage among Spanish, indigenous, African, and mixed populations; ecclesiastical marriage records proliferate as documentation requirements intensify; fertility remains adequate for population maintenance across all groups.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Indigenous population stabilizes after two centuries of post-conquest decline, beginning slow recovery; creole and mestizo populations grow; African slave imports continue for coastal agriculture; total viceregal population approaches two million by 1780; density remains low outside urban centers and mining zones.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: The mit'a labor draft continues to extract working-age males from indigenous communities for Potosi service, leaving women, children, and elderly as dependents; mortality in mines and mercury works creates widows and orphans absorbed by extended kin networks; dependency load is chronic but contained within indigenous social structures.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: Indigenous communities maintain subsistence through traditional agriculture augmented by European crops and livestock; tribute obligations and labor drafts extract surplus but rarely push below subsistence; periodic droughts and earthquakes disrupt provisioning locally but reserves and reciprocity networks buffer shortfalls.

Energy Capture & Conversion: Human and animal muscle remain the primary power sources; watermills serve grain processing; draft animals (mules, llamas) power transport and some mining operations; no significant technological advance in energy capture occurs during the period; per-capita energy ceiling remains constrained.

Labor Organization & Coercion: The mit'a system continues to draft indigenous labor for Potosi mines under formal legal coercion; wage labor expands in urban centers and haciendas; African slavery persists on coastal plantations; Bourbon reforms attempt to regulate labor conditions without fundamentally altering the coercive structure.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Silver production at Potosi declines but remains the primary export; textile obrajes produce for regional markets; agricultural haciendas expand; Bourbon commercial reforms (comercio libre from 1778) stimulate trade; surplus flows to Spain as remittances and taxes, leaving limited local accumulation.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: Royal treasury maintains reserves in Lima; merchants hold inventories; indigenous communities maintain traditional storage practices; credit networks centered on Lima merchant houses provide liquidity; reserves adequate for normal fluctuations, stressed by major disasters like the 1746 earthquake.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: The 1778 comercio libre decree opens additional ports to direct trade with Spain, bypassing the Cadiz monopoly; internal trade flows along established mule routes; Bourbon reforms improve customs documentation and reduce contraband; logistics remain slow but increasingly documented.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: Silver peso remains the unit of account and medium of exchange; merchant credit networks extend throughout the viceroyalty; the Tribunal del Consulado regulates commercial disputes; bills of exchange circulate among merchants; indigenous communities maintain traditional reciprocity obligations alongside monetary transactions.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: Bourbon fiscal reforms intensify tax collection, introducing new levies and improving enforcement; the alcabala (sales tax) expands; tribute collection from indigenous communities continues; customs duties increase under comercio libre; fiscal pressure rises but remains below levels that provoke open resistance until the late 1770s.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Wealth concentrates among peninsular merchants, creole hacendados, and the Church; indigenous communities hold communal lands under legal protection but face encroachment; the Jesuit expulsion (1767) transfers substantial ecclesiastical property to secular administration; inequality deepens as commercial reform favors established capital.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Mining waste continues to accumulate at Potosi and Huancavelica; urban waste managed through traditional channels; no significant change in waste routing practices; financial malinvestment limited by conservative credit practices and colonial oversight.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Spanish inheritance law governs creole families with primogeniture for entailed estates; indigenous communities maintain bilateral inheritance with communal land tenure; the casta system regulates intermarriage and determines legal status of offspring; ecclesiastical marriage remains the only legitimate union, extensively documented in parish registers.

Association & Mutual Aid: Indigenous cofradias (confraternities) provide mutual aid and organize religious festivals; artisan guilds regulate urban crafts; merchant consulados coordinate trade; indigenous communities maintain traditional ayllu structures for labor coordination and resource sharing; the fabric of association remains dense and functional.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: Religious festivals structure the calendar with processions, bullfights, and public celebrations; urban tertulias gather creole elites for conversation and literary discussion; indigenous festivals syncretize Catholic and traditional elements; sociability reinforces both colonial hierarchy and community solidarity.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: The casta system formally stratifies society by racial category with peninsular Spaniards at apex, creoles below, then mixed categories (mestizo, mulato, zambo), indigenous tribute-payers, and African slaves at bottom; boundaries remain legally rigid but social practice permits some mobility through wealth, education, or whitening (gracias al sacar); stratification is hardening as Bourbon reforms favor peninsulares over creoles for high office.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: The intendancy system (introduced 1784, anticipated by earlier reforms) replaces the corregimiento, centralizing provincial administration under royally appointed intendants; the Audiencia of Lima retains judicial functions; visitadores (inspectors) audit colonial administration; documentary production multiplies as each reform generates new record requirements, reports, and correspondence; administrative capacity increases but corruption persists.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: The colonial militia system provides local defense; regular army units garrison Lima and major cities; fortifications protect Callao harbor; indigenous communities lack formal military organization but retain capacity for coordinated resistance; the apparatus suffices for internal order but proves inadequate when confronted with mass uprising in the 1780s.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: Low-level disorder persists in banditry, smuggling, and occasional local riots; judicial records document criminal proceedings; indigenous grievances accumulate as tribute and labor burdens intensify under Bourbon fiscal pressure; the apparatus contains disorder but does not resolve underlying tensions; friction accretes toward the crisis of the 1780s.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: Viceroys appointed from Spain exercise formal authority; local caciques (indigenous chiefs) mediate between communities and colonial state; creole elites lack access to highest offices; no charismatic leader emerges to channel discontent until Tupac Amaru II in 1780; leadership is bureaucratic rather than personal.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: The Spanish Crown retains formal legitimacy through tradition, religion, and established authority; indigenous communities accept colonial rule as established fact while maintaining separate identity; creole allegiance is instrumental, eroding as discrimination intensifies; legitimacy weakens gradually but has not yet cracked.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: Bourbon reformers in Madrid drive policy with centralizing will; local viceregal administration implements directives with variable enthusiasm; creole elites lack collective organization to resist; indigenous communities conserve energy, waiting; collective will is dispersed, reactive, not yet mobilized for resistance.

External Relations & Posture: The viceroyalty functions as colony, its external posture determined by Madrid; British and Portuguese pressure on Spanish American periphery is felt as distant threat; no independent diplomatic capacity exists; the stance is defensive, inward-looking, focused on internal administration.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: Creole resentment grows as Bourbon reforms systematically favor peninsular Spaniards for high office; indigenous communities maintain outward compliance while inward grievance deepens over tribute increases and labor demands; public sentiment is cautious, watchful, increasingly strained; trust contracts along ethnic and status lines.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: Creole disaffection deepens as career paths narrow; indigenous communities harbor deep but unexpressed grievance; the combination creates potential energy for revolt; will is not spent but suppressed, accumulating pressure that will discharge in the Tupac Amaru rebellion.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Spanish remains the language of administration and commerce; Quechua and Aymara serve indigenous communities with some bilingual intermediaries; literacy remains confined to clerical, administrative, and commercial elites; the majority accesses public information through oral transmission and public proclamations read aloud; the shared code is stratified, not universal.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Official correspondence travels by mule courier along established routes, Lima to Cusco in two to three weeks, to Potosi in four to six weeks; the correo system improves under Bourbon administration; no newspaper exists until the Mercurio Peruano (1791, outside this window); transmission is slow, reliable for official channels, slower for private communication.

Record, Storage & Persistence: Administrative manuscript production expands dramatically as Bourbon reforms generate census records, tribute rolls, commercial registers, judicial proceedings, and inspection reports; notarial archives accumulate in Lima and provincial capitals; ecclesiastical records (baptism, marriage, death) continue systematic documentation; the Jesuit expulsion (1767) transfers vast documentary holdings to secular archives; persistence is systematic, survival rates high for official records.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: The Inquisition retains censorship authority over print and manuscript; Enlightenment texts circulate clandestinely among creole elites; scientific expeditions (Hipólito Ruiz botanical expedition 1777-1788) produce officially sanctioned secular knowledge; the permitted band remains narrow but widens slightly as Enlightenment influences penetrate; discourse norms remain formally Catholic, practically more diverse in elite circles.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: Literate audiences remain small, perhaps 5-10% of the population; public proclamations reach broader audiences through oral transmission; rumors circulate rapidly through market networks and indigenous communities; amplification follows established social channels, privileging urban centers and commercial networks.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: Official records maintain high integrity through notarial protocols and archival practices; oral transmission introduces distortion; the information load increases as reforms multiply documentation requirements; verification capacity keeps pace within official channels but cannot penetrate oral networks where rumor and misinformation circulate; noise load is moderate, concentrated in non-official channels.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Catholic moral teaching provides the official foundation; natural law arguments from scholastic tradition justify colonial hierarchy; indigenous communities maintain parallel moral frameworks emphasizing reciprocity and communal obligation; Enlightenment ideas of natural rights begin to circulate among creole elites; the sense of justice is plural, stratified by culture and education.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: The Laws of the Indies remain the foundational legal code; Bourbon reforms add layers of regulatory legislation, commercial ordinances, and administrative procedures; the Recopilación de las Leyes de Indias (1680) is supplemented by royal decrees (cédulas reales) that accumulate as manuscript copies in colonial archives; codification is active, expanding, increasingly complex.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: The Audiencia of Lima serves as supreme court; corregidores (later intendants) exercise local jurisdiction; ecclesiastical courts handle matrimonial and clerical matters; the Inquisition prosecutes heresy and some moral offenses; indigenous communities retain limited jurisdiction over internal disputes; adjudication is slow, expensive, favors those with resources to pursue litigation; sanction ranges from fines to imprisonment to corporal punishment to execution for serious crimes.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Indigenous communities retain legal protections under the Laws of the Indies, including communal land rights and prohibition of enslavement, but these are inconsistently enforced; compliance burden increases as Bourbon reforms multiply regulatory requirements; predictability of rules improves within official channels but local variation persists; rights are formal rather than effective for most of the population.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: Corregidores notoriously abuse their positions through forced sales (repartimiento de mercancias) despite prohibition; tribute collectors extract unauthorized payments; mine operators evade labor regulations; impunity for powerful actors is endemic; indigenous petitions document grievances but rarely obtain effective redress; the justice gap is wide and widening as fiscal pressure intensifies.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: Enlightenment natural philosophy reaches creole elites through clandestine circulation; Spanish scientific expeditions (Ruiz-Pavón botanical expedition, Alejandro Malaspina's later voyage) apply systematic observation to Andean flora, fauna, and geography; the University of San Marcos continues scholastic curriculum but some professors introduce modern ideas; the paradigm is transitional, scholasticism dominant but challenged.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Mining technology stagnates at established levels; agricultural practice continues traditional methods augmented by colonial introductions; textile production uses established techniques; no significant technical innovation originates locally; applied knowledge is conservative, adequate for existing production but not advancing.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: The University of San Marcos trains clergy, lawyers, and physicians; Jesuit colleges educate creole elites until the 1767 expulsion; literacy remains confined to perhaps 10% of the population, concentrated in urban centers and among clergy; the knowledge stock is substantial within elite circles, largely inaccessible to the majority; skill distribution is highly uneven.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: Indigenous knowledge systems persist in oral tradition but transmission weakens as Spanish cultural hegemony deepens; quipu use has ceased except as antiquarian curiosity; some traditional agricultural and medical knowledge survives through practice; scholastic learning ossifies as Enlightenment alternatives emerge; obsolescence is gradual, loss continuing from earlier periods.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: Creole identity crystallizes around American birth and resentment of peninsular privilege; indigenous communities maintain pre-Columbian memory through oral tradition, ritual, and encoded symbols; the Inca past becomes a resource for both creole patriotism and indigenous resistance; memory is plural, contested, politically charged.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: The colonial order is justified by Catholic mission, royal authority, and civilizing project; Bourbon reformers add Enlightenment rhetoric of rational administration and useful knowledge; indigenous subjects are framed as childlike wards requiring Spanish tutelage; the narrative remains officially unchallenged but creole intellectuals begin articulating alternative patriotic visions.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: Baroque religious art continues in churches and convents with distinctively Andean inflections (Cuzco School painting); elite architecture follows Spanish models with local materials; indigenous textile traditions persist with syncretic imagery; the visual culture is richly layered, officially Catholic, privately preserving indigenous forms; color palette emphasizes gold, crimson, and deep blue in religious contexts, earth tones in domestic settings.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: Baroque forms remain vital in religious contexts; colonial ceremonial retains meaning for participants; indigenous rituals maintain significance within communities; exhaustion is not yet evident; the symbolic vocabulary is stable, even expanding as creole patriotism develops new imagery.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: Catholic cosmology provides the official frame, with heaven, hell, purgatory structuring afterlife expectations; indigenous communities maintain syncretic beliefs integrating Pachamama, mountain spirits (apus), and ancestor veneration with Catholic saints; fatalism and piety predominate; Enlightenment skepticism remains confined to tiny elite circles; the outlook is traditional, stable, providing meaning and orientation for most of the population.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: Catholic sacraments (baptism, marriage, extreme unction) mark life transitions with extensive documentary record; daily devotion includes rosary, prayer, and saint veneration; indigenous festivals syncretize Catholic feast days with agricultural and ancestral rituals; pilgrimage to regional shrines continues; the sacred is enacted regularly, communally, binding society together across ethnic lines.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: The Archbishop of Lima heads the colonial church; religious orders (Franciscans, Dominicans, Augustinians, Mercedarians) maintain parishes, missions, and schools; the Jesuit expulsion (1767) removes the most intellectually active order and transfers substantial property; Inquisition authority persists but activity declines; doctrinal orthodoxy is enforced but accommodation of indigenous practice is pragmatic.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: Catholicism is universal but syncretic, incorporating indigenous elements that the Church tolerates when not openly heterodox; no competing religious system is spreading; the dominant cosmology's reach is stable, perhaps deepening as indigenous populations internalize Catholic forms over generations.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: Enlightenment ideas introduce incipient skepticism among tiny elite circles, but disenchantment is negligible for the vast majority; the sacred remains potent, meaningful, actively practiced; no significant drift toward secularism is yet evident; spiritual need is fully addressed within existing structures.

docs.title: 1400 CE – 1532 CE — Inca Imperial Administration and Quipu Statecraft
docs.text: Summary: Tawantinsuyu at its height, the largest empire in pre-Columbian America, with governance running entirely on the quipu system — knotted-string records that stored census, tribute, labor obligations, and possibly narrative across four thousand kilometers of territory. The binding constraint is the Manuscript Stage: external records kept outside living memory became the medium imperial administration ran on, with khipukamayuq specialists maintaining the accounting that made central coordination of millions possible, even without alphabetic script.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: Tawantinsuyu stretched along the Andean spine from southern Colombia to central Chile, approximately 4,000 km north-to-south but rarely more than 500 km east-to-west, bounded by Pacific coast, high cordillera, and Amazonian escarpment; the Qhapaq Ñan (royal road) system of 30,000+ km overcame extreme topographic friction through paved surfaces, suspension bridges, and switchbacks, reducing transit time from weeks to days for chasqui relay runners who could move a message from Quito to Cusco in five to seven days.

Climate Regime & Volatility: The vertical ecology ranged from hyper-arid coastal desert through temperate highland valleys to frigid puna above 4,000 m, with seasonal rains concentrated in the austral summer (November–March); ENSO events periodically devastated coastal irrigation while bringing drought to highlands, but the empire's multi-zone structure distributed risk across elevation bands.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: The Pacific Ring of Fire subjected the region to frequent seismic activity; major earthquakes periodically damaged Cusco and provincial centers; volcanic activity affected the southern highlands; the infrastructure of agricultural terraces and irrigation canals required continuous maintenance against erosion and collapse.

Resource & Energy Endowment: Gold, silver, and copper concentrated in highland deposits fueled elite material culture; tin from the altiplano enabled bronze metallurgy; obsidian, salt, and coca circulated through state-controlled redistribution; llama and alpaca herds provided transport, wool, and dried meat (charki); the resource base was rich but extraction limited by muscle-powered technology.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Population density in core valleys (Cusco, Mantaro, Cajamarca) stressed local wood supplies for fuel and construction; terrace agriculture prevented erosion but required labor investment; the environmental footprint remained manageable given the absence of large-scale smelting or intensive fuel consumption beyond subsistence needs.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: The Andean population carried its own endemic disease load — tuberculosis, treponematoses, parasitic infections — but was isolated from Old World crowd diseases; mortality from violence during conquests and from altitude-related stress on lowland populations moved to highland mines represented significant but localized pressures; baseline mortality was moderate by pre-modern standards.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: The vertical archipelago model ensured dietary diversity — maize, potatoes, quinoa, beans from different elevations; freeze-dried potato (chuño) and dried meat provided storable protein and carbohydrates; nutritional status appears adequate in most regions, with skeletal evidence showing populations generally well-nourished though shorter than coastal predecessors.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Andean medicine combined herbalism, surgery (including trepanation with high survival rates), and ritual healing; coca leaf served analgesic and stimulant functions; specialist healers (hampicamayoc) practiced throughout the empire; healing capacity was distributed through kinship networks and state-provisioned specialists at major centers.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: The Inca institutionalized controlled reproduction through the aqllakuna (chosen women) system, with selected females serving religious, textile, and reproductive functions for the state; commoner marriage was regulated through annual ceremonies; polygyny was an elite privilege scaled to rank.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Population estimates range from 6 to 14 million at contact; the mit'akuna (forced relocation) policy moved entire communities to consolidate conquests and break resistance, redistributing population across the empire; density concentrated in core highland valleys and irrigated coastal zones.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: The ayllu (kinship community) structure absorbed dependent members through reciprocal obligations; the state extracted labor rather than goods, leaving communities responsible for their own elderly and infirm; mit'a labor drafts removed productive adults but the system rotated burdens across households.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: State granaries (qollqa) stored maize, chuño, dried meat, and other provisions across the road network; this buffer protected against local crop failures and sustained armies and labor corvées on the move; the provisioning floor was higher and more secure than in most pre-modern states due to systematic storage.

Energy Capture & Conversion: Human and camelid muscle provided all motive power; the absence of the wheel for transport (though known for toys) reflected terrain unsuited to wheeled vehicles; bronze tools improved agricultural efficiency over stone but remained muscle-powered; per-capita energy remained low but labor mobilization achieved massive works through sheer scale.

Labor Organization & Coercion: The mit'a system drafted rotational labor for state projects — road construction, terrace building, mining, military service — with communities responsible for quotas rather than individuals; this was coerced but rotational, distinct from permanent slavery; yanakuna were a separate class of permanent state servants removed from ayllu membership.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Agricultural terracing expanded cultivable land dramatically; state and religious lands produced surplus extracted as labor on those lands rather than as goods taxation; textile production by aqllakuna and community quotas generated vast quantities of cumbi cloth, a medium of state wealth and diplomatic exchange.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: The qollqa system represented perhaps history's largest pre-modern state storage network, with thousands of storehouses along the road system containing food, weapons, textiles, and sandals; this buffer enabled rapid military deployment and famine relief; quipu recorded exact inventories across the system.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: Markets in the Mesoamerican sense were absent or minimal; the state redistributed goods through administrative channels; long-distance exchange occurred through state caravans and elite reciprocity; the road system enabled logistics at unprecedented scale, with relay stations (tampu) every 20–30 km.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: No currency existed; value storage took the form of accumulated goods — textiles, metal objects, coca — or claims on future labor; reciprocity obligations tracked through quipu constituted a form of deferred exchange accounting without monetary abstraction.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: The state extracted labor rather than goods, avoiding the grain-taxation problem of perishable tribute; mit'a obligations were encoded on quipu by ayllu, enabling precise tracking of who owed what; surplus redistribution through feasts, gifts, and emergency relief legitimated extraction.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Extreme concentration at the top — the Sapa Inca's mummified predecessors maintained their own estates and servants; the panaca (royal descent groups) accumulated wealth across generations; commoners held usufruct land rights through ayllu membership but could not alienate land, limiting wealth accumulation.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Organic waste recycled through agriculture; minimal industrial waste given craft production scales; the system generated negligible non-biodegradable refuse; no financial mispricing residue existed in the absence of credit markets and currency.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: The ayllu structured all commoner life — land access, labor obligations, marriage, and ritual all ran through this kinship corporation; inheritance followed ayllu rules with property remaining within the group; Inca elites followed different rules, with panaca corporations holding royal lineage property in perpetuity for the cult of dead rulers.

Association & Mutual Aid: Ayllu reciprocity (ayni) obligated mutual labor assistance for house-building, planting, and harvest; the minka system organized communal work for community benefit; these horizontal solidarities persisted beneath and alongside state extraction, providing the actual safety net for daily life.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: State festivals structured the ceremonial calendar — Inti Raymi (sun festival), Qhapaq Raymi (royal festival) — with feasting, chicha (maize beer) distribution, music, and dance; local festivities marked agricultural and life-cycle events; competitive games and ritual combat had ceremonial functions.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: A rigid hierarchy descended from the Sapa Inca through the Inca nobility (panaca members), to Incas-by-privilege (allied elites granted status), to curacas (local hereditary lords), to hatun runa (commoner taxpayers), to yanakuna (permanent servants) and aqllakuna (chosen women); ethnic identity persisted beneath Inca overlay, with conquered groups maintaining dress markers and local structures under supervision.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: Provincial administration operated through a decimal hierarchy — overseers of 10, 100, 1,000, and 10,000 households — with quipu recording all obligations and compliance; khipukamayuq maintained records at each level, reporting upward to Cusco; the system achieved remarkable reach for a pre-literate state, though it depended on the integrity of oral interpretation accompanying the quipu.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: The Inca army mobilized through mit'a, with each ethnic group providing units under their own curacas but commanded by Inca generals; weapons included bronze-headed clubs, slings, axes, and bows; fortifications (pukara) controlled strategic points; the army could field tens of thousands, overwhelming smaller polities through sheer numbers and logistical superiority backed by the tampu-qollqa system.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: Succession crises represented the system's greatest vulnerability — the civil war between Atahualpa and Huascar (1529–1532) killed tens of thousands and was still resolving when Pizarro arrived; conquered populations retained resentments exploited by Spanish later; the apparatus otherwise functioned until external shock, with no significant internal rebellion recorded in the final decades.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: The Sapa Inca embodied divine authority as son of Inti (the sun), with elaborate ritual reinforcing his unique status; his person was sacred, his movements accompanied by thousands, his clothing worn only once; provincial curacas exercised local authority under Inca supervision, their legitimacy partly traditional, partly delegated.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: Inca legitimacy rested on military success, the claim of divine mandate, and the material benefits of incorporation — roads, storage, security; for core populations this was genuine belief; for recently conquered groups, compliance was pragmatic; the speed of defection to Spanish revealed how shallow allegiance ran among many subject peoples.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: The succession crisis paralyzed political will at the moment of Spanish contact; Atahualpa's capture at Cajamarca decapitated a system where authority concentrated in the divine ruler; the inability to coordinate resistance after 1532 reflected both the system's centralization and the divisions the civil war had opened.

External Relations & Posture: Tawantinsuyu expanded continuously until the 1520s, incorporating new territories through conquest or intimidation; the frontier zones — Amazonian lowlands, Chilean Araucanía, northern jungles — marked the limits where terrain made conquest unprofitable; no peer competitor existed in the hemisphere, leaving no tradition of diplomatic balance among equals.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: Subject populations experienced Inca rule as an imposition backed by overwhelming force, softened by redistributive feasts and the security of the qollqa buffer; loyalty varied by how recently conquest had occurred and how harshly mit'a was extracted; the core Inca population around Cusco exhibited genuine attachment to the system that elevated them.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: Resentment among subject peoples remained suppressed but real; the mit'akuna policy of forced relocation deliberately disrupted potential resistance networks; when Spanish arrived, Cañari, Huanca, and other groups saw opportunity for revenge against Inca overlords, converting stored disaffection into active collaboration with invaders.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Quechua served as the administrative lingua franca, spread by Inca policy, though local languages persisted; the quipu system was accessible only to trained khipukamayuq, creating a specialist monopoly on record interpretation; oral transmission accompanied all quipu readings, with the cords serving as mnemonic aids rather than fully autonomous texts.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: The chasqui relay system achieved remarkable speed — messages traveled 240+ km per day through continuous runner relays at tampu stations; this velocity enabled central coordination across vast distances; quipu content moved physically with runners or officials, the information embedded in the cords themselves.

Record, Storage & Persistence: Quipu stored numerical data — census counts, tribute tallies, inventory quantities — in a decimal positional system using knot types and positions; categorical information was encoded in cord color, ply, and attachment position; whether quipu recorded narrative content remains debated, but they certainly fixed quantitative data beyond any single memory, enabling cumulative accounting across generations of khipukamayuq.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: Official history was recited at state festivals, with the Sapa Inca controlling historical narrative; conquered peoples' histories were subordinated or suppressed; the quipu system recorded what the state wanted recorded, with no independent documentation tradition to contest official accounts.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: State communications reached populations through curacas and public ceremonies; the ritual calendar ensured regular occasions for message transmission; quipu readings occurred in administrative contexts, not public forums, limiting direct popular access to information content.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: The quipu system's integrity depended on the khipukamayuq corps — their training, honesty, and accurate oral supplementation of cord data; redundancy (multiple khipukamayuq at each level) provided some verification; Spanish chroniclers noted occasional discrepancies between quipu accounts, suggesting some noise in the system, but overall integrity appears high for a pre-literate record-keeping technology.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Inca moral order centered on ama sua, ama llulla, ama qella (don't steal, don't lie, don't be lazy) — principles encoding property security, truthfulness essential for quipu reliability, and the labor obligation that sustained the system; reciprocity (ayni) at the community level and between state and subjects framed obligations as mutual rather than merely extractive.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: Law was oral, transmitted through administrative hierarchy and embodied in precedent; no written code existed, but quipu could record judgments and penalties for reference; Inca law distinguished offenses by status — crimes against the state, the Sapa Inca, or religious objects carried death; ordinary disputes were resolved locally by curacas.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: Curacas adjudicated local disputes; serious matters escalated to provincial governors; capital cases might reach Cusco; punishments included death (by hanging, stoning, or pushing from cliffs), exile, loss of position, flogging, and assignment to onerous labor; collective liability attached to ayllu for members' offenses in some cases.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Commoners held usufruct rights to ayllu land, protection from arbitrary dispossession, and access to state redistribution in hardship; these were not rights against the state but entitlements within a system of mutual obligation; compliance burden was heavy — mit'a could demand months of labor annually — but predictable and theoretically reciprocated by state protection and storage access.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: Elite impunity existed — Inca nobles faced different standards than commoners, and the Sapa Inca was above ordinary judgment; the succession conflict revealed how elite violence operated outside normal constraints; for ordinary disputes, the system appears to have functioned with rough justice, but no appeal beyond the hierarchy existed.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: Astronomical observation determined the ceremonial calendar, with the Coricancha (sun temple) functioning as an observatory; agricultural knowledge was empirically refined over centuries — crop selection, terrace construction, irrigation engineering; medical knowledge combined empirical herbalism with cosmological interpretation; no tradition of abstract inquiry independent of practical application or religious function existed.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Engineering achievement was remarkable — suspension bridges spanning 50+ meters, roads through extreme terrain, terrace systems transforming mountainsides, precisely fitted stone architecture without mortar; metallurgical knowledge produced bronze tools and gold/silver work of high quality; textile technology achieved extraordinary complexity and fineness; technique was highly developed within its domains.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: Specialized training occurred for khipukamayuq (quipu keepers), amautas (scholars/teachers), and various craft specialists; the aqllawasi (house of chosen women) trained women in textile production and religious service; commoner education was informal, through ayllu apprenticeship; literacy in the alphabetic sense did not exist, but quipu competence required years of training.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: Knowledge transmission depended on living practitioners; the khipukamayuq corps preserved accumulated data across generations, but meaning was vulnerable to interpretive drift; post-conquest extermination of khipukamayuq and suppression of quipu led to catastrophic knowledge loss within decades.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: Inca origin myths centered on Manco Cápac and Mama Ocllo emerging from Lake Titicaca or the cave of Pacaritambo, sent by Inti to civilize humanity; each ethnic group retained its own origin narratives subordinated to Inca cosmology; the cult of royal mummies (mallqui) kept dead rulers present in political life, their panaca descendants maintaining their estates and cults.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: The Sapa Inca ruled as Intip Churin (son of the sun), with divine mandate to extend civilization through conquest; Inca expansion was framed as bringing order to chaos, civilization to barbarism; subject peoples were incorporated into a hierarchy where proximity to Inca culture conferred status; this ideology legitimated extraction as reciprocity for the benefits of Inca order.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: Imperial style was standardized — aryballoid vessels, polychrome geometric ceramics, cumbi textiles with tocapu designs (possibly encoding meaning), precisely fitted stone architecture with trapezoidal doorways and niches, gold and silver worked into figures and vessels; provincial elites adopted Inca style as status markers while local traditions continued at lower social levels.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: The empire was too young (under a century old) for significant form exhaustion; imperial iconography was vigorously deployed; the speed of collapse prevented internal cultural decay, though the post-conquest period saw rapid hollowing of Inca symbols as Spanish replaced them with Christian imagery.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: A layered cosmos — hanan pacha (upper world), kay pacha (this world), ukhu pacha (lower world) — with spirits (huacas) inhabiting features of the landscape; Inti (sun) and Mama Quilla (moon) headed the celestial hierarchy; Pachamama (earth mother) received offerings for agricultural fertility; the dead remained present, requiring feeding and consultation; time was cyclical, with world ages ending in cataclysm (pachacuti).

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: The ceremonial calendar organized state and local ritual throughout the year; major festivals involved mass gatherings, processions of royal mummies, sacrifices (including human sacrifice for major occasions), feasting, and chicha consumption; daily offerings to huacas maintained cosmic order; divination through coca, fire, and animal entrails guided decision-making.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: The Willaq Uma (high priest) headed the religious hierarchy; the Coricancha in Cusco served as the central temple complex, staffed by priests and mamaconas (consecrated women); provincial temples replicated the center; the Sapa Inca's divine status made religious and political authority inseparable at the apex.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: Inca religion incorporated conquered peoples' huacas into a hierarchy beneath Inti, holding significant idols hostage in Cusco; this was syncretic incorporation rather than replacement; local cults continued under Inca overlay; no missionary impulse sought to eliminate other beliefs, only to subordinate them.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: The cosmos remained fully enchanted; huacas inhabited every significant landscape feature; the sacred was omnipresent; no secularizing tendency existed; the catastrophe of conquest would create spiritual crisis, but within the pre-contact period the cosmology retained full explanatory power and ritual efficacy for its adherents.

docs.title: 1780 CE – 1810 CE — Late Colonial Crisis and Revolutionary Manuscript Culture
docs.text: Summary: The Viceroyalty of Peru from the Tupac Amaru II rebellion through Napoleon's invasion of Spain, where the accumulated tensions of Bourbon reform erupt in the largest indigenous uprising since the conquest, generating massive judicial documentation, while the 1808 imperial crisis unleashes revolutionary manuscript circulation among creole elites debating constitutional responses, binding constraint remaining the Manuscript Stage medium through which both repression and revolution are recorded, argued, and organized.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: The truncated viceroyalty retains the Peruvian coast and central sierra after the 1776 creation of the Rio de la Plata viceroyalty that absorbed Upper Peru (modern Bolivia) including Potosi; the rebellion of 1780-1782 sweeps across the southern highlands from Cuzco to Lake Titicaca, terrain that advantages insurgent guerrilla movement and disadvantages royalist conventional forces; Lima remains the administrative center, connected to the crisis zone by weeks of difficult transit.

Climate Regime & Volatility: The Little Ice Age continues with no exceptional climate events; ENSO cycles produce normal variation; no climate shock correlates with the rebellion's timing, which is driven by political and fiscal triggers rather than environmental stress.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: No major seismic event disrupts the period; the 1746 Lima earthquake's reconstruction is complete; volcanic activity in the southern Andes does not significantly affect population centers; the hazard regime provides no unusual stress.

Resource & Energy Endowment: Silver production continues its long decline from 17th-century peaks but remains economically significant; mercury from Huancavelica sustains amalgamation processes; the mining economy's reduced dynamism removes one source of colonial vitality while tribute and labor extraction continue at full pressure; resource endowment is adequate but not expanding.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Mining pollution continues to accumulate at established rates; no change in waste routing or sink pressure; the physical environment absorbs loads without crisis; degradation continues gradually from earlier periods.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: Endemic disease patterns continue; the rebellion and its suppression add violent mortality, with perhaps 100,000 deaths in the 1780-1782 conflict concentrated in southern highland indigenous communities; baseline mortality returns to normal after 1782; no major epidemic coincides with the crisis.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: The rebellion disrupts agricultural production in affected zones, creating temporary food stress; royalist forces and rebels both requisition supplies; after pacification, nutritional status recovers to baseline; overall physiological vitality is not permanently impaired.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Colonial medical infrastructure proves inadequate for conflict casualties; traditional indigenous healing serves both sides; battlefield wounds and subsequent infections kill many who might otherwise survive; healing capacity is overwhelmed during the acute crisis, adequate during peacetime.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: The rebellion disrupts normal life in affected zones; some displacement and refugee movement occurs; after pacification, pairing and reproduction resume normal patterns; demographic recovery begins within a decade; the crisis is severe but not catastrophic for reproductive capacity.

Demographic Renewal & Density: The rebellion's mortality falls disproportionately on indigenous highland populations, temporarily reversing demographic recovery; estimates suggest 100,000 deaths in a regional population of perhaps one million; the demographic shock is absorbed over the following generation; density remains low by global standards.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: The rebellion creates widows, orphans, and displaced persons in affected zones; royalist reprisals target indigenous leadership, removing community heads; the dependency load spikes during and after the conflict; extended kin networks absorb the burden over time; attrition is severe but not permanent.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: The rebellion disrupts production and trade in the southern highlands for two years; forced requisitions by both sides stress communities; the Spanish response includes economic warfare against rebel-held areas; after pacification, subsistence agriculture recovers; the floor holds despite severe stress.

Energy Capture & Conversion: No change in energy technology; human and animal muscle remain primary; the rebellion demonstrates the limits of colonial energy mobilization against dispersed highland resistance; conversion efficiency remains at established levels.

Labor Organization & Coercion: The rebellion is triggered partly by intensified labor coercion through the mita system and repartimiento abuses; Tupac Amaru II's program explicitly attacks forced labor and tribute; after suppression, the Crown reforms the mita and abolishes repartimiento de mercancias (1780s), moderating the coercive system without eliminating it; labor organization continues under modified colonial structures.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Mining production continues at reduced levels; the rebellion disrupts textile obrajes and agricultural haciendas in affected zones; trade routes through the southern highlands are interrupted; after pacification, production resumes at pre-war levels; surplus capacity is damaged but not destroyed; the long-term economic trend remains stagnant.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: Royal treasury absorbs the cost of military mobilization against the rebellion, depleting reserves; merchant credit networks are strained; indigenous community reserves are exhausted by requisitions and tribute demands; buffering capacity is degraded, leaving less margin for future shocks.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: The rebellion interrupts the Lima-Potosi trade route, the viceroyalty's commercial spine; smuggling and informal exchange continue; after pacification, formal trade resumes; comercio libre continues to reshape Atlantic commerce; logistics infrastructure is not permanently damaged.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: Silver peso remains stable as currency; the rebellion does not trigger monetary crisis; credit networks recover after pacification; no fundamental change in value storage practices; the monetary system absorbs the shock without transformation.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: The rebellion explicitly protests excessive tribute and the repartimiento system; Spanish response includes moderate fiscal reforms (abolition of corregimiento, reduction of some exactions) alongside intensified military spending; net extraction pressure may slightly decrease after reform, but fundamental colonial fiscal structure persists; redistribution continues to favor Spain and colonial elites.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: The rebellion targets Spanish and creole property in affected zones; some haciendas and obrajes are destroyed; royalist victory restores property rights; wealth concentration continues with perhaps slightly greater caution among elites; no fundamental redistribution occurs.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: War debris and unburied dead constitute temporary waste load in conflict zones; normal waste patterns resume after pacification; no lasting change in waste routing; financial system absorbs war costs through debt and deferred obligations.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: The rebellion disrupts families through death, displacement, and separation; widows and orphans require reintegration into kin networks; indigenous kinship structures prove resilient, absorbing the shock; creole family structures are unaffected outside immediate conflict zones; inheritance patterns continue unchanged.

Association & Mutual Aid: Indigenous communities demonstrate remarkable capacity for coordinated action during the rebellion; cofradias and ayllu structures provide organizational infrastructure; after suppression, Spanish authorities attack these structures, banning indigenous political organization, traditional dress, and Quechua language in official contexts; the associational fabric is deliberately damaged by colonial repression.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: Public festivals are suspended during the emergency; after pacification, religious celebrations resume with heightened surveillance; indigenous festivals face new restrictions as authorities suspect them of harboring resistance; sociability is constrained by security concerns and ethnic suspicion.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: The rebellion threatens the racial hierarchy, with indigenous leadership claiming Inca legitimacy; royalist victory reinforces colonial stratification; Spanish response eliminates the indigenous nobility (cacique class) that had mediated between communities and the state, flattening the indigenous social structure; creole-peninsular tensions continue; stratification is violently reinforced, boundaries hardened by trauma.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: The intendancy system, fully implemented by 1784, proves more effective than the corregimiento it replaced; military administration dominates the immediate post-rebellion period; judicial documentation of the rebellion generates thousands of pages of testimony, sentences, and administrative correspondence; administrative capacity is enhanced by crisis, bureaucratic procedures refined, manuscript production intensified.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: The colonial military apparatus, initially overwhelmed by the rebellion's scale, ultimately mobilizes sufficient force to defeat dispersed resistance; regularized military units garrison key points; militia reorganization improves response capacity; fortifications are reinforced; the coercive apparatus emerges from the crisis stronger, more professionalized, better documented; force advantage shifts decisively to the colonial state.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: The rebellion represents maximum discharge of accumulated grievance through violent uprising; suppression does not eliminate grievance but drives it underground; banditry and low-level resistance persist in remote areas; the apparatus contains post-war disorder through intensified surveillance and punishment; underlying tensions are managed, not resolved; the social fabric is damaged, scarred, not broken.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: Jose Gabriel Condorcanqui (Tupac Amaru II) briefly galvanizes indigenous and some mestizo support through personal charisma and Inca symbolism before his capture and execution (1781); no comparable leader emerges thereafter; colonial administration relies on bureaucratic authority rather than personal leadership; the vacuum of indigenous leadership is deliberately maintained through elimination of the cacique class.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: Spanish royal legitimacy survives the rebellion but is damaged; indigenous allegiance becomes instrumental compliance under coercion rather than willing acceptance; creole allegiance is complicated by fear of indigenous uprising, which paradoxically ties them to Spanish protection even as they resent peninsular privilege; legitimacy is hollowed, functional, no longer deep.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: The rebellion demonstrates indigenous capacity for collective action, terrifying colonial authorities; Spanish response deploys overwhelming will to suppress, reform, and prevent recurrence; creole elites lack independent political organization; after 1808, Napoleon's invasion of Spain creates a legitimacy crisis that will eventually mobilize creole will, but within this window collective resolve remains reactive, fragmented.

External Relations & Posture: The viceroyalty remains subordinate to Spain; the rebellion is entirely internal; British naval pressure during European wars creates peripheral concern but no direct engagement; external posture is determined by Madrid; no independent diplomatic capacity exists.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: Fear predominates after the rebellion's suppression; indigenous communities adopt protective silence; creole elites are shaken by the specter of racial warfare; peninsular administrators are anxious and vigilant; trust collapses across ethnic lines; the public mood is dark, watchful, traumatized; risk aversion intensifies among all groups.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: Indigenous disaffection is suppressed but not extinguished; the rebellion's defeat produces exhaustion and apparent resignation that masks continuing resentment; creole disaffection grows through the period, fed by continued discrimination; apathy is protective strategy, not genuine acceptance; will is not spent but constrained, awaiting opportunity.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Spanish colonial authorities attack indigenous communication by banning Quechua in official contexts and restricting indigenous assembly; this drives indigenous communication further underground; Spanish and creole literate circles continue normal communication; the shared code fragments further along ethnic lines; accessibility narrows for indigenous populations, widens slightly for creoles as newspapers emerge after 1790.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: The rebellion demonstrates indigenous capacity for rapid mobilization through oral networks and runner systems; colonial authorities respond by attempting to disrupt these channels; official channels (correo system) continue functioning; after 1790, the Mercurio Peruano (1791-1795) provides Lima's first periodical, mixing print and manuscript circulation; transmission velocity unchanged, channel diversity slightly increased for creole elites.

Record, Storage & Persistence: The rebellion generates massive judicial documentation: interrogations of prisoners, testimony of witnesses, sentences, correspondence, and administrative reports; these records are preserved in colonial archives (much survives in the Archivo General de Indias and the Archivo Nacional del Peru); the event is exhaustively documented from the Spanish perspective; indigenous perspectives are filtered through interrogation records; persistence is systematic for official records, oral indigenous memory persists in parallel.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: Post-rebellion censorship intensifies; representations of Inca history and imagery are banned; indigenous political expression is prohibited; Enlightenment texts continue to circulate clandestinely among creole elites; after 1808, censorship weakens as the imperial crisis opens debate; discourse norms are restrictive during the 1780s-1800s, loosening after 1808 as constitutional questions become unavoidable.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: News of the rebellion spreads throughout Spanish America, inspiring fear among elites and hope among subordinate populations; the execution of Tupac Amaru II is staged as public spectacle to maximize deterrent effect; after 1808, manifestos, constitutional arguments, and political correspondence circulate among creole elites with unprecedented attention; amplification follows established elite networks.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: Official documentation of the rebellion maintains high integrity within colonial administrative norms; rumor and oral transmission introduce distortion; after 1808, competing political claims generate confusion and contested narratives; verification capacity is overwhelmed by the volume of political argument; noise load increases as consensus fractures.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: The rebellion articulates indigenous grievances in terms of justice violated: excessive tribute, forced labor, abusive officials; Spanish response frames the uprising as treason against legitimate authority; both sides appeal to Catholic moral foundations while reaching opposite conclusions; the sense of justice is contested, fractured along ethnic and status lines; after 1808, natural rights arguments enter creole discourse, introducing new moral foundations.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: The rebellion triggers reform: abolition of the repartimiento de mercancias (forced sale of goods to indigenous communities), modification of the mita, replacement of corregidores with intendants; these reforms are codified in royal decrees extensively documented in manuscript; the Laws of the Indies are supplemented but not replaced; after 1808, constitutional debates (Spanish Cortes of Cadiz, 1810-1812) introduce new legal frameworks, circulating as manuscript copies and early printed texts.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: The rebellion's suppression demonstrates colonial judicial capacity at maximum extension: mass trials, collective punishments, public executions; Tupac Amaru II is executed by quartering (1781) after watching his family killed; subsequent leaders are hanged, exiled, or imprisoned; liability is collective, extending to communities associated with rebellion; sanction is exemplary, designed to terrorize; adjudication is rapid, severe, documented in exhaustive detail.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Post-rebellion reforms nominally improve indigenous legal protections by eliminating the most abusive practices; compliance burden shifts from corregidor extraction to more regular tributary obligations; indigenous political rights are further restricted (bans on assembly, dress, language); the net effect is mixed: some economic relief, increased cultural repression; rights remain limited, protection dependent on official enforcement.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: The rebellion itself is an attempt to redress accumulated wrongs through violence after legal channels failed; its suppression demonstrates that resistance is punished, not accommodated; impunity for pre-rebellion abuses goes unaddressed; new abuses during suppression create fresh grievances; the justice gap widens even as specific practices are reformed; unredressed wrong accumulates, feeding future conflict.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: Enlightenment thought continues to penetrate creole intellectual circles through clandestine circulation of French and Spanish texts; the Society of Lovers of the Country (Sociedad de Amantes del País) publishes the Mercurio Peruano (1791-1795), promoting scientific and patriotic inquiry; after 1808, constitutional theory and political philosophy become urgent concerns; the paradigm is transitional, moving from scholasticism toward Enlightenment rationalism among elites.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: No significant technical innovation occurs; mining, agriculture, and manufacturing continue established methods; the rebellion demonstrates indigenous organizational capacity but introduces no new techniques; applied knowledge remains static throughout the period.
