Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: The University of San Marcos continues training clergy, lawyers, and physicians; post-Jesuit educational decline continues; literacy remains confined to perhaps 10% of the population; indigenous education is neglected or actively suppressed; the knowledge stock stagnates; skill distribution remains highly uneven, perhaps becoming more so as indigenous cultural transmission is disrupted.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: Indigenous oral traditions continue gradual erosion under colonial pressure; post-rebellion bans on Quechua in official contexts accelerate this process; European scholastic knowledge is increasingly superseded by Enlightenment alternatives; obsolescence affects both indigenous and colonial intellectual traditions; knowledge decay continues at established rates, accelerated for indigenous traditions.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: The rebellion invokes Inca imperial memory, with Tupac Amaru II claiming descent from the last Inca; Spanish response attacks this memory, banning Inca imagery, dress, and the Comentarios Reales of Garcilaso de la Vega; creole identity develops in tension between American patriotism and fear of indigenous mobilization; indigenous identity is driven underground but not destroyed; memory is contested, politicized, dangerous.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: Colonial legitimation based on Catholic mission and royal authority is maintained but strained; the rebellion exposes the narrative's failure to convince its subjects; after 1808, constitutional liberalism offers alternative legitimation for political reform; the narrative is in transition, the old order defended but not secure, alternatives emerging.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: Post-rebellion restrictions ban indigenous symbols in public display; Inca imagery disappears from legitimate circulation; creole baroque art continues in churches and elite residences; material culture becomes more explicitly Spanish in public contexts, indigenous forms retreating to private and rural settings; the visual culture is disciplined, censored, divided between public conformity and private persistence.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: Colonial baroque forms retain meaning in religious contexts; indigenous symbols retain power precisely because they are forbidden; no form exhaustion is evident; meaning is contested, suppressed, but not exhausted; the symbolic vocabulary is charged with political significance.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: Catholic cosmology remains officially dominant; indigenous syncretic beliefs persist despite suppression; the rebellion is sometimes interpreted in millenarian terms, with Tupac Amaru II cast as messianic restorer; after suppression, fatalism predominates among indigenous populations; Enlightenment skepticism remains confined to tiny elite circles; the outlook is traditional for most, troubled, uncertain about providence's favor.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: Catholic sacraments continue marking life transitions; indigenous festivals face new restrictions; pilgrimage continues; devotional practice is intensified among some as response to crisis; the sacred is enacted regularly, providing consolation and continuity despite political trauma.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: The Archbishop of Lima and religious orders maintain authority; the Church supports colonial order against the rebellion, excommunicating Tupac Amaru II; doctrinal orthodoxy is enforced; institutional property remains substantial; the Church emerges from the crisis with authority intact, aligned with colonial power.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: No new religious movement spreads; syncretic practice continues despite official disapproval; the dominant Catholic cosmology maintains its reach, perhaps deepening as populations seek spiritual solace after trauma; no displacement is occurring; the spiritual landscape is stable.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: Enlightenment skepticism reaches tiny elite circles without mass effect; for the vast majority, the sacred remains potent, meaningful, necessary; no significant disenchantment is evident; spiritual need is met within existing structures; the residue is minimal, not accumulating.

docs.title: 1000 CE – 1400 CE — Late Intermediate Period and Regional Record Systems
docs.text: Summary: The central Andes during the Late Intermediate Period, following the collapse of Wari and Tiwanaku and preceding Inca expansion — an era of regional polities, notably Chimu and Lambayeque on the north coast, each developing distinct administrative traditions. The binding constraint is the Manuscript Stage: quipu record-keeping persisted and diversified across independent polities, with regional variations in cord conventions maintaining the essential function — external records outlasting their makers, consultable by officials never told in person, accumulating administrative memory beyond any individual — while the absence of a single imperial standard allowed local experimentation within the knotted-string medium.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: The Late Intermediate Period saw political fragmentation along natural boundaries. The north coast between Piura and the Casma Valley hosted the Chimu Empire centered at Chan Chan, exploiting a series of irrigated river valleys separated by desert corridors. The Lambayeque (Sican) polity occupied the La Leche and Lambayeque valleys to the north. Highland basins supported independent polities (Chanka, Lupaca, Colla, Huanca) separated by high passes. The friction of distance and terrain that had constrained Middle Horizon integration now defined smaller regional units.

Climate Regime & Volatility: The Little Ice Age began around 1300 CE, bringing modest cooling to the highlands. El Nino events continued to cycle, with major floods disrupting coastal irrigation systems and droughts stressing highland agriculture. A severe El Nino around 1100 CE may have contributed to Lambayeque's political transition. Climate variability created administrative demand for tracking reserves across bad years.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: Coastal polities remained vulnerable to El Nino flooding that could destroy canal infrastructure requiring years of labor to rebuild. Highland polities faced drought, frost, and the ever-present seismic hazard. Chimu's massive irrigation works represented substantial accumulated investment vulnerable to catastrophic loss.

Resource & Energy Endowment: Coastal polities commanded marine resources (fish, shellfish, seabird guano), irrigated agricultural production (maize, cotton, beans, squash), and access to Spondylus shell from Ecuador for ritual and prestige use. Highland polities exploited tuber agriculture, camelid pastoralism, and mineral resources. Inter-regional exchange linked ecological zones, with coastal states trading marine products and craft goods for highland camelids and metals.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Coastal irrigation concentrated population in narrow valley floors, with intensive cultivation maintaining productivity through guano fertilization. Agricultural terracing continued in highlands. The system operated within carrying capacity, with periodic El Nino destruction forcing rebuilding rather than cumulative degradation.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: Endemic disease patterns continued from the Middle Horizon. Coastal populations faced parasitic infections from irrigation agriculture; highland populations dealt with respiratory stress at altitude. No major epidemic events appear in the archaeological record. Life expectancy remained constrained by infant mortality and infectious disease, but populations were generally healthy by pre-modern standards.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: The diversified subsistence base continued to provide adequate nutrition for most populations. Chimu state storehouses and coastal fishing ensured protein availability. Skeletal evidence shows continued adequate nutrition, with elite access to higher-quality foodstuffs marked by better dental health and larger stature.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Medical traditions continued from earlier periods, with herbal knowledge, surgical techniques, and ritual healing. Specialist curers served elite households. The absence of major epidemic stress meant healing capacity generally matched demand.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Marriage patterns continued to follow ayllu and ethnic group boundaries, with elite polygyny and commoner monogamy. Coastal states may have drawn populations from conquered valleys, complicating traditional kin structures in urban centers like Chan Chan.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Population continued to grow during the Late Intermediate Period. Chan Chan reached an estimated 30,000–60,000 inhabitants, making it one of the largest pre-Columbian cities. Highland populations remained dispersed in smaller settlements. Overall Andean population may have reached 10–12 million by 1400 CE.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: Extended family and ayllu structures continued to absorb dependent populations. Urban aggregation at Chan Chan may have created new dependency patterns as craft specialists relied on state provisioning rather than kin-based subsistence.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: Ayllu-based subsistence production continued in highland regions. Coastal states overlaid state extraction on village agriculture, with Chan Chan's population provisioned through tribute from conquered valleys. The subsistence floor remained secure for most populations outside drought or flood years.

Energy Capture & Conversion: Human and camelid muscle continued as the sole power sources. Coastal irrigation systems represented massive embodied labor, channeling Andean runoff across desert to cultivated fields. The energy ceiling remained unchanged from the Middle Horizon, constraining transport and construction to human-scale efforts.

Labor Organization & Coercion: Chimu continued mit'a-style labor mobilization, with conquered populations owing rotational service for canal maintenance, construction, and craft production. Craft specialists (metalworkers, weavers, potters) were concentrated in barrios within Chan Chan, working under state direction. This represented more intensive labor organization than the Middle Horizon model.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Chimu's expansion incorporated multiple river valley irrigation systems, generating substantial agricultural surplus. Craft production reached high levels, with standardized mass production of bronze tools, ceramics, and textiles. The scale of Chan Chan's ciudadelas (royal compounds) indicates massive wealth accumulation.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: State storehouses at Chan Chan and provincial centers held tribute goods. The administrative architecture included storage facilities for tracking accumulated reserves. Managing reserves across multiple conquered valleys required external record-keeping — quipu accounting that could be consulted to verify stocks, assess obligations, and plan distributions.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: Chimu controlled long-distance exchange networks, with state-managed maritime trade extending to Ecuador for Spondylus and south along the coast. Llama caravans connected coastal and highland zones. Market exchange may have operated more extensively than in the Middle Horizon, alongside state redistribution.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: No currency existed, but standardized bronze tools and prestige textiles functioned as value stores. Reciprocal obligations continued to track debits and credits between groups. Quipu recorded these obligations, enabling deferred transactions to be verified by officials who had not witnessed the original agreement.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: Chimu extracted tribute in labor and goods from conquered valleys, concentrating wealth at Chan Chan. Redistribution through feasting and ceremonial gifting legitimated extraction. Tributary obligations required record-keeping to track which populations owed what and whether they had fulfilled their assessments.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Extreme concentration characterized Chimu wealth distribution. Each ruler built a new ciudadela, with previous rulers' compounds sealed as mortuary monuments. Elite burials included hundreds of sacrificed retainers and vast quantities of prestige goods. Commoners retained subsistence access but owed heavy labor obligations.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Urban concentration at Chan Chan generated waste management challenges, with refuse middens accumulating around residential areas. Craft production byproducts (slag, ash, spoiled goods) were disposed in designated areas. The system managed waste within urban constraints.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Ayllu organization persisted in highland regions. Coastal states complicated kin structures through population transfers and urban aggregation. Chimu royal succession may have followed split inheritance, with each ruler's ciudadela and retainers passing to his lineage while the throne passed to a successor — creating accumulated mortuary complexes rather than consolidated royal estates.

Association & Mutual Aid: Ayllu-based reciprocity continued in rural areas. Urban craft specialists in Chan Chan may have formed guild-like barrio associations, though these operated under state direction rather than independently. The thick fabric of highland mutual aid persisted outside state structures.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: Feasting continued as the primary venue for sociability and political negotiation. Chimu iconography depicts warriors, rulers, and ritual scenes suggesting ceremonial occasions that brought populations together. Chicha consumption and music remained central to festive life.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: Sharp hierarchy separated Chimu royalty from nobility, nobility from commoners, and all from the servile populations attached to elite households. Conquered ethnic groups maintained distinct identities within the tributary structure, administered through their own curacas subordinate to Chimu authorities. Highland polities showed similar stratification at smaller scales.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: Chimu developed sophisticated administration for managing conquered valleys, with provincial governors, tribute assessors, and quipu keepers maintaining records of obligations and payments. Chan Chan's ciudadelas included audiencia structures — administrative spaces with standardized plans suggesting bureaucratic function. This apparatus reached further than Middle Horizon administration, directly managing production in conquered territories rather than simply extracting tribute.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: Chimu military expansion conquered the north coast from Tumbes to the Casma Valley. Fortifications protected boundaries. Warriors equipped with bronze weapons, slings, and clubs enforced state authority. The highland polities maintained smaller military forces adequate for regional conflicts and raiding.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: The period ended with Inca conquest of Chimu around 1470 CE. Prior to that, regional conflicts characterized inter-polity relations. The Chanka-Inca conflict around 1438 CE reshaped highland politics. Internal tensions within Chimu may have facilitated Inca conquest — accumulated grievances from intensive extraction finding release when external force weakened state control.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: Chimu rulers exercised highly concentrated authority, with each reign marked by construction of a new ciudadela. Royal iconography emphasized the ruler's role as intermediary with cosmic forces and guarantor of irrigation. Highland curacas held more limited authority within ethnic territories, mediating between communities and external powers.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: Chimu legitimacy rested on maintaining irrigation infrastructure and providing for subjects through redistribution. The visible wealth of Chan Chan projected power; whether it inspired allegiance or resentment likely varied by proximity to benefits. Highland polities relied on traditional ayllu loyalties reinforced by shared ethnic identity.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: Chimu's sustained expansion demonstrated concentrated political will. The capacity to mobilize labor for massive irrigation works and to field armies for conquest indicated effective command. Highland polities showed sufficient resolve for self-defense, with the Chanka challenging early Inca expansion and the Lupaca maintaining independence until Inca diplomacy incorporated them.

External Relations & Posture: Chimu's posture was expansionist on the coast, though it may have avoided highland entanglements. Highland polities existed in competitive balance, raiding and negotiating without achieving regional hegemony. The Inca emergence from Cusco around 1400–1438 CE began to reshape the highland system, setting the stage for rapid imperial expansion.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: Subject populations in Chimu's conquered valleys likely experienced rule as extraction rather than reciprocity, given the intensity of labor demands and the concentration of wealth at Chan Chan. Highland populations in independent polities retained stronger ayllu-based trust networks. The fragmented political landscape created multiple local loyalties rather than broad imperial allegiance.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: The Chimu collapse under Inca pressure around 1470 CE suggests that accumulated disaffection facilitated conquest — subjects unwilling to fight for rulers who had extracted heavily without adequate reciprocity. Highland polities fragmented in the face of Inca pressure, with some (Lupaca, Chincha) aligning diplomatically rather than resisting.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Multiple languages continued in use across the fragmented political landscape. Muchik (the Chimu language) dominated the north coast, distinct from Quechua and Aymara in the highlands. Administrative communication required multilingual capacity at boundaries. No alphabetic literacy existed; quipu served administrative recording needs.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Information moved at human speed via messenger and caravan. Chimu's coastal empire was relatively compact, allowing faster communication than the spread-out Middle Horizon polities. Highland terrain continued to impose transmission delays.

Record, Storage & Persistence: Quipu record-keeping continued and diversified across regional polities. Without a single imperial standard, local variations in cord conventions likely developed — regional "dialects" of the quipu system encoding similar information types (census, tribute, inventory) with different specific conventions. The function remained constant: records outlasting their makers, consultable by officials at a distance, accumulating administrative memory. Khipukamayuq specialists maintained and transmitted these conventions within each polity.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: State iconography in each polity conveyed legitimating messages. Chimu's visual program emphasized maritime themes, royalty, and ritual sacrifice. Highland polities developed local iconographic traditions. Control of prestige goods production gave states authority over the symbolic vocabulary.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: Monumental architecture, ceremonial performance, and prestige goods distribution disseminated state messages. Chan Chan's scale projected Chimu power to all who saw it. Feasting occasions concentrated attention on royal generosity.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: Quipu provided verification for numerical and categorical information within each administrative system. Regional fragmentation may have created communication difficulties at boundaries, where different quipu conventions required translation. Within polities, the khipukamayuq system maintained consistency.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Reciprocity continued as the fundamental moral frame: those who took must give in return. Chimu's intensive extraction created tension with this norm, potentially experienced as exploitation rather than legitimate exchange. Highland ayllu ethics maintained stronger reciprocity expectations.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: No written law codes existed. Customary norms governed conduct, with disputes adjudicated by curacas and state officials. Quipu may have recorded judgments and precedents, creating a form of case law retrievable across time, though direct evidence is lacking.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: Dispute resolution operated through hierarchical adjudication, with appeals from local curaca to regional authorities. Sanctions included compensation, corporal punishment, and death for serious offenses. State authority in Chimu could override local custom.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Subjects retained customary rights to subsistence plots and ayllu membership. The compliance burden of labor obligations was heavy in Chimu territories, with intensive demands for canal maintenance, construction, and craft production. The predictability of state demands varied with the distance from Chan Chan.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: Elite privilege enabled impunity. The Chimu practice of sacrificing retainers at royal funerals demonstrated the ultimate elite prerogative over subject lives. Grievances against extraction accumulated without formal channels for redress, contributing to weak resistance when Inca conquest offered an alternative.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: Empirical knowledge remained embedded in practice. Chimu hydraulic engineers understood gradients, flow rates, and canal construction techniques at a sophisticated level. Metallurgists developed arsenical bronze and refined gold and silver working. Astronomical observation served calendrical and agricultural purposes. No theoretical treatises existed; knowledge was practical and transmitted through apprenticeship.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Chimu metallurgy produced exceptional work, including gilded copper that appeared to be solid gold — sophisticated deception technique serving status display. Bronze tools (chisels, axes, tweezers) reached mass production. Textile production continued at high levels. Quipu conventions were refined and transmitted as technical method.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: Specialist knowledge passed through apprenticeship within craft barrios and administrative lineages. Khipukamayuq training transmitted quipu skills. Mass production in Chan Chan workshops spread standardized craft skills among specialist populations. Broader agricultural and pastoral knowledge remained distributed through ayllu transmission.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: Some Middle Horizon techniques may have been lost in the fragmentation after 1000 CE, though continuity appears stronger than discontinuity. Regional experimentation produced innovations (Chimu's advanced metallurgy) that would later be appropriated by Inca expansion. The knowledge stock grew rather than contracted during this period.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: Chimu origin narratives centered on Taycanamo, a founder arriving by sea to establish the dynasty. Lambayeque's Naymlap legend told a similar maritime origin. Highland polities maintained origin narratives linking them to landscape features — emergence from caves, lakes, or mountains. These foundational stories legitimated ruling lineages and ethnic distinctiveness.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: Chimu ideology emphasized the ruler's role in maintaining irrigation and cosmic order. The ciudadela system — each ruler building anew rather than inheriting — projected each reign as a fresh foundation while honoring predecessors as ancestors. Highland curacas legitimated authority through genealogical claims and ritual performance.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: Chimu blackware ceramics, produced in standardized molds, achieved wide distribution. Textile production continued at high levels, with distinctive coastal styles. Metalwork reached new heights of technical sophistication. Chan Chan's adobe architecture created monumental ciudadelas with elaborate relief decoration. Highland polities maintained regional ceramic and textile traditions distinct from coastal styles.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: Chimu's standardized mass production may have represented form exhaustion — repetition replacing innovation as the same molds produced thousands of identical vessels. The accumulation of ciudadelas, each repeating the pattern of predecessors, suggests formulaic repetition. This exhaustion may have facilitated Inca cultural replacement after conquest.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: The three-tiered Andean cosmos continued to structure understanding. Chimu's maritime orientation added emphasis on the sea and moon over highland sun cults. The ocean was a realm of power and origin — rulers arrived by sea, ancestors departed by sea. This distinguished coastal cosmology from highland traditions centered on mountains and the sun.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: Elaborate ritual cycles continued, with Chimu practice emphasizing lunar observation, maritime offerings, and human sacrifice at key transitions. Huaca veneration persisted at local shrines. Pilgrimage to major centers created networks of devotion across ethnic boundaries. Chicha consumption remained central to ritual practice.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: Chimu rulers combined political and religious authority, performing rituals that maintained cosmic order and irrigation. Priestly specialists conducted ceremonies at major huacas. The Moon (Si) held prominence in Chimu religion, contrasting with highland sun emphasis. Religious institutions held property and commanded labor for shrine maintenance.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: Regional fragmentation produced spiritual diversity, with coastal and highland traditions developing along separate trajectories after the Middle Horizon unity faded. Chimu conquest imposed coastal cults on subject valleys without fully displacing local traditions. The stage was set for Inca religious imperialism, which would spread the solar cult while tolerating local huaca veneration.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: No evidence of secularizing disenchantment exists. The sacred remained potent, with elaborate ritual investment at all levels. The fragmentation of political authority distributed rather than diminished spiritual power, with multiple regional centers hosting active cult practice. Inca conquest would redirect rather than extinguish this spiritual energy.

docs.title: 1650 CE – 1700 CE — Mature Colonial Society and Creole Literary Culture
docs.text: Summary: The Viceroyalty of Peru at its mature colonial consolidation, when Lima functions as the cultural capital of Spanish South America, baroque literary and artistic production flourishes in manuscript circulation before and alongside print, ecclesiastical and administrative archives grow vast, and a distinctly creole identity emerges among American-born Spaniards who increasingly see the viceroyalty as their patria; the binding constraint is the Manuscript Stage, where handwritten documents—letters, poetry, legal briefs, theological treatises, administrative records—constitute the medium through which colonial society conducts its public, intellectual, and devotional life, accumulating in archives that preserve the era's transactions beyond any living memory.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: Lima anchors the viceroyalty from the coastal desert, connected to the highland mining centers by mule train; Potosí remains the economic pole though declining; maritime links through Callao tie the viceroyalty to Panama and Spain; spatial friction remains high, measured in weeks of travel.

Climate Regime & Volatility: The coastal desert receives minimal rainfall; highland regions experience seasonal wet-dry cycles; ENSO events bring periodic disruption; the garúa mist moderates Lima's climate; agricultural systems adapted to these conditions produce documentary records of harvests and irrigation.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: The 1687 earthquake devastates Lima and Callao, killing thousands and destroying buildings including parts of the cathedral and university; reconstruction generates extensive notarial documentation; seismic risk shapes architecture toward lower, more massive construction.

Resource & Energy Endowment: Potosí silver production declines from its peak but remains substantial; Huancavelica mercury continues to supply amalgamation; agricultural resources support colonial population; timber and building materials circulate through documented trade networks.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Mercury contamination persists around mining centers; urban sanitation in Lima remains primitive; environmental degradation from a century of extraction accumulates; no systematic remediation occurs; waste loads continue without clearance.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: Endemic diseases persist with periodic epidemic flares; yellow fever and other tropical diseases affect coastal populations; smallpox recurs; mortality remains elevated but the demographic catastrophe of the conquest era has passed its worst phase.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: Colonial elites enjoy adequate nutrition; indigenous and African populations face nutritional stress from labor extraction; mita workers continue to suffer physiological degradation; the provisioning system supports urban populations adequately.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Hospital foundations in Lima (San Andrés, Santa Ana, San Bartolomé) serve different racial categories; religious orders provide nursing care; indigenous healing persists; medical knowledge transmitted through manuscript treatises and apprenticeship.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Complex casta system documents interracial unions and their offspring; creole families maintain endogamous marriage strategies to preserve status; demographic recovery among indigenous populations slowly begins; African slave population maintained through continued importation.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Indigenous population begins slow recovery from its nadir; Lima grows to approximately 30,000–40,000 inhabitants; Potosí declines from its peak; urban concentration in Lima creates the density for literary and cultural life; parish registers document demographic flows.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: Aging religious personnel, widows supported by capellanías (chantry endowments), and orphans in church care constitute documented dependency; cofradías provide mutual support; the institutional apparatus absorbs dependency through ecclesiastical charity.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: Lima's provisioning depends on coastal valleys, highland supply, and maritime trade; urban poor face periodic scarcity; indigenous communities maintain subsistence agriculture while meeting tribute obligations; the provisioning floor is adequate but uneven across populations.

Energy Capture & Conversion: Human and animal muscle remain the primary energy sources; water power drives some mills; the energy ceiling constrains productive capacity; mita labor continues to provide the human energy for mining, though at declining intensity as silver output falls.

Labor Organization & Coercion: Mita obligations persist but enforcement weakens as indigenous population remains depleted; wage labor expands in cities; African slavery concentrated in coastal agriculture and urban service; obraje textile workshops employ coerced labor; labor relations documented in contracts and disputes.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Silver production declines but remains the viceroyalty's primary export; textile obrajes, sugar haciendas, and wine production generate regional surplus; artisan production in Lima serves elite consumption; surplus supports elaborate religious and cultural institutions.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: Colonial treasuries and merchant houses hold reserves; church wealth accumulates in censos (loans secured on property) documented in notarial records; buffer capacity against crisis exists but is unevenly distributed; public granaries inadequate for major crisis.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: The Lima-Callao axis dominates Pacific trade; the consulado (merchant guild) regulates commerce; annual fleet arrivals from Spain bring European goods; contraband trade with other colonial powers documented in seizure records; internal trade networks link regions.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: Silver remains the monetary standard; censos provide credit secured on urban and rural property; ecclesiastical institutions become major creditors; notarial records document complex credit relationships; merchant credit networks extend across the empire.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: Royal taxes, tribute, tithes, and merchant profits extract surplus; redistribution flows to Spain, to ecclesiastical institutions, and to elite consumption; public works and charity provide limited redistribution downward; fiscal documentation extensive.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Wealth concentrates among peninsular merchants, mine owners, and creole landholders; ecclesiastical institutions accumulate property through donations and mortmain; indigenous communities defend remaining lands through documented títulos; entail (mayorazgo) protects elite fortunes.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Urban waste disposal primitive; industrial byproducts from tanneries, obrajes, and workshops discharged into waterways; no systematic waste management; environmental costs externalized without documentation or remediation.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Creole elite families deploy marriage strategy to consolidate status and property; mayorazgo entails protect patrimonies; complex documentation of lineage supports status claims; indigenous ayllu kinship persists beneath colonial overlay; African family formation constrained by slavery.

Association & Mutual Aid: Cofradías proliferate, organizing devotional life and mutual support by occupation, ethnicity, and parish; the merchant consulado regulates commerce; university and religious communities provide institutional identity; associational life generates extensive documentary records.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: Elite sociability centers on tertulias (literary salons), religious festivals, and public celebrations; theater performances documented in municipal records; bullfights and processions mark civic calendar; cofradía feasts provide popular sociability; gambling and taverns serve lower orders.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: The casta system reaches full elaboration with documented categories (español, criollo, mestizo, mulato, indio, negro, and complex mixtures); status anxiety drives documentary proof of limpieza de sangre (blood purity); social boundaries legally and ecclesiastically enforced through recorded procedures.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: Mature colonial bureaucracy functions routinely; audiencia, cabildo, and viceregal administration produce continuous documentation; corruption endemic but predictable; administrative capacity adequate for extraction though not development; institutional integrity maintained through record-keeping conventions.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: Standing military force remains minimal; urban watch maintains order; Inquisition exercises spiritual police power; coercive capacity sufficient against dispersed population; no serious military threat tests the apparatus during this period.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: Crime, banditry, and popular disturbance occur at manageable levels; litigation absorbs disputes; cofradías channel social energy; the system maintains stability through routine and document; grievance is processed rather than suppressed, preventing accumulation into explosive potential.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: Viceroys rotate from Spain, exercising delegated authority; archbishops command spiritual respect; creole families produce local notables; no charismatic figure dominates the era; authority is institutional rather than personal; leadership documented through official correspondence.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: Spanish rule accepted as established order; creole identity develops within imperial framework rather than against it; indigenous compliance reflects accommodation rather than allegiance; the system's legitimacy rests on routine and benefit distribution rather than fervent loyalty.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: Colonial state maintains extraction and order without ambitious projects; no major reforms or conquests occur; institutional inertia rather than dynamic will characterizes the period; collective resolve is adequate for maintenance, not expansion.

External Relations & Posture: The viceroyalty faces no serious external threat; English and Dutch piracy affects trade; border regions with Portuguese Brazil remain peripheral; foreign rivalries documented in correspondence but produce no military crisis during this period.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: Colonial society settles into stable hierarchy; elite confidence rests on established position; creole resentment of peninsular privilege simmers; indigenous and African populations endure under coercion; the general temper is stable though not content; trust operates within casta boundaries.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: Indigenous resistance largely channeled into legal frameworks; no major rebellions occur; creole discontent remains cultural rather than political; the system absorbs potential disaffection through routine; apathy among subordinated populations serves stability.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Spanish literacy spreads among creole population; indigenous literacy remains limited to elites trained in church schools; the lettered city (ciudad letrada) maintains documentary culture; oral communication dominates among non-elites; the literate fraction expands slowly.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Manuscript letters carry information across the viceroyalty over weeks; official dispatches move through established channels; news from Spain arrives with fleet sailings; local networks spread information through personal correspondence and oral report; velocity constrained by distance and transport.

Record, Storage & Persistence: Archives accumulate systematically: notarial protocols, parish registers, audiencia records, viceregal correspondence, Inquisition files, cofradía books; documents survive earthquake and decay in institutional custody; the record persists beyond living memory, fulfilling the Manuscript Stage criterion; retrieval requires institutional access.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: Inquisition monitors circulation of prohibited books and heterodox manuscripts; print requires license; manuscript circulation evades some controls; discourse norms permit baroque elaboration within orthodoxy; political critique remains circumscribed; literary expression flourishes within conventional bounds.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: Literary works circulate in manuscript among elite readers before and alongside print; poetry competitions and academic exercises create audiences; sermons reach broader publics; attention concentrated in Lima's lettered circles; amplification limited by manuscript reproduction constraints.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: Notarial conventions maintain documentary reliability; legal copies (traslados) preserve originals; the formulaic character of records ensures consistency; rumor and gossip circulate alongside formal documentation; verification depends on institutional witness and notarial authentication.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Catholic moral theology provides the official framework; honor codes govern elite conduct; indigenous moral frameworks persist in community practice; the sense of justice operates within casta hierarchy, accepting differential treatment as natural order.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: Spanish colonial law stabilizes with the Recopilación de Leyes de Indias (1680) consolidating previous legislation; local ordinances address specific conditions; legal evolution slows as the system matures; manuscript copies of laws circulate in administrative and judicial settings.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: Audiencia courts hear major cases; alcaldes ordinarios judge lesser disputes; ecclesiastical courts handle marriage, morals, and clerical matters; Inquisition prosecutes heresy; caseloads manageable; sanctions documented in judicial records; the system processes disputes routinely.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Theoretical indigenous protections persist alongside practical exploitation; compliance with colonial regulations burdensome but predictable; legal representation available though expensive; the documented legal system offers recourse within its own terms; rights are casta-differentiated.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: Elite impunity persists; residencia reviews of officials rarely produce sanctions; wrongs against indigenous and African populations routinely unredressed; the gap between formal justice and lived experience remains wide but stable; accumulated impunity generates no crisis during this period.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: Scholastic philosophy and baroque theology dominate; the University of San Marcos produces graduates in law, medicine, and theology; natural history inquiry continues in manuscript; no paradigm shift occurs; intellectual life remains within established frameworks; European scientific revolution has minimal impact.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Mining technology adapts to declining ore grades; architectural and engineering knowledge applied to earthquake-resistant construction after 1687; medical practice follows humoral theory; practical knowledge transmitted through apprenticeship and manuscript treatises.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: Jesuit colleges educate creole elites; parish schools provide basic literacy to some indigenous youth; the university trains professional cadre; knowledge stock preserved in institutional libraries; skill distribution remains narrow; the educated constitute a thin elite layer.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: Pre-conquest indigenous knowledge continues to decay as elders die; quipu reading capacity effectively lost; some practical knowledge (metallurgy, agriculture, medicine) persists in practice without documentation; baroque learning accumulates without displacing older stock; no major knowledge loss occurs during the period.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: Creole identity crystallizes around American birth and devotion to local saints (especially Santa Rosa of Lima, canonized 1671); indigenous communities maintain ancestral memory through oral tradition; African populations preserve cultural elements within constraints of slavery; the viceroyalty develops a sense of itself as a distinct society.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: Spanish imperial ideology legitimates colonial order through Christian mission and civilizing role; creole writers celebrate Peru's glories (silver wealth, baroque culture, holy saints) while remaining loyal to crown; no counter-narrative challenges the system; legitimation operates through religious and civic ceremonial documented in contemporary accounts.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: Baroque reaches its height in architecture, painting, and sculpture; churches and convents display elaborate retablos and paintings; silverwork achieves distinctive Andean-baroque synthesis; literary production flourishes in manuscript—poetry, theater, hagiography, theological treatises; material culture documented in inventories and artistic commissions.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: Baroque forms remain vital though increasingly elaborate; religious symbols retain potency; no form-exhaustion apparent yet; cultural production continues within established modes without staleness; innovation occurs within convention rather than against it; meaning remains anchored in living practice.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: Catholic cosmology dominates officially; providentialist interpretation of events (earthquakes as divine punishment) shapes public discourse; indigenous cosmology persists in syncretic forms; creole piety centers on local devotions; the sacred remains pervasive and unquestioned in public life.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: Mass, confession, and festival cycles structure temporal experience; processions and public devotions mark the civic calendar; convent life absorbs substantial female population; devotion to Santa Rosa and local shrines develops distinctly Peruvian character; ritual practice documented in ecclesiastical records.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: The church reaches institutional maturity: archbishop, cathedral chapter, parishes, convents, and religious orders form comprehensive structure; Inquisition maintains doctrinal boundaries; ecclesiastical wealth extensive; institutional authority stable; church records constitute a major portion of the documentary archive.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: Syncretic forms consolidate as indigenous and African populations incorporate Catholic elements into their practice while retaining older beliefs; extirpation campaigns diminish; practical tolerance of popular religiosity increases; the church claims universal adherence while actual belief remains layered.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: No disenchantment occurs; the sacred suffuses colonial society; creole baroque spirituality represents an intensification rather than diminution of religious sensibility; spiritual need met through elaborated Catholic practice; the era represents a high point of colonial religious culture rather than any secularizing drift.

docs.title: 600 CE – 1000 CE — Middle Horizon Empires and the Origins of Quipu Administration
docs.text: Summary: The central Andes during the Middle Horizon, when the Wari and Tiwanaku polities developed complex administrative systems requiring record-keeping beyond oral memory. The binding constraint is the Manuscript Stage: knotted-string quipu emerged as external records that could outlast their makers, be consulted by officials never told in person, and accumulate information beyond any single memory — the Andean functional equivalent of cuneiform administration, storing census, tribute, and calendar data in a durable, retrievable medium.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: The central Andes present extreme vertical relief — Pacific coastal desert, sierra valleys between 2,500 and 4,000 meters, the altiplano above 3,800 meters around Lake Titicaca, and the eastern montaña slopes. Wari centered in the Ayacucho basin (2,700 m) while Tiwanaku occupied the southern Titicaca basin (3,850 m). Movement between zones required traversing passes and descending thousands of meters, imposing severe logistical friction that favored decentralized administration with local record-keeping rather than constant messenger traffic to capitals.

Climate Regime & Volatility: The Middle Horizon fell within a relatively stable climatic interval. Highland agriculture depended on seasonal rainfall (November–April) and frost-free growing seasons; the altiplano's extreme diurnal temperature swings limited crop options to frost-tolerant tubers and hardy grains. Coastal valleys relied on Andean runoff channeled through irrigation. Interannual variability from El Nino-Southern Oscillation cycles brought periodic coastal flooding and highland drought, requiring buffer stocks and administrative tracking of reserves.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: The Andes sit along the Pacific Ring of Fire, exposing settlements to seismic and volcanic hazard. Mudslides (huaycos) threatened narrow valley floors during heavy rains. Drought cycles imperiled highland agriculture. Administrative centers like Wari's Pikillacta were built with massive walls suggesting both defense and earthquake resistance.

Resource & Energy Endowment: The vertical archipelago offered complementary resources: marine protein from the coast, maize and cotton from irrigated lowland valleys, potatoes and quinoa from highland basins, llama and alpaca pastoralism on the puna, and coca from the eastern slopes. Obsidian, copper, and gold deposits supported craft production. The diversity was accessible only through coordinated exchange across ecological tiers.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Population densities remained modest relative to carrying capacity. Agricultural terracing and irrigation modified landscapes but did not saturate the sink. The residue was localized soil depletion in intensively farmed basins, managed through fallow rotation and the application of guano fertilizer from coastal islands.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: Pre-Columbian Andean populations faced endemic parasitic and respiratory infections but lacked the crowd diseases (smallpox, measles, typhus) that would arrive with European contact. High-altitude populations exhibited physiological adaptations to hypoxia. Infant mortality was elevated by altitude and nutrition constraints, but endemic disease pressure was moderate by global standards.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: The vertical archipelago model ensured dietary diversity: protein from camelids and marine sources, carbohydrates from tubers and grains, fats from guinea pigs and fish. Freeze-dried potato (chuno) and dried meat (charqui) enabled storage. Skeletal evidence suggests adequate nutrition in most periods, though periodic drought caused localized famine.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Medical knowledge combined herbal pharmacopoeia, surgical techniques (including trepanation with high survival rates), and ritual healing. Specialist practitioners served elite households; commoner care relied on kin networks and local curers.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Household formation centered on monogamous pairs among commoners, with polygyny common among elites. Ayllu (kin-corporate group) membership structured marriage patterns, with preferred endogamy within ecological zones.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Population expanded during the Middle Horizon, with Wari and Tiwanaku controlling perhaps 500,000 to 1,000,000 people each at their height. Settlement aggregation in administrative centers increased local densities. The expansion suggests birth rates exceeding mortality, enabled by intensified agricultural production.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: Extended family structures absorbed dependent populations. Mit'a (rotational labor service) drew on able-bodied adults, implicitly leaving dependents in kin-group care. The system functioned within the carrying capacity of the agricultural regime.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: The ayllu provided the baseline subsistence unit, pooling labor for agriculture and pastoralism. Household plots combined with communal fields ensured a provisioning floor. State intervention layered extraction on top of subsistence production rather than displacing it.

Energy Capture & Conversion: Human and llama muscle powered all production and transport. No wheeled vehicles or draft animals beyond camelids existed. The llama caravan served as the primary long-distance transport mode, carrying roughly 30 kg per animal over 15–25 km daily. This limited bulk goods movement and favored high-value, low-weight commodities over distances.

Labor Organization & Coercion: The mit'a system mobilized labor for state projects — construction, agriculture, craft production, military service — on a rotational basis by ayllu quotas. This was corvee rather than slavery: households retained their own production while owing periodic state service. The obligation required accounting to track which groups had served and when.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Agricultural intensification through terracing and irrigation enabled surplus extraction. Wari and Tiwanaku both maintained state storehouses (qollqa) holding food, textiles, and craft goods. The scale of storage facilities at Pikillacta and other centers indicates substantial surplus accumulation.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: Massive state storehouses buffered against interannual variability. The qollqa system required inventory management — knowing what was stored where, what had been withdrawn, what remained — creating demand for durable external records beyond oral memory.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: Vertical archipelago exchange moved goods between ecological tiers through kin-based reciprocity and state redistribution rather than market mechanisms. Long-distance exchange linked coastal shell (Spondylus) to highland centers. Llama caravans following established routes connected administrative nodes.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: No coinage or currency existed. Value was stored in textiles (cumbi cloth), agricultural surplus, and camelid herds. Reciprocal obligations tracked debits and credits between groups — who owed labor, goods, or services to whom — creating the accounting demand that quipu would serve.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: The state extracted labor (mit'a) and goods (tribute in kind) from subject populations, redistributing through feasting, military support, and emergency relief. Tracking obligations required records that could be consulted across time and by officials who had not been present when the obligation was incurred.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Elite lineages controlled the finest agricultural lands and largest herds. Sumptuary distinctions in dress and ornament marked status. Craft specialists attached to elite households produced prestige goods. Commoner households retained subsistence plots but owed labor and tribute above that floor.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Organic waste returned to agricultural fields as fertilizer. The system operated within a closed loop at the household level, with minimal persistent waste accumulation.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: The ayllu structured social organization: a corporate kin group holding land collectively, tracing descent from a common (often mythical) ancestor, and providing the unit for labor mobilization and tribute assessment. Inheritance passed through both male and female lines (parallel descent), with property and obligations transmitted within the ayllu.

Association & Mutual Aid: Ayllu membership entailed reciprocal labor obligations (ayni) for agriculture, construction, and life-cycle events. Mutual aid cushioned individual household misfortune. This thick fabric of reciprocity operated below the state level and persisted across political regimes.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: Communal feasting, music, dance, and ritual drinking (chicha consumption) marked agricultural cycles and life transitions. These events reinforced ayllu solidarity and provided the context for negotiating obligations.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: Sharp hierarchy separated ruling lineages from commoner ayllus, with intermediate curacas (local lords) mediating between state and community. Ethnic groups maintained distinct identities within the broader polity. Status was marked by dress, ornament, and access to prestige goods.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: Wari developed a network of administrative centers (Pikillacta, Viracochapampa, Cerro Baul) with standardized architectural plans — orthogonal compounds, storage facilities, residential sectors for administrators. This infrastructure suggests bureaucratic presence coordinating labor, tribute, and redistribution. The scale implies record-keeping beyond what individual memory could manage, though direct evidence of Middle Horizon quipu remains inferential.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: Both Wari and Tiwanaku maintained military capacity, evident in fortified sites and warrior imagery. Wari expansion appears to have involved conquest; Tiwanaku's spread combined colonization with ideological influence. Weaponry included slings, clubs, axes, and spear-throwers.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: Both polities collapsed around 1000 CE, with abandonment of administrative centers and fragmentation into regional successor polities. The causes remain debated: drought, overextension, internal conflict, or some combination. The collapse discharged accumulated tensions as the administrative apparatus failed.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: Wari rulers remain anonymous in the archaeological record, though elite burials suggest concentrated authority. Tiwanaku iconography centers on the Gateway God (Viracocha) and suggests theocratic leadership, with authority legitimated through ritual performance and cosmological association.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: State architecture and iconography projected power and cosmological order. Participation in state-sponsored feasting created reciprocal obligations and reinforced legitimacy through generosity. When redistribution faltered, allegiance eroded.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: The construction of massive administrative centers and the coordination of labor across hundreds of kilometers demonstrate substantial political will and organizational capacity during the Middle Horizon florescence. The collapse suggests that will exhausted itself or fractured under stress.

External Relations & Posture: Wari and Tiwanaku appear to have coexisted with a buffer zone rather than direct conflict, though Wari's expansion into the Moquegua Valley brought it adjacent to Tiwanaku territory. Relations with unconquered highland and lowland groups involved trade, alliance, and periodic raiding.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: Subject populations apparently accepted Wari and Tiwanaku hegemony during their florescence, participating in state labor projects and adopting elements of imperial material culture. Whether this reflected genuine allegiance, pragmatic accommodation, or coerced compliance cannot be directly assessed.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: The collapse around 1000 CE suggests accumulated disaffection or exhaustion. Administrative centers were abandoned, sometimes deliberately destroyed or ritually terminated. Successor polities were smaller, suggesting fragmented loyalties and spent imperial will.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Multiple languages (proto-Quechua, Aymara, Puquina, coastal tongues) coexisted within the Middle Horizon polities. State administration required communication across linguistic boundaries, likely through bilingual intermediaries or a prestige administrative language. No evidence of writing in the alphabetic sense exists; the quipu served as a mnemonic and accounting device.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Information traveled at the speed of human runners or llama caravans. The later Inca chasqui relay system may have had Middle Horizon precursors. Administrative centers along routes facilitated message transmission across the polity.

Record, Storage & Persistence: Quipu — knotted cords using a decimal positional system, with color, ply, and attachment position encoding categorical information — likely developed during this period, though direct Middle Horizon specimens are scarce. The administrative complexity evident in Wari storage facilities implies external record-keeping beyond oral memory. Quipu enabled records to outlast their makers and be consulted by officials who had not been present at the original transaction — the defining characteristic of the Manuscript Stage.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: State iconography disseminated through textiles, ceramics, and architecture conveyed cosmological and political messages. Control of these prestige media shaped the narrative framework within which subjects understood the order.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: State messages were amplified through architectural monumentality, ritual performance, and the distribution of standardized prestige goods. Reception occurred through participation in feasts, ceremonies, and the labor obligations that brought subjects into contact with state infrastructure.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: Quipu provided a verification mechanism for numerical information — tribute obligations, census counts, inventory levels — that could be cross-checked against physical stocks. The specialist khipukamayuq (quipu keeper) training ensured consistency in encoding and decoding. Oral transmission of narrative content remained vulnerable to drift and loss.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Andean moral economy centered on reciprocity (ayni) and redistribution. The state's legitimacy rested on fulfilling obligations to subjects — providing feasts, emergency relief, and protection — in exchange for labor and tribute. Failure to reciprocate undermined moral standing.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: No written law codes existed; customary norms governed conduct within ayllus, with disputes adjudicated by curacas and, at higher levels, state officials. The quipu may have recorded judgments and precedents, but direct evidence is lacking.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: Dispute resolution operated through kin-group mediation, with escalation to curaca authority. Sanctions ranged from compensation and shaming to corporal punishment and death for serious offenses. The state reserved ultimate sanction authority.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Subjects possessed customary rights to subsistence plots and ayllu membership. The compliance burden of mit'a service was substantial but rotational, spreading the load across the population. Elite obligations to redistribute softened extraction.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: Elite privilege enabled differential treatment. The collapse of the Middle Horizon polities may have involved accumulated grievances against extraction perceived as unreciprocated — impunity experienced as exploitation rather than legitimate rule.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: Understanding of agricultural cycles, astronomical observation for calendrical purposes, and architectural engineering reached sophisticated levels. Empirical knowledge was embedded in practice rather than formalized in theoretical treatises. The cosmological paradigm framed natural phenomena as animated by spiritual forces.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Terrace construction, irrigation engineering, metallurgy (bronze, gold, silver), textile production, and ceramic manufacture all demonstrated advanced technique. The quipu itself represented a sophisticated information technology — a positional notation system enabling arithmetic operations and categorical classification.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: Specialist knowledge passed through apprenticeship within craft and administrative lineages. Khipukamayuq training transmitted quipu encoding and decoding skills. Broader populations held agricultural and pastoral knowledge appropriate to their ecological zone. Formal schooling did not exist.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: The collapse around 1000 CE disrupted some knowledge transmission. Architectural and administrative techniques declined in the following Late Intermediate Period before revival under the Inca. Some Middle Horizon craft traditions persisted in regional successor polities.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: Origin narratives likely centered on emergence from landscape features (caves, lakes, mountains) and descent from founding ancestors. Tiwanaku's Gateway of the Sun and associated iconography suggest a cosmological charter linking rulership to cosmic order. Ayllu identity provided the primary frame for commoner self-understanding.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: State iconography — the Staff God, winged attendants, trophy heads — projected a narrative of divine authority and military prowess. The visual program disseminated through textiles and ceramics created a shared symbolic vocabulary legitimating the order.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: Wari textiles achieved exceptional technical and aesthetic sophistication, with complex iconographic programs in tapestry weave. Tiwanaku stone carving created monumental gateways and stelae. Both traditions influenced regional styles across their spheres. Ceramics, metalwork, and architecture followed standardized prestige forms that marked participation in the imperial sphere.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: The abandonment of Middle Horizon administrative centers and the fragmentation of the iconographic program after 1000 CE suggest exhaustion of the symbolic complex. Successor polities developed distinct regional styles, though some motifs persisted in transformed contexts.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: A three-tiered cosmos — upper world (hanan pacha), this world (kay pacha), lower world (ukhu pacha) — structured Andean cosmology. Landscape features (mountains, springs, caves) served as huacas — sacred places connecting the realms. Ancestors mediated between the living and cosmic forces.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: Elaborate ritual cycles marked agricultural seasons and life transitions. Offerings (including human sacrifice at major events) propitiated spiritual forces. Chicha consumption in ritual contexts facilitated communion with the sacred. Pilgrimage to major shrine centers like Tiwanaku integrated populations across the polity.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: Priestly specialists controlled access to the sacred and conducted major rituals. Tiwanaku's monumental ceremonial complex suggests concentrated religious authority. The integration of political and religious functions made the ruler a sacred figure whose ritual performance maintained cosmic order.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: Wari and Tiwanaku iconography spread across their spheres of influence, overlaying or syncretizing with local traditions. The Staff God complex achieved wide distribution, suggesting either religious conversion or adoption of prestige symbols. Regional traditions persisted beneath the imperial overlay.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: The collapse around 1000 CE terminated the state cults, though localized huaca veneration continued. The fragmentation discharged accumulated spiritual authority as regional centers developed their own sacred complexes. No evidence of secularizing disenchantment exists; the sacred remained potent, merely redistributed to local shrines and successor polities.

docs.title: 1532 CE – 1570 CE — Spanish Conquest and the Introduction of Alphabetic Writing
docs.text: Summary: The forty-year rupture from Pizarro's arrival at Cajamarca to the capture of Vilcabamba and consolidation of colonial rule, during which two information regimes collided and overlapped — Spanish notaries recording conquest in alphabetic script while indigenous khipukamayuq continued maintaining quipu records that conquistadors initially exploited before suppressing. The binding constraint is the Manuscript Stage transition: alphabetic manuscript culture arrived with the conquerors, began displacing quipu administration, and established the documentary infrastructure that would govern the colonial Andes for three centuries.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: Spanish forces operated across the same extreme terrain the Inca had mastered — coastal desert, highland valleys, altiplano, and the forested eastern slopes where the neo-Inca state at Vilcabamba resisted until 1572; the Qhapaq Ñan road system now served Spanish movement; horses gave conquistadors tactical mobility but mule and llama trains handled bulk transport through terrain impassable to wheeled vehicles.

Climate Regime & Volatility: The period experienced normal Andean climate variability; ENSO events continued their pattern of coastal flooding and highland drought; Spanish newcomers suffered from altitude sickness in highland campaigns; the climate itself posed no exceptional stress during the conquest decades, though the disruption of Inca storage and irrigation systems exposed populations to failures that the pre-conquest buffer would have absorbed.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: Earthquakes damaged settlements but did not decisively affect conquest outcomes; the primary hazard for Spanish was disease acquired in lowland campaigns — tropical fevers in the Amazonian fringe; for indigenous populations, the catastrophic hazard was biological, carried by the invaders themselves.

Resource & Energy Endowment: Spanish conquest was driven by precious metals — gold from Atahualpa's ransom (estimated at 6,000 kg of gold, 12,000 kg of silver), then systematic extraction from highland deposits; Potosí (discovered 1545) would become the world's largest silver source; the resource base that had sustained Inca imperial culture now funded Spanish imperial ambitions and Atlantic trade.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Mercury amalgamation introduced at Potosí (1571) began contaminating highland water systems, though full environmental impact would accumulate over subsequent centuries; the disruption of Inca terrace maintenance initiated erosion that would compound over generations; conquest-period environmental damage was initial rather than severe.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: Old World epidemic diseases — smallpox, measles, typhus, influenza — devastated Andean populations lacking immunological exposure; smallpox preceded Pizarro, killing Huayna Capac (the previous Sapa Inca) and precipitating the succession war; subsequent waves struck repeatedly; demographic collapse of 50–90% occurred over the conquest century, the most lethal sustained mortality event in human history.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: The collapse of Inca storage and redistribution systems exposed populations to food insecurity previously buffered by state granaries; displacement, warfare, and epidemic created cascading nutritional stress; skeletal evidence shows declining health indicators in conquest-period populations; the synergy of disease, malnutrition, and overwork compounded mortality.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Neither Andean nor Spanish medicine could treat epidemic disease; Spanish introduced some Old World remedies while Andean herbalism continued; the scale of mortality overwhelmed any healing capacity; religious responses — both Christian and Andean — attempted to address the incomprehensible catastrophe, but medical intervention was essentially futile against virgin-soil epidemics.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Spanish males arrived without Spanish women initially, taking indigenous concubines and producing the first mestizo generation; the aqllakuna system dissolved as Spanish seized these women; epidemic mortality disrupted pair-bonding and family formation; birth rates could not compensate for death rates.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Population collapsed from pre-contact estimates of 6–14 million toward perhaps 600,000–1.5 million by century's end; entire communities disappeared; highland populations fared somewhat better than coastal; the mit'akuna (relocated populations) were especially vulnerable, lacking local kin networks and environmental knowledge; demographic recovery would take centuries.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: The epidemic killed across age cohorts but especially the young and old; surviving communities carried enormous dependency loads — orphans, widows, the debilitated; the ayllu system that had absorbed dependents buckled under unprecedented death tolls; Spanish missionaries established hospitals and orphanages, inadequate to the scale but representing new institutional responses to attrition.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: The Inca qollqa system was looted by conquistadors and collapsed through administrative neglect; local subsistence continued but the supra-local buffer disappeared; encomenderos demanded tribute in goods and labor, squeezing populations already devastated; the provisioning floor dropped catastrophically for indigenous communities even as Spanish established new production for Atlantic markets.

Energy Capture & Conversion: Spanish introduced horses, cattle, and donkeys — new sources of animal power; water mills appeared for grain grinding; fundamental energy regime remained muscle-powered but the addition of larger draft animals represented a genuine increment; mining operations mobilized vast human labor at Potosí, extending rather than replacing the Inca mit'a system's reliance on human muscle.

Labor Organization & Coercion: The encomienda granted Spanish rights to indigenous labor and tribute from assigned populations; this was coerced labor, theoretically in exchange for Christianization and protection, practically exploitative extraction; the mita was adapted for Potosí, drafting highland communities for rotational mining labor under brutal conditions; mortality at Potosí was extreme; the labor system was more extractive than Inca mit'a had been, without the reciprocal storage and redistribution.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Silver production transformed the Andean economy, linking it to global trade; indigenous communities continued agricultural production but surplus was extracted as tribute rather than stored for redistribution; Spanish introduced wheat, grapes, and livestock, transforming production patterns; the colonial economy extracted rather than developed, draining surplus toward the metropole.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: The qollqa system's collapse eliminated the pre-conquest buffer; encomiendas maintained stores for their own use but nothing replaced the empire-wide reserve network; indigenous communities retained household-level storage but faced increased extraction; the systematic resilience of the Inca system disappeared, leaving populations more vulnerable to localized shocks.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: Monetary exchange replaced Inca redistribution; silver coinage circulated; markets developed in Spanish towns; indigenous peoples entered the cash economy to pay tribute; the mule train became the primary freight system, supplementing llama caravans; Lima became the commercial hub, replacing Cusco's political centrality with mercantile dominance; Atlantic trade routes connected Andean silver to global commerce.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: Silver currency provided a universal value medium absent under Inca rule; Spanish merchants extended credit; debt relations increasingly bound indigenous communities; the transition from labor and goods obligations tracked by quipu to monetary obligations recorded in account books represented a fundamental shift in the medium of economic coordination.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: The encomienda and mita extracted labor and tribute without Inca reciprocity; the quinto (royal fifth) on silver went to the Crown; ecclesiastical tithes added further extraction; tribute assessments recorded by Spanish notaries replaced quipu accounting; extraction intensified while redistribution collapsed — a pure taking without the ideological frame of mutual obligation.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Conquistadors accumulated encomiendas, mining claims, and estates; indigenous elites (curacas) who collaborated retained some property and privileges; commoner populations lost access to state redistribution and faced tribute demands on diminished resources; wealth polarized between Spanish encomenderos and indigenous communities stripped of the buffer system that had protected them.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Mercury contamination from silver processing began its long accumulation in highland watersheds; mining generated slag and debris; the scale was still modest compared to later centuries but the pattern was established; organic waste continued recycling through agriculture.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: The ayllu persisted as the basic unit of indigenous social organization, though under enormous stress; Spanish inheritance law applied to settlers, with encomiendas initially heritable; mestizo children occupied ambiguous positions; indigenous kinship structures adapted to demographic collapse through amalgamation of depleted communities.

Association & Mutual Aid: Ayllu reciprocity (ayni) continued among survivors; Spanish cofradías (religious brotherhoods) provided new associational frameworks incorporating indigenous and mestizo members; encomenderos organized no mutual aid; indigenous communities maintained solidarity under pressure, with ayllu membership becoming more critical as state support disappeared.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: Spanish festivals, particularly religious celebrations, introduced new public rituals; bullfights and European games appeared in Spanish towns; indigenous festivals continued in modified form, sometimes overlaid with Christian calendars; chicha consumption persisted as a social practice despite occasional Spanish attempts at suppression.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: A new racial hierarchy emerged — peninsulares (Spanish-born) at top, criollos (American-born Spanish) below, mestizos in ambiguous middle positions, indigenous commoners at bottom; curacas retained intermediate status as indigenous nobles collaborating with Spanish rule; African slaves (arriving by the 1540s) and their descendants added another stratum; the Inca status hierarchy was replaced by a sistema de castas based on ancestry and race.
