Discharge, Disorder & Decay: Endemic low-level violence — brigandage, local feuding, peasant resistance — persists in regions where central authority is weak. The apparatus cannot contain all disorder; chronic insecurity becomes normalized. Roman administrative structures decay; ecclesiastical institutions partially compensate.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: Visigothic kingship is elective and contested; royal authority depends on military success and magnate support. Individual kings rise and fall by assassination and coup. Episcopal leaders — figures like Leander of Seville — command moral authority that sometimes exceeds royal reach.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: Visigothic kings claim Roman imperial legitimacy but hold it thinly. Arian religion separates them from the Catholic majority's allegiance. Legitimacy is negotiated rather than assumed; consent is conditional on protection and justice delivery. Erosion is chronic until conversion resolves the religious divide.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: The Visigothic elite displays collective resolve sufficient for conquest and defense but fractures over succession and policy. Factional struggle among magnates limits unified action. The will to govern is present but contested; the regime survives through adaptation rather than consolidation.

External Relations & Posture: The Visigothic kingdom faces Byzantine enclaves on the southern coast (Spania), Frankish pressure across the Pyrenees, and residual Suevi resistance in the northwest. Posture is defensive: holding territory rather than expanding. Diplomacy alternates with warfare; no hegemonic ambition animates external policy.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: Uncertainty and insecurity color public sentiment. Trust contracts to kin and local patrons. The Hispano-Roman majority accommodates Visigothic rule pragmatically but without enthusiasm. Religious division generates latent tension. The overall temper is defensive and localized.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: Chronic succession crises and religious division generate elite disaffection. The Hispano-Roman majority endures rather than supports the regime. Apathy settles where participation is neither invited nor rewarded. This disaffection feeds periodic rebellion and limits state capacity.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Latin remains the shared code for administration, law, and liturgy. Spoken Latin diverges toward proto-Romance vernaculars. Gothic language persists among the Visigothic elite but leaves minimal written record. Literacy contracts to clergy and a diminished lay elite; the shared ground narrows.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Roman road network persists but maintenance declines. Messenger systems depend on royal and episcopal networks. Transmission velocity slows with infrastructure decay. Information travels with travelers — merchants, pilgrims, emissaries — rather than through institutional channels.

Record, Storage & Persistence: Manuscript production continues in episcopal scriptoria and nascent monasteries. Church archives preserve legal documents, correspondence, and liturgical texts. Roman public archives decay; ecclesiastical records become the primary persistence medium. Survival depends on institutional continuity.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: Arian-Catholic theological controversy structures permissible discourse. Episcopal correspondence circulates among Catholic networks; Arian texts are less well preserved. No systematic censorship apparatus exists, but religious division shapes what is copied and preserved.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: Sermons, liturgy, and episcopal letters reach the literate minority. Oral transmission carries information to the majority. Amplification depends on ecclesiastical networks and the prestige of individual bishops. Attention is local and episodic rather than continuous.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: Document survival is uneven; many records are lost to destruction, neglect, or institutional collapse. Surviving texts require interpretation across linguistic and cultural distance. Noise increases as Roman administrative precision fades; verification depends on witness and oath rather than documentary cross-reference.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Both Visigothic and Hispano-Roman populations share basic Mediterranean moral foundations: honor, kinship loyalty, reciprocity, and divine sanction. Christian teaching shapes conscience; the church articulates moral standards. Tension arises where Arian and Catholic norms diverge.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: Roman law persists for the Hispano-Roman population; Visigothic customary law governs the Gothic minority. Dual legal systems coexist, codified in texts like the Codex Euricianus (c. 480 CE) for Goths. Manuscript transmission preserves and transmits legal knowledge. Unification awaits later consolidation.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: Bishops assume judicial roles in the absence of Roman magistrates. Visigothic counts judge their followers. Adjudication is localized and personalized. Sanction includes fines (wergild), corporal punishment, and exile. Church councils legislate on moral and ecclesiastical matters.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Property rights depend on local power rather than imperial guarantee. Church asylum offers limited sanctuary. Free status remains contested; enslavement through debt or capture expands. Compliance burden is irregular: heavy where lords are demanding, light where authority is absent.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: Impunity is endemic for the powerful. Royal and magnate violence often goes unsanctioned. Episcopal mediation provides some redress for those with access. The gap between justice owed and delivered is wide; backlog and non-enforcement accumulate as standing injustice.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: Classical learning survives in ecclesiastical custody. Bishops and monks preserve Roman educational texts — grammar, rhetoric, computus. No active discovery frontier exists; the task is preservation, not innovation. Theological inquiry focuses on Christological controversy and anti-Arian polemic.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Roman agricultural, building, and craft techniques persist but diffuse less widely as urban workshops decline. Monastic communities preserve and practice technical knowledge. Metalworking for weapons and liturgical objects continues; architectural ambition contracts.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: Education contracts to episcopal and monastic schools. Literacy rates decline; the knowledge stock narrows to religious and legal texts. Skill distribution concentrates in ecclesiastical institutions. The classical canon survives but circulates among fewer readers.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: Much Roman technical and literary knowledge becomes obsolete or is lost as institutions that transmitted it collapse. Manuscript destruction through warfare and neglect depletes the stock. Error propagates as copying becomes less careful. The residue of loss is significant but not total; ecclesiastical custody preserves the core.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: Hispano-Roman identity persists among the majority, rooted in Roman provincial heritage and Catholic Christianity. The Visigothic elite carries its own Gothic origin mythology and martial tradition. The two identities coexist without synthesis; Catholic religious identity increasingly bridges the ethnic divide.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: Visigothic kings claim succession to Roman authority, minting coins with imperial imagery and using Latin titles. Arian Christianity legitimates Gothic distinctiveness. Catholic bishops offer an alternative legitimating framework, available upon conversion. The narrative is contested and unstable.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: Visigothic material culture blends Germanic metalwork styles — fibulae, belt buckles, eagle motifs — with late Roman forms. Church architecture adapts Roman basilica plans to smaller scale. Manuscript illumination begins in scriptoria. The visual surface is hybrid: Roman inheritance modified by Germanic imports.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: Roman civic forms — forums, baths, spectacles — hollow out as resources and populations contract. Visigothic forms have not yet achieved canonical expression. The period is transitional: old forms decay, new forms gestate. Neither exhaustion nor vigor dominates; the cultural register is muted.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: Christian cosmology dominates both Arian Visigoths and Catholic Hispano-Romans: creation, fall, redemption, judgment. Eschatological anxiety colors the age; political disorder is read through apocalyptic lenses. Piety is serious and pervasive; doubt is not articulated.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: Liturgical practice structures daily and annual cycles. Baptism, Eucharist, and penance organize Christian life. Saints' cults and relic veneration expand. Arian and Catholic rites differ in detail but share core forms. Monastic life begins to spread as a devotional vocation.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: The Catholic episcopate holds institutional continuity from Roman times; bishops administer dioceses, convene councils, and accumulate property. Arian clergy serve the Visigothic elite but lack comparable institutional depth. Doctrinal authority is contested until Catholic conversion resolves the division.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: Catholicism holds the majority and slowly absorbs the Visigothic elite through intermarriage, episcopal influence, and political calculation. Arian Christianity contracts. Residual paganism in rural areas faces episcopal suppression. The trajectory is toward Catholic consolidation, achieved formally in 589 CE.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: No disenchantment marks this period; the sacred remains potent and contested. The spiritual need is not unmet but channeled through competing institutional forms. Conversion resolves the contest by absorbing Arianism into the Catholic mainstream, leaving no residue of unanchored spiritual need.

docs.title: 1350 CE – 1400 CE — Black Death and Late Medieval Crisis
docs.text: Summary: The Iberian Peninsula and Western Mediterranean in crisis mode, as plague, pogroms, and political instability devastate population and disrupt the manuscript culture that had flourished under high medieval conditions; the binding constraint remains the Manuscript Stage, with written records essential for administering shrunken kingdoms, documenting legal succession, and preserving learning through catastrophic mortality, yet production contracts sharply as scriptoria lose personnel and patronage collapses.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: The peninsula's geography remains fixed — the Meseta's interior plateau, the Ebro and Guadalquivir valleys, the Pyrenean barrier, and the Mediterranean and Atlantic coasts — but plague disrupts the spatial networks that connected them; trade routes contract as commerce falters and towns depopulate, increasing effective friction between regions that had been well-linked under the high medieval commercial expansion.

Climate Regime & Volatility: The Little Ice Age onset brings cooler, wetter conditions across Iberia; the favorable climate of the Medieval Warm Period that had supported agricultural expansion gives way to greater interannual variability, contributing to harvest failures that compound plague mortality and economic disruption.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: The biological hazard of plague dwarfs all other exposures; the pandemic reaches Iberia via Mediterranean shipping routes in 1348, spreading rapidly through port cities and along trade corridors; urban concentrations suffer catastrophic mortality while isolated rural areas escape more lightly.

Resource & Energy Endowment: Agricultural land remains abundant but labor-scarce; the dramatic population collapse leaves fields uncultivated, vineyards untended, and pastoral systems disrupted; mineral resources in the peninsula continue extraction at reduced levels as mining communities suffer mortality.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: The mass mortality generates unprecedented volumes of human remains; urban burial capacity is overwhelmed, with plague pits and emergency interments becoming necessary; the sanitary crisis compounds the epidemiological disaster, though reduced population ultimately lessens long-term waste loads.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: Yersinia pestis devastates the peninsula from 1348 onward; mortality estimates range from thirty to sixty percent in affected areas, with recurrent waves in 1362–1363 and 1374–1375 preventing demographic recovery; the disease baseline shifts catastrophically upward, and plague becomes endemic in Iberian cities for generations.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: Surviving populations paradoxically experience improved nutrition as labor scarcity raises wages and reduces competition for food resources; those who survive multiple plague waves show acquired resilience, though the overall biological vitality of the population is shattered by mortality.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Medical knowledge proves impotent against plague; Galenic theory attributes the pestilence to miasma and corrupted air, leading to ineffective fumigation and aromatic treatments; quarantine measures develop empirically but cannot halt transmission; the healing professions suffer proportional mortality, reducing care capacity.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Mortality disrupts marriage patterns as widows and widowers remarry rapidly; fertility may temporarily rise among survivors as remarriage rates increase and opportunities open for younger cohorts, but population replacement remains insufficient against recurring plague waves.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Population collapse is catastrophic and sustained; Iberia's population falls from perhaps six million to three or four million, with urban areas suffering disproportionately; Barcelona, Valencia, and other commercial centers lose half or more of their inhabitants; density falls well below pre-plague carrying capacity.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: Plague mortality is somewhat indiscriminate but hits productive adult cohorts heavily; the dependency ratio shifts as orphans multiply and family structures fragment; monastic communities that had provided care services suffer mortality, reducing the institutional capacity to absorb dependents.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: Labor scarcity raises the subsistence floor for survivors; wages rise, rents fall, and peasant conditions improve materially even as the overall economy contracts; abandoned villages dot the landscape, but remaining settlements consolidate around better land and resources.

Energy Capture & Conversion: The labor force that powered agricultural and artisanal production collapses; watermills and other capital equipment stand idle without operators; energy conversion contracts proportionally to population, though per-capita work output may rise among survivors with access to better tools and land.

Labor Organization & Coercion: Labor relations shift toward the worker as scarcity empowers survivors to demand better terms; seigneurial attempts to reimpose corvee and freeze wages meet resistance; the balance between coercion and compensation tilts toward compensation, though lords attempt legal enforcement of labor obligations.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Total output collapses with population; surplus generation falls catastrophically as both producers and consumers die; luxury production, including manuscript illumination and fine book production, contracts as patronage disappears and skilled artisans perish.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: Accumulated wealth provides some cushion, but granaries and treasuries draw down rapidly; the fiscal capacity of crowns contracts as tax bases shrink; monasteries and cathedrals lose income from depopulated estates, reducing their capacity to maintain scriptoria and libraries.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: Mediterranean commerce contracts sharply as plague spreads along trade routes; the Catalan-Aragonese commercial network that had linked Barcelona to Italy, North Africa, and the Levant shrinks; Castilian wool exports to Flanders decline; internal trade networks fray as towns depopulate.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: Credit networks seize as debtors die and creditors face collection failures; Jewish moneylenders, already targeted by popular resentment, face violence in the 1391 pogroms partly driven by debt obligations survivors wished to extinguish; price instability reflects collapsing demand and disrupted supply.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: Royal revenues collapse as the tax base contracts; the Castilian and Aragonese crowns struggle to maintain administrative capacity and military forces; fiscal crisis compounds political instability, driving succession conflicts and civil wars.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Mortality creates opportunities for wealth consolidation among survivors who inherit from multiple deceased relatives; land values fall but labor values rise; noble families face extinction of lineages, enabling cadet branches and new men to acquire estates.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Material waste decreases with economic contraction, but the biological waste of mass death creates acute disposal crises; abandoned properties and unclaimed goods create legal complications that generate documentary production even as other manuscript activity declines.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Family structures shatter under mortality; complex inheritance disputes arise as entire lineages die out or collateral heirs emerge; orphans and widows multiply; remarriage patterns shift rapidly; the documentary apparatus of wills, testaments, and succession records works intensively to process the mortality.

Association & Mutual Aid: Guilds and confraternities lose members to mortality; mutual aid networks strain under unprecedented demands; some institutions collapse entirely while others consolidate surviving populations; charitable foundations face overwhelming need with reduced resources.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: Public gatherings become vectors of contagion; festivals and markets are suspended or restricted; the dance of death motif enters popular culture, and the carnivalesque takes darker tones; sociability contracts as fear of contagion discourages assembly.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: Social mobility accelerates as mortality creates vacancies in all strata; servile tenures weaken as lords compete for scarce labor; Jewish communities, already marginal, face scapegoating culminating in the 1391 pogroms that destroy major aljamas in Seville, Cordoba, Valencia, and Barcelona.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: Royal administration strains under mortality among clerks and officials; record-keeping continues but with reduced personnel and capacity; the Castilian civil war (1366–1369) between Pedro I and the Trastamara pretender Henry compounds administrative disruption, while the Aragonese crown faces its own succession crises.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: Military capacity declines with population; the Castilian civil war demonstrates how contracted forces still enable decisive conflict; mercenary companies (routiers) displaced from France by the Peace of Bretigny enter Iberia, adding to violence; the 1391 pogroms reveal breakdown of public order as royal authority fails to protect Jewish communities.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: Social disorder reaches crisis levels; the pogroms of 1391 represent catastrophic failure of the coercive apparatus to maintain order; forced conversions create the converso population whose ambiguous status will generate conflict for generations; banditry and local violence increase as central authority weakens.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: Royal authority weakens under mortality and political crisis; Pedro I of Castile's brutal rule and eventual assassination (1369) by his half-brother Henry of Trastamara reflects legitimacy collapse; the Aragonese dynasty faces extinction crises; personal authority of surviving leaders rests on force more than consent.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: Dynastic legitimacy fractures in Castile's civil war; Henry of Trastamara's usurpation creates a Castilian monarchy dependent on noble support and compromised by illegitimate origins; the Aragonese succession dispute (resolved at Caspe in 1412) reflects similar legitimacy fragmentation.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: Political will fragments among competing factions; the Castilian civil war demonstrates how contested succession paralyzes collective action; the Aragonese crown similarly experiences reduced capacity for unified action; the post-plague political order lacks the confident expansionism of the high medieval Reconquista.

External Relations & Posture: External ambitions contract; the Castilian civil war draws in English and French intervention as part of the Hundred Years' War; Granada gains respite as Christian kingdoms turn inward; the Aragonese Mediterranean empire faces challenges from Genoa and others with reduced capacity to respond.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: Terror and despair dominate public mood; the inexplicable and seemingly divine punishment of plague generates apocalyptic anxiety; trust collapses as neighbors become potential plague vectors; scapegoating of Jews and other marginal groups channels fear into violence.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: Exhaustion pervades post-plague society; the trauma of mass death, civil war, and pogrom leaves populations depleted of energy and will; resignation and fatalism replace the confident expansion of the high medieval period; the collective will settles into survival mode.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Latin remains the language of church, law, and learning; Castilian, Catalan, Aragonese, Portuguese, and other vernaculars continue their expansion into documentary use; literacy concentrations suffer mortality proportionally, reducing the population capable of encoding and decoding written communication.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Information channels contract with commercial networks; news of plague spreads rapidly along the same trade routes that carry infection; royal communication networks strain under reduced personnel; the velocity of official correspondence slows as administrative capacity contracts.

Record, Storage & Persistence: Archives survive plague but face reduced maintenance; cathedral and monastic libraries continue but with fewer personnel to copy, preserve, and organize manuscripts; some scriptoria close entirely; the accumulated documentary heritage of the high medieval period persists but ceases to grow at former rates.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: Plague generates new genres of documentation — plague treatises, testament records, death registers — while the crisis narrative frames public discourse; explanatory frameworks range from astrological to theological, with Jewish poisoning accusations representing the darkest edge of plague discourse.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: Public attention focuses on survival and the meaning of catastrophe; the danse macabre and memento mori themes spread through visual and literary culture; attention to learning and intellectual production declines as immediate crisis absorbs capacity.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: Documentary production becomes essential for processing the mortality crisis — wills, inheritances, property transfers — while the informational infrastructure that processes these records strains under volume and reduced capacity; some records are lost to disruption; noise increases as administrative continuity breaks.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Plague shakes confidence in cosmic justice; the apparently random mortality challenges theodicy; scapegoating of Jews represents a morally catastrophic attempt to locate human agency behind divine punishment; the forced conversions and pogroms of 1391 mark moral collapse of the convivencia ideal.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: Legal systems strain to process unprecedented volumes of succession and property disputes; sumptuary legislation attempts to restrain social mobility enabled by mortality; labor regulations try unsuccessfully to fix wages and bind workers to lords; legal development continues but addresses crisis conditions.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: Courts face backlogs as normal processes of justice are overwhelmed by mortality-related disputes; succession litigation multiplies; the 1391 pogroms proceed with minimal judicial consequences, demonstrating failure of the legal order to protect minority populations.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Jewish rights of residence and protection collapse in 1391 as royal authority fails to enforce them; converso status creates new legal categories of ambiguous protection; peasant rights strengthen de facto as labor scarcity enables negotiation, though formal servile statuses persist.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: Impunity prevails in the pogroms; perpetrators of mass violence against Jewish communities face minimal consequences; the Trastamara usurpation demonstrates how successful violence can establish new legitimacy; unredressed wrong accumulates as the judicial system loses capacity to impose consequences.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: Plague treatises represent active inquiry into causes and responses, though within Galenic and astrological frameworks that prove inadequate; the University of Salamanca continues teaching but with reduced enrollment and faculty; intellectual production contracts but does not cease entirely.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Empirical development of quarantine measures represents practical knowledge generation outside theoretical frameworks; maritime quarantine practices that will become standard in Mediterranean ports begin in this period; medical technique remains ineffective against plague but sanitary knowledge accumulates.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: University enrollment declines; cathedral schools lose faculty; the transmission of specialized skills is interrupted as masters die without training successors; literacy rates may fall as educational institutions contract; the accumulated knowledge stock persists in libraries but ceases to grow.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: Some specialized knowledge is lost through mortality; scribal traditions suffer as trained copyists die and apprentices are not trained; Hebrew learning in Iberia faces catastrophic disruption as Jewish communities are destroyed or converted; some manuscripts are lost to violence and disruption.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: The plague becomes a foundational trauma reshaping collective memory; the danse macabre and ars moriendi traditions embed death-consciousness into cultural identity; the destruction of Jewish communities eliminates a constituent element of Iberian cultural synthesis; converso identity emerges as a new, ambiguous category.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: The Trastamara dynasty must construct legitimating narratives for usurpation; Henry of Trastamara's propaganda emphasizes Pedro I's tyranny and alliance with Jews and Muslims; religious orthodoxy becomes more central to political legitimation as crisis demands explanatory frameworks.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: Artistic production contracts with patronage; monumental architecture slows; manuscript illumination becomes less elaborate; death imagery proliferates in what survives; the aesthetic register shifts toward the stark and morbid; material culture becomes less exuberant as resources contract.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: The high medieval cultural synthesis shows strain; convivencia as a lived reality collapses with the 1391 pogroms; the confident expansion of Romanesque and Gothic forms gives way to more austere expressions; cultural forms struggle to process unprecedented trauma.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: Plague is interpreted through apocalyptic and providentialist frameworks; the mortality appears as divine punishment for sin; flagellant movements spread briefly; fatalism deepens as mortality seems inescapable; the existential outlook darkens toward acceptance of imminent death.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: Death rituals intensify and transform under mass mortality; normal burial practices become impossible; masses for the dead multiply; votive devotion to plague saints (Sebastian, Roch) spreads; processions and collective devotional practices continue despite contagion risk, sometimes spreading infection.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: Monasteries and cathedrals suffer proportional mortality; some houses collapse entirely; clerical ranks thin, reducing pastoral capacity; the institutional church persists but with diminished personnel and resources; religious orders face recruitment challenges.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: The forced conversions of 1391 create the converso phenomenon — a large population of nominal Christians of Jewish descent whose sincerity becomes suspect; this represents violent displacement of Judaism rather than organic religious change; Crypto-Judaism persists among some conversos.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: Rather than disenchantment, the crisis produces intensified religious anxiety; the sacred remains potent but threatening; the failure of religious explanations to make plague meaningful generates not doubt but desperate searching for spiritual answers; the residue is not secularizing drift but traumatized piety.

docs.title: 1212 CE – 1350 CE — High Medieval Iberia and the Translation Movement
docs.text: Summary: The Iberian Peninsula following the decisive Christian victory at Las Navas de Tolosa through the arrival of the Black Death, bound by the Manuscript Stage constraint where external records kept outside the body become the medium public life runs on. The binding constraint is the documentary apparatus reaching its high medieval peak: Toledo's translation schools transfer Arabic philosophical and scientific learning into Latin manuscripts that reshape European scholasticism; Alfonso X's court produces vernacular Castilian prose in history, law, and science; royal chanceries, episcopal archives, and university scriptoria generate unprecedented documentary volume, while the approaching plague will disrupt but not destroy this manuscript-based information regime.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: The geography of reconquest shifts dramatically: after Las Navas de Tolosa opens the Guadalquivir valley, Christian advance reaches the sea at Cadiz (1262) and Murcia, leaving only Granada as Muslim territory; the Meseta remains Castilian heartland; Aragon expands into Valencia and the Balearics; Portugal completes its reconquest to the Algarve; Atlantic and Mediterranean coastlines open to maritime expansion.

Climate Regime & Volatility: The Medieval Warm Period peaks and begins transitioning toward cooler conditions by the fourteenth century; agricultural productivity remains high through most of the period; drought affects southern regions periodically but without catastrophic impact; climate supports the colonization of newly conquered Andalusian territories.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: The peninsula experiences no major environmental catastrophes during this period; localized earthquakes in the south cause limited damage; flooding in river valleys disrupts agriculture occasionally; the predictable hazard regime permits sustained agricultural and urban development.

Resource & Energy Endowment: Andalusian conquest brings rich agricultural lands, mineral deposits, and established irrigation infrastructure under Christian control; Cantabrian iron supports expanded metalworking; Mediterranean salt pans and Atlantic fisheries provide essential resources; timber from northern forests supplies construction and shipbuilding.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Expanding urban centers generate increasing waste loads; livestock raising on the Meseta, organized through the Mesta, creates environmental pressure; no evidence of sink saturation constraining development; abandoned Muslim agricultural lands in some frontier zones experience temporary degradation before Christian resettlement.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: Pre-plague mortality rates remain at Mediterranean baseline; endemic diseases continue without major epidemic disruption until 1348; urban populations face higher disease exposure than rural; port cities experience occasional imported outbreaks; the Black Death at period's end devastates populations, killing perhaps thirty to sixty percent.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: Diverse agricultural production supports adequate nutrition; Andalusian irrigation permits fruit and vegetable cultivation; Castilian Meseta produces grain and supports transhumant sheep; Mediterranean coast combines fishing, horticulture, and trade; nutritional adequacy permits population growth through most of the period.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Arabic medical knowledge, translated into Latin and increasingly into vernacular, provides theoretical foundation; hospitals in major cities serve urban populations; Jewish physicians enjoy reputation for skill despite periodic restrictions; monastic infirmaries serve rural populations; medical capacity proves wholly inadequate against plague.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Marriage patterns follow religious and social norms: noble families arrange strategic alliances; urban and rural commoners marry within their communities; church regulates consanguinity and marriage formation; Jewish and mudejar communities maintain separate marriage customs under respective religious law.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Population grows steadily through colonization of conquered territories and agricultural expansion; urban centers grow as commerce and administration concentrate; density increases in irrigated zones and along trade routes; the catastrophic mortality of 1348-1350 reverses demographic gains abruptly.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: Normal demographic dependency ratios prevail before plague; conquest warfare produces casualties among military classes; frontier colonization absorbs surplus population; the plague's arrival creates massive orphan and widow populations, disrupting normal dependency structures catastrophically.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: Agricultural production expands through colonization of Andalusian and Valencian territories; Mediterranean irrigation sustains intensive cultivation; Castilian Meseta supports grain and wool production; fueros establish peasant holdings in newly colonized areas while reserving lands for nobility and military orders; subsistence security prevails until plague disruption.

Energy Capture & Conversion: Human and animal muscle power remains dominant; water mills proliferate along rivers for grain processing and textile production; irrigation systems captured from Al-Andalus represent sophisticated hydraulic engineering; wind power emerges for milling in some regions; overall energy regime continues medieval baseline.

Labor Organization & Coercion: Mudejars work conquered lands as free peasants or sharecroppers; serfdom exists in some regions but is less prevalent than northern Europe; slave labor from captives and trade supplements agricultural and domestic work; the Mesta organizes transhumant sheep herding with complex labor arrangements; guilds regulate urban craft production.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Wool production for export becomes major Castilian industry, organized through the Mesta; textile manufacturing continues in Andalusian cities; agricultural surplus funds urban growth and ecclesiastical construction; shipbuilding develops in Mediterranean and Atlantic ports; overall productive capacity expands through the period.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: Urban granaries and commercial storage buffer against harvest variation; wool exports create monetary reserves; royal treasuries accumulate through taxation and tribute from Granada; the fiscal system develops sufficient capacity to fund Alfonso X's ambitious cultural projects; reserves prove insufficient against plague disruption.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: Mediterranean trade connects Barcelona, Valencia, and Majorca to Italian and North African markets; Atlantic trade develops through Seville and Portuguese ports; wool exports to Flanders drive northern commerce; the Mesta's transhumance routes create internal logistics network; fairs at Medina del Campo and elsewhere facilitate exchange.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: Coinage stabilizes under strong monarchies; Jewish and Italian merchants provide credit and banking services; bills of exchange facilitate long-distance trade; Alfonso X's monetary reforms attempt standardization; credit networks connect Iberian commerce to broader Mediterranean and European systems.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: Royal taxation develops more systematic bases; ecclesiastical tithes claim agricultural surplus; seigneurial dues burden peasant production; tribute from Granada continues to flow northward; the administrative apparatus for extraction produces extensive documentary records.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Nobility consolidates landholdings from conquest; military orders control vast territories; Jewish communities maintain commercial wealth while facing increasing restrictions; urban oligarchies emerge in major cities; primogeniture and entail protect aristocratic estates from fragmentation.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Urban craft production generates localized pollution; tanning and textile industries in cities create waste streams; transhumant herding affects pasture lands; no systemic environmental crisis constrains development during the period.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Noble lineages solidify through primogeniture and mayorazgo (entail); partible inheritance among commoners in some regions; Jewish communities follow rabbinic inheritance law; mudejar communities apply Islamic rules; marriage alliances cement political relationships among noble houses and between kingdoms.

Association & Mutual Aid: Urban guilds (gremios) organize craft production and provide mutual aid; confraternities proliferate for religious and charitable purposes; Jewish aljamas and Muslim morerías constitute semi-autonomous communities; the Mesta organizes pastoral interests into powerful corporate body; universities at Salamanca, Valladolid, and elsewhere create scholarly communities.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: Tournaments, hunting, and court festivities occupy nobility; religious festivals and saints' days structure popular recreation; bull-running and bull-fighting emerge as popular entertainment; university life creates distinctive student culture; troubadour poetry and music entertain courts.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: Three-religion society hardens into more rigid hierarchy: Christians at apex, Jews and mudejars as tolerated but subordinate communities; within Christian society, nobility, clergy, and commons form distinct estates; urban patriciate emerges as distinct status group; religious identity increasingly determines legal standing and social access.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: Royal chanceries achieve unprecedented documentary output; Alfonso X's Siete Partidas attempts comprehensive legal codification; cortes (representative assemblies) develop in Castile, Aragon, and Portugal; episcopal and monastic administration maintains ecclesiastical records; university organization institutionalizes learning; the documentary apparatus of governance reaches high medieval peak.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: Heavy cavalry remains dominant military arm; castle networks define territorial control; military orders maintain standing forces; urban militias supplement royal armies; naval forces develop in Mediterranean and Atlantic; Granada maintains defensive capability behind mountain barriers; the balance of force favors Christian kingdoms decisively.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: Frontier violence diminishes as conquest stabilizes; noble factionalism triggers periodic civil conflicts; disputed successions create instability in multiple kingdoms; anti-Jewish violence increases, presaging 1391 pogroms; mudejar communities face increasing pressure; plague's arrival in 1348 overwhelms social order catastrophically.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: Alfonso X of Castile ("el Sabio") exemplifies learned kingship, sponsoring translation, law codes, and vernacular literature despite political failures; Jaume I of Aragon leads Mediterranean expansion; strong monarchs alternate with weak ones and disputed successions; episcopal and abbatial leadership guides ecclesiastical communities.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: Monarchical legitimacy rests on lineage, divine sanction, and law; Alfonso X's claim to Holy Roman Empire demonstrates expansive legitimacy aspirations; noble challenges to royal authority recur; ecclesiastical authority derives from papal sanction and sacramental power; Granada's Nasrid dynasty maintains legitimacy through cultural patronage and jihad rhetoric.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: Sustained will for reconquest completion; Alfonso X's imperial ambitions overextend Castilian resources; Aragonese expansion into Mediterranean demonstrates focused will; Portuguese consolidation after reconquest completion; plague disrupts collective will catastrophically through mortality and psychological trauma.

External Relations & Posture: Castile claims Mediterranean and European roles; Aragon builds Mediterranean empire through conquest and diplomacy; Portugal develops Atlantic orientation; all kingdoms maintain papal relationships; Granada cultivates North African and Egyptian ties; commercial relations with Italian city-states, Flanders, and France intensify.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: Triumphalism follows reconquest victories; court culture reaches high refinement under Alfonso X; religious devotion intensifies through confraternities and pilgrimage; anti-Jewish sentiment increases, especially during economic stress; mudejar communities experience growing insecurity; plague arrival produces panic, scapegoating, and social breakdown.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: Noble factionalism indicates elite disaffection with royal authority; minority communities experience increasing marginalization; frontier populations settle into post-conquest routines; plague arrival induces despair and social breakdown; the period ends in crisis of collective will.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Latin remains language of learning and ecclesiastical administration; Castilian emerges as language of royal administration and literary culture under Alfonso X; Catalan develops parallel literary tradition; Arabic persists in Granada and mudejar communities; Hebrew serves Jewish religious and scholarly purposes; vernacular literacy begins expanding beyond clergy.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Royal messengers carry official correspondence; merchant networks transmit commercial information; pilgrimage routes carry religious and cultural communication; university scholars circulate between Iberian and European institutions; manuscript copying in scriptoria remains the technology of textual transmission.

Record, Storage & Persistence: Royal archives develop systematic preservation; cathedral and monastic archives maintain ecclesiastical records; university libraries accumulate scholarly texts; the translation movement creates a massive new corpus of Latin manuscripts transmitting Arabic learning; Alfonso X's literary projects produce extensive vernacular documentation; plague disrupts but does not destroy archival institutions.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: Ecclesiastical authorities police doctrinal boundaries; royal patronage shapes chronicle writing; university disputation follows scholastic norms; Alfonso X's projects frame Castilian as language capable of learning and law; anti-Jewish rhetoric intensifies in popular discourse; plague generates religious explanation and scapegoating.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: Manuscript circulation reaches literate elites; sermon and oral recitation reach broader populations; vernacular literature expands potential audience; legal texts communicate rights and obligations; university teaching transmits translated learning to new generations of scholars; the translation movement's impact extends across European Christendom.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: Archival preservation in stone buildings protects manuscripts; copying errors accumulate in transmission; competing chronicle traditions generate conflicting narratives; translation introduces interpretive variation; overall signal integrity maintained through institutional copying and preservation; plague mortality disrupts transmission chains.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Religious law provides moral foundation; Alfonso X's Siete Partidas synthesizes Roman, canon, and Castilian legal traditions into comprehensive code; chivalric ethics regulate noble conduct; guild statutes govern craft behavior; the codification project represents high medieval confidence in legal rationality.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: The Siete Partidas represents most ambitious Iberian legal codification, drawing on Roman law, canon law, and Castilian custom; fueros continue regulating local communities; ecclesiastical law governs church matters and marriage; minority communities apply internal religious law under crown supervision; the documentary volume of legal production reaches unprecedented levels.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: Royal courts claim increasing jurisdiction; seigneurial courts retain local authority; ecclesiastical courts handle clerical and certain moral cases; inquisitorial procedure develops for heresy; appellate structures emerge connecting local to royal justice; minority communities maintain internal adjudication for internal matters.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Fueros guarantee community rights against royal encroachment; urban charters define municipal privileges; noble privileges limit royal authority; minority communities hold defined but subordinate legal status; the compliance burden of legal complexity falls on those navigating multiple jurisdictions.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: Noble violence often escapes royal sanction; anti-Jewish violence receives inadequate response; frontier violence diminishes but is not eliminated; captive-taking continues with Granada; plague overwhelms normal adjudication, leaving wrongs unaddressed and social order disrupted.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: Toledo remains the premier center of translation and transmission: Gerard of Cremona's work continues through successors; Arabic versions of Aristotle with Islamic and Jewish commentaries enter Latin circulation; Ptolemaic astronomy, Galenic medicine, and Arabic mathematics transform European learning; the Alfonsine Tables provide the most accurate astronomical calculations in Christendom; scholastic philosophy absorbs and debates the new learning; Jewish scholars including Abraham ibn Ezra contribute original philosophical and scientific work.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Agricultural techniques continue adapting Arabic methods; shipbuilding advances for Mediterranean and Atlantic navigation; military engineering in fortification and siege craft develops; textile and metallurgical industries maintain skilled production; the gap between theoretical and practical knowledge characteristic of the period persists.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: University of Salamanca achieves prominence as major European center; cathedral schools prepare clergy; Jewish academies maintain rabbinic learning; Alfonso X's court functions as center of vernacular scholarship; literacy expands among urban elites while remaining confined to small minority overall; the translation movement dramatically expands the Latin knowledge stock available to European scholars.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: Some Arabic learning not translated remains inaccessible; mudejar communities gradually lose access to Arabic scholarly tradition; practical techniques survive better than theoretical knowledge in disrupted contexts; plague mortality breaks some transmission chains; overall the period represents knowledge accumulation rather than loss.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: Reconquista ideology reaches triumphal expression; chronicles construct continuous narrative from Visigothic kingdom through Muslim interlude to Christian restoration; Santiago remains patron of Christian Iberia; the Cid story elaborates into legendary epic; Alfonso X's historiography constructs Castilian identity within universal history; Sephardic Jewish identity maintains distinctiveness; Granada cultivates Andalusian Islamic memory.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: Monarchical legitimacy rests on divine sanction, lineage, and law; Alfonso X's imperial claims extend legitimacy aspirations beyond Iberia; the Siete Partidas provides comprehensive legitimating framework; Nasrid Granada claims Islamic legitimacy through cultural patronage and jihad; chronicle writing serves legitimating purposes throughout.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: Gothic architecture spreads across Iberia in cathedrals at Burgos, Leon, and Toledo; Mudejar style blends Islamic decorative techniques with Christian patronage; illuminated manuscripts reach high refinement in Alfonsine projects; troubadour poetry continues in Catalan and Portuguese-Galician; vernacular prose develops under royal patronage; textiles, ceramics, and metalwork maintain high craft standards.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: Convivencia model strains under increasing pressure on minorities; some cultural forms fossilize as political context shifts; Gothic style reaches maturity without evident exhaustion; vernacular literary forms remain vital and expanding; the period represents cultural florescence rather than exhaustion, though plague will disrupt cultural production severely.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: Christian cosmology dominates public life; scholastic synthesis integrates Aristotelian philosophy with Christian theology; Jewish philosophical tradition engages same questions from different premises; Islamic cosmology persists in Granada and among mudejars; pilgrimage to Santiago expresses devotion and identity; plague arrival challenges providential confidence catastrophically.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: Latin liturgy standardized through Gregorian reform; confraternities multiply devotional practice; pilgrimage to Santiago reaches peak; mendicant orders (Franciscans, Dominicans) bring new forms of urban spirituality; Jewish communities maintain Sabbath, festival, and dietary observance; Islamic prayer and fasting continue in Granada and mudejar communities.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: Episcopal and monastic structures maintain ecclesiastical order; mendicant orders expand urban presence; inquisition against heresy develops in Aragon; papal authority accepted though sometimes resisted; Jewish communities maintain rabbinic authority; kabbalah develops distinctive mystical tradition in Catalonia and Castile, with the Zohar composed circa 1280s in Castile.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: Christianity consolidates dominance; Islam contracts geographically to Granada; conversion pressure increases on Jews and mudejars; some religious boundary-crossing occurs despite prohibitions; Jewish mysticism spreads within Sephardic communities; Christian mysticism develops through mendicant influence.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: No significant secularizing trend evident; religious commitment remains strong across communities; plague arrival will test but not break religious framework, redirecting spiritual anxiety into intensified devotion, flagellant movements, and anti-Jewish scapegoating rather than disenchantment; the period ends with spiritual crisis rather than drift.

docs.title: 100 CE – 400 CE — Imperial Hispania and Roman Provincial Manuscript Culture
docs.text: Summary: The Iberian Peninsula reaches its apex of Roman integration as fully pacified provinces supplying emperors, senators, and literary figures to the imperial center, with a mature manuscript culture sustaining urban administration, legal practice, and intellectual life; the binding constraint of the Manuscript Stage manifests in the dense infrastructure of archives, libraries, and scriptoria that fix law, property, and knowledge in written form — a documentary substrate that will prove both invaluable and vulnerable when the political order supporting it contracts.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: The Roman road network — the Via Augusta tracing the Mediterranean coast, the Via de la Plata linking Emerita to Asturica — has reduced spatial friction to its practical minimum for pre-modern technology; the peninsula functions as an integrated economic zone despite interior uplands; the geographic frame established under conquest now enables rather than impedes movement.

Climate Regime & Volatility: The Mediterranean climate continues its seasonal rhythm of wet winters and dry summers in the south and east; Atlantic influence moderates the northwest; the central Meseta endures continental extremes; the Roman Climatic Optimum (circa 200 BCE – 150 CE) brings relatively warm, stable conditions that favor agriculture, though cooling begins by the 3rd century.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: Drought occasionally stresses the arid south; seismic activity affects the southeast periodically; floods along the Guadalquivir and Ebro disrupt but do not destroy lowland settlement; the hazard regime remains local; no catastrophic events mark the period; infrastructure and granaries buffer against ordinary volatility.

Resource & Energy Endowment: Mining output declines from its Augustan peak as the richest veins are exhausted; gold extraction at Las Medulas ends by the 3rd century; agricultural resources remain robust; timber depletion affects some regions; the energy endowment contracts slightly but remains adequate for provincial needs; the peninsula shifts from mineral extraction to agricultural export.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Mining spoil and deforestation mark the northwest; urban waste accumulates in cities lacking active maintenance by the 4th century; lead pollution from smelting leaves traces in soils; the landscape absorbs these loads without systemic degradation; localized damage does not yet loop back as constraint.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: Endemic malaria persists in coastal wetlands; the Antonine Plague (165–180 CE) and Plague of Cyprian (249–262 CE) elevate mortality across the empire including Hispania; urban populations suffer disproportionately; the mortality baseline rises and falls with these epidemics but does not permanently spike; endemic disease remains manageable.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: The agricultural surplus of Baetica and the Mediterranean littoral sustains adequate nutrition for most of the population; urban populations access varied diets; rural populations subsist on grain, legumes, and olive oil; skeletal evidence suggests stable physiological status until the 3rd-century crisis brings localized stress.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Roman medical knowledge reaches provincial cities through trained physicians; public baths promote hygiene; military medicine maintains standards; rural populations rely on folk healing and itinerant practitioners; the healing capacity is unevenly distributed but functional; hospitals (valetudinaria) serve military and some urban populations.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Roman marriage patterns predominate among citizens; provincial elites adopt Roman family norms; reproductive rates remain positive through most of the period; the plagues may temporarily depress fertility; pairing dynamics are stable within the Roman legal framework.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Population peaks in the 2nd century, perhaps reaching 6–9 million; the plagues and 3rd-century crisis reduce numbers; urban populations contract in the 4th century; density remains highest along the coasts and in the Guadalquivir valley; the interior Meseta never achieves high density; demographic renewal slows but does not collapse.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: An aging population structure emerges in mature cities; plague mortality creates widows and orphans; the Church begins to assume charitable functions for dependents by the 4th century; the dependency load is manageable where institutional capacity persists but burdens communities where it decays.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: The provisioning floor remains secure for most of the period; the annona system ensures grain supply to cities; agricultural productivity sustains the population; the 3rd-century crisis brings disruption but not famine; by the 4th century, provisioning depends increasingly on local circuits as long-distance trade declines.

Energy Capture & Conversion: Human and animal muscle remain the primary movers; water mills spread for grain processing; the per-capita energy ceiling does not advance; Roman organization extracts maximum output from available sources; the energy regime is mature and stable rather than expanding.

Labor Organization & Coercion: Slavery persists but the supply of war captives diminishes; the colonate emerges, binding tenant farmers to the land in quasi-servile status; wage labor exists in cities; the labor relation shifts from chattel slavery toward tied tenancy as the empire ages; coercion remains fundamental but changes form.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Agricultural production — olive oil, wine, grain, garum — sustains export flows to Rome and other provinces; manufacturing (pottery, textiles, metalwork) serves regional markets; production capacity remains high through the 2nd century, contracts in the 3rd, and stabilizes at lower levels in the 4th; the surplus shrinks but persists.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: Granaries, horrea, and treasuries hold reserves in provincial capitals and municipalities; private wealth buffers elite households; the state's fiscal reserves contract during the 3rd-century crisis; the buffer against shock diminishes but does not vanish; localized scarcity becomes more common by the 4th century.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: Mediterranean trade networks integrate Hispania into empire-wide commerce; Baetican olive oil reaches Rome in millions of amphorae; the road network maintains internal connectivity; trade contracts in the 3rd century as security deteriorates and currency debases; by the 4th century, exchange is increasingly regional rather than Mediterranean-wide.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: The denarius and later the solidus circulate as currency; inflation and debasement in the 3rd century erode monetary value; credit networks contract; written contracts and debt instruments depend on functioning archives and courts; the monetary system stabilizes under Diocletian and Constantine but never fully recovers its earlier liquidity.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: Taxation funds the army, bureaucracy, and public works; the tax burden rises in the 3rd–4th centuries as military costs increase; redistribution flows through imperial administration, municipal governments, and increasingly the Church; extraction capacity tightens as the tax base contracts.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Wealth concentrates in senatorial and equestrian hands; provincial elites hold vast landed estates (latifundia); the 3rd-century crisis and subsequent reforms redistribute some wealth downward through military service; asset defense strategies include conversion to land, hoarding, and church donations; inequality remains extreme.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Urban waste management decays in cities losing population and municipal resources; rural waste is dispersed; financial waste in the form of bad debt and malinvestment accumulates during the 3rd-century crisis but is partially cleared by inflation and debt cancellation; the residue does not cripple the system.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Roman family law governs citizens; the paterfamilias structure persists among elites; inheritance follows Roman rules with testamentary freedom; kinship networks remain the basic unit of social organization; the family adapts to Christian influence by the 4th century, with the Church acquiring rights over marriage and inheritance.

Association & Mutual Aid: Collegia (guilds and burial societies) organize urban populations; Christian communities emerge as mutual aid networks by the 3rd century; rural villages maintain communal structures; the fabric of association thickens with Christian institutional growth even as municipal institutions decay.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: Amphitheaters, theaters, baths, and circuses remain centers of public life through the 3rd century; elite sociability revolves around villas, banquets, and literary culture; Christian communities develop their own social spaces — churches, cemeteries, charitable institutions; public spectacles decline in the 4th century as Christian influence grows.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: The citizen/non-citizen divide dissolves with the Constitutio Antoniniana (212 CE) extending citizenship to all free inhabitants; a new hierarchy emerges: honestiores (elites) versus humiliores (commoners); the senatorial and curial orders define the top; slaves, coloni, and the poor occupy the bottom; social mobility decreases as status becomes hereditary in the 4th century.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: Provincial and municipal administration reaches its peak in the 2nd century; the 3rd-century crisis disrupts governance; Diocletian's reforms (284–305 CE) reorganize the provinces and expand bureaucracy; administrative capacity stabilizes at a more centralized, authoritarian level; archives, record-keeping, and legal procedure sustain the manuscript regime; corruption increases as resources contract.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: The legions garrison the northwest through the 2nd century; thereafter, frontier defense draws troops away; the 3rd-century crisis brings Germanic raids and internal usurpers; Diocletian and Constantine reorganize the army into limitanei (border troops) and comitatenses (mobile field armies); the apparatus of force remains formidable but stretched thin.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: The 3rd-century crisis brings raids, usurpations, and economic disruption; Bagaudae (rural bandits or rebels) appear in the northwest; urban populations decline; municipal institutions atrophy; the 4th century sees partial recovery but the social fabric frays at the edges; disorder is contained but not eliminated; decay accumulates as maintenance fails.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: The Antonine emperors command respect from afar; the 3rd-century soldier-emperors hold power by force; Constantine and his successors claim divine sanction; provincial governors and bishops exercise local authority; personal leadership becomes more important as institutional authority weakens; charisma substitutes for procedure.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: Imperial legitimacy is strong in the 2nd century; the 3rd-century crisis erodes it through rapid imperial turnover and military usurpation; Constantine's dynasty and Christian endorsement rebuild legitimacy on new foundations; by the 4th century, the Christian emperor claims divine mandate; allegiance is genuine among Christians, pragmatic among others.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: The will to maintain the empire persists; elites defend their positions; the army fights on; no alternative attracts loyalty; political will concentrates in the emperor and his court; provincial populations are subjects rather than participants; the resolve to hold Hispania remains, though the peninsula is peripheral to frontier pressures.

External Relations & Posture: Hispania remains an interior province, insulated from frontier threats until the 5th century; its external posture is passive, supplying resources and recruits to imperial campaigns elsewhere; Germanic raids in the 3rd century are episodic rather than existential; the peninsula faces inward toward Rome and outward toward Africa and Gaul.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: The 2nd century is confident and prosperous; the 3rd-century crisis breeds anxiety, distrust, and apocalyptic expectation; Constantine's stabilization and Christian triumph restore a measure of confidence; the 4th century combines Christian hope with awareness of decline; the radius of trust contracts toward local and religious communities.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: The 3rd-century crisis generates disaffection visible in tax evasion, flight to the countryside, and Bagaudae; the 4th-century recovery is partial; apathy affects decayed municipalities where elites flee curial responsibilities; spent will is re-anchored for some through Christian hope but settles as resignation for others.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Latin is the universal language of administration, law, and literature; Greek is known among educated elites; indigenous languages persist in rural speech but vanish from the written record; literacy remains confined to perhaps 10–20% of urban populations, concentrated among elites, administrators, clergy, and scribes; the code is standardized but access is restricted.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: The cursus publicus (imperial post) maintains official communication; trade routes carry informal messages; the road network ensures provincial connectivity; transmission velocity remains high by pre-modern standards — a message can cross the peninsula in days; channel capacity is stable but does not expand.

Record, Storage & Persistence: This is the apex of Roman provincial manuscript culture: archives hold tax records, census data, property registers, legal proceedings, and official correspondence; libraries in major cities hold literary and scholarly texts; scriptoria produce copies; the Church develops its own archival and literary infrastructure; persistence is systematic but depends on institutions that will not survive intact.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: Imperial ideology frames public discourse; Christian discourse gains ground through the 4th century; censorship targets political dissent and, increasingly, religious heterodoxy; discourse norms valorize classical rhetoric and Latin eloquence; Christian Latin develops its own conventions; the permitted band shifts as Christianity becomes orthodox.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: Public inscriptions, imperial edicts, and ecclesiastical letters reach literate populations; sermons and oral proclamation extend the reach to the illiterate; amplification follows patronage, ecclesiastical, and trade networks; attention concentrates on imperial news, religious controversy, and local affairs; the Christian communication network rivals and then surpasses the secular.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: The manuscript system maintains signal integrity through archival redundancy and legal citation; forgery exists but is constrained by institutional verification; the 3rd-century crisis and subsequent disruptions introduce noise through lost records and broken transmission; the 4th century stabilizes but cannot fully recover lost material; surveillance is limited to political and religious threats.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Roman law provides the framework; Christian morality increasingly influences the sense of right and wrong; the provincial population internalizes a hybrid code; justice is expected to flow from emperor and magistrate, increasingly from bishop; the moral universe shifts from civic virtue to Christian sin and salvation.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: Roman law reaches its classical peak; jurists (Gaius, Papinian, Ulpian, Paul, Modestinus) produce authoritative texts; the Theodosian Code (438 CE) compiles imperial legislation; Christian influence shapes family and criminal law; codification intensifies as memory alone cannot hold the accumulating rules; the law is written and must be looked up, not recalled.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: Courts function at provincial and municipal levels; the governor's tribunal handles serious cases; bishops acquire jurisdiction over church matters and, by the 4th century, some civil disputes; liability follows Roman categories; sanctions include fines, exile, torture, and death; adjudication capacity strains as resources contract but does not collapse.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: The Constitutio Antoniniana extends citizenship but distinguishes honestiores from humiliores in criminal procedure; rights thin as status degrades; the compliance burden of taxation, corvée, and tied occupation increases in the 4th century; predictability decreases as emergency measures multiply; the rule framework hardens and constrains.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: Powerful landowners evade justice; the poor have limited recourse; slaves and coloni have few legal protections; impunity grows as state capacity contracts; the Church offers an alternative forum but cannot compel enforcement; the gap between justice owed and delivered widens but does not become a chasm.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: Hispania produces major intellectual figures: Seneca, Lucan, Quintilian, Martial in the early period; later, Christian thinkers emerge; the dominant paradigm is Greco-Roman philosophical tradition, increasingly fused with Christian theology; the discovery frontier lies in doctrinal elaboration rather than natural inquiry; preservation and transmission matter more than innovation.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Roman engineering maintains aqueducts, roads, and buildings through the 2nd century; maintenance decays in the 3rd–4th centuries; agricultural technique remains stable; no significant technical advances occur; the peninsula applies received knowledge rather than generating new technique; skills persist but institutional support weakens.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: Elite education continues in rhetoric, law, and philosophy; Christian education emerges in episcopal schools; literacy remains low but stable; the knowledge stock is preserved in libraries and transmitted through teaching; skill distribution narrows as municipal schools decay; the Church becomes the primary educational institution by the 4th century.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: The 3rd-century crisis disrupts intellectual life; some texts are lost; libraries decay; teaching positions go unfilled; the 4th-century recovery is partial and selective — Christian texts gain priority; pagan philosophy and literature survive but transmission is precarious; knowledge decay accelerates at the edges while core texts are preserved.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: Hispano-Roman identity matures: provincial elites claim Roman civilization as their own; indigenous identities have faded from public memory; the new Christian identity layers onto the Roman, creating a hybrid Hispano-Roman-Christian foundational narrative; the empire is now the natural order of things, sanctioned by God.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: The ideology of eternal Rome persists but is supplemented and gradually supplanted by Christian eschatology; the emperor rules by divine mandate; the Church teaches obedience to legitimate authority; the legitimating narrative holds the empire together even as its material base contracts; the story of Christian Rome justifies the order.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: Classical artistic forms continue in elite contexts — mosaics, sculpture, silver plate — but provincial production declines in quality; Christian art emerges in funerary contexts (sarcophagi, catacombs) and church decoration; architectural activity shifts from secular public buildings to churches; the material surface becomes increasingly Christian by the 4th century.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: Classical forms show signs of exhaustion: repetition replaces innovation; provincial art becomes derivative; yet Christian forms are fresh and vital, carrying new meaning; the pagan sacred decays while the Christian sacred rises; form exhaustion affects one tradition while another is born; meaning is transferred rather than lost.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: The shift from pagan to Christian cosmology is the defining spiritual movement: a universe of many gods gives way to the one God; fate yields to providence; the afterlife gains centrality; existential outlook shifts from civic immortality (through fame) to personal salvation; the 4th century completes this transformation among elites while popular syncretism persists.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: Pagan cult declines; the imperial cult loses meaning after Constantine; Christian liturgy — Eucharist, baptism, festivals, daily prayer — becomes the dominant ritual framework; devotion to saints and martyrs develops; sacred practice becomes more frequent, more personal, and more institutionally mediated; the calendar Christianizes.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: The Christian Church emerges as the dominant religious institution: bishops hold authority in cities; councils define doctrine; heresy is persecuted after Theodosius; church property grows through donations; the clergy becomes a parallel elite; institutional religion achieves a density and reach unknown to paganism; doctrinal authority is contested but increasingly enforced.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: Christianity spreads from urban communities to rural populations through the 4th century; paganism retreats but persists in countryside (pagani = rural dwellers); mystery religions and philosophy are absorbed or displaced; Judaism survives in small communities facing increasing legal restriction; the direction is toward Christian monopoly with syncretic residue.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: The pagan sacred empties: temples close, priesthoods end, festivals fade; this is not secularization but replacement — the Christian sacred fills the void; disenchantment with the old gods enables enchantment with the new; the spiritual need is vigorously re-anchored; no existential vacuum opens; the discharge of one cosmology is the foundation of the next.

docs.title: 711 CE – 756 CE — Islamic Conquest and the Establishment of Al-Andalus
docs.text: Summary: The Manuscript Stage's binding constraint — external records kept outside the body becoming the medium public life runs on — here manifests as the abrupt displacement of Visigothic Latin manuscript culture by Arabic administrative and religious writing, as Umayyad and Berber forces overrun Hispania, collapse the Visigothic state, and install a new governing apparatus whose ledgers, treaties, and quranic texts rewire the peninsula's documentary substrate within two generations.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: The Strait of Gibraltar, barely fourteen kilometers wide, collapses the distance between North Africa and Iberia, permitting rapid troop ferry once Visigothic naval watch fails; the Guadalquivir valley then funnels invaders northeast toward Toledo and the Meseta heartland with minimal terrain resistance, while the Cantabrian mountains in the north impose the friction that halts expansion and shelters the Asturian remnant.

Climate Regime & Volatility: Mediterranean semi-arid conditions in Andalusia and the Levant favor cavalry operations year-round; wetter Atlantic conditions in the northwest limit campaigning seasons but also support the agrarian surplus that sustains refugee populations; no exceptional drought or flood is recorded during the conquest window.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: Seismic risk along the Betic-Rif zone poses latent danger to urban centers but no major earthquake disrupts the conquest; flash-flood exposure in Guadalquivir tributaries remains a seasonal logistical concern for supply trains.

Resource & Energy Endowment: Hispania's gold and silver deposits in the Sierra Morena and Galicia, together with grain surpluses from the Guadalquivir basin and iron from the Basque region, make the peninsula a high-value prize; the conquerors inherit rather than exhaust these stocks.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Siege and sack leave localized debris fields around contested towns — Cordoba, Toledo, Merida — but population displacement and agricultural disruption reduce the aggregate waste load on land and waterways; no systemic sink saturation occurs.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: Endemic Mediterranean fevers and intestinal parasites persist at pre-conquest levels; no major epidemic is recorded during the invasion window, leaving combat, flight, and famine as the principal mortality drivers rather than disease.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: Agricultural disruption during the 711–716 CE campaigns degrades provisioning in war zones, producing localized hunger among refugees fleeing north; Berber and Arab troops arrive provisioned by North African supply lines and face no reported starvation.
