Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Visigothic monasteries and episcopal centers that provided wound-care and herbal remedy are abandoned or repurposed in conquered zones; Arab field medicine, drawing on Galenic and Persian traditions, accompanies the armies but reaches only combatants, leaving civilian casualties largely unattended.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Conquest disrupts Visigothic marriage patterns as Christian elites flee north; intermarriage between Arab commanders and Visigothic noble women (including the family of Count Julian) produces mixed lineages that will later claim ruling status; Berber settlers bring their own kinship structures into the demographic mix.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Population in the conquered south initially declines through flight and war mortality, then stabilizes as Berber colonists settle depopulated estates; the Christian north absorbs refugees, raising density in Asturias and Galicia beyond pre-conquest levels.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: War widows, orphans, and the displaced form a substantial dependent load in both zones; monastic and episcopal charity in the north and nascent Islamic alms systems in the south absorb portions of this burden, though neither clears it entirely.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: Grain stores in the Guadalquivir and Ebro basins pass intact to the conquerors, who levy tribute rather than destroy agriculture; subsistence in the north tightens as refugees compete for arable land in the Cantabrian valleys.

Energy Capture & Conversion: Human and animal muscle remain the sole prime movers; the conquerors inherit Roman-era irrigation works in Andalusia that multiply agrarian output, while horse-breeding intensifies to supply cavalry remounts.

Labor Organization & Coercion: Visigothic serfs and freedmen largely remain on the land under new landlords, their labor status shifting from Visigothic servitude to dhimmi taxation; enslaved war captives augment the labor pool for public works and domestic service.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Agricultural surplus continues to flow from the Guadalquivir, Ebro, and Levantine coasts; urban craft production contracts initially as artisans flee or are displaced, then recovers as new demand from governors and garrisons emerges.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: Visigothic royal treasuries — including the famed treasure of Toledo — pass to the conquerors, providing immediate liquidity; grain reserves in episcopal and monastic storehouses are requisitioned or redistributed.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: Mediterranean sea lanes reopen to North African and Eastern trade as Islamic control reunites Iberia with the Umayyad commercial sphere; overland routes to Gaul are severed after the failed push beyond the Pyrenees (732 CE), but trans-Strait traffic intensifies.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: Visigothic gold tremisses give way to Islamic dinars and dirhams; the conquerors impose tribute in kind and coin, establishing a new unit of account that will dominate Iberian commerce for centuries.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: Jizya (poll tax) and kharaj (land tax) replace Visigothic fiscus levies, extracting surplus from dhimmi Christians and Jews while Arab and Berber settlers receive land grants (qati'a) and military stipends; the fiscal apparatus is rebuilt from scratch using Arabic records.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Visigothic aristocrats who submit retain portions of their estates; those who flee lose everything to confiscation; Berber settlers receive hill and frontier lands, Arab commanders the richer lowland estates, creating a new stratified distribution.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Urban disruption leaves rubble and abandoned structures in sacked towns; reconstruction absorbs some debris as building material; no systemic waste crisis emerges.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Arab tribal ('asabiyya) and Berber clan structures overlay and partially displace Visigothic kindred networks; Islamic inheritance rules apply to Muslim settlers, while dhimmi Christians retain their own family law under episcopal jurisdiction.

Association & Mutual Aid: Episcopal and monastic networks collapse in the conquered south; nascent Islamic waqf and neighborhood solidarity (hisba) structures begin to form in urban centers; the surviving Christian communities coalesce around their bishops and monasteries in the north.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: Public baths (hammams) and communal prayer at Friday mosques introduce new sociability patterns; horse-racing and hunting continue as elite pastimes shared across confessional lines.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: A new status hierarchy emerges: Arab ashraf (nobles) at the apex, Berber tribesmen below, then muwallad (Iberian converts), dhimmi Christians and Jews at the bottom but protected, and slaves lowest; Visigothic aristocrats who convert may ascend, those who do not descend sharply.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: The Visigothic royal administration disintegrates with the death of Roderic (711 CE); Umayyad governors (walis) appointed from Damascus or Qayrawan rebuild a provincial apparatus using Arabic chancery practice, though reach remains shallow beyond garrison towns until mid-century.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: Arab cavalry and Berber infantry, numbering perhaps 20,000–30,000 initially, defeat Visigothic levies piecemeal; fortified garrison towns (jund) and frontier ribats anchor control; the Asturian remnant fields only a few thousand warriors in the mountains.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: Brigandage and vendetta fill the vacuum between collapsing Visigothic order and incomplete Umayyad control; ethnic tension between Arab and Berber settlers erupts periodically (the Berber Revolt of 740–743 CE); the disorder is contained but not cleared.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: Tariq ibn Ziyad and Musa ibn Nusayr embody the conquest's charismatic impetus; subsequent governors lack comparable personal pull until Abd al-Rahman I arrives (756 CE) to found the independent emirate.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: Umayyad legitimacy rests on caliphal appointment from Damascus; when the Abbasid revolution (750 CE) overthrows the Umayyads in the East, Iberian governors face a legitimacy crisis that only Abd al-Rahman's arrival resolves by founding a rival dynasty.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: The conquerors' will to expand drives campaigns into Gaul until the defeat at Tours (732 CE); thereafter, consolidation replaces expansion; internal rivalries (Arab-Berber, Qaysi-Yemeni) fragment collective will until the emirate's establishment.

External Relations & Posture: Al-Andalus orients toward Damascus and Qayrawan for legitimacy and reinforcement; relations with the Frankish north are hostile after Tours; the Asturian kingdom is too weak to threaten and is largely ignored.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: Shock and despair pervade conquered Christian populations; among Berber and Arab settlers, triumphalism and piety merge; the Asturian remnant cultivates defiant resolve around the Covadonga legend (722 CE).

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: Berber settlers, assigned marginal lands and excluded from Arab privilege, harbor resentment that explodes in the 740s revolt; Arab factional strife (Qaysi vs. Yemeni) saps collective will; neither is cleared until Abd al-Rahman imposes emirate authority.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Arabic becomes the language of administration and religion; Latin persists among Mozarabic Christians; Romance vernaculars continue in daily speech; Berber dialects circulate among settlers — a multilingual regime emerges, with Arabic as the prestige code.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Courier routes along Roman roads carry gubernatorial orders; sea lanes to North Africa and the East transmit caliphal directives; the shift from Latin to Arabic chancery practice slows initial transmission as scribal corps are retrained or replaced.

Record, Storage & Persistence: Visigothic Latin archives survive where monasteries remain intact (primarily in the north); in the conquered south, Arabic registers replace them, documenting tax rolls, land grants, and treaties; the transition destroys or orphans much Visigothic documentary heritage.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: Islamic religious discourse now frames public speech in the conquered zones; Christian preaching retreats to churches and monasteries; blasphemy against Islam becomes punishable, narrowing the permitted band for non-Muslims.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: Friday sermons (khutba) become the principal mass communication channel, amplifying gubernatorial decrees and caliphal directives; Christian liturgy and episcopal letters serve the same function for Mozarabic communities.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: The rupture of Visigothic chancery practice introduces noise as records are lost, scribes flee, and new Arabic systems are still being calibrated; by 756 CE, the emirate's establishment begins to stabilize signal integrity under a unified administration.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Islamic notions of justice (adl) and contract (ahd) now govern relations between rulers and ruled in the conquered zones; dhimmi status codifies the protected but subordinate position of Christians and Jews; Visigothic legal categories persist only in the north.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: The Lex Visigothorum ceases to apply in the south; Islamic fiqh (jurisprudence), still in formative stages, governs Muslims; dhimmi communities retain internal legal autonomy under episcopal or rabbinic courts for personal status matters.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: Qadis (Islamic judges) adjudicate disputes among Muslims and between Muslims and dhimmis; Christian bishops retain jurisdiction over intra-Christian matters; the dual system introduces jurisdictional complexity but functions.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Dhimmi status guarantees life and property in exchange for jizya and behavioral restrictions (no proselytizing, no new church construction, distinctive dress); compliance burden is heavier than under Visigothic rule but predictable.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: Conquest violence — killings, enslavements, property seizures — goes unredressed; the victors define legality; impunity for Arab and Berber soldiers is near-total in the initial campaigns, narrowing only as gubernatorial authority consolidates.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: Isidoran encyclopedism and Visigothic Latin learning retreat to northern monasteries; the conquerors bring Quranic exegesis, hadith studies, and the first stirrings of Arabic grammar and jurisprudence, but no major intellectual center emerges until Cordoba flourishes later.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Arab and Berber settlers introduce improved irrigation techniques (noria, qanat) and horse-breeding methods; Visigothic metallurgy and building crafts persist where artisans remain.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: Cathedral and monastic schools collapse in the south; quranic schooling (kuttab) begins for Muslim children; literacy in Arabic spreads among administrators and religious scholars while Latin literacy contracts geographically.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: Visigothic Latin manuscripts in conquered zones are abandoned, burned, or repurposed as palimpsests; the knowledge stock they carried — church councils, legal codes, Isidoran compilations — survives only where monasteries remain intact in the north.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: The Visigothic origin story — Gothic migration, Arian past, Catholic conversion — is displaced in the south by Islamic narratives of conquest and righteous expansion; the Asturian kingdom begins constructing a counter-narrative of Christian reconquest rooted in the Covadonga legend.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: Umayyad governors legitimate rule through caliphal appointment and jihad ideology; dhimmi subordination is framed as just protection; the Asturian court, still nascent, invokes divine election and Visigothic succession.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: Mosque construction begins — early examples are repurposed churches or simple hypostyle halls; Arabic epigraphy replaces Latin inscriptions on official structures; Visigothic horseshoe arches, ironically, are adopted into early Andalusian mosque architecture, seeding the fusion style that will flower later.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: Visigothic court ritual and regalia lose their settings and audiences; the symbolism of Visigothic kingship — the Toledo treasury, the anointing rite — becomes inert once the state collapses; no equivalent form-exhaustion afflicts the incoming Islamic repertoire, still charged with the energy of recent revelation.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: Islamic monotheism, with its eschatology of judgment and paradise, becomes the dominant cosmology in the conquered zones; Nicene Christianity persists among Mozarabs, and Judaism among Iberian Jews, but both are now subordinate frames.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: The five daily prayers, Friday congregational worship, and Ramadan fasting structure Muslim devotional life; Christian liturgy continues in Mozarabic churches under episcopal supervision; synagogue worship persists under rabbinic authority.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: Visigothic episcopal hierarchy survives in diminished form under dhimmi status; mosques and nascent waqf endowments anchor Islamic institutional presence; doctrinal authority for Muslims flows from qadis and ulama appointed by governors, not yet from a local scholarly establishment.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: Conversion to Islam begins immediately — some opportunistic, some coerced, some sincere — producing the muwallad population; Christianity contracts geographically but retains adherents as a protected minority; Judaism persists with similar protected status.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: For Mozarabic Christians, the collapse of the Visigothic Catholic kingdom produces a crisis of sacred meaning — was God's favor withdrawn? — that later Asturian ideology will address by recasting the conquest as a test and the reconquista as redemption; for Muslims, no such crisis arises, the conquest confirming rather than challenging their cosmology.

docs.title: 1400 CE – 1479 CE — Late Medieval Consolidation and Manuscript Production
docs.text: Summary: The Iberian Peninsula and Western Mediterranean in recovery and consolidation, as the Trastamara dynasties stabilize Castile and Aragon, population slowly rebuilds, and manuscript production resumes in royal courts, monasteries, and emerging universities; the binding constraint remains the Manuscript Stage, with written records essential for the administrative consolidation, legal codification, and vernacular literary florescence that characterize the period, while humanist influences from Italy introduce new scholarly currents that manuscript circulation propagates.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: The peninsula's geography remains unchanged, but spatial integration improves as recovery proceeds; the Meseta reconnects to peripheral regions through reviving trade networks; Castilian control extends more firmly over the Guadalquivir valley; Aragonese maritime connections across the Western Mediterranean rebuild; the effective friction between regions diminishes as depopulated corridors repopulate.

Climate Regime & Volatility: Little Ice Age conditions persist with cooler, more variable weather than the Medieval Warm Period; periodic droughts and harsh winters punctuate the recovery; agricultural systems adapt to the changed climate baseline, with some shift toward hardier crops and pastoral activities in marginal zones.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: Plague remains endemic, with outbreaks in 1422, 1434, 1448, and 1465–1466, though mortality is lower than the initial pandemic; the biological hazard becomes a persistent background condition rather than an acute crisis; other environmental hazards remain at typical Mediterranean levels.

Resource & Energy Endowment: Abandoned agricultural land gradually returns to cultivation as population recovers; pastoral resources, particularly Castilian merino wool, become increasingly valuable for export; mining of iron, silver, and other metals continues at modest levels; the resource endowment remains abundant relative to recovering population.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Reduced population lessens environmental pressure; forests regenerate on abandoned marginal land; sanitary conditions in recovering towns improve gradually; the sink capacity remains well within the loads arriving from the contracted economic activity.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: Plague recurs periodically but with declining mortality; endemic diseases remain present at typical pre-industrial levels; the mortality baseline, while elevated compared to the high medieval period, no longer represents a catastrophic crisis; population begins sustained recovery after mid-century.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: Survivors and their descendants benefit from abundant land relative to population; per-capita food availability is higher than in the crowded pre-plague era; nutritional status and stature likely improve among the lower orders; the biological vitality of the population gradually rebuilds.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Medical knowledge remains within Galenic frameworks but incorporates empirical lessons from plague management; hospitals and charitable institutions rebuild; the Salamanca medical faculty continues training physicians; healing capacity gradually recovers toward pre-plague levels as institutional structures restabilize.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Marriage rates normalize as demographic crisis recedes; age at first marriage may decline, facilitating higher completed fertility; the reproductive effort of the population shifts toward recovery, though growth remains slow against recurrent plague outbreaks.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Population growth resumes, though slowly; by 1479 Iberian population reaches perhaps five million, still below pre-plague levels; urban recovery is uneven, with some centers regaining vigor while others remain depressed; overall density increases but remains below the medieval maximum.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: The dependency burden normalizes as age structure rebalances over generations; the acute crisis of orphans and disrupted families from the plague years passes; monastic and charitable institutions that care for dependents recover capacity; the overhang clears gradually.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: The subsistence situation stabilizes well above crisis levels; peasants benefit from improved terms of tenure negotiated during the labor scarcity; the provisioning floor rises as land-labor ratios remain favorable; famines become less common than in the densely populated pre-plague era.

Energy Capture & Conversion: The labor force rebuilds, enabling fuller utilization of water and wind power; agricultural energy capture increases as abandoned land returns to cultivation; the energy conversion system operates within capacity as population remains below pre-plague density.

Labor Organization & Coercion: Labor relations settle into new equilibria; attempts to reimpose strict serfdom largely fail; wage labor and sharecropping arrangements become more common; the balance between coercion and compensation remains tilted toward workers, though lords consolidate control where they can.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Production recovers gradually across sectors; wool production for export becomes increasingly important for Castile, feeding Flemish textile industries; Catalan and Valencian manufactures resume growth; surplus generation increases, though total output remains below pre-plague peaks; manuscript production resumes in scriptoria with new patronage from stabilized courts.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: Royal and noble treasuries rebuild as tax revenues recover; commercial credit networks restabilize; the fiscal capacity of crowns improves, enabling more ambitious state-building; buffering capacity against shock increases though remains modest by later standards.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: Mediterranean commerce revives, with Catalan-Aragonese merchants reconnecting Barcelona to Italian, North African, and Eastern Mediterranean markets; Castilian wool exports through Burgos to Flemish ports grow substantially; internal trade networks strengthen as towns recover; commercial infrastructure improves.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: Credit systems restabilize; Genoese and Florentine banking houses operate in Iberian markets; the converso community, drawing on commercial skills, becomes important in finance and trade; monetary systems remain stable under Castilian and Aragonese crowns; capital formation resumes.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: Royal revenues increase with economic recovery; the Castilian crown develops more sophisticated fiscal machinery; the Cortes retain power over extraordinary taxation while regular revenues grow; the Aragonese crown similarly consolidates fiscal capacity; taxation supports court culture and manuscript patronage.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Wealth concentration increases as noble families consolidate holdings acquired during the crisis; the converso community accumulates commercial wealth; peasant conditions remain better than pre-plague but begin to erode in some regions; land values recover, benefiting established holders.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Economic activity generates increasing waste as production grows, but the expanded sink capacity absorbs the load; urban waste management remains rudimentary but adequate for population levels; the economic residue clears without significant accumulation.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Family structures restabilize after plague disruption; inheritance patterns normalize; noble lineages that survived the crisis consolidate; the converso population establishes new family networks while maintaining some connections across the conversion divide; kinship remains central to social organization.

Association & Mutual Aid: Guilds and confraternities rebuild membership; urban associations recover organizational capacity; mutual aid networks strengthen; the associational fabric thickens as crisis conditions recede; the mesta, the Castilian sheepherders' guild, becomes increasingly powerful as wool exports grow.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: Festive life resumes; royal courts become centers of display and sociability; tournaments, hunting, and courtly entertainments flourish; urban festivals return; the carnivalesque and ludic dimensions of social life recover from plague-era contraction.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: The converso population constitutes a new and ambiguous social category, nominally Christian but suspect; limpieza de sangre (purity of blood) concerns emerge, distinguishing Old Christians from New; noble status remains prestigious while commercial wealth grows among conversos and others; social boundaries harden in some respects while remaining permeable in others.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: Royal administration consolidates under the Trastamara dynasties; the Castilian councils (Consejo Real, later specialized councils) develop greater capacity; the Aragonese crown maintains its composite structure with distinct administrations for Aragon, Catalonia, and Valencia; universities at Salamanca, Valladolid, and elsewhere train administrators and jurists; documentary apparatus becomes more sophisticated.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: Military capacity rebuilds; the Castilian crown develops more direct control over armed force, reducing dependence on noble levies; the Aragonese crown maintains Mediterranean naval capacity; fortification continues; the coercive apparatus strengthens relative to the chaos of the crisis years.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: Social order improves as central authority consolidates; banditry declines; the violence of the crisis years recedes; however, tension around converso status creates new sources of friction; rural unrest occasionally flares as lords attempt to claw back concessions made during labor scarcity; the disorder residue diminishes but does not fully clear.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: Strong monarchs emerge in both crowns: in Castile, John II (1406–1454) and the contested reign of Henry IV (1454–1474); in Aragon, the Compromise of Caspe (1412) installs the Trastamara Fernando I, followed by Alfonso V (1416–1458) and John II (1458–1479); personal authority of monarchs increases, though constrained by noble factions.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: Trastamara legitimacy consolidates over generations; the usurpation origins fade from active memory; however, the Castilian succession crisis of 1474–1479 between Isabella and Juana la Beltraneja shows continuing vulnerability; legitimacy is contested but the principle of dynastic monarchy holds firm.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: Political will coheres around dynastic consolidation; the Castilian and Aragonese crowns pursue state-building with increasing effectiveness; the wars against Granada resume intermittently, signaling reviving expansionist will; the marriage of Ferdinand and Isabella (1469) represents successful coordination of political will across the crowns.

External Relations & Posture: External ambitions revive; Alfonso V of Aragon conquers Naples (1442), extending Aragonese power into Italy; Castilian rivalry with Portugal over Atlantic expansion intensifies; relations with Granada shift toward renewed pressure; the posture moves from defensive consolidation toward renewed expansion.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: Public mood recovers from plague-era despair; confidence slowly returns as normal life resumes; however, suspicion of conversos creates an undercurrent of distrust; the collective temper moderates toward cautious optimism without fully recovering the confident expansionism of the high medieval period.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: The exhaustion of the crisis years gradually dissipates; however, noble factionalism creates ongoing political instability, particularly in Castile during Henry IV's reign; converso communities face mounting hostility; the disaffection residue partly clears but new sources of tension emerge around religious identity.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Latin remains central for learning, law, and church; vernacular languages continue expanding into documentary use; Castilian becomes increasingly standardized through royal and literary production; Catalan maintains its literary tradition; Hebrew use declines catastrophically with the destruction of Jewish communities; conversos largely adopt Christian communicative codes.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Communication networks strengthen with commercial recovery; royal courier systems become more regular; Mediterranean shipping carries correspondence as well as goods; the velocity and reliability of information transmission improve, though the fundamental technologies remain unchanged.

Record, Storage & Persistence: Archival practices develop greater sophistication; royal chancelleries produce growing volumes of documentation; cathedral and monastic archives are maintained and organized; the Crown of Aragon's archival system becomes particularly systematic; manuscript copying resumes in scriptoria with improved capacity; libraries grow through new production and acquisition.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: Royal courts shape discourse through patronage of approved narratives; chronicles commissioned by monarchs frame political events; religious orthodoxy increasingly constrains public discourse about conversos and religious identity; the Inquisition, established in Castile in 1478, begins to systematize censorship.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: Courtly audiences for literature and learning expand; university-trained readers form a growing public for scholarly and literary works; humanist texts from Italy circulate among educated elites; vernacular literature reaches broader audiences through public readings and performance.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: Documentary systems achieve greater reliability as administrative capacity improves; record-keeping becomes more systematic; however, the ambiguity around converso identity creates informational noise about genealogy and religious sincerity; the verification of lineage becomes increasingly important and contested.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Religious orthodoxy becomes more central to moral foundations; the sin of heresy and its detection preoccupy moral discourse; limpieza de sangre begins to function as a moral category distinguishing pure from impure lineages; the convivencia ethos of the high medieval period yields to more exclusivist moral frameworks.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: Legal codification advances; the Ordenamiento de Montalvo (1484) compiles Castilian law; royal legislation proliferates; university-trained jurists apply Roman and canon law principles; the legal framework for the emerging Inquisition develops; law becomes more systematized and written.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: Royal justice extends its reach relative to noble and local jurisdictions; the Audiencias develop as appellate courts; the Inquisition, from 1478, creates a parallel jurisdiction for matters of faith; adjudicative capacity improves though access remains uneven; sanction becomes more regularized.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Converso rights remain formally equal to Old Christians, but informal discrimination increases; peasant rights achieved during labor scarcity face erosion in some regions; noble privileges consolidate; the compliance burden of proving religious orthodoxy and lineage begins to weigh on converso populations.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: The unpunished violence of 1391 continues to cast a shadow; converso communities seeking justice for past wrongs find little recourse; noble factionalism sometimes enables violence without consequence; however, ordinary crime faces more effective prosecution as royal justice expands; the impunity residue partly clears while new forms emerge.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: Humanist learning from Italy reaches Iberian courts and universities; classical studies develop, with new attention to Latin style and Greek texts; scholasticism continues to dominate university curricula at Salamanca and elsewhere; the two currents coexist, with humanism gaining ground among courtly elites while scholasticism holds the institutions.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Practical techniques in navigation, cartography, and shipbuilding advance, laying groundwork for Atlantic exploration; agricultural and pastoral techniques adapt to changed demographic conditions; manuscript production techniques continue without major innovation, though paper becomes more widely used alongside parchment.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: Universities recover and expand; Salamanca remains Castile's premier institution; new foundations emerge; literacy spreads slowly among urban populations; the knowledge stock grows through humanist acquisition of classical texts and continued scholastic production; skill distribution remains heavily concentrated among clergy and urban elites.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: Hebrew learning in Iberia faces severe contraction as the Jewish scholarly community is destroyed or dispersed; some classical Arabic learning preserved in translation; Latin scholastic tradition shows continuity; humanist recovery of classical texts counters earlier losses; overall, the knowledge stock stabilizes and begins to grow again.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: The Reconquista narrative strengthens as legitimating mythology; the crusading identity of Castilian and Aragonese kingdoms consolidates; the memory of convivencia fades as exclusivist Christian identity becomes more central; converso identity remains ambiguous and contested, neither fully Christian nor permitted to remain Jewish.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: Trastamara monarchs commission chronicles and literary works celebrating their rule; Alfonso V's Neapolitan court becomes a center of humanist culture; the ideology of religious unity and limpieza de sangre develops; royal patronage shapes cultural production toward legitimating narratives.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: Late Gothic style flourishes in ecclesiastical and civil architecture; manuscript illumination reaches new heights of elaboration in royal and noble commissions; Hispano-Flemish painting emerges; material culture becomes more refined as prosperity returns; courtly display intensifies as competition for prestige through cultural patronage increases.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: The Gothic style shows elaboration rather than exhaustion, with Isabelline Gothic developing distinctive features; vernacular literary forms flourish, from the romancero to courtly poetry; however, the meaning systems of the pre-plague era, including the convivencia synthesis, have decayed and been replaced by more exclusivist frameworks.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: Christian cosmology dominates more exclusively than in the high medieval period; the existential outlook remains shaped by plague memory but moderates toward conventional late medieval piety; apocalyptic anxiety recedes; the confidence of a unified Christian order gradually returns.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: Devotional practices intensify around Marian and Christocentric piety; religious confraternities proliferate; pilgrimage to Santiago de Compostela revives; the liturgical calendar structures public life; conversos must perform Christian devotion under increasing scrutiny, creating anxiety around ritual practice.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: The Church rebuilds institutional strength; mendicant orders remain influential; monasteries recover endowments and recruitment; the Castilian crown gains increasing control over Church appointments; the establishment of the Inquisition (1478) represents the crown's assertion of doctrinal authority in partnership with Rome.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: Judaism is suppressed rather than displaced; Crypto-Judaism persists among some conversos; the surviving Muslim population (Mudejars) faces increasing pressure toward conversion; the spiritual landscape moves toward uniformity, with diversity driven underground rather than accommodated; the direction is toward consolidation of Catholic orthodoxy.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: Rather than disenchantment, the period sees re-enchantment through intensified orthodoxy; the sacred remains potent and is defended through institutional means (the Inquisition); the spiritual residue is not secularizing drift but rather the anxiety and suspicion generated by the converso question and the apparatus of enforcement emerging to police belief.

docs.title: 200 BCE – 100 CE — Roman Conquest and the Latinization of Hispania
docs.text: Summary: The Iberian Peninsula undergoes gradual transformation from a mosaic of indigenous polities into integrated Roman provinces, with Latin script and administrative record-keeping displacing Iberian and Celtiberian writing systems; the binding constraint of the Manuscript Stage manifests as Roman provincial administration depends upon written records — census rolls, tax registers, military dispatches, and legal documents — that fix obligations beyond memory and outlast their makers, establishing the documentary infrastructure upon which public life will run for the next four centuries.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: The peninsula's rugged interior — the Meseta plateau ringed by mountain chains, the Pyrenean barrier to the north, and the river valleys of the Ebro, Tagus, Guadiana, and Guadalquivir cutting through uplands — imposes severe spatial friction that fragments indigenous resistance but also slows Roman consolidation; conquest proceeds valley by valley, siege by siege, over two centuries.

Climate Regime & Volatility: Mediterranean climate prevails in the south and east with dry summers and mild winters; Atlantic influence brings wetter conditions to the northwest; the continental Meseta endures harsh winters and summer heat; this climatic mosaic supports varied agricultural regimes from olive and vine in the south to grain and cattle in the center and north.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: Drought periodically stresses the arid south and central plateau; seismic activity affects parts of the southeast; flooding along major rivers disrupts lowland settlement; these hazards remain local and episodic, never threatening the provincial system as a whole.

Resource & Energy Endowment: The peninsula holds rich mineral deposits — gold in the northwest (Las Medulas), silver and lead in the Sierra Morena, copper in the Huelva region, tin in Galicia — that draw Roman extraction efforts; agricultural surplus flows from the Guadalquivir valley and Mediterranean littoral; timber from mountain forests feeds construction and mining.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Mining operations leave spoil heaps, deforestation, and mercury contamination from gold extraction; urban centers generate refuse and sewage; the landscape absorbs these loads without systemic saturation, though localized degradation marks mining districts.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: Endemic malaria affects coastal wetlands and river valleys; gastrointestinal diseases circulate in densely settled areas; the mortality baseline remains elevated by ancient Mediterranean standards but is not catastrophic; Roman military camps and urban concentrations create new disease foci.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: The Mediterranean diet of grain, olive oil, wine, and legumes provides adequate nutrition where surplus flows; mining slaves and war captives suffer degraded nutrition and elevated mortality; skeletal evidence suggests robust physiological status among settled agricultural populations.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Roman military medicine reaches legionary camps and veteran settlements; indigenous healing traditions persist in rural areas; urban centers acquire public physicians and bathhouses that improve sanitary conditions; healing capacity concentrates unevenly along lines of Roman settlement.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Indigenous kinship patterns persist alongside Roman marriage customs; intermarriage between Roman settlers and local populations produces mixed lineages; reproductive patterns remain stable, with high fertility offset by childhood mortality.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Population grows as Roman peace ends endemic warfare and opens new agricultural land; urban centers — Tarraco, Corduba, Emerita Augusta — draw migrants; density remains highest along the Mediterranean coast and in the Guadalquivir valley; the interior Meseta remains thinly settled.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: War casualties thin fighting-age males in the conquest decades; enslavement removes productive labor from indigenous communities to mines and latifundia; Roman veteran settlement introduces a population requiring land grants; dependency loads remain manageable as growth continues.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: Indigenous agriculture — wheat, barley, olives, vines — continues under Roman rule; the provisioning floor rises as Roman infrastructure reduces transport friction and markets integrate; famine risk declines but remains present in marginal upland zones.

Energy Capture & Conversion: Human and animal muscle power dominates; water mills appear by the late period for grain processing; mining operations deploy enslaved labor at scale for ore extraction and processing; the per-capita work ceiling remains low but Roman organization multiplies its aggregate effect.

Labor Organization & Coercion: Conquest generates masses of war captives channeled into mining and agricultural slavery; free indigenous cultivators owe tribute and labor obligations; wage labor exists in urban crafts and construction; the coercion spectrum runs from chattel slavery in mines to tenant farming on latifundia.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Mineral extraction — gold, silver, copper, lead, tin — constitutes the primary surplus flow to Rome; agricultural surplus from the Baetica region supplies olive oil and garum (fish sauce) for Mediterranean markets; production capacity expands as Roman capital and organization reach the peninsula.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: Granaries in urban centers and military camps store grain reserves; provincial treasuries hold tax revenues; private wealth accumulates in land and moveable goods; the buffer against shock improves with administrative integration.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: Roman road construction — the Via Augusta along the coast, the Via de la Plata inland — integrates markets; Mediterranean shipping connects ports from Gades to Tarraco to Italian markets; the denarius circulates as the standard medium; logistics friction falls dramatically as infrastructure matures.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: The Roman monetary system displaces indigenous coinage and barter; credit networks link provincial elites to Italian financiers; debt obligations are recorded in written contracts that outlast memory; value storage shifts from cattle and metal objects to coined money and documented claims.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: Roman taxation — tribute, customs, mining royalties — extracts surplus for the imperial center; provincial administration redistributes a portion locally for roads, aqueducts, and public buildings; the extraction load is heavy but sustainable as long as peace holds and production expands.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Conquest transfers land and mineral wealth to Roman citizens and the imperial treasury; indigenous elites who accommodate Rome retain and sometimes expand their holdings; wealth concentrates in the hands of Roman colonists, provincial administrators, and collaborating local aristocrats.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Mining spoil accumulates at extraction sites; urban refuse is dumped outside walls or channeled through sewers in larger cities; the waste load remains local and does not yet strain regional sinks.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Indigenous kinship systems — Iberian bilateral descent, Celtiberian patrilineal clans — persist in rural areas while Roman familia structures dominate colonial settlements and spread through intermarriage and acculturation; inheritance increasingly follows Roman legal forms as citizenship expands.

Association & Mutual Aid: Indigenous clan and tribal solidarities weaken as Roman administrative units (civitates, conventus) supplant them; collegia (trade and religious associations) appear in urban centers; mutual aid persists through kinship and neighborhood networks but loses its political-military dimension.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: Roman entertainment infrastructure — amphitheaters, theaters, circuses — transforms urban leisure; public baths become centers of sociability; indigenous festivals persist alongside Roman religious calendars; elite sociability revolves around banquets and patronage networks.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: A new status hierarchy emerges: Roman citizens at the apex, Latinized provincial elites obtaining citizenship, free peregrini (non-citizens) in the middle, slaves at the bottom; indigenous ethnic distinctions blur as Latinization proceeds; the rigid citizen/non-citizen divide softens over the period as citizenship spreads.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: Roman provincial administration establishes governors, procurators, and a hierarchy of conventus and civitates; tax rolls, census records, and legal documents create a paper trail that fixes obligations; administrative capacity deepens as provincial infrastructure matures; corruption exists but is constrained by imperial oversight.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: Roman legions complete the conquest by 19 BCE and thereafter garrison the northwest; auxiliary units recruited locally police the interior; the apparatus of force is overwhelming and resistance after the Cantabrian Wars becomes futile; fortifications protect key points but the interior pacifies.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: Indigenous resistance collapses after two centuries of war; banditry persists in mountain zones but poses no systemic threat; the social friction of conquest — mass enslavement, land confiscation, cultural disruption — is absorbed rather than discharged as the system stabilizes under the Principate.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: Indigenous leaders — Viriathus, the defenders of Numantia — command fierce loyalty in resistance; after conquest, authority shifts to Roman governors and provincial elites who derive personal pull from their connection to imperial power; charismatic indigenous leadership is crushed or co-opted.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: Roman rule initially lacks legitimacy among conquered peoples; over generations, the benefits of peace, trade, and access to citizenship build acquiescence; by 100 CE, provincial elites actively identify with Rome and seek imperial honors; legitimacy is constructed, not inherited.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: Rome's will to conquer and hold Hispania is implacable, sustained across two centuries of costly wars; indigenous will to resist fragments as tribes are defeated piecemeal; after pacification, political will flows through provincial councils and municipal governments within Roman structures.

External Relations & Posture: Hispania shifts from a theater of conquest to a pacified interior province; its external posture is passive, supplying troops and tribute to imperial campaigns elsewhere; no external threat presses the peninsula after the Cantabrian Wars; the provinces face inward toward Rome.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: The conquest era breeds fear, defiance, and despair among indigenous populations; as Roman peace consolidates, a resigned acceptance and gradual identification with the empire spreads among elites; trust extends along patronage networks but interethnic suspicion lingers.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: The exhaustion of resistance leaves a residue of cultural disruption and identity loss among indigenous populations; this disaffection fades over generations as Romanization creates new identities; by the late 1st century CE, the will has re-anchored around provincial Roman identity.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Latin spreads as the administrative and elite language, displacing Iberian, Celtiberian, and Lusitanian scripts; bilingualism is common during the transition; by 100 CE, Latin dominates public life while indigenous languages survive in rural speech; literacy remains confined to elites, administrators, and scribes.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Roman roads and the cursus publicus (imperial post) accelerate message transmission; couriers carry official dispatches across the province in days; informal communication follows trade routes; the channel network is denser and faster than anything preceding it.

Record, Storage & Persistence: The manuscript regime takes hold: census records, tax registers, military diplomas, legal contracts, and municipal archives fix information beyond living memory; records are stored in provincial capitals and municipal tabularia; papyrus and wooden tablets serve as media; persistence is systematic but vulnerable to fire and neglect.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: Imperial ideology frames discourse; public inscriptions celebrate Roman power and benefaction; censorship is light but criticism of emperors can be dangerous; discourse norms favor Latin eloquence and Greco-Roman cultural references; indigenous traditions are marginalized in the written record.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: Public inscriptions, monuments, and official proclamations reach urban populations; amplification follows patronage networks and trade routes; rural populations receive information through markets and periodic gatherings; attention concentrates on imperial news and local affairs.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: The manuscript system reduces noise by fixing information in durable form; forgery and interpolation remain possible but are constrained by archival cross-reference; the signal-to-noise ratio improves over oral transmission; surveillance is limited to politically sensitive matters.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Roman justice coexists with indigenous customary norms; the provincial population gradually internalizes Roman concepts of law, contract, and citizenship; a hybrid sense of justice emerges, acknowledging Roman authority while preserving local expectations of reciprocity and honor.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: Roman law extends to the provinces through edicts, senatus consulta, and imperial constitutions; local custom is incorporated where not contradictory; the lex provinciae establishes the framework; written law displaces oral custom as the authoritative source.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: Roman courts handle serious cases; municipal magistrates judge local disputes; the governor's tribunal is the court of last resort; liability follows Roman categories; sanctions range from fines to exile to death; adjudication capacity keeps pace with caseload in the pacified provinces.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Roman citizens enjoy legal protections; non-citizens have limited standing; the compliance burden of taxation and military service is heavy but predictable; rights expand as citizenship spreads; the rule framework is more regularized than indigenous alternatives.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: Provincial governors sometimes abuse their power; slaves have no legal recourse; conquered peoples suffer mass enslavement and land confiscation without redress; impunity exists at the margins but the system delivers rough justice for those within its protection.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: Hispania imports Greco-Roman intellectual traditions rather than generating them; provincial elites educate their sons in rhetoric, philosophy, and literature; the paradigm is receptive rather than innovative during this period; natural philosophy and history are studied but the discovery frontier lies elsewhere.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Roman engineering — roads, bridges, aqueducts, mines — transfers to the peninsula; hydraulic mining at Las Medulas represents cutting-edge technique; agricultural methods improve with Roman tools and crop rotations; technical knowledge spreads through military and civilian channels.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: Elite education follows Greco-Roman models; grammatici and rhetores teach in provincial cities; literacy is confined to perhaps 10-15% of the urban population, lower in rural areas; the knowledge stock is imported from Rome and Greece; local schools emerge in major cities.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: Indigenous Iberian and Celtiberian scripts fall out of use; oral traditions weaken as their social contexts dissolve; some indigenous technical knowledge — metallurgy, agriculture — is absorbed into Roman practice while other traditions are lost; the shift is absorptive rather than catastrophic.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: Indigenous identities — Iberian, Celtiberian, Lusitanian, Turdetanian — persist in rural memory but lose political salience; new Hispano-Roman identities form around provincial and municipal belonging; the foundational mythos shifts from tribal origins to Roman foundation stories and the civilizing mission.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: Roman rule is legitimated through the narrative of pacification, civilization, and incorporation into the universal empire; public monuments celebrate military victory and imperial benefaction; the ideology of Romanitas offers a positive identity to provincial elites who embrace it.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: Roman styles dominate public architecture — forums, temples, amphitheaters, baths — while domestic material culture hybridizes Roman and indigenous elements; Latin inscriptions mark the landscape; coinage carries imperial imagery; dress shifts toward Roman fashions among elites while rural populations retain indigenous elements.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: Indigenous artistic forms — Iberian sculpture, Celtiberian metalwork — decline as their social context dissolves; Roman forms arrive fresh and vital; no exhaustion marks this period of active cultural transfer; meaning is created rather than decayed as new hybrid identities form.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: Indigenous polytheisms encounter and syncretize with Roman religion; the Greco-Roman cosmology of ordered universe under divine providence spreads among elites; existential outlook shifts from tribal to imperial, from local gods to universal cult; fatalism and piety coexist.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: Roman public cult — the Capitoline triad, the imperial cult — is established in provincial centers; indigenous deities are assimilated to Roman equivalents (interpretatio romana); domestic cult, ancestor veneration, and rural shrines continue; the sacred calendar blends Roman festivals with local observances.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: Priesthoods follow Roman models; provincial councils administer the imperial cult; no centralized doctrinal authority exists; indigenous priestly classes lose their social base; religious institutions serve political integration as much as spiritual need.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: Roman religion absorbs and reframes indigenous cults rather than displacing them entirely; mystery religions from the eastern Mediterranean — Isis, Mithras — begin to appear; Judaism exists in small communities; Christianity arrives by the 2nd century but remains marginal; the direction is toward syncretic imperial religion.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: The conquest disrupts sacred landscapes and priestly orders; some sacredness drains from indigenous sites reframed as Roman; yet new sacred meanings attach to imperial cult and imported deities; the period is one of transformation rather than disenchantment; spiritual need is redirected rather than left unfilled.

docs.title: 1031 CE – 1212 CE — Taifa Fragmentation and Reconquista Advance
docs.text: Summary: The Iberian Peninsula during the collapse of the Cordoban Caliphate and the accelerating Christian southward expansion, bound by the Manuscript Stage constraint where external records kept outside the body become the medium public life runs on. The binding constraint is the documentary apparatus of competing polities: taifa courts issuing decrees in Arabic, Christian kingdoms generating fueros, donation charters, and administrative records in Latin and emerging vernaculars, with the fragmentation of political authority multiplying centers of manuscript production even as the translation of Arabic learning into Latin begins reshaping intellectual life across the region.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: The peninsula's geography shapes the reconquest dynamic: the Meseta's open plateau permits cavalry operations and mobile warfare; the Tagus, Guadiana, and Guadalquivir valleys channel advance and mark defensive lines; mountain ranges like the Sierra Morena and Sistema Central provide fallback positions; Mediterranean and Atlantic coasts offer separate axes for Aragonese-Catalan and Portuguese expansion respectively.

Climate Regime & Volatility: The Medieval Warm Period continues, favoring agricultural colonization of newly conquered territories; the Ebro and Guadalquivir valleys produce surplus grain; irrigation networks inherited from Al-Andalus sustain intensive horticulture in Valencia and Murcia; periodic droughts stress southern taifa economies, compounding political fragmentation.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: Seismic activity in the Pyrenees and Betic ranges poses localized risk; flooding in river valleys disrupts agriculture periodically; the absence of catastrophic volcanic or climatic events allows military campaigns to proceed on predictable seasonal cycles.

Resource & Energy Endowment: Iron deposits in the Basque Country and Catalonia supply weapon forges; Andalusian silver and gold reserves fund taifa tribute payments (parias) to Christian kings; mercury from Almaden, salt from multiple coastal and interior sites, and timber from northern forests provide strategic materials.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Urban centers in both taifas and Christian kingdoms generate modest waste loads absorbed by surrounding agricultural hinterlands; abandoned or depopulated frontier zones recover quickly; no evidence of significant environmental degradation constrains the period.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: Endemic diseases persist at pre-plague Mediterranean baseline levels; periodic local epidemics occur but no peninsula-wide pestilence disrupts demographic trends; warfare deaths concentrate among military classes rather than civilian populations except in sieges.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: Irrigated agriculture in Al-Andalus territories produces varied diet including fruits, vegetables, and grains; Christian territories rely more heavily on cereals, legumes, and pastoral products; overall nutritional adequacy supports population growth in both zones.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Arabic medical manuscripts and practices, translated and adapted, provide the most advanced healing knowledge; hospitals in major cities serve urban populations; monastic infirmaries care for Christian communities; battlefield casualties rely on limited surgical knowledge.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Marriage patterns follow religious law: Islamic polygyny among elites, Christian monogamy enforced by church; interfaith unions occur in frontier zones despite prohibitions; elite marriage alliances cement political agreements across kingdoms.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Christian north experiences steady population growth, generating pressure for southward expansion and colonization; taifa territories maintain denser populations in irrigated zones; frontier warfare and resettlement create demographic flux in contested regions.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: Warfare casualties fall disproportionately on military-age males; widows and orphans in frontier communities rely on kin networks and ecclesiastical charity; monastic institutions absorb some dependent population.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: Agricultural systems vary by region: irrigated horticulture in Andalusia and Levante, dryland cereals on the Meseta, pastoral economies in mountains; newly conquered lands redistributed through fueros establish peasant holdings while reserving lands for military orders and nobility.

Energy Capture & Conversion: Human and animal muscle power predominates; water mills expand along Iberian rivers for grain processing; irrigation systems in former Al-Andalus territories represent sophisticated hydraulic engineering captured and maintained by Christian conquerors.

Labor Organization & Coercion: Mudejars (Muslims under Christian rule) work conquered lands as free peasants or sharecroppers; serfdom exists but is less prevalent than in northern Europe; slave labor from captives supplements agricultural and domestic work; frontier fueros often grant favorable terms to attract settlers.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Taifa economies generate surplus through intensive agriculture, textile production, and metalwork; Christian kingdoms expand productive capacity through colonization; Toledo, Cordoba, Seville, and Valencia remain major manufacturing centers for textiles, leather, ceramics, and metalwork.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: Urban granaries and commercial storage in major trading centers buffer against harvest failure; chronic warfare depletes reserves in contested zones; parias payments drain taifa treasuries while enriching Christian monarchs.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: Trans-Mediterranean trade connects Iberian ports to North Africa, Italy, and the Levant; overland routes link Christian kingdoms to France and beyond; Muslim and Jewish merchants facilitate cross-religious commerce; gold dinars and silver dirhams circulate alongside emerging Christian coinage.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: Jewish and Muslim merchants operate credit networks spanning the Mediterranean; bills of exchange facilitate long-distance trade; parias payments constitute systematic tribute extraction from taifas to Christian kingdoms, denominated in gold and recorded in royal archives.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: Christian kings extract tribute from taifas through parias system; within kingdoms, royal taxation, ecclesiastical tithes, and seigneurial dues claim agricultural surplus; military orders receive extensive land grants funded by conquest.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Conquest redistributes wealth from Muslim to Christian elites; military orders accumulate vast landholdings; Jewish communities maintain commercial wealth while facing increasing restrictions; nobility consolidates territorial holdings through royal grants.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Urban craft production generates waste absorbed by surrounding agricultural zones; tanning and dyeing industries in cities like Cordoba and Toledo create localized pollution; no systemic environmental degradation evident at regional scale.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Noble lineages consolidate through primogeniture and strategic marriage; partible inheritance among commoners in some regions fragments holdings; Islamic inheritance law applies in taifas and among mudejars; Jewish communities follow rabbinic law.

Association & Mutual Aid: Urban guilds emerge in Christian cities, particularly in textile and metal trades; confraternities provide mutual aid and funeral benefits; Jewish aljamas and Muslim morerías constitute semi-autonomous communities with internal governance; frontier communities develop cooperative defense arrangements.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: Tournaments, hunting, and feasting occupy noble leisure; saints' days and religious festivals structure popular recreation; cross-cultural contact in frontier zones produces cultural exchange in music, poetry, and material culture despite religious boundaries.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: Religious identity constitutes primary social boundary: Christians, Muslims, Jews each occupy defined legal positions; within Christian society, nobility, clergy, and commons form distinct orders; conversos (converts) occupy ambiguous status; mudejars and Jews face increasing restrictions.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: Royal chanceries produce growing documentary output in Latin and vernacular; episcopal and monastic scriptoria maintain ecclesiastical records; taifa courts continue Arabic administrative traditions; fueros codify local law and privileges; the documentary apparatus of governance multiplies with political fragmentation.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: Heavy cavalry dominates warfare; castle networks define territorial control; military orders (Templars, Hospitallers, Calatrava, Santiago, Alcantara) institutionalize frontier warfare; Almoravid and Almohad interventions introduce North African military systems; fortification and siege warfare define Reconquista rhythm.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: Frontier violence, raiding, and captive-taking constitute endemic disorder; disputed successions trigger civil conflicts within kingdoms; taifa fragmentation produces chronic inter-Muslim warfare; factional conflicts among nobility destabilize royal authority periodically.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: Charismatic kings like Alfonso VI of Castile-Leon and Alfonso I of Aragon lead major conquests; the Cid (Rodrigo Diaz de Vivar) exemplifies frontier warrior leadership; Almoravid and Almohad commanders bring disciplined religious zeal; bishops and abbots exercise moral authority alongside secular lords.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: Christian kings claim legitimacy through lineage, divine sanction, and crusading achievement; taifa rulers face legitimacy deficits from fragmentation and dependence on Christian tribute arrangements; Almoravid and Almohad rulers claim reformist religious authority.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: Sustained reconquest momentum demonstrates Christian political will; taifa fragmentation reflects failure of collective Muslim resistance; periodic crusading campaigns (Las Navas de Tolosa 1212) mobilize pan-Iberian Christian coalitions.

External Relations & Posture: Christian kingdoms cultivate ties to papacy and French nobility; Almoravid and Almohad dynasties connect Iberia to North African empires; commercial relations with Italian city-states intensify; pilgrimage to Santiago de Compostela links Iberia to European Christendom.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: Crusading fervor mobilizes Christian populations for reconquest; taifa courts maintain refined cultural patronage despite political insecurity; frontier communities develop pragmatic tolerance alongside religious hostility; popular anti-Muslim sentiment intensifies with Almohad invasions.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: Taifa populations exhibit resignation to Christian advance; internal conflicts within Christian kingdoms periodically divert crusading energy; mudejar communities adapt to Christian rule with varying degrees of accommodation and resistance.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Arabic remains the language of learning and administration in taifa territories; Latin dominates ecclesiastical and royal documentation in Christian kingdoms; Romance vernaculars emerge in everyday speech and increasingly in written form; Hebrew serves Jewish religious and commercial communities; multilingual intermediaries enable cross-cultural communication.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Royal messengers carry official correspondence between courts; merchants transmit commercial information along trade routes; pilgrimage routes carry religious and cultural information; manuscript copying in scriptoria multiplies texts slowly but systematically.

Record, Storage & Persistence: Cathedral and monastic archives preserve charters and administrative records; royal chanceries develop systematic record-keeping; Arabic libraries in taifa capitals maintain philosophical and scientific texts; the translation movement in Toledo transfers Arabic learning to Latin manuscripts, creating a new documentary corpus for European scholarship.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: Religious authorities police doctrinal boundaries in all three traditions; crusading rhetoric frames Muslim presence as requiring elimination; Christian chroniclers construct narratives of reconquest legitimacy; Arabic court poetry celebrates refined culture despite political decline.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: Manuscript circulation limits audience to literate elites; sermon and oral recitation reach broader populations; epic poetry (Cantar de Mio Cid) transmits heroic narratives across social strata; legal texts (fueros) communicate rights and obligations to affected communities.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: Archival preservation in stone buildings protects manuscripts from decay; war and conquest destroy some Arabic libraries; copying errors accumulate in manuscript transmission; competing chronicle traditions generate conflicting historical narratives.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Religious law provides moral foundation in all three traditions; crusading ideology justifies violence against Muslims; chivalric codes regulate noble conduct; fueros establish local justice norms balancing royal authority with community rights.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: Fueros proliferate as conquest generates new communities requiring legal frameworks; Visigothic legal traditions persist in modified form; Islamic law continues in taifas and among mudejars; Jewish communities apply rabbinic law internally; the diversity of legal frameworks reflects political fragmentation.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: Royal and seigneurial courts adjudicate disputes within their jurisdictions; ecclesiastical courts claim jurisdiction over clergy and certain moral offenses; frontier justice often depends on local power rather than formal procedure; ordeal and judicial combat persist alongside emerging rational procedure.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Fueros grant specific rights and obligations to settlers; mudejars and Jews hold defined but subordinate legal status; nobility claims exemptions from common obligations; church properties enjoy immunity from secular taxation.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: Frontier violence generates unpunished wrongs; powerful nobles evade royal justice; captive-taking and ransom operate outside formal legal framework; conquest itself redistributes property without compensation to dispossessed.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: The translation movement transforms European intellectual life: Arabic versions of Aristotle, Ptolemy, Galen, and their commentators enter Latin circulation through Toledo; Gerard of Cremona translates over eighty works; astronomical tables, medical treatises, and philosophical texts reshape scholastic inquiry; Jewish scholars contribute translations and original work in philosophy and science.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Irrigation techniques transfer from Muslim to Christian cultivators; Andalusian metalwork, textile, and ceramic methods continue under new rule; military engineering in fortification and siege craft advances; navigational knowledge develops along Mediterranean and Atlantic coasts.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: Cathedral schools in Toledo, Barcelona, and elsewhere train clergy in Latin learning; Arabic and Hebrew education continues in respective communities; the translation movement creates a new Latin knowledge stock accessible to European scholars; literacy remains confined to clerical, administrative, and commercial elites.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: Some Arabic libraries destroyed in conquest; knowledge not translated into Latin remains inaccessible to Christian scholars; practical techniques survive conquest better than theoretical learning; oral traditions of mudejar communities gradually erode under Christian rule.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: Reconquista ideology constructs Christian Iberia as continuous with Visigothic kingdom, defining Muslim presence as interruption requiring reversal; Santiago (Saint James) emerges as patron of reconquest; the Cid becomes legendary hero; taifa courts cultivate memory of Cordoban golden age; Jewish communities maintain diaspora identity and Sephardic distinctiveness.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: Christian kings claim divine mandate for reconquest; papal endorsement confers crusading legitimacy; Almoravid and Almohad rulers deploy reformist Islamic ideology against taifa decadence; chronicle writing constructs historical narratives supporting current claims.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: Mudejar architecture blends Islamic decorative techniques with Christian patronage; Romanesque churches spread across northern Spain; illuminated manuscripts in scriptoria produce distinctive Iberian styles; textile, ceramic, and metalwork industries continue Andalusian traditions; troubadour poetry flourishes in Catalonia and Portugal-Galicia.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: Taifa court culture maintains refinement despite political decline; convivencia model strains under intensified crusading pressure and Almohad intolerance; some cultural forms fossilize as communities lose political autonomy; the translation movement renews Latin intellectual culture with Arabic learning.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: Crusading ideology frames reconquest as sacred duty; Islamic fatalism accepts divine will in political reverses while maintaining ultimate confidence in the faith; Jewish messianic hopes persist amid political marginalization; pilgrimage to Santiago expresses Christian devotion and Iberian identity.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: Latin liturgy spreads with reconquest, replacing Mozarabic rite in some regions; Islamic prayer, fasting, and pilgrimage obligation continue in taifas and mudejar communities; Jewish Sabbath, dietary law, and festival observance maintain communal identity; relics and saints' cults proliferate.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: Gregorian reform strengthens papal authority over Iberian churches; military orders combine monastic discipline with crusading warfare; Almoravid and Almohad movements enforce strict Islamic orthodoxy; Jewish communities maintain rabbinic authority through academies and responsa literature.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: Christianity expands geographically with reconquest; Islam contracts but intensifies under Almoravid and Almohad reform; some conversion occurs in both directions; interfaith intellectual exchange continues despite hardening religious boundaries; kabbalah develops in Jewish communities of Catalonia and Castile.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: No significant secularizing trend evident; religious commitment intensifies on all sides; crusading fervor and jihad rhetoric frame conflict in maximalist sacred terms; the period represents religious mobilization rather than disenchantment.

docs.title: 756 CE – 1031 CE — Umayyad Cordoba and Andalusian Manuscript Florescence
docs.text: Summary: The Manuscript Stage's binding constraint — external records kept outside the body becoming the medium public life runs on — here reaches its Iberian apogee as the Umayyad emirate and caliphate of Cordoba builds the largest library in Western Europe, supports Arabic manuscript production across philosophy, medicine, astronomy, poetry, and religious sciences, and establishes the documentary infrastructure that makes Al-Andalus a peer to Baghdad and Constantinople, with paper manufacture arriving by the eleventh century to multiply the substrate's abundance.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: Cordoba, astride the Guadalquivir at the Meseta's southern edge, commands the fertile lowlands while the Sierra Morena screens the north; the Mediterranean coast from Almeria to Tortosa provides sea access to the Islamic East; the Duero valley frontier with Christian kingdoms hardens into a marchland of castles and ribats.

Climate Regime & Volatility: The Medieval Warm Period (onset ~900 CE) lengthens growing seasons and raises yields across Andalusia; periodic droughts stress the irrigated huerta but do not collapse the system; Atlantic moisture sustains the Christian north, enabling its demographic recovery.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: Seismic risk persists along the Betic zone; a damaging earthquake strikes Cordoba in 881 CE, requiring mosque and palace repairs; flash floods in the Guadalquivir tributaries occasionally disrupt harvests but are absorbed by the buffered agrarian system.

Resource & Energy Endowment: Silver from the Sierra Morena funds state expenditure; iron from the Basque marches and North African trade routes supplies armament; olive oil, grain, and silk from Andalusian estates generate exportable surplus; esparto grass and, by the eleventh century, rag-based paper pulp provide writing substrates.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Urban Cordoba, population perhaps 100,000–500,000 at its peak, produces substantial organic waste; the Guadalquivir absorbs sewage, while municipal hisba regulations manage refuse; no systemic sink crisis is recorded, though localized nuisance complaints appear in legal texts.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: Endemic Mediterranean fevers, dysentery, and intestinal parasites persist; urban density in Cordoba elevates transmission, but no catastrophic epidemic is recorded during the caliphal apogee; smallpox circulates but does not reach pandemic intensity.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: Irrigated agriculture — citrus, rice, sugarcane, vegetables — diversifies the Andalusian diet; grain surplus keeps famine rare in the core; caloric intake and stature likely exceed contemporary Christian Europe; the north remains more dependent on grain and livestock.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Galenic and Arabic medical traditions merge in Cordoban practice; physicians (tabib) serve the court and urban elites; bimaristans (hospitals) appear by the tenth century; the poor rely on folk remedy and charitable dispensaries attached to mosques.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Polygyny among elites and concubinage with enslaved women produce large elite households; muwallad families (Iberian converts) adopt Arab kinship norms; interfaith marriage is asymmetric — Muslim men may wed Christian or Jewish women, the reverse prohibited — shaping demographic flows toward Islam.
