docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Written Japanese (kanji-kana mixed script) serves administrative, literary, and commercial functions; classical Chinese (kanbun) remains the prestige medium for official documents, Buddhist texts, and scholarship; literacy concentrates among warriors, clergy, and urban merchants.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Couriers and relay stations (later formalized as the gokaido system) carry official communications; the Tōkaidō route enables Kyoto-Edo transmission in approximately two weeks; local information circulates through temple networks and merchant travel.

Record, Storage & Persistence: Manuscript remains the dominant medium; domain archives accumulate administrative records, land surveys (kenchi), and household registers; temple archives preserve religious texts and parish records; the bakufu establishes documentary requirements for domain governance.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: Tokugawa authority controls official narrative through chronicle sponsorship and temple regulation; Christian texts face prohibition and destruction (intensifying through 1612–1614 edicts); political criticism remains dangerous though literary expression continues relatively free.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: Elite audiences receive texts through manuscript circulation, reading aloud, and performance (Nō, puppet theater); commoner access to written material remains limited outside urban centers; oral transmission carries news and rumor.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: Official documentation achieves high reliability through bureaucratic verification; manuscript copying introduces scribal variation but maintains functional accuracy; rumor and misinformation circulate regarding Osaka campaign events but are eventually settled by official accounts.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Loyalty (chū) to lord and domain structures warrior ethics; Buddhist karmic causation and Confucian social hierarchy provide complementary moral frameworks; revenge obligations (katakiuchi) remain legitimate under regulated conditions.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: The bakufu issues the Buke Shohatto (Laws for Warrior Households, 1615) and Kinchū Narabini Kuge Shohatto (Laws for the Imperial Court and Nobility, 1615), establishing written codes governing daimyō and courtiers; domain laws regulate local populations; the Kōsatsu (public notice boards) announce regulations to commoners.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: Domain lords exercise judicial authority within their territories; the bakufu adjudicates inter-domain disputes and supervises daimyō conduct; punishments include execution, exile, confiscation, and domain transfer; vendetta operates under regulated procedures.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Status determines obligations and protections; warriors owe military service and receive stipends; peasants owe tax and receive cultivation rights; the compliance burden is substantial but predictable under stable administration.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: The defeated have no recourse; Toyotomi survivors face execution or exile without appeal; victorious daimyō enjoy wide discretion within their domains; the shogunate monopolizes ultimate judgment while tolerating substantial domain autonomy.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: Neo-Confucian thought (especially Zhu Xi school) gains bakufu favor as a framework for social order; Buddhist scholasticism continues in major temples; empirical inquiry remains limited to practical domains (medicine, agriculture, military science).

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Surveying techniques enable accurate land assessment; castle engineering reaches sophisticated levels before construction ceases; firearms manufacture is mastered though innovation slows without competitive pressure; Korean captive artisans introduce ceramic techniques.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: Temple schools provide basic literacy to elite children; domain schools for warrior families emerge; Confucian scholars find patronage at Kyoto and domain courts; the Jesuit mission schools close with the Christian suppression.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: Military techniques developed during Sengoku warfare begin losing relevance as peace prevails; Jesuit-introduced knowledge (European science, movable type) is partially suppressed or abandoned; earlier manuscript traditions continue with gradual copying loss.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: The imperial house retains mythological authority as descendant of Amaterasu; warrior identity draws on medieval tale traditions (Heike, Taiheiki); the Tokugawa cultivate a legitimating narrative linking their house to the Minamoto through genealogical construction.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: The bakufu presents itself as restorer of order after a century of warfare; Confucian framing emphasizes hierarchical harmony under benevolent rule; the destruction of Osaka is narrated as necessary elimination of disruptive elements threatening peace.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: Momoyama aesthetic of gold leaf, bold color, and monumental scale persists in castle interiors and screen paintings; the Kanō school dominates official art; tea ceremony maintains refined simplicity; Nō drama continues under warrior patronage; early kabuki emerges in Kyoto pleasure quarters.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: The Momoyama exuberance shows no exhaustion in this window; rather, the end of warfare enables concentrated patronage and refinement; form-fatigue is minimal as new political circumstances generate fresh commemorative and celebratory expression.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: Buddhist karma, Shinto kami, and Confucian cosmic order coexist in layered complementarity; Pure Land Buddhism's promise of salvation through faith appeals broadly; the impermanence (mujō) of worldly glory remains a persistent theme.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: Temple attendance, festival participation, and household devotion continue established patterns; pilgrimage routes attract travelers; funeral rites and memorial services structure the household relationship with the dead; Christian practice is driven underground (the kakure kirishitan).

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: The bakufu mandates temple registration (terauke) for all households, incorporating Buddhist institutions into state surveillance; major temple-shrine complexes retain landed wealth and local influence; Christian institutions are destroyed and missionaries expelled or executed.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: Christianity faces comprehensive suppression after 1614; Buddhist sectarian boundaries harden under bakufu regulation; Shinto shrines operate in complementary relationship with Buddhist temples through the shinbutsu-shūgō synthesis; Confucian ethics penetrate warrior education without displacing Buddhist soteriology.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: No significant disenchantment occurs; rather, the elimination of Christian competition and the routinization of Buddhist registration channel spiritual practice into stable institutional forms; existential security accompanies political pacification; the sacred remains vividly present in daily practice and annual ritual.

docs.title: 1568 CE – 1600 CE — Unification Wars and Azuchi-Momoyama Era
docs.text: Summary: Three successive warlords — Oda Nobunaga, Toyotomi Hideyoshi, and Tokugawa Ieyasu — consolidated Japan through innovative warfare and administration, while manuscript culture reached its apogee as cadastral surveys, diplomatic correspondence, and house codes documented the emerging unified state, even as Jesuit and Korean movable type introduced the technology that would soon transform information circulation.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: The central Kinai region around Kyoto and the approaches to it from Owari and Mino became the strategic focus as Nobunaga fought his way to supremacy; the archipelago's mountainous terrain required each province to be subdued individually, making unification a decades-long military campaign across distinct geographic compartments.

Climate Regime & Volatility: The late sixteenth century fell within the early phase of the Little Ice Age, with cooler and more variable conditions than the medieval optimum; agricultural productivity remained sufficient for the armies fielded, but climate stress may have contributed to the desperate quality of the final resistance to unification.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: The 1586 Tensho earthquake devastated central Honshu, destroying castles and disrupting Hideyoshi's consolidation; tsunamis, typhoons, and floods continued to strike unpredictably; the Korean campaigns (1592-1598) exposed armies to unfamiliar disease environments.

Resource & Energy Endowment: Gold and silver production peaked as mining technology improved; the Iwami Ginzan, Sado, and Kai gold mines poured bullion into the unifiers' treasuries; iron for weapons and timber for castle construction were systematically exploited; Nobunaga's control of productive Owari and Mino provinces provided his initial economic base.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Castle town construction and naval shipbuilding accelerated deforestation; battlefield carnage and the destruction of enemy territories left localized devastation; the scale of military operations exceeded anything in previous Japanese history.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: Endemic diseases persisted; the Korean campaigns exposed Japanese armies to different disease environments with significant mortality; the displacement of populations during unification campaigns created conditions for epidemic spread in some regions.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: The end of chronic warfare allowed agricultural recovery in pacified regions; Hideyoshi's cadastral surveys (kenchi) rationalized taxation and may have reduced the arbitrary exactions that had impoverished peasants; nutritional status likely improved in the final decade of the period.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Military medicine advanced through practical necessity; Jesuit missionaries introduced European medical knowledge alongside Christianity; temple-based care continued; the wars produced large numbers of wounded requiring treatment.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: The unifiers used marriage strategically to bind subordinate daimyo; Hideyoshi's elevation from peasant origins demonstrated that talent could transcend birth; the samurai class began to crystallize as a hereditary status group.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Population probably reached 15-18 million by 1600; the cessation of endemic warfare removed a constant drain on manpower; urbanization accelerated as castle towns became administrative and commercial centers.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: The pacification process created numerous dispossessed warriors from defeated houses; these ronin would remain a social problem; war widows and orphans found varying degrees of support in the consolidating social order.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: Hideyoshi's nationwide cadastral surveys standardized land measurement and tax assessment, providing accurate information for administration and enabling more efficient extraction; the kokudaka system assessed domain wealth in rice equivalents, rationalizing the economic basis of the warrior class.

Energy Capture & Conversion: Human and animal muscle remained primary; water power served milling and some metallurgy; charcoal fueled intensive weapons production; the energy demands of building Osaka Castle and other massive construction projects mobilized unprecedented labor forces.

Labor Organization & Coercion: Hideyoshi's separation edicts (1588-1591) fixed peasants to the land and reserved weapons-bearing to samurai, beginning the crystallization of status categories; corvee labor built castles and infrastructure; the Korean campaigns forcibly relocated thousands of Korean artisans to Japan.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Agricultural production increased as warfare ended and investment in irrigation resumed; craft production concentrated in castle towns achieved new scales; the Portuguese trade brought Chinese silk in exchange for Japanese silver at enormous profit.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: The great castles incorporated massive rice storehouses; Osaka Castle became the center of a national logistics system; Hideyoshi accumulated unprecedented wealth that funded the Korean campaigns and grandiose building projects.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: Maritime trade expanded dramatically; the nanban (Southern Barbarian) trade with Portuguese and Spanish merchants linked Japan to global commerce; Sakai, Hakata, and Nagasaki served as entrepots; Hideyoshi's issuing of vermilion-seal ships regularized foreign trade authorization.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: Gold and silver coinage began to supplement copper coins; Hideyoshi minted gold coins (koban) that would become the basis of Tokugawa currency; merchant houses extended credit on an unprecedented scale to finance trade and military logistics.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: The cadastral surveys enabled systematic taxation at approximately 40% of assessed yield; confiscated lands from defeated daimyo were redistributed to loyal followers; Hideyoshi's personal domains yielded enormous revenue.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Wealth concentrated dramatically in unifier hands; Osaka Castle's treasury held vast stores of gold, silver, and rice; defeated daimyo lost everything while successful retainers rose to great wealth; the merchant class of port cities accumulated commercial fortunes.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Construction debris from castle building, battlefield carnage, and the devastation of resistant territories accumulated; the Korean campaigns left destruction across the peninsula; captured Korean artisans including potters established new craft traditions in Japan.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Hideyoshi's lack of a capable heir proved decisive; adoption and succession politics dominated the final years; the Tokugawa house carefully cultivated lineage claims while building vassal networks through marriage alliance; kinship remained central to political organization.

Association & Mutual Aid: Village communities (mura) were formalized as administrative units under the cadastral system; guilds and merchant associations continued to operate in castle towns; temple networks provided mutual aid and communication channels.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: Tea ceremony reached its classical form under Sen no Rikyu's guidance, patronized by both Nobunaga and Hideyoshi; Noh drama was performed at official occasions; Hideyoshi staged elaborate entertainments demonstrating his magnificence.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: The separation edicts created rigid status categories (shi-no-ko-sho: warrior, farmer, artisan, merchant) that would characterize Tokugawa society; social mobility that had characterized Sengoku narrowed dramatically; Hideyoshi's own rise from peasant to supreme ruler would become impossible under the system he created.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: The unifiers built sophisticated administrative machines; cadastral surveys required trained staff and systematic record-keeping; correspondence archives documented diplomacy and command; the five magistrates (go-bugyo) and council of regents (go-tairo) that Hideyoshi established to govern after his death represented institutional solutions to succession problems.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: Armies reached unprecedented sizes; firearms became standard infantry equipment; castle architecture reached its most elaborate forms; naval forces supported amphibious operations in Korea; the apparatus of military force that achieved unification would be maintained by the Tokugawa for internal control.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: The transition to peace created structural unemployment among warriors; the ronin problem would persist; the succession crisis after Hideyoshi's death (1598) produced renewed warfare culminating at Sekigahara (1600); victory there allowed Tokugawa Ieyasu to establish lasting order.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: Nobunaga combined ruthless violence with cultural patronage; Hideyoshi added diplomatic skill and organizational genius; Ieyasu embodied patient calculation; all three commanded intense personal loyalty from their followers while inspiring fear in opponents.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: Imperial appointment provided formal legitimation — Nobunaga never sought the shogunate, Hideyoshi became kampaku (regent), Ieyasu would become shogun — but real authority derived from military success and administrative effectiveness; oaths of loyalty documented in written pledges bound vassals to lords.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: The unifiers demonstrated extraordinary political will sustained over decades; their retainer bands shared commitment to victory; defeated populations acquiesced to superior force while hoping for better governance.

External Relations & Posture: Hideyoshi's Korean invasions (1592-1598) represented aggressive external posture unprecedented in Japanese history; the stated goal of conquering Ming China proved wildly unrealistic; relations with Europeans combined commercial interest with growing concern about Christian proselytizing.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: War-weariness and longing for peace coexisted with admiration for successful warlords; the dramatic rise of Hideyoshi from peasant to ruler captured popular imagination; religious movements continued to offer consolation and community.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: Resistance to unification was suppressed violently; the Ikko-ikki leagues were destroyed; Christian communities faced increasing suspicion; defeated samurai faced dispossession and social death; by 1600 the will to resist Tokugawa hegemony was largely exhausted.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Literacy continued spreading among warriors, merchants, and some commoners; the unified realm enabled standardization of administrative practices; written Japanese (kanji-kana mixture) served all domestic purposes while kanbun (classical Chinese) remained important for formal documents.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: The pacified realm enabled reliable messenger services; post stations were established along major routes; maritime communication linked distant domains; information moved faster and more reliably than during Sengoku fragmentation.

Record, Storage & Persistence: Cadastral survey documents (kenchicho) systematically recorded land holdings throughout Japan; diplomatic correspondence with Korea and Ming China was carefully preserved; Jesuit missionaries produced detailed reports for Rome; house archives documented family histories and legal precedents.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: The unifiers controlled official messaging about their achievements; Hideyoshi's humble origins were managed through elaborate genealogical fabrications; criticism of authority was dangerous; diplomatic correspondence followed elaborate formal conventions.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: War tales documenting recent events circulated in manuscript; popular religious movements spread simplified teachings; commercial entertainment in castle towns attracted growing audiences; the technology of movable type printing arrived via Jesuits (1591) and Korean captives (1593).

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: The centralization of authority reduced the deliberate disinformation of Sengoku warfare; authenticated documents with vermilion seals carried legal force; the cadastral surveys established an authoritative information base; forgery remained a concern requiring verification procedures.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Buddhist karma doctrine persisted; Confucian ethics emphasized loyalty and hierarchy; the unifiers dispensed harsh but predictable justice; peasant communities maintained customary morality; Christian converts adopted new ethical frameworks.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: Hideyoshi issued edicts with realm-wide force — sword hunts (1588), status separation (1591), restrictions on Christianity (1587) — representing a new scale of legal authority; the Council of Five Elders was charged with maintaining order after his death; house laws continued to govern individual domains.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: The unifiers served as supreme judges; punishments were public and severe, including crucifixion for serious offenses; collective responsibility bound families and villages; legal process was summary by later standards but provided some predictability.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Peasants were fixed to the land but protected from arbitrary samurai violence; merchants operated within guild structures that provided collective representation; Christian practice became illegal (1587 edict) though enforcement was initially lax.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: The powerful operated by their own rules; Nobunaga's massacre of the Enryaku-ji monks (1571) went unpunished; Hideyoshi's execution of Sen no Rikyu (1591) demonstrated arbitrary power; the defeated had no recourse beyond submission or death.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: Buddhist philosophy remained dominant though sectarian competition continued; Confucian scholarship was patronized by some daimyo; European Jesuits introduced natural philosophy, mathematics, and geography that intrigued Japanese scholars; practical military and administrative knowledge was systematically developed.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Firearms technology reached high levels with Japanese improvements on European designs; castle architecture achieved its most sophisticated forms; mining technology advanced; shipbuilding enabled oceangoing vessels; printing technology arrived but manuscript remained dominant for most purposes.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: Jesuit schools educated converts including some high-ranking samurai; temple schools continued basic education; warrior households trained sons in military and administrative skills; Korean artisans brought ceramic and other craft techniques.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: The destruction of the Enryaku-ji library represented significant knowledge loss; some esoteric Buddhist traditions declined; classical court learning survived in attenuated form; practical knowledge displaced speculative scholarship.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: Imperial mythology remained foundational though practically irrelevant; warrior house identity emphasized martial achievement and loyal service; the drama of unification was beginning to generate its own heroic narratives; regional identities persisted beneath the emerging national framework.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: Hideyoshi constructed elaborate fictitious genealogies to justify his unprecedented rise; the Tokugawa would develop sophisticated ideological justifications for their rule; military success remained the ultimate proof of legitimacy; divine favor was claimed by all sides.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: The Azuchi-Momoyama aesthetic combined gold, bold colors, and monumental scale; castle keeps (tenshu) reached their most elaborate forms; screen paintings depicted scenes of grandeur; tea ceremony utensils were valued as political gifts; gorgeous textiles and lacquerware demonstrated wealth and taste.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: Classical court culture persisted marginally in Kyoto; new warrior aesthetics displaced traditional refinement; some tea masters like Rikyu sought simplicity against Hideyoshi's love of gold; religious forms were disrupted by the destruction of major temple complexes.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: Buddhist impermanence remained a dominant theme, dramatized by the violent deaths of great lords; Pure Land faith offered salvation through devotion; Zen discipline appealed to warriors; Christianity introduced radically different cosmology emphasizing salvation through Christ.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: Buddhist funerary rites continued universally; tea ceremony acquired quasi-sacred significance; Christian converts practiced mass and confession; Shinto rites continued at local shrines; Hideyoshi's deification after death (as Toyokuni Daimyojin) created a new cult.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: Nobunaga destroyed the military power of Buddhist temples, razing Enryaku-ji (1571) and crushing the Ikko-ikki (1580); Hideyoshi initially tolerated Christianity before restricting it (1587); the Tokugawa would make Buddhist temple registration compulsory; religious institutions lost independent political power.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: Christianity spread rapidly until restriction, claiming perhaps 300,000 converts by 1600; Buddhist schools competed for patronage from the new rulers; syncretic combinations of Buddhist, Shinto, and folk elements characterized popular religion; no single orthodoxy prevailed.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: The destruction of militant Buddhism removed a major spiritual-political force; the turn against Christianity would intensify under Tokugawa; warriors cultivated aesthetic disciplines as secular spirituality; the question of meaning in a violent world remained urgent as the era closed with the battle of Sekigahara.

docs.title: Manuscript Stage in The Mexican Highlands and Yucatan Lowlands — 400 BCE – 1810 CE

- 250 CE – 550 CE — Early Classic Maya and Teotihuacan Influence
- 550 CE – 800 CE — Late Classic Maya Florescence
- 800 CE – 1000 CE — Classic Maya Collapse and Terminal Classic
- 1000 CE – 1200 CE — Early Postclassic and Toltec Horizon
- 1200 CE – 1428 CE — Late Postclassic Transformations and Mexica Rise
- 1428 CE – 1519 CE — Aztec Empire and Tribute Administration
- 1519 CE – 1550 CE — Spanish Conquest and Early Colonial Transition
- 1550 CE – 1650 CE — Colonial Consolidation and Documentary Synthesis
- 1650 CE – 1750 CE — Mature Colonial Society and Baroque Culture
- 1750 CE – 1810 CE — Bourbon Reforms and Independence Ferment
- 400 BCE – 1810 CE — Codex Traditions Across Mesoamerican History
1428 CE – 1519 CE — Aztec Empire and Tribute Administration
docs.text: Summary: The Triple Alliance at its height stands as a tributary hegemony whose cohesion rests on the pictographic codex as instrument of state: tribute schedules, calendrical regulation, and dynastic legitimation run on painted records kept outside memory, making the administrative manuscript the binding constraint that holds the imperial fabric together against the centrifugal pull of subject polities.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: The Basin of Mexico sits at 2,240 meters on the Mesa Central, its five interconnected lakes (Texcoco, Xochimilco, Chalco, Xaltocan, Zumpango) providing waterborne transit that lowers friction within the core while surrounding mountain ranges impose steep gradients on landward approaches; Tenochtitlan occupies an island whose causeways and canoe traffic make it both defensible and logistically central, while the empire's outer provinces stretch from the Gulf coast lowlands to the Pacific littoral and southward into Oaxaca and Soconusco, each separated by rugged terrain that lengthens tribute transit to weeks of porter travel.

Climate Regime & Volatility: A semi-arid highland regime with summer monsoon rains (May–October) supports maize agriculture, though interannual variability brings periodic drought years that stress the provisioning base; the "one-rabbit" famine years recorded in annals mark failures of the rain-fed harvest, while lowland tribute zones contribute tropical products buffered against highland volatility.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: Volcanism (Popocatepetl, Iztaccihuatl) and seismic activity threaten intermittently; lake flooding periodically inundates Tenochtitlan, prompting massive dike construction (the Nezahualcoyotl dike separating salt and fresh water); frost at altitude limits the highland growing season.

Resource & Energy Endowment: Obsidian from Pachuca and Otumba sustains tool and weapon production; lacustrine clays support ceramic industries; timber from surrounding forests and tribute cotton, cacao, feathers, jade, and gold from distant provinces flow inward; no metallurgical base for bronze or iron leaves stone and wood as the primary tool substrate.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Urban concentration in Tenochtitlan (150,000–300,000 inhabitants) produces organic waste absorbed by chinampa agriculture as fertilizer; lake waters carry effluent but show no evidence of severe eutrophication; the sink remains functional within the period.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: A relatively benign disease environment compared to Old World ecumenes; no epidemic smallpox, measles, or plague circulates; endemic gastro-intestinal and parasitic infections carry baseline mortality, but no mass die-off punctuates the window; life expectancy at birth likely in the low thirties.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: Maize-bean-squash polyculture provides protein complementation; lake resources (fish, waterfowl, algae, insects) supplement calories; chinampa agriculture yields two to three harvests per year in favorable conditions; skeletal evidence suggests generally adequate nutrition among commoners, though periods of drought induce visible stress markers.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Healers (ticitl) practice herbal medicine, wound care, and obstetrics; botanical knowledge extensive (Badianus Manuscript records colonial-era preservation of pre-Columbian pharmacopoeia); temazcal sweat baths serve hygienic and therapeutic functions; no hospital institutions exist, but household and specialist care absorbs routine illness.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Polygyny among elites expands elite lineages; commoner monogamy prevails; marriage arranged through kin negotiation with gift exchange; reproductive rates sufficient to sustain population growth through the period.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Central Mexico's population reaches perhaps 15–25 million by 1519; the Basin of Mexico alone holds 1–2 million, among the densest pre-industrial concentrations; growth continues through the period, pressing against the carrying ceiling in marginal zones.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: Warfare extracts a toll of young male casualties (including sacrificial captives), but demographic structure remains balanced; orphan and widow support falls to kin networks and calpulli communal structures; no crushing dependency overhang evident.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: Chinampa raised-bed agriculture in the southern lakes (Xochimilco, Chalco) anchors the urban food supply; rain-fed terraces and irrigation in surrounding basins supplement; maize, beans, squash, chili, amaranth, and maguey provide caloric foundation; the provisioning floor sits above subsistence for most years, with tribute grain buffering shortfalls.

Energy Capture & Conversion: Human muscle remains the sole prime mover; no draft animals, no wheel for traction; porterage (tlameme) carries all overland freight at roughly 23 kilograms per porter per day; water transport on lakes and canals multiplies throughput within the basin; firewood and charcoal fuel cooking and craft production.

Labor Organization & Coercion: Commoners (macehualtin) owe labor service (tequitl) to their calpulli and to the state; war captives and slaves (tlacotin) perform domestic and agricultural labor; craft specialists (featherworkers, goldsmiths, scribes) organized in occupational wards; coercion moderate within the core, heavier in recently conquered provinces.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Intensive agriculture, craft specialization, and tribute inflows generate substantial surplus; elite consumption absorbs featherwork, textiles, and precious goods; temple and palace construction employs corvée labor; surplus extraction peaks under Motecuhzoma II's expansionist wars.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: State granaries (petlacalco) hold tribute maize; merchant (pochteca) networks provide distribution flexibility; no coined money constrains liquidity, but cacao beans and cotton cloaks (quachtli) serve as media of exchange and stores of value; reserves sufficient to absorb single-year harvest failures.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: Periodic markets (tianquiztli) operate on five-day cycles; Tlatelolco market serves 60,000 daily according to Spanish accounts; long-distance pochteca merchants carry luxury goods to and from distant provinces; no external blockade vulnerability exists, though internal route disruption by rebellious provinces occasionally interrupts tribute flow.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: Cacao beans and quachtli function as commodity money; no coinage or precious-metal currency; credit arrangements exist among merchants; tribute obligations constitute a form of deferred extraction recorded in codices.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: The Matricula de Tributos and Codex Mendoza record biannual tribute quotas from 400+ subject towns: cotton cloaks, warrior costumes, feathers, cacao, gold, foodstuffs, labor service; extraction heavy on distant provinces (up to half of local production in some accounts), lighter on core allies; redistribution flows to warriors, priests, and palace consumption.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Pipiltin nobility hold patrimonial lands (pillalli) and receive tribute shares; macehualtin hold usufruct through calpulli; social mobility possible through military achievement (commoner warriors elevated to cuauhpilli status); wealth concentration substantial but not impermeable.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Organic waste recycled into chinampa agriculture; no industrial effluent; craft production generates modest ceramic and lithic debris; no accumulated financial imbalance beyond the tribute obligations themselves.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Patrilineal descent governs inheritance of noble titles and lands; commoner households embedded in calpulli, territorial-kin units that allocate land and labor obligations; marriage strengthens inter-calpulli and inter-polity alliances.

Association & Mutual Aid: Calpulli provide mutual aid, land allocation, and collective labor mobilization; occupational guilds (featherworkers, merchants) maintain internal solidarity and ritual obligations; no autonomous civil association beyond these structures.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: Ball courts host ritual ullamaliztli games; pulque consumption accompanies festivals; market gatherings provide sociable space; calendrical festivals structure collective celebration across the year.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: Sharp divide between pipiltin nobility and macehualtin commoners; tlacotin (slaves) occupy the bottom; warrior grades confer status through captive counts; priests form a parallel hierarchy; ethnic Mexica privileged over incorporated groups; boundaries permeable through military achievement but otherwise rigid.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: Triple Alliance (excan tlatoloyan) coordinates Tenochtitlan, Texcoco, and Tlacopan, though Tenochtitlan dominates by 1500; each altepetl (city-state) under a tlatoani; tribute collectors (calpixque) stationed in provinces; codex-based record-keeping tracks obligations; administrative reach extends to 400+ subject polities but relies on local elites for enforcement; no standing provincial bureaucracy beyond tribute collection.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: Standing warrior orders (Eagle, Jaguar) supplemented by levies from calpulli; obsidian-edged macuahuitl, atlatl darts, and quilted cotton armor constitute armament; conquest warfare expands tribute base while flower wars (xochiyaoyotl) with Tlaxcala provide captives without territorial gain; fortifications minimal; coercive capacity sufficient to suppress rebellion but dependent on rapid mobilization and allied contingents.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: Subject polities periodically rebel (Chalco, Tlaxcala, Huexotzinco maintain independence or resistance); tribute exactions generate resentment exploitable by external powers; internal factional rivalry over succession occasionally erupts (succession crisis after Ahuitzotl's death 1502); the apparatus holds but resentment accumulates in the periphery.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: The tlatoani ("speaker") holds supreme authority, combining military, judicial, and ritual roles; Motecuhzoma II (r. 1502–1520) concentrates power, restricting noble access to his person; charismatic authority reinforced by ritual seclusion and cosmic framing.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: Core Mexica populations accept the tlatoani's divine-right authority; Texcoco and Tlacopan allies maintain cooperative allegiance; subject provinces comply under coercion rather than consent; legitimacy erodes at the periphery where tribute extractions outrun any reciprocal benefit.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: The warrior elite displays high resolve for expansion; succession proceeds through elite selection (not strict primogeniture), occasionally contested; Motecuhzoma II's reign shows continued expansion (Oaxaca, Soconusco) though pace slows as resistant polities (Tlaxcala, Tarascan) hold firm.

External Relations & Posture: Expansionist posture toward the unconquered; Tarascan state to the west resists incorporation; Tlaxcala and allies remain hostile enclaves within Aztec territory; long-distance trade connects to Maya and beyond; no peer competitor threatens the core, but the unconquered buffer zones reveal the limits of hegemonic reach.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: A martial ethos pervades public culture; warrior achievement honored; fatalism infused by cosmology of cyclical destruction; public sentiment in the core expresses pride in imperial ascendancy, while subject provinces harbor resentment masked by outward compliance.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: Peripheral disaffection accumulates; some evidence of war weariness among allied contingents; the Tlaxcalan-Aztec enmity hardens into irreconcilable hostility; no collapse of will in the core, but the periphery's resentment constitutes latent fragility.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Nahuatl functions as the imperial lingua franca; subject populations speak diverse languages (Otomi, Zapotec, Mixtec, Maya) with varying Nahuatl proficiency; pictographic-logographic writing accessible only to trained scribes (tlacuilos); oral proclamation carries state commands to non-literate populations.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Relay runners (paynani) transmit urgent messages at approximately 300 kilometers per day; routine information travels with porters and merchants at walking pace; no postal system but established routes and way stations facilitate official communication.

Record, Storage & Persistence: Screenfold codices (amoxtli) on bark paper (amatl) record tribute lists, genealogies, historical annals, calendrical cycles, and ritual prescriptions; state archives (amoxcalli) preserve records in Tenochtitlan and Texcoco; codices survive fire and flood poorly, requiring recopying; the Matricula de Tributos demonstrates the administrative function of written records in sustaining tribute extraction.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: Official histories (xiuhamatl) frame Mexica ascendancy as cosmic destiny; Itzcoatl's burning of earlier histories (c. 1428) indicates deliberate framing of the past; public discourse regulated by decorum and rank; commoners may not address rulers directly.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: Market criers and ritual proclamations reach mass audiences; calendrical ceremonies synchronize public attention; codex information circulates only among literate elites and their oral interpreters.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: The pictographic system's ambiguity requires trained readers; no evidence of severe corruption or noise; oral transmission carries higher distortion risk than painted records; verification rests on scribal authority and archival comparison.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: A cosmic moral order positions the Mexica as the people of the sun, obligated to nourish it with blood; earthly justice reflects this cosmic hierarchy; theft, adultery, drunkenness, and rebellion carry severe sanctions; commoners expect protection from noble abuse through judicial appeal.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: Customary law codified in oral tradition and painted records; Nezahualcoyotl of Texcoco credited with systematic legal codes (eighty laws); courts (teccalli) adjudicate disputes; sumptuary laws regulate dress and consumption by rank.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: Judges (tecutli) hear cases in public courts; testimony, witnesses, and codex evidence inform judgment; sanctions include death (for adultery, treason, certain thefts), slavery, restitution, and corporal punishment; noble offenders face harsher penalties for same offenses in some accounts.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Commoners hold usufruct land rights through calpulli; slaves retain certain protections (cannot be killed arbitrarily, can purchase freedom); compliance burden heavy for subject provinces; predictability of rules moderate within the core, more arbitrary at the periphery.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: Elite impunity exists but is checked by intra-elite rivalry and occasional royal intervention; subject provinces suffer tribute extraction with limited recourse; the gap between cosmic justice proclaimed and peripheral experience constitutes a standing grievance.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: A cosmological paradigm structures knowledge: the universe operates through cyclical destruction and renewal, divine forces require human action to sustain, and specialist priests interpret celestial and calendrical patterns; empirical observation of astronomy and agriculture serves ritual and practical ends without separating from cosmological framing.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Hydraulic engineering (dikes, aqueducts, chinampas) reaches high sophistication; architectural techniques support massive temple construction; obsidian knapping, featherwork, goldsmithing, and textile production embody accumulated craft knowledge; no iron or bronze metallurgy.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: Calmecac schools train noble youth in priestly and administrative arts, including codex reading and composition; telpochcalli schools train commoner youth in warfare and civic duty; scribal literacy remains restricted to perhaps a few thousand specialists; oral transmission carries the bulk of technical and cultural knowledge.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: The burning of pre-1428 histories deliberately erases prior knowledge; otherwise, scribal copying preserves and updates records; no evidence of large-scale knowledge loss within the period, though reliance on specialist scribes creates transmission bottlenecks.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: The Mexica origin narrative traces migration from Aztlan under Huitzilopochtli's guidance to the prophesied eagle-on-cactus site of Tenochtitlan; this narrative, fixed after 1428, legitimates Mexica supremacy and the obligation of war and sacrifice.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: The sun requires blood to rise; the Mexica are chosen to provide it; imperial expansion fulfills cosmic duty; tribute extraction compensates subject peoples' failure to provide sufficient captives; this ideology justifies both warfare and extraction.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: Monumental sculpture (Coatlicue, Sun Stone) expresses cosmological themes; featherwork mantles and mosaics display status; stepped pyramids (Templo Mayor) dominate urban space; polychrome codices combine pictorial narrative with symbolic color coding (turquoise for royalty, red for blood); body paint, jade ear spools, and lip plugs mark rank.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: No evidence of cultural exhaustion; forms remain potent and generative; the artistic vocabulary expands with each temple reconstruction (Templo Mayor rebuilt seven times); meaning decay does not appear within this window.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: A layered cosmos (thirteen heavens, nine underworlds) surrounds the earthly plane; cyclical destruction by the elements (water, wind, fire, jaguars) has ended four prior suns; the current Fifth Sun requires human blood to continue; existence is precarious, sustained by ritual action.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: Calendrical festivals structure the year (veintena ceremonies every twenty days); human sacrifice at temples, markets, and on campaign nourishes the gods; auto-sacrifice (bloodletting) by elites demonstrates piety; household shrines, incense, and offerings maintain daily practice.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: Temple priesthoods (tlamacazque) maintain cult sites and ritual calendars; the high priest (Quetzalcoatl Totec Tlamacazqui) holds doctrinal authority alongside the tlatoani's politico-religious role; Templo Mayor at Tenochtitlan houses Huitzilopochtli and Tlaloc cults; institutional property includes temple lands and labor.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: Aztec religion incorporates and subordinates conquered deities (Huitzilopochtli elevated over earlier Nahua gods); provincial cults continue under imperial overlay; no missionary displacement from outside; the Mexica cosmology expands its reach with the empire.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: No secularizing drift; the sacred remains potent; omens preceding 1519 (comets, temple fires, the weeping woman) suggest anxiety about cosmic continuity rather than disenchantment; the spiritual order holds firm through the window's close, only to shatter with the conquest.

docs.title: 1750 CE – 1810 CE — Bourbon Reforms and Independence Ferment
docs.text: Summary: The Bourbon reforms impose rationalized extraction and centralized administration on New Spain, generating unprecedented documentary apparatus while simultaneously cultivating the creole grievances and Enlightenment-inflected print culture that will dissolve the colonial order; the binding constraint is the contradiction between administrative intensification and the political exclusion it enforces.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: The viceroyalty spans from Guatemala to California, with the Mexican highlands concentrating population, administration, and the richest mining districts at Guanajuato, Zacatecas, and Real del Monte; distance from Madrid remains a fundamental friction that Bourbon efficiency campaigns cannot overcome — orders take months to arrive, responses months more, and local officials retain discretionary space regardless of reformist intent.

Climate Regime & Volatility: The decades after 1785 bring severe climatic stress: the agricultural crisis of 1785–1786 follows failed rains and early frosts, producing famine mortality exceeding 300,000 and revealing the fragility of the maize-provisioning floor; subsequent droughts in 1808–1810 intensify the social pressures accumulating toward insurgency.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: Earthquakes strike Mexico City in 1753 and periodically damage provincial towns; the rebuilding generates administrative records and architectural commissions but drains treasury reserves needed elsewhere.

Resource & Energy Endowment: Silver extraction reaches its colonial apogee: the Guanajuato district alone produces over 20 million pesos annually by the 1790s; mercury supply from Almaden remains the critical bottleneck, and Bourbon efforts to increase allocation and reduce smuggling aim to maximize Crown revenues from this irreplaceable resource base.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Mining operations intensify deforestation for timber and charcoal; hacienda expansion degrades marginal lands; urban growth concentrates waste in capitals without sanitary infrastructure adequate to the load — the viceroy's repeated public health ordinances document the saturation.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: Epidemic cycles continue: smallpox returns in 1761–1762 and typhus (matlazahuatl) strikes in 1761–1764 and 1813; mortality remains heavily stratified, with indigenous communities bearing the greatest burden; the Crown sponsors smallpox vaccination campaigns after 1804, documenting inoculation in parish records.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: The 1785–1786 famine exposes structural vulnerability: maize prices triple, urban poor starve, rural communities sell land to survive; physiological indicators suggest chronic undernutrition among lower strata even in non-crisis years.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Hospital capacity expands modestly under Bourbon stimulus: the Hospital de San Andres and Hospital Real de Naturales serve Mexico City; provincial hospitals remain few; botanical expeditions document medicinal plants but healing practice reaches only limited strata.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Marriage patterns remain heavily regulated by caste legislation; the 1776 Royal Pragmatic on Marriages requires parental consent, generating extensive documentation and litigation when families contest unsuitable unions.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Population recovers strongly: the indigenous population, which had bottomed near 1.5 million in the seventeenth century, exceeds 3.5 million by 1810; total viceregal population approaches 6 million; this growth outpaces employment and land availability, generating the mobile poor who will become insurgent recruits.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: Famine orphans, mining casualties, and epidemic survivors accumulate; ecclesiastical and municipal charity struggles to absorb the dependent load; the dependency is documented in parish death registers and poor relief petitions.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: The alhondiga system regulates maize distribution to cities; the 1785–1786 crisis reveals its inadequacy — granaries empty, speculators hoard, the poor starve; Viceroy Galvez's emergency measures generate extensive documentation but cannot prevent mass mortality.

Energy Capture & Conversion: Mining consumes vast labor and animal power; draft animals multiply; charcoal and firewood extraction accelerates; the energy base remains organic, with no mechanical innovation breaking the ceiling.

Labor Organization & Coercion: The repartimiento system declines but hacienda debt peonage intensifies; mining labor combines free wage workers, draft indigenous labor, and convict gangs; obraje textile workshops employ coerced labor; the labor regime generates grievances documented in petitions and litigation.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Silver production peaks around 27 million pesos annually in the 1800s; textile obrajes, tobacco monopoly manufactures, and agricultural haciendas generate substantial output; the surplus flows disproportionately to peninsular interests and Crown coffers.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: The viceregal treasury chronically remits surplus to Spain; reserves are thin when crisis arrives; the consolidacion de vales reales (1804–1809) forces redemption of Church capital, draining the colony's accumulated credit reserves and generating lasting resentment.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: Bourbon comercio libre reforms (1778 onward) diversify Atlantic ports but disrupt established merchant networks; internal trade expands along improved roads; the consulado (merchant guild) documents commercial flows while resisting liberalization.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: The Church functions as the primary credit institution; capellanias and obras pias provide capital; the consolidacion forces liquidation, disrupting the entire credit system and impoverishing borrowers from hacendados to parishes.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: Bourbon taxation intensifies: alcabala rates increase, new monopolies (tobacco, pulque, playing cards) extract revenue, mining taxes are rationalized; total Crown revenue from New Spain doubles between 1765 and 1800; this extraction is meticulously documented in treasury accounts.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Wealth concentrates in merchant and mining oligarchies; the creole elite accumulates but faces peninsular competition for highest offices; land titles proliferate as elites document holdings against reform threats.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Mining waste accumulates in tailings; urban refuse concentrates; the economic expansion generates material and social detritus — vagrants, unemployed castas, displaced peasants — that administrative reforms cannot absorb.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Elite families practice strategic marriage to consolidate landholding; entailed estates (mayorazgos) preserve patrimony across generations; the 1776 marriage pragmatic inserts state authority into family formation.

Association & Mutual Aid: Confraternities (cofradias) remain the primary mutual aid structure; they manage burial insurance, festival organization, and community funds; Bourbon anticlerical pressure threatens their autonomy; indigenous cajas de comunidad (community treasuries) face royal appropriation.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: Tertulias (salon gatherings) among the elite circulate Enlightenment texts; bullfights, religious festivals, and theatrical performances structure public sociability; the Coliseo de Mexico stages plays; sociability generates the networks through which independence sentiment will spread.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: The sistema de castas hardens: elaborate racial taxonomies (casta paintings) document the stratification; peninsulares monopolize high office; creoles resent exclusion; indigenous communities retain corporate land but face encroachment; castas occupy ambiguous middle positions.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: Bourbon reforms create intendancies (1786) to rationalize provincial administration; the Tribunal de Mineria regulates mining; the tobacco monopoly builds state capacity; census-taking (1790–1793) generates comprehensive population documentation; yet corruption persists and reforms generate resistance.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: The colonial militia expands under Bourbon stimulus; creole officers gain military experience; fortifications are upgraded; yet the apparatus remains thin — fewer than 30,000 regular and militia forces for 6 million inhabitants; this weakness will enable insurgent success.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: Rural banditry increases; the 1767 expulsion of Jesuits provokes riots; indigenous communities resist tribute increases and land encroachment; the social fabric frays at the margins even as administrative documentation expands.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: Viceroy Revilla Gigedo II (1789–1794) exemplifies enlightened administration; later viceroys lack his capacity; creole leaders — Allende, Aldama, the Corregidora — emerge in conspiracies; Hidalgo's personal authority among his parishioners proves decisive.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: The French invasion of Spain (1808) and Ferdinand VII's captivity shatter the legitimacy basis; the question of sovereignty — residing in king, junta, or people — becomes open; colonial subjects debate where allegiance lies when the king is captive.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: The 1808 Mexico City crisis reveals factional division: the audiencia coup against Viceroy Iturrigaray demonstrates peninsular determination to retain control; creole conspiracies proliferate thereafter; by September 1810 Hidalgo's grito marshals collective will toward open revolt.

External Relations & Posture: The colony remains subordinate to Madrid; Atlantic communication carries orders, goods, and ideas; the French Revolution and Haitian Revolution generate anxiety and inspiration in equal measure; Spanish alliance shifts and conflicts affect colonial trade and defense.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: Creole resentment intensifies: exclusion from high office, commercial restrictions, and peninsular arrogance generate grievances; the consolidacion enrages propertied classes; by 1808 the sentiment has crystallized toward autonomy if not yet independence.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: The 1785–1786 famine exhausts the rural poor; repeated tribute demands exhaust patience; by 1810 accumulated disaffection is ready to discharge in insurgency.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Literacy remains restricted but expands among urban elites and colonial administrators; indigenous literacy in alphabetic Nahuatl and Maya persists in community documentation; the printing press in Mexico City produces religious works, administrative decrees, and increasingly secular texts.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: The Gazeta de Mexico (founded 1784) establishes regular periodical circulation; pamphlets multiply after 1808; correspondence networks among conspirators demonstrate the velocity of manuscript communication within the elite.

Record, Storage & Persistence: Administrative documentation reaches unprecedented density: census records, tax rolls, mining accounts, ecclesiastical registers, notarial archives; the consolidacion requires detailed inventories of Church capital; the archive as institution expands.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: Inquisition censorship persists but cannot prevent circulation of prohibited texts; Enlightenment works reach New Spain through smuggling and official channels; the 1808 crisis generates open debate in print and pamphlet.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: Tertulias and reading circles amplify texts among the lettered elite; sermons carry messages to the illiterate; the Grito de Dolores demonstrates how oral proclamation can mobilize masses beyond the reach of print.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: Rumor networks carry distorted information; the 1808 crisis generates competing accounts; the documentary record accumulates but verification lags — the archive grows faster than interpretation can follow.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Enlightenment natural rights discourse penetrates creole consciousness; the traditional compact between Crown and colonies is questioned; taxation without representation becomes a grievance; equality before law is asserted against casta hierarchy.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: The Bourbon program generates extensive legislation: the 1786 Ordinance of Intendants, mining ordinances, commercial regulations; law proliferates but enforcement remains uneven.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: Colonial courts handle expanding caseloads; appeals to Spain take years; indigenous communities litigate land disputes; the system delivers justice slowly and unevenly.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Casta status restricts rights differentially; the compliance burden of Bourbon documentation falls on all strata; indigenous communities spend heavily to defend land titles in court.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: The peninsular coup against Iturrigaray (1808) demonstrates that law yields to force; creole grievances accumulate unaddressed; the gap between justice owed and delivered widens.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: Enlightenment science reaches New Spain: the Royal Botanical Expedition (1787–1803) surveys flora; the Mining Seminary teaches modern mineralogy; geography, astronomy, and natural history advance.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Mining technology improves modestly; the patio process for silver amalgamation is refined; agricultural technique remains traditional; the gap between European innovation and colonial application persists.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: The Royal and Pontifical University graduates theologians and lawyers; the School of Mines trains engineers; Jesuit expulsion (1767) disrupts secondary education; literacy expands slowly but remains minority.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: Scholastic paradigms persist in universities while Enlightenment thought circulates outside; indigenous technical knowledge continues in communities; the transition between frameworks generates both innovation and loss.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: Creole patriotism develops: the cult of the Virgin of Guadalupe anchors Mexican identity; pre-Columbian antiquities are recuperated as creole heritage; Clavijero's Storia antica del Messico (1780–1781) defends American civilization.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: The colonial order legitimates itself through divine right and paternal protection; Bourbon reforms invoke rational improvement; creole counter-narratives invoke natural rights, historical rights of the conquered, and American exceptionalism.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: Late Baroque and Neoclassical styles coexist; Mexico City's rebuilt cathedral combines both; portraiture documents the elite; casta paintings codify racial hierarchy in visual form; material culture reflects both metropolitan fashion and local adaptation.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: Baroque forms exhaust themselves; Neoclassicism arrives as official style but lacks popular roots; the symbolic vocabulary of the old regime begins to hollow as independence sentiment rises.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: Catholic cosmology remains dominant but Enlightenment deism penetrates the elite; the question of Providence in political change becomes urgent after 1808; faith and reason are renegotiated.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: Public religious festivals remain central to urban life; Marian devotion intensifies; confraternities maintain ritual calendars; the rhythm of the sacred year structures experience.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: The Church retains immense wealth and institutional reach; Bourbon regalism subjects it to royal control; the 1767 Jesuit expulsion demonstrates state power over ecclesiastical institutions; the consolidacion attacks Church capital.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: Indigenous Christianity maintains syncretic elements; popular devotion incorporates pre-Columbian practices; the Church tolerates what it cannot eradicate.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: Elite Enlightenment generates skepticism; anticlericalism spreads among the lettered; yet popular piety remains strong — Hidalgo's banner of Guadalupe demonstrates that insurgency will mobilize sacred symbols, not secular abstractions.

docs.title: 800 CE – 1000 CE — Classic Maya Collapse and Terminal Classic
docs.text: Summary: The dissolution of Classic Maya lowland civilization as a rapid, disruptive turning point — a two-century span in which the southern lowlands lose ninety percent of their population, monument construction ceases, and the hieroglyphic tradition contracts northward, revealing that the agricultural intensification, political fragmentation, and environmental degradation accumulated during the florescence had exhausted the system's buffering capacity, leaving it unable to absorb the multi-decadal droughts that struck after 800 CE.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: The southern Maya lowlands — Peten, Usumacinta drainage, Copan valley, Belize interior — remain the geographic frame, but the spatial calculus inverts: the forest that once supported dense populations now reclaims abandoned centers. Rivers and causeways that carried tribute and trade fall silent. Survivors concentrate in remaining pockets or migrate toward the northern Yucatan Peninsula, where shallower soils but accessible cenote water sources offer different constraints. The northern centers — Uxmal, Chichen Itza — inherit the political center of gravity.

Climate Regime & Volatility: Paleoclimate proxies (Lake Chichancanab sediments, Macal Chasm speleothems) document severe multi-year droughts centered on 810, 860, and 910 CE — the most intense aridity in two millennia. Rainfall deficits of 25–40% below normal persisted for years to decades. The drought regime is the precipitating shock; the system's vulnerability is its inability to buffer such volatility after centuries of agricultural intensification.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: Drought is the dominant hazard. Reduced rainfall intensifies fire risk in secondary growth. The hazard is not unprecedented — earlier droughts are recorded — but the system's margin has narrowed to the point where it cannot recover.

Resource & Energy Endowment: Forest resources are depleted; the timber and fuel that enabled construction and lime production are exhausted in many areas. Agricultural soils are degraded by centuries of cultivation. The resource base that supported the florescence has been drawn down below the level that can sustain the population.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Accumulated deforestation and soil erosion have reduced the land's capacity to retain water and support agriculture. The feedback loop closes: degraded sinks worsen drought impacts, which further degrade the agricultural base. The environmental debt accumulated during the florescence comes due.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: No catastrophic epidemic is documented, but nutritional stress from crop failures would elevate mortality from endemic diseases. Skeletal evidence from Terminal Classic contexts shows increased nutritional stress markers. The mortality baseline rises as the provisioning floor falls.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: Crop failures from drought directly reduce food availability. Skeletal analysis from Terminal Classic sites shows increased enamel hypoplasias, cribra orbitalia, and reduced stature — markers of childhood malnutrition and physiological stress. The nutritional floor collapses.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Healing capacity depends on stable communities and specialist knowledge. As populations disperse and die, the knowledge base contracts. Recovery capacity is overwhelmed by the scale of the crisis.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Nutritional stress reduces fertility. Social disruption breaks the alliance networks that structured elite marriage. Reproductive rates fall; the demographic base cannot regenerate.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Population decline in the southern lowlands exceeds ninety percent over two centuries. Major centers are abandoned: Tikal's last monument dates to 869 CE, Copan's to 822 CE. The dense settlement pattern that defined the florescence disappears. Survivors concentrate in remnant communities or migrate northward. The demographic collapse is the defining outcome of the event.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: The dependency ratio shifts catastrophically. As productive adults die or flee, remaining dependents cannot be supported. Entire communities dissolve. The demographic structure cannot sustain itself.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: Maize agriculture fails when rains do not come. Intensified systems (terraces, raised fields) require maintenance labor and water availability; both fail. The provisioning floor drops below subsistence. Famine drives abandonment and death.

Energy Capture & Conversion: The human labor pool contracts with population loss. No technological shift compensates. The energy available for any organized activity — agriculture, construction, warfare — diminishes below the threshold required to maintain complex society.

Labor Organization & Coercion: Corvee systems collapse when there is no surplus to extract and no population to extract it from. Coercive capacity depends on concentrated population and agricultural surplus; both disappear. Labor relations dissolve into survival-level household autonomy.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Surplus production ceases. The elaborate craft specialization, monumental construction, and elite luxury production of the florescence end. The economy contracts to subsistence and below.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: Reserves accumulated during good years are exhausted by successive drought years. The buffering capacity that allowed the system to survive earlier shocks is depleted. There is nothing left to draw on.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: Long-distance trade networks fragment as production and demand collapse. Obsidian and jade imports cease. The exchange system that integrated the region dissolves. Centers that depended on trade for obsidian and prestige goods lose access.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: Cacao and jade retain notional value but cannot be eaten. The value-storage function collapses when there is nothing to exchange value for. Tribute obligations become meaningless.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: No surplus exists to extract. The tributary system that supported elites collapses. Rulers who cannot redistribute lose legitimacy. The entire extraction-redistribution cycle breaks down.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Elite wealth becomes worthless when there is no one to impress and no surplus to appropriate. Tombs are looted. Jade and ceramics are scattered. The wealth defense strategies of the florescence fail completely.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: The question is moot. Production has ceased; there are no byproducts. The environmental waste accumulated earlier continues to degrade the land, but no new waste is generated by a collapsed economy.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Lineage structures fragment as populations disperse. Inheritance becomes meaningless when there is nothing to inherit and no heirs to inherit it. The kin scaffolding that organized society dissolves.

Association & Mutual Aid: Local mutual aid networks are overwhelmed by the scale of the crisis. Communities that survive do so through remnant solidarity, but most communities do not survive. The associational fabric shreds.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: Ball courts fall silent. Feasting ceases. The ritual calendar that structured collective life continues in diminished form at surviving centers but disappears in abandoned ones. Sociability contracts to the household level.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: The elite-commoner divide collapses when there are no commoners to rule and no surplus to support elites. Some elites survive by migrating to northern centers; most disappear from the record. The rigid stratification of the florescence becomes irrelevant.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: The palace bureaucracies that managed tribute and record-keeping dissolve. The last dated monuments mark the end of administrative capacity: centers stop recording their own existence. The k'uhul ajaw institution persists at some sites (Seibal, with inscriptions to 889 CE showing foreign influence) but these are exceptions. Administrative capacity collapses.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: Warfare intensifies initially as polities compete for shrinking resources. But the armies that fought the wars of the eighth century cannot be maintained without agricultural surplus. Coercive capacity dissolves with the economic base. The warfare that accelerated the collapse becomes impossible to sustain.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: Disorder is total. The system does not merely strain — it ceases to exist. Abandoned cities are reclaimed by forest. Populations scatter into remnant communities or migrate. The apparatus does not merely decay; it vanishes. This is not a residue to be cleared but an endpoint.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: Rulers lose authority when they cannot deliver rain, victory, or redistribution. The last monuments often show rulers in diminished circumstances or adopt new, non-traditional iconography. Personal authority drains away with the system that sustained it.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: Cosmological legitimacy requires performance — rituals that bring rain, sacrifices that sustain the cosmos. When rains do not come despite ritual observance, legitimacy fails. The divine kingship that grounded the florescence loses its credibility. This is not gradual erosion but sudden collapse: the system either works or it does not.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: Collective will cannot mobilize without resources and hope. The massive construction projects that demonstrated collective resolve in the florescence are impossible. Will fragments into household-level survival. There is no collective project left.

External Relations & Posture: Inter-polity relations dissolve with the polities themselves. Northern Yucatan (Uxmal, Chichen Itza) continues and absorbs some refugees and influences. But the southern lowlands cease to be actors in any external system. The posture is not retreat but disappearance.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: Morale collapses with the system. Trust erodes when reciprocity fails. Fear and desperation replace the confidence of the florescence. The surviving inscriptions at Seibal and other late sites suggest attempts to restore legitimacy through foreign (Chontal Maya or central Mexican) ideological elements — a sign that indigenous confidence has broken.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: The emotional residue is total exhaustion. The will that built Tikal and Copan is spent. Survivors carry forward whatever they can; most carry nothing. The affective collapse is as complete as the demographic one.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: The hieroglyphic script survives where literate specialists survive — in the northern centers and among migrant elites. But the southern lowland scribal tradition ends with the collapse. The last dated southern monuments (Tonina 909 CE, among the latest) mark the end of local literacy. The script's accessibility contracts geographically.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Messenger networks collapse with the polities they served. Diplomatic communication ceases. The channel infrastructure depends on political organization that no longer exists.

Record, Storage & Persistence: Stone monuments persist — the corpus of Classic Maya inscriptions survives as the record of a dead civilization. But no new records are produced in the southern lowlands. Codices presumably perish with the centers that housed them; none from the Classic period survive. The persistence of the medium outlasts the persistence of the tradition.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: The last inscriptions attempt to maintain traditional framing — royal triumph, cosmic order — but the disjunction between claim and reality is total. Censorship is irrelevant when there is no discourse to censor. The norms of elite monumentality become empty forms.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: There is no audience. The public rituals that amplified elite messaging cease. Monuments stand in empty plazas. The reception infrastructure collapses with the population.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: The signal ends. Physical destruction (burning, vandalism, weathering) affects some monuments, but the main loss is the cessation of production. Noise is irrelevant when there is no signal.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: The cosmological reciprocity that grounded moral order — humans feed gods, gods send rain — fails when rain does not come. The sense that the universe operates justly collapses with the agricultural system. Moral foundations erode when the cosmos appears indifferent.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: Whatever customary law governed conduct becomes moot when there is no community to regulate. Legal evolution ceases.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: No authority remains to adjudicate. Disputes presumably devolve to household or band-level violence. The judicial function of rulership disappears with rulership itself.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Rights and obligations become meaningless abstractions. Compliance burden evaporates because there is nothing to comply with.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: All wrong goes unredressed. The collapse is the ultimate impunity: no one is held accountable because there is no one to hold accountable. The moral residue is total.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: Astronomical observation and calendrical calculation continue at surviving centers (Chichen Itza will become a major astronomical center). But in the southern lowlands, the inquiry tradition ends with the institutions that supported it. The paradigm does not fail intellectually; it fails socially.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Construction technique, hydraulic engineering, and agricultural intensification knowledge cannot be applied without labor and resources. The technical methods of the florescence become useless. Some knowledge transfers to northern centers; most is lost.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: Scribal schools close when there are no patrons and no students. The knowledge stock disperses with surviving specialists or dies with them. Skill distribution contracts to zero in the southern lowlands.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: The knowledge decay is catastrophic. The entire corpus of specialized knowledge — scribal, calendrical, agricultural, architectural — accumulated over centuries is lost in the southern lowlands within two generations. This is not obsolescence through replacement but loss through social collapse.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: Maya identity persists — survivors remain Maya, and the northern tradition continues. But the specific dynastic identities (Tikal, Copan, Calakmul) that grounded southern lowland culture end. Memory of the florescence becomes ancestral rather than living.
