Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: The royal ideology that legitimated the k'uhul ajaw becomes a dead letter. At surviving northern centers, new legitimating narratives emerge incorporating central Mexican elements. The Classic Maya ideology does not evolve; it is replaced.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: The polychrome ceramic tradition, the carved stela tradition, the featherwork and jade mosaic tradition — all cease in the southern lowlands. Material culture regresses to utilitarian forms. The artistic florescence ends as completely as the political one.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: The forms do not exhaust through repetition; they die through abandonment. The symbols retain meaning — survivors presumably understand what the monuments represent — but no one produces new symbolic forms. This is not decay but termination.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: The cosmology does not change; the universe remains the three-tiered cyclical structure. But the existential outlook shifts from confident piety to something grimmer. The covenant between humans and gods — sacrifice for rain — has failed. Doubt or despair presumably enters, though survivors cannot record it.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: Public ritual ceases at abandoned centers. Some practice continues at household level among remnant populations. The elaborate period-ending ceremonies of the florescence require resources and populations that no longer exist. Sacred practice contracts to survival level.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: Temple priesthoods dissolve with the courts they served. Doctrinal authority disperses or dies. Whatever orthodoxy existed becomes unenforceable.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: In the north, new religious elements enter — feathered serpent imagery (Kukulkan) associated with central Mexican influence appears at Chichen Itza. The Classic Maya religion is not exactly displaced but syncretically transformed in the surviving centers. In the south, there is no one left to transform.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: The sacred has failed. Rituals did not bring rain. Sacrifices did not sustain the cosmos. The divine kings were not divine enough. This is disenchantment in its most literal sense: the magic did not work. The spiritual residue is not secularizing drift but catastrophic loss of confidence. The survivors carry forward what they can — the calendar, the gods, the memory — but they carry it into a world where the covenant has broken.

docs.title: 400 BCE – 1810 CE — Codex Traditions Across Mesoamerican History
docs.text: Summary: The screenfold codex constitutes Mesoamerica's distinctive manuscript form, carrying calendrical, divinatory, genealogical, tributary, and historical knowledge across two millennia through pre-Columbian florescence and colonial adaptation; the binding constraint is the restricted specialist class that controls production and interpretation, making the tradition vulnerable to the demographic and institutional catastrophe of conquest even as alphabetic transcription partially preserves its content.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: The codex tradition spans ecological zones from highland basins to tropical lowlands: bark paper (amatl, huun) derives from ficus trees abundant in tierra caliente; deerskin substrates come from highland and lowland game; pigments — cochineal red, Maya blue, carbon black — require specific regional resources; the material chain connects environments across Mesoamerica.

Climate Regime & Volatility: Tropical humidity destroys organic materials: no Classic Maya codices survive in the wet Peten, though fragments appear in dry caves and tombs; the three surviving pre-Columbian Maya books (Dresden, Madrid, Paris) reached European collections and escaped the climate that consumed their counterparts.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: Fire destroys libraries: the 1520s burning of codices by Spanish friars eliminates the bulk of Aztec manuscript production; Bishop Diego de Landa's 1562 auto-da-fe in Mani destroys Maya books by the cartload; accidental fires in colonial archives continue the loss; the hazard regime is primarily anthropogenic.

Resource & Energy Endowment: Paper production requires substantial labor and botanical knowledge: bark is harvested, soaked, beaten, and plastered with lime; the energy investment in a single codex represents weeks of specialized work; this resource constraint limits production to elite patronage contexts.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: The organic materials return to soil when discarded; the tradition leaves no physical residue beyond the exceptional survivals; the primary accumulation is informational loss — the unrecoverable content of destroyed books.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: The colonial demographic catastrophe (1520–1600) kills 90% of the indigenous population, including the scribal specialists who maintain the tradition; epidemics of smallpox, measles, and cocoliztli eliminate the knowledge-bearers faster than they can transmit their skills.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: Scribes occupy elite positions with adequate nutrition; their physical capacity for the fine motor work of painting and writing is not constrained; the tradition's vulnerability is demographic, not nutritional.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Medicinal knowledge is itself codex content: the Badianus Manuscript (1552) records Aztec herbal medicine in Latin and Nahuatl; healing traditions survive partially through colonial transcription.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Scribal lineages transmit knowledge through family training; disruption of these lineages by conquest mortality breaks transmission chains; the biological continuity of specialist families is inseparable from the tradition's continuity.

Demographic Renewal & Density: The pre-Columbian population supports extensive specialist classes; post-conquest collapse eliminates the demographic base for maintaining the full range of scribal expertise; recovery is too slow to restore what the first generation of epidemics destroys.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: The elderly scribes who survive the initial epidemics become the critical knowledge-bearers; their death without adequate successors closes transmission; this attrition is the immediate cause of the tradition's contraction.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: Scribes are provisioned by elite patronage, temple institutions, or state tribute; they do not produce their own subsistence; this dependence ties the tradition's survival to the survival of the institutions that support it.

Energy Capture & Conversion: Paper-making and pigment preparation require organized labor; the energy cost of a single codex is substantial; this limits production to contexts where surplus supports specialist work.

Labor Organization & Coercion: Scribes (tlacuilos, ah ts'ib) constitute a specialized class trained from youth; their labor is skilled and honored, not coerced; colonial disruption reduces this class but does not eliminate it — indigenous scribes continue producing documents throughout the colonial period.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Pre-Columbian states produce codices as administrative necessity and ritual requirement; the Aztec tribute system generates extensive pictographic records; colonial administration continues to require indigenous documentation, sustaining demand for scribal production.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: Codices themselves are the storage medium: genealogies preserve lineage claims across generations; tribute records enable consistent extraction; calendrical codices store astronomical observations accumulated over centuries; the manuscript is the buffer against memory loss.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: Paper and pigments circulate as tribute goods; finished codices do not typically circulate as trade items but remain with the institutions that commission them; the colonial period sees codices reach European collections as curiosities, trophies, and legal evidence.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: Land titles encoded in pictographic documents store property claims across generations; genealogical codices preserve inheritance rights; the manuscript functions as a store of legal and economic value.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: The Matricula de Tributos and Codex Mendoza document the Aztec tribute system in pictographic form; these records are instruments of extraction, enabling systematic taxation; colonial adaptations continue this administrative function.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Indigenous nobles defend land claims through pictographic titles (titulos primordiales) into the colonial period; the codex tradition serves elite property defense.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Worn or superseded codices are discarded, recycled, or ritually disposed; little is known of pre-Columbian practices; colonial authorities destroy books as idolatrous; the waste stream is primarily informational loss.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Mixtec screenfold codices (Nuttall, Bodley, Selden) record genealogies and marriage alliances across generations; these are instruments of lineage legitimation; inheritance claims depend on documentary proof.

Association & Mutual Aid: Scribal training occurs within lineage and institutional contexts — palace schools, temple colleges, family workshops; the calmecac schools of Aztec Tenochtitlan train elite youth including scribes; these associations maintain technique across generations.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: Codices include calendrical games and divinatory practices that structure social interaction; the tonalpohualli (260-day count) governs personal fate; reading codices is both ritual and social practice.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: Scribes occupy elite positions; literacy is restricted; the ability to read and produce codices marks high status; this restriction makes the tradition dependent on a narrow specialist class.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: The Aztec state's administrative capacity rests partly on pictographic record-keeping; tribute lists, census records, and judicial documents are maintained in codex form; colonial administration inherits and adapts this capacity.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: Codices record warfare and conquest; the Aztec tribute system depends on military coercion documented in pictographic form; the colonial state uses documentary evidence to enforce its claims.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: The conquest constitutes catastrophic institutional decay; palace schools are abolished; temple colleges disappear; the institutional infrastructure that maintains the tradition collapses within a generation, though indigenous scribes continue working in adapted forms.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: Rulers commission and interpret codices; the ability to read historical and divinatory books marks royal competence; colonial caciques continue to use pictographic documents to legitimate their authority.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: Genealogical codices anchor lineage legitimacy; rulers trace descent through painted records; the manuscript makes the claim visible and persistent; legitimacy is documented, not merely claimed.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: The determination to preserve the tradition survives conquest: indigenous scribes adapt to alphabetic transcription, preserving content if not form; the Florentine Codex project (1545–1590) demonstrates sustained collective effort to document pre-Columbian knowledge.

External Relations & Posture: Codices record diplomatic relations, tribute obligations, and warfare between polities; the painted record documents the posture of polities toward each other across time.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: The codex tradition commands reverence: books are sacred objects containing ancestral wisdom; the colonial destruction of codices registers as sacrilege and loss; indigenous communities continue to value surviving manuscripts as objects of identity.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: By the seventeenth century the intensive transcription effort wanes; the specialists who could interpret pre-Columbian conventions die; disaffection is not the cause — exhaustion and demographic loss are.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Codex reading requires specialized training; the systems are not fully phonetic and depend on oral interpretation; accessibility is restricted to the trained elite; this restriction makes the tradition fragile when specialists die.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Codices are produced for specific patrons and remain in their possession; they do not circulate rapidly; the channel is local and slow, but the record persists across generations.

Record, Storage & Persistence: The codex is the technology of persistence: bark paper and deerskin outlast memory; pigments remain legible for centuries; the screenfold format allows efficient storage and retrieval; the technology enables accumulation beyond individual lifespan.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: Pre-Columbian codex production follows established conventions — calendrical formats, genealogical layouts, tribute tabulations; colonial censorship targets religious and divinatory content while permitting administrative and historical documentation; the norms shift radically after 1520.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: Codex reading is a performance: the painted page provides cues for oral exposition; the reader-interpreter (tlamatini) elaborates the content in speech; the system combines graphic record and oral transmission.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: The pictographic system tolerates variation in style while maintaining semantic integrity; conventions ensure that different painters produce legible results; the signal is robust within its conventions; noise enters when conventions are forgotten.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Divinatory codices assign fate according to calendrical position; moral responsibility is negotiated within this framework; the painted record establishes what is owed and when.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: Land titles, tribute records, and judicial precedents are codified in pictographic form; the codex is an instrument of law; colonial courts accept pictographic evidence as legally binding.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: Pictographic records provide evidence in disputes; colonial indigenous communities litigate using traditional documents; the codex serves adjudication.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Documentary proof establishes rights to land, tribute, and office; the compliance burden of producing and maintaining records falls on indigenous communities defending their claims.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: The destruction of codices by colonial authorities violates indigenous conceptions of justice; this wrong remains unredressed; the burned books cannot be recovered.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: The codex tradition embodies astronomical, calendrical, and historical knowledge: the Dresden Codex contains lunar and Venus tables of high precision; the 260-day and 365-day calendrical cycles encode sophisticated mathematical understanding; the paradigm integrates cosmic and human time.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Paper-making, pigment preparation, and painting techniques constitute a specialized craft tradition; apprenticeship transmits technique; the methods are refined over centuries.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: Scribal training occurs in palace schools (calmecac) and through lineage apprenticeship; the knowledge stock is concentrated in specialist hands; distribution is narrow by design.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: The colonial transition makes pre-Columbian reading conventions obsolete for most practical purposes; by 1600 few can interpret the old books; the knowledge decays through demographic loss and institutional collapse, not intellectual supersession.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: Codices preserve mythic history, migration narratives, and origin accounts; the Mixtec codices trace lineages to divine ancestors; the Aztec painted histories record migration from Aztlan; the manuscript anchors identity to documented past.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: Genealogical and historical codices legitimate ruling lineages; the record shows descent from gods and ancient kings; colonial adaptations continue to make legitimating claims through pictographic documentation.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: The codex is a visual art form: stylized figures, standardized color conventions, and sophisticated composition characterize the tradition; the material culture of painting — brushes, pigments, paper — constitutes a specialized production system; aesthetic standards persist through colonial adaptations.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: The pre-Columbian conventions lose meaning as their institutional context disappears; colonial codices become increasingly Europeanized in style; by 1700 the distinctive pictographic conventions are vestigial; the form exhausts itself through loss of interpretive community rather than internal stagnation.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: Divinatory codices (tonalamatl) place human life within cosmic cycles; the 260-day count assigns fate; the Long Count (in Maya tradition) situates the present within vast temporal spans; the codex is a window onto cosmic order.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: Codices guide ritual practice: calendrical books indicate propitious days; screenfolds are consulted before undertakings; the painted record structures devotion.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: Temple institutions maintain and interpret sacred books; priests control access to divinatory knowledge; the colonial destruction of religious codices targets institutional authority as much as physical objects.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: Christian content enters colonial codices; the Testerian catechisms adapt pictographic conventions to Christian instruction; syncretism appears in documents that combine pre-Columbian forms with Christian content; displacement is incomplete — indigenous spiritual content persists in adapted forms.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: The destruction of sacred books constitutes forced disenchantment; the colonial Church attempts to eliminate the indigenous sacred; yet the sacred content survives in oral tradition, community memory, and the codices that escaped the fires — the discharge is partial, leaving a residue of hidden practice alongside public conversion.

docs.title: 1550 CE – 1650 CE — Colonial Consolidation and Documentary Synthesis
docs.text: Summary: The century after conquest establishes a hybrid documentary regime where indigenous scribes adapt pre-Columbian pictographic traditions to alphabetic literacy, producing an unprecedented volume of legal, administrative, and ecclesiastical records that embed the colonial order in written form — the binding constraint being the demographic catastrophe that reduces the indigenous population by over ninety percent, concentrating surviving knowledge in a diminishing corps of trained scribes whose documents become the sole surviving medium of land tenure, community identity, and political claim.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: The colonial territory encompasses the high volcanic basins of central Mexico — the Valley of Mexico at 2,240 meters, the valleys of Puebla, Oaxaca, and Michoacan — alongside the tropical lowlands of the Yucatan Peninsula and the coastal plains of both oceans; Spanish administration concentrates in highland centers where climate suits European settlement, while the hot lowlands remain understaffed and difficult to govern, creating a persistent spatial gradient between administrative intensity and peripheral neglect.

Climate Regime & Volatility: The monsoon-driven wet-dry cycle continues to pattern agricultural life, with maize cultivation dependent on summer rains from June through October; the period witnesses several severe droughts (1558, 1579, 1616) that compound epidemic mortality and deepen demographic crisis, while the Little Ice Age onset after 1550 brings slightly cooler and more variable conditions than the late pre-Columbian period.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: The volcanic axis delivers periodic seismic shocks — major earthquakes strike Mexico City in 1575 and 1611 — while the Gulf coast suffers hurricane impacts that disrupt shipping and coastal settlements; the lacustrine environment of the Basin of Mexico produces chronic flooding, requiring constant drainage works that intensify after the catastrophic 1555 and 1607 floods that submerge significant portions of the capital.

Resource & Energy Endowment: Silver extraction at Zacatecas (discovered 1546), Guanajuato, and other northern sites becomes the colony's economic engine, with ore bodies of exceptional richness; the highland forests supply timber and charcoal for smelting, while draft animals (horses, mules, oxen) introduced by the Spanish expand the available muscle power beyond human porters.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Mercury amalgamation for silver refining (patio process, introduced 1554) deposits toxic residues around mining centers; deforestation accelerates around highland cities and mining zones as timber and charcoal demand rises; urban waste accumulates in the canal-and-lake system of Mexico City, degrading water quality, though the sparse post-epidemic population limits pressure on most sinks.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: The catastrophic epidemics continue through this period: cocoliztli outbreaks in 1545–48 and 1576–78 each kill millions, with the latter reducing the surviving indigenous population by perhaps half; measles, typhus, and influenza recur in epidemic waves of roughly generational spacing, maintaining mortality pressure throughout the century.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: The surviving indigenous population experiences nutritional stress from land loss, labor demands, and ecological disruption of traditional agricultural systems; Spanish settlers and the emerging mestizo population enjoy more varied diets incorporating Old World grains, livestock products, and continued access to maize and native foods; stature and vitality data remain sparse but the documentary record shows frequent famine years.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Spanish hospitals (hospitales de indios) are established in major centers, with the Hospital de Jesus founded by Cortes in 1524 and expanded through the period; indigenous healing traditions continue alongside Spanish humoral medicine, but the trained indigenous physicians (ticitl) decline with the demographic collapse; the regular orders provide the primary care infrastructure in indigenous communities.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: The massive gender imbalance among early Spanish settlers drives extensive unions with indigenous women, creating the mestizo population that grows throughout the period; indigenous communities struggle to maintain reproduction under labor drafts and epidemic pressure; Church marriage enforcement gradually transforms pairing patterns, with parish registration creating the documentary record of family formation.

Demographic Renewal & Density: The indigenous population falls from perhaps 16–25 million at contact to approximately 1–2 million by 1620, the most catastrophic demographic collapse in recorded history; the nadir occurs around 1620–1650, after which slow recovery begins; Spanish and mestizo populations grow but remain small relative to the pre-contact indigenous base; urban concentrations in Mexico City, Puebla, and Oaxaca serve as primary population centers.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: The demographic collapse creates a severe labor shortage that the colonial administration addresses through the repartimiento system (rotational labor drafts) and eventually the concentration of surviving indigenous populations into congregaciones; orphaned, widowed, and displaced individuals strain the already diminished community structures.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: Maize agriculture continues as the dietary foundation for indigenous and mestizo populations, though land tenure disruptions and labor drafts reduce output per capita; wheat cultivation expands for Spanish consumption; the introduction of livestock provides new protein sources but also competes with indigenous agriculture for land.

Energy Capture & Conversion: The introduction of draft animals — horses, mules, oxen — dramatically expands the work ceiling beyond human muscle power; water mills for grinding grain and processing ore supplement animal power; mining operations depend on mule trains for ore transport and require massive charcoal inputs for smelting.

Labor Organization & Coercion: The encomienda system (grants of indigenous tribute and labor to Spanish holders) yields to the repartimiento (rotational labor drafts administered by the state) and eventually wage labor (naborios) as the demographic collapse renders traditional extraction unsustainable; mining increasingly relies on nominally free but often debt-bonded workers; indigenous communities retain internal labor organization for agriculture and local projects.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Silver production dominates the colonial economy, with annual output rising from negligible levels in the 1540s to 10–15 million pesos by 1600, making New Spain the world's leading silver producer; agricultural surplus supports the urban populations but remains constrained by labor shortage and the disruption of pre-contact irrigation and intensification systems.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: Colonial granaries (alhondigas) are established to buffer grain supply in major cities; silver reserves accumulate in treasury coffers and ecclesiastical holdings; indigenous communities maintain diminished communal reserves (cajas de comunidad); periodic supply crises reveal thin buffers.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: The silver economy generates a monetized exchange system centered on the Mexico City mint (established 1535); the camino real connects mining zones to the capital and the port of Veracruz; the Manila galleon trade (from 1565) links New Spain to Asian markets; internal trade networks expand along Spanish roads while indigenous tianguis (markets) continue.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: Silver coinage provides a stable monetary medium; credit networks link merchants, miners, and the treasury; the Church accumulates substantial capital through donations, tithes, and mortgages (censos), becoming the colony's primary lending institution; indigenous communities hold land and cajas de comunidad as collective stores.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: The colonial state extracts through tribute (from indigenous communities), tithes (to the Church), the quinto real (royal fifth on mining), and various taxes on trade and consumption; ecclesiastical tithes and bequests channel substantial surplus to religious institutions; local elites extract through land rents and commerce.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Land concentration accelerates as Spanish settlers and their descendants acquire haciendas, while indigenous communities fight to retain lands through legal processes documented in the colonial archive; encomienda holders transition to landowners; mining wealth creates a volatile elite with rapid turnover.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Mining generates toxic mercury wastes and tailings; deforestation residues and urban refuse accumulate; the thin population limits most waste impacts beyond mining zones and immediate urban peripheries.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Spanish inheritance law (partible, with mejoras) replaces indigenous patterns; the Church enforces marriage registration and monogamy; compadrazgo (godparent) relations create cross-cutting kin ties; indigenous noble lineages (principales, caciques) are recognized but constrained; mestizo and mulato families occupy ambiguous positions in the emerging social hierarchy.

Association & Mutual Aid: Indigenous communities (republicas de indios) retain internal governance and mutual aid functions under Spanish supervision; cofradias (religious brotherhoods) proliferate, providing burial, feast sponsorship, and credit functions; guilds (gremios) organize urban crafts; the regular orders provide institutional support.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: Feast days proliferate under the colonial religious calendar, with major celebrations for patron saints and Corpus Christi; bullfighting arrives as elite spectacle; indigenous dance and music traditions continue, often incorporated into Christian festival contexts.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: The sistema de castas crystallizes, ranking Spaniards (peninsulares and criollos) above mestizos, indigenous people, and those of African descent; within indigenous communities, principales and caciques retain status distinctions; urban society stratifies by race, occupation, and wealth in elaborate hierarchy.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: The viceregal administration matures, with the Audiencia of Mexico providing judicial and administrative oversight; corregidores administer provincial districts; the Church operates a parallel hierarchy of bishops, cathedral chapters, and parish priests; indigenous cabildos (town councils) manage local affairs under Spanish oversight; recordkeeping becomes systematic.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: A small professional military force guards against external threats; internal order relies on local officials, ecclesiastical authority, and the militia; the Inquisition (established 1571 for New Spain) provides ideological enforcement, primarily targeting crypto-Jews and Protestant infiltrators rather than indigenous populations (who were exempt).

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: Social displacement from demographic collapse and congregation policies generates rootless populations absorbed into haciendas or urban margins; banditry increases in areas of thin administration; indigenous communities experience cumulative stress from tribute demands and labor drafts.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: Viceroys serve as the crown's personal representatives, with figures like Luis de Velasco (both father and son) and the Marquis of Villamanrique providing effective governance; bishops exercise substantial influence; indigenous caciques retain diminished but real authority within their communities; hacienda owners command local loyalty and labor.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: The colonial order derives legitimacy from the dual pillars of crown and Church; indigenous acceptance remains pragmatic rather than enthusiastic, grounded in the Church's spiritual monopoly and the legal protections that the crown formally extends; creole loyalty to the crown remains strong through this period.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: The colonial administration maintains sufficient coherence to govern a vast territory with limited European population; indigenous communities demonstrate collective will through legal action, petition, and the maintenance of community institutions; major challenges to colonial authority remain absent through this period.

External Relations & Posture: New Spain sits within the broader Spanish imperial system, sending silver to the metropole and receiving administrative appointments and trade goods; the Manila galleon links the colony to Asian commerce; English and Dutch corsairs threaten coastal shipping, spurring fortification of Veracruz and San Juan de Ulua.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: The indigenous population carries profound collective trauma from epidemic mortality and social collapse; survivors adapt through strategic accommodation with colonial institutions; Spanish settlers exhibit frontier assertiveness and anxiety about maintaining status in the racial hierarchy; religious fervour provides emotional anchorage across groups.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: The weight of demographic catastrophe, labor extraction, and cultural dislocation leaves indigenous communities in a state of depleted collective energy; millenarian undercurrents occasionally surface but do not produce sustained resistance; Spanish settler satisfaction with the colonial arrangement remains generally high.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: The colonial period witnesses a remarkable expansion of written communication as indigenous scribes learn alphabetic script; Nahuatl, Maya, Zapotec, and Mixtec documents proliferate; Spanish remains the language of high administration; Latin serves ecclesiastical and academic contexts; oral communication continues to dominate everyday life.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Information travels by foot, horse, and ship; the courier system (correos) links major centers to the capital and to Spain via the annual fleets; news from Europe arrives months after events; internal communications move faster along the camino real.

Record, Storage & Persistence: This period sees the creation of the vast colonial archive: parish registers of baptism, marriage, and burial; notarial records of property and contract; viceregal correspondence; Audiencia judicial records; tribute and census rolls; ecclesiastical archives; indigenous community documents in native languages; survivability depends on institutional care.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: The Inquisition reviews imported books and surveils heretical discourse; the printing press (active since 1539) operates under licensing; indigenous religious expression is monitored for idolatry; acceptable discourse frames colonial rule as divinely ordained and benevolent.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: Written communication reaches primarily the literate minority — clergy, officials, merchants, indigenous scribes — while sermons, public readings, and visual media (church art, processional displays) convey messages to broader audiences; rumor networks carry information through oral channels.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: The documentary record of this period shows high preservation rates in institutional archives but significant loss in peripheral areas and indigenous communities; translation and transcription introduce errors; forgery of land documents becomes a recognized problem.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Competing moral frameworks coexist: Spanish Catholic natural law traditions justify hierarchy and colonial rule while also mandating protection of indigenous peoples; indigenous moral traditions survive in adapted forms; the tension between exploitation and protection defines the period's moral ambiguity.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: The Leyes Nuevas (New Laws, 1542) and subsequent legislation establish the legal framework; the Recopilacion de Leyes de Indias (compiled through this period, codified 1680) systematizes colonial law; indigenous communities retain customary law for internal matters; ecclesiastical law governs marriage, wills, and clerical conduct.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: The Audiencia serves as the supreme court; corregidores and alcaldes mayores provide local justice; indigenous cabildos handle minor matters; ecclesiastical courts adjudicate clergy and matters touching religion; the Inquisition tries heresy; multiple jurisdictions create complexity and opportunities for appeal.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Indigenous peoples are formally recognized as vassals of the crown with defined rights and protections; these rights provide the legal basis for countless petitions and lawsuits documented in the archive; compliance burden on indigenous communities includes tribute payment, labor service, and conformity to Christian norms.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: Despite formal protections, indigenous peoples face systematic exploitation with limited effective redress; powerful Spaniards evade sanctions; distance from supervisory authorities enables local abuses; the legal system provides some check but the gap between law and practice remains substantial.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: The major intellectual project of this period is ethnographic documentation: Sahagun's Florentine Codex (completed 1577), Diego Duran's histories, the Relaciones Geograficas (1579–85), and numerous lesser works record indigenous knowledge, history, and practice within Catholic interpretive frameworks; natural history inquiry documents the American environment for European audiences.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Mining technology advances with the introduction of the patio process (mercury amalgamation) for silver extraction; agricultural techniques combine indigenous and European methods; architectural and engineering knowledge produces the colonial built environment; hydraulic engineering addresses Mexico City's chronic flooding.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: The University of Mexico (founded 1551) trains clergy and administrators; colegios educate elite youth; indigenous scribal training occurs within communities and some ecclesiastical institutions; literacy remains restricted but the corps of literate indigenous scribes maintains remarkable productivity; skill in traditional arts and crafts continues though master practitioners decline.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: Pre-contact knowledge undergoes rapid loss as the generation educated before conquest dies; pictographic literacy declines as alphabetic script displaces it; astronomical, calendrical, and ritual knowledge is preserved in some documents but much is lost to persecution and mortality; practical craft knowledge erodes with demographic collapse.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: Indigenous communities struggle to maintain historical memory through documentary strategies — the creation of primordial titles, community histories, and maps that anchor identity in documented claims; Spanish settlers develop a proto-creole identity rooted in conquest narratives and American birth; ecclesiastical culture provides shared symbols and narratives.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: The colonial order justifies itself through the dual narrative of spiritual salvation (conversion) and political protection (pacification); indigenous nobles legitimize their status through documented genealogies linking them to pre-contact rulers who accepted Spanish sovereignty; the conquest itself becomes mythologized in competing Spanish and indigenous accounts.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: The colonial artistic synthesis emerges: Christian iconography executed by indigenous artists incorporates native techniques and subtle symbolic elements; church architecture adapts European forms to local materials and labor; featherwork and manuscript painting continue in hybrid contexts; the material culture of everyday life mixes indigenous and Spanish elements.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: Pre-contact artistic and expressive traditions undergo fragmentation as the demographic catastrophe removes master practitioners and patrons; some forms survive through adaptation to Christian contexts while others are actively suppressed or simply abandoned; the colonial synthesis is generative but built on indigenous loss.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: The colonial Church enforces Catholic cosmology while indigenous populations maintain syncretic practices; the Virgin of Guadalupe apparition narrative (codified 1648 but claimed for 1531) bridges indigenous and Christian worldviews; fatalistic acceptance of colonial rule as divinely ordained competes with millenarian hopes.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: The sacramental system structures life from baptism through burial; feast days, processions, and cofradias organize communal religious practice; indigenous ritual elements persist within Christian frameworks, sometimes openly incorporated, sometimes covertly maintained; domestic devotion centers on household altars and saint images.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: The regular orders (Franciscans, Dominicans, Augustinians, later Jesuits) dominate early evangelization; the secular clergy expands through the period; the episcopal structure consolidates; the Inquisition guards orthodoxy; ecclesiastical wealth and institutional power rival the secular state.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: Mass conversion of indigenous populations creates a Catholic majority that incorporates significant pre-contact elements; the boundaries between acceptable syncretism and prohibited idolatry are actively policed; African religious traditions arrive with enslaved populations; Judaism survives covertly among crypto-Jews (marranos) until Inquisition persecution.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: The sacred remains intensely present across society; disenchantment in the European sense does not characterize this period; rather, the spiritual landscape is one of fervent religiosity channeled through Catholic forms that absorb indigenous sacred energies; the loss of pre-contact cosmological coherence creates spiritual wounds that the new synthesis imperfectly heals.

docs.title: 250 CE – 550 CE — Early Classic Maya and Teotihuacan Influence
docs.text: Summary: The Early Classic Maya lowlands experience the florescence of dynastic writing and monumental record-keeping alongside profound external influence from Teotihuacan, the central Mexican metropolis whose intervention at Tikal in 378 CE reorganizes political alignments across the lowlands — the binding constraint is the tension between indigenous manuscript tradition deepening its hold on Maya statecraft and the disruptive entry of an imperial power operating through a different information regime.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: The Maya lowlands retain their Preclassic configuration — the Peten interior (Tikal, Uaxactun, Calakmul), the Usumacinta drainage (Palenque, Yaxchilan, Piedras Negras), the Copan valley on the southeastern periphery, and Kaminaljuyu in the Guatemala highlands bridging lowland and central Mexican worlds. Teotihuacan lies 1,000 kilometers northwest in the Basin of Mexico at 2,240 meters altitude, connected to the lowlands through highland Guatemala trade corridors and possibly coastal routes. Spatial friction between central Mexico and the Maya world is immense — the "entrada" of 378 CE represents a remarkable projection of influence across this distance.

Climate Regime & Volatility: Seasonal monsoon patterns continue; paleoclimate reconstructions show no catastrophic drought episodes in this window, permitting agricultural expansion and population growth. The central Mexican highlands experience different seasonality but similarly supportive conditions for Teotihuacan's demographic peak.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: No major volcanic or seismic disruption affects the lowlands. Teotihuacan's position in the volcanic central highlands exposes it to seismic risk but no catastrophic event is documented in this period.

Resource & Energy Endowment: Obsidian flows intensify from Teotihuacan-controlled sources (Pachuca green obsidian becomes prestige marker in lowland elite contexts). Jade from the Motagua Valley, cacao from Pacific piedmont, and marine shell from both coasts continue circulating. Teotihuacan's control of obsidian gives it leverage over long-distance exchange networks.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Population growth at major centers increases pressure on local environments, but sink capacity remains adequate. Agricultural intensification around Tikal, Copan, and other centers alters local forest cover without triggering collapse-level degradation.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: Endemic tropical disease continues as background mortality factor. No evidence of epidemic crisis in this window. Population growth at major centers suggests mortality rates remain within demographic replacement capacity.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: Agricultural surplus supports population growth; skeletal evidence from elite and commoner burials shows variable nutritional status by social position. Teotihuacan's maize-based agriculture supports its massive population (100,000–200,000), though long-distance provisioning becomes necessary.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Healing remains embedded in ritual-specialist practice. No significant change from Preclassic patterns.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Elite polygyny continues; dynasties documented through inscriptions show concern with succession and legitimate offspring. Commoner household patterns less visible archaeologically.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Population grows at major lowland centers; Tikal reaches significant scale (though estimates vary widely, 50,000–100,000 in the urban core and sustaining area). Teotihuacan peaks as the largest city in the pre-Columbian Americas. The Early Classic sees demographic expansion across Mesoamerica.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: Growing populations generate larger dependent cohorts; household and kinship structures absorb this load. Elite tombs show elaborate mortuary treatment indicating resources devoted to honoring the dead.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: Maize agriculture intensifies; raised-field and terrace systems expand around major centers. Provisioning floor rises with technique but remains vulnerable to sequential drought (not yet tested in this window).

Energy Capture & Conversion: Human labor remains the sole power source. Monumental construction continues — Tikal's North Acropolis, temple-pyramids across the lowlands — funded by corvee labor mobilization.

Labor Organization & Coercion: Tributary labor obligations support elite construction and craft production. Warfare generates captives for sacrifice and possibly labor. The degree of coercion likely increases with state complexity.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Surplus funds specialists — scribes, artists, architects, priests — and monumental construction. Long-distance trade in prestige goods requires surplus production for exchange.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: Reservoir construction continues at major centers. Granary storage documented but scale unclear. Buffering capacity sufficient for normal variation.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: Teotihuacan's influence transforms exchange networks. Pachuca green obsidian appears in elite lowland contexts as prestige marker. Kaminaljuyu emerges as intermediary between Teotihuacan and the lowlands. Trade routes consolidate; middleman centers profit from transit.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: Cacao likely functions as currency or near-currency in prestige exchange. Tribute obligations recorded (later documented; likely extend to this period) defer exchange across time.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: Dynastic states extract surplus through tribute; redistribution through feasting, monument construction, and warfare maintains elite legitimacy. Teotihuacan-affiliated elites at Tikal may redirect some extraction toward central Mexican interests.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Inequality intensifies. Elite tombs contain Teotihuacan-style goods (green obsidian, tripod cylinders, talud-tablero architectural elements) marking affiliation with distant power. Prestige goods circulation reinforces stratification.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Construction debris accumulates at major sites. Organic waste recycles through agricultural systems. No crisis evident.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Patrilineal descent governs dynastic succession, now documented in hieroglyphic inscriptions. Tikal's Stela 31 (erected 445 CE) records royal genealogy across generations, including the disruptive entrada of 378 CE that installs a new lineage. Royal kinship networks extend across polities through marriage alliance.

Association & Mutual Aid: Village-level cooperation continues. Urban centers develop more complex occupational differentiation — scribes, artists, merchants, priests forming distinct groups with internal solidarities.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: Ballcourts proliferate. Feasting occasions mark ritual calendar. The ballgame carries cosmological significance and provides spectacle reinforcing political hierarchy.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: Divine-kingship ideology matures. The ajaw (ruler) occupies apex of hierarchy; noble lineages (sajal, aj k'uhuun) serve as administrators and subsidiary lords. Commoner-elite distinction sharpens. Teotihuacan-affiliated elites at some centers form distinct faction.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: Hieroglyphic writing becomes essential to administration. Emblem glyphs identify polities. Tribute records (later documented in codices) likely emerge. Scribal specialists (aj tz'ihb) form professional class trained in palace schools. Administrative capacity grows but remains personalized around royal authority.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: Warfare intensifies and becomes documented in hieroglyphic texts. The 378 CE entrada — Siyaj K'ahk' arrives at Tikal from Teotihuacan, the existing king dies, a Teotihuacan-affiliated ruler is installed — demonstrates military intervention at inter-regional scale. Elite warriors lead; mass levies mobilize for campaigns. Fortifications appear at some sites.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: The entrada of 378 CE represents imposed regime change — the existing Tikal dynasty is disrupted, new rulers installed. Political disorder at this moment of foreign intervention is absorbed by installing a hybrid regime claiming both Teotihuacan and local legitimacy. Endemic inter-polity warfare generates chronic low-level disorder.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: Siyaj K'ahk' ("Fire Is Born") emerges as the key figure of the 378 entrada — a military-political leader projecting Teotihuacan authority into the lowlands. At Tikal, Yax Nuun Ahiin I (installed 379 CE) combines Teotihuacan affiliation with Maya kingship. Leadership authority rests on military success, lineage claims, and ritual performance.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: Legitimacy at Tikal after 378 requires careful negotiation — the new regime claims both Teotihuacan and local ancestry, erecting monuments (Stela 31) that explain the succession in acceptable terms. Allegiance is secured through ritual spectacle, successful warfare, and continuity of elite privilege.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: The capacity to project influence from Teotihuacan to Tikal — 1,000 kilometers — implies extraordinary political will and coordination. Within the lowlands, sustained inter-polity competition (Tikal vs. Calakmul rivalry emerges) demonstrates resolve.

External Relations & Posture: Teotihuacan-Maya relations define the period. Whether the entrada represents military conquest, elite alliance, or trade-network control remains debated, but Teotihuacan influence is undeniable — green obsidian, talud-tablero architecture, and iconographic elements appear across the lowlands. Maya polities navigate between attraction to prestige goods and resistance to foreign domination.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: Monumental inscriptions and architecture project confidence and stability. The disruption of 378 CE is retrospectively framed as legitimate succession rather than conquest, suggesting concern for public acceptance.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: No evidence of mass disaffection; elite factional conflict around the entrada may generate localized resistance but is absorbed by the hybrid regime's success in subsequent decades.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Maya script reaches mature logosyllabic form capable of recording spoken language. Literacy remains elite-restricted — scribes trained in palace schools, writing serves royal legitimation and administration. Teotihuacan's writing system (minimally attested; limited corpus) contrasts with Maya's elaborate inscription tradition.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Information travels at walking/canoe speed. Long-distance communication between Teotihuacan and the lowlands requires weeks of transit; the coordination implied by the 378 entrada suggests either advance planning or local agents acting with pre-authorized discretion.

Record, Storage & Persistence: Hieroglyphic inscriptions on stone stelae, altars, architectural elements, and painted ceramics proliferate. The corpus from this period documents dynastic history, warfare, ritual, and calendrical computation. Codices (bark-paper books) are used but none survive archaeologically from this period. The manuscript tradition deepens — texts accumulate beyond living memory, consultable by scribes trained to read them.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: Texts controlled by ruling elites frame events to legitimize power. The 378 entrada is recorded as legitimate succession; defeated enemies appear as sacrificial offerings. No competing public discourse — writing serves the ruler.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: Monumental texts address ritual audiences; the carved image communicates to non-literate viewers while the text rewards trained readers. Stelae erected in public plazas serve as permanent proclamation.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: Stone inscriptions durable across centuries. The signal survives where monuments survive; destruction through warfare or weathering causes information loss. Painted texts on stucco and ceramics more vulnerable than carved stone.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Cosmic justice — rulers maintain world order through proper ritual; disorder results from moral failure. The defeated in warfare suffer because they (or their gods) failed. Victory demonstrates divine favor.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: No codified law corpus attested; custom and royal judgment govern. Inscriptions do not carry legal code — their function is commemorative and legitimating.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: Royal judgment settles disputes. Sanction for serious offense includes sacrifice. Captives from warfare face ritual execution; this is framed as cosmic necessity, not punishment.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: No individual rights framework. Subjects owe tribute and labor; rulers owe protection and cosmic mediation. The bargain remains hierarchical.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: Elite impunity structural. Foreign intervention (378 entrada) imposes new rulers without recourse for displaced dynasty — might makes right, retrospectively legitimized through inscription.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: Astronomical observation continues; the Venus cycle documented in later codices likely studied in this period. Mathematical and calendrical systems elaborate. Inquiry remains embedded in cosmological framework — observation serves ritual prediction.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Architectural technique develops — corbeled vaults, massive platform construction, stucco modeling. Ceramic technology produces polychrome vessels for elite use and exchange. Writing technology matures — the logosyllabic system now capable of recording any spoken Maya utterance.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: Scribal training occurs in palace schools. Knowledge transmission follows master-apprentice patterns within elite lineages and specialist guilds. Literacy remains restricted; technical skills concentrate among specialists serving elite patrons.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: No significant knowledge decay in this period of elaboration and accumulation. The manuscript tradition grows.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: Maya identity crystallizes around shared cosmology, divine-kingship ideology, and the inscribed record that now anchors memory across generations. The 378 entrada introduces Teotihuacan elements — talud-tablero architecture, goggle-eyed war deity iconography — that blend with Maya tradition into hybrid forms.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: Dynastic legitimacy rests on documented succession, military victory, and ritual performance. Tikal's Stela 31 (erected 445 CE by Siyaj Chan K'awiil II) narrates the entrada and subsequent succession, framing foreign intervention as legitimate transfer of authority. The inscribed text makes the claim permanent and authoritative.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: Polychrome ceramics reach high refinement. Architectural style blends Maya corbeled vault and massive platform tradition with Teotihuacan-influenced talud-tablero facades at some sites. Stela portraiture elaborates royal iconography. Jade, shell, and obsidian working continue at high level.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: No exhaustion — forms are in creative elaboration. The Teotihuacan influence introduces new vocabulary rather than replacing exhausted traditions.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: Layered cosmos with heavens, underworlds, and earth plane continues as framework. The maize god, jaguar god of the underworld, and ancestral deities populate the sacred realm. Teotihuacan contact may introduce or reinforce certain deities (feathered serpent imagery appears, though how much is influence versus independent development is debated).

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: Bloodletting, sacrifice, calendrical ceremony, ballgame, and pyramid-temple ritual continue. The ritual round governed by interlocking calendars structures public and elite religious life. Caves and cenotes retain sacred significance.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: Rulers combine political and priestly functions. Specialist priests serve particular cults and calendrical knowledge. No separate ecclesiastical hierarchy — religious authority fuses with political power.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: Teotihuacan religious elements — war imagery, specific deity forms — diffuse into Maya lowlands, blending with indigenous tradition rather than displacing it. The result is syncretism that enriches rather than disrupts Maya religion.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: No disenchantment — the cosmological system remains vital, elaborating through contact with Teotihuacan traditions. The sacred suffuses political and artistic life.

docs.title: 1000 CE – 1200 CE — Early Postclassic and Toltec Horizon
docs.text: Summary: The Early Postclassic sees Mesoamerica reorganize after the Classic Maya collapse, with Toltec Tula and Chichen Itza emerging as major powers while long-distance trade networks, intensified militarism, and new artistic-scribal traditions reshape the cultural landscape; the binding constraint is the fragmentation of the Classic-period political order and the need for new mechanisms of integration across a depopulated southern lowland zone.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: The Mexican Highlands center on the Basin of Mexico and the Tula region (modern Hidalgo) at 2,000–2,200 meters elevation, connected by highland corridors to Oaxaca and the Gulf Coast; the northern Yucatan Peninsula provides a limestone platform of low relief, with cenotes (sinkholes) supplying water in the absence of surface rivers; the abandoned southern lowland jungle of the Peten creates a demographic void between these poles, increasing the friction of north-south movement.

Climate Regime & Volatility: The period follows severe droughts that contributed to the Classic Maya collapse; paleoclimate proxies suggest somewhat recovered but still variable rainfall in the northern Yucatan, while highland central Mexico maintains its predictable wet-dry monsoonal regime, with summer rains supporting rainfed maize agriculture and winter dry seasons constraining surplus.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: Highland volcanic and seismic risk persists around the Basin of Mexico; Yucatan faces hurricane exposure along coastal zones; drought remains the primary civilizational threat, the memory of the ninth-century collapse shaping settlement patterns and agricultural strategies toward more resilient configurations.

Resource & Energy Endowment: Obsidian sources at Pachuca and other highland deposits fuel long-distance exchange; cacao, feathers, jade, and marine shell flow through trade networks; salt from northern Yucatan coastal salinas becomes a major commodity; firewood and timber available in highland pine-oak zones, scarcer in the scrub-covered northern Yucatan.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Population remains well below Classic-period peaks in most zones, leaving ample absorptive capacity; localized degradation around major centers like Tula and Chichen Itza accumulates but does not approach crisis thresholds; the abandoned southern lowlands slowly regenerate forest cover.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: Endemic tropical disease persists in lowland zones; highland populations face lower pathogen burdens; overall mortality baselines stable within the Mesoamerican disease ecology, with no novel epidemic introductions until the sixteenth century.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: Maize, beans, squash, and chili form the dietary base; protein from turkey, dog, deer, and lake fish in highland basins; coastal populations access marine resources; skeletal evidence suggests adequate nutrition at major centers, with elite access to cacao and other luxuries.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Herbalism, bone-setting, and ritual healing practiced by specialists; sweat baths (temazcalli) serve hygienic and therapeutic functions; healing integrated with cosmological frameworks attributing illness to supernatural causes.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Polygyny practiced among elites; marriage alliances cement political relationships between lineages and polities; average household size and fertility patterns follow Mesoamerican norms.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Population slowly recovers in northern Yucatan after the collapse; Chichen Itza reaches perhaps 30,000–50,000 inhabitants; Tula perhaps 40,000–60,000; the southern Peten remains largely depopulated, with scattered remnant communities.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: Warfare casualties create cohorts of widows and orphans absorbed through kinship networks; no evidence of catastrophic demographic imbalance; the demographic recovery phase generates relatively favorable dependency ratios.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: Milpa agriculture (maize-bean-squash polyculture) provides the subsistence base; Yucatan adds henequen fiber cultivation; chinampas (raised fields) expand in highland lake basins; household production supplemented by market exchange.

Energy Capture & Conversion: Human labor remains the primary energy source; no draft animals; fire for cooking, lime-burning for construction, and metallurgy (copper-gold alloys) emerging from West Mexican traditions; canoe transport on waterways reduces energy costs of bulk movement.

Labor Organization & Coercion: Corvee labor mobilized for monumental construction and agricultural intensification; slavery exists as a social institution, with war captives, debtors, and criminals constituting an unfree labor pool; tribute systems extract labor and goods from subordinate communities.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Craft specialization intensifies, with dedicated workshops for obsidian, ceramics, textiles, and metallurgy; surplus supports warrior elites, priest-scribes, and merchant classes; production organized through both household and state-directed modes.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: Granaries hold maize reserves; tribute warehouses at major centers accumulate goods; household strategies include drying, smoking, and multi-year crop storage; vulnerability to sequential drought years remains.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: Long-distance trade networks expand dramatically, with professional merchant groups (pochteca-like precursors) linking highland Mexico, the Gulf Coast, Yucatan, and Central America; turquoise from the American Southwest, gold from Central America, obsidian, cacao, and feathers circulate; port sites like Isla Cerritos serve Chichen Itza's maritime trade.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: Cacao beans serve as currency; copper axes and T-shaped ingots emerge as exchange media; reciprocal obligation networks structure elite exchange; no formal credit institutions but debt bondage functions as deferred obligation.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: Tribute flows to Tula and Chichen Itza from subordinate communities; warrior elites claim shares of conquest goods; temples accumulate offerings; redistribution through feasting, ritual, and elite gifting.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Marked inequality between noble (pilli) and commoner (macehual) strata; elite residence compounds concentrate luxury goods; land held communally through calpulli-like units with differential access by status; wealth defended through kinship alliance and military force.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Obsidian debitage accumulates at workshop sites; organic waste composted or discarded in middens; lime-burning depletes local fuel supplies; no evidence of systemic waste management beyond household-level practices.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Patrilineal descent predominates with bilateral elements; noble lineages (tecalli) control land and offices; commoner households organized in calpulli-like territorial units; inheritance passes through male lines with provisions for elite polygynous households.

Association & Mutual Aid: Calpulli structures provide mutual aid, collective labor mobilization, and local governance; craft and merchant guilds emerge as associational forms; temple complexes organize devotional communities; neighborhood solidarity buffers individual household risk.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: The ballgame (ullamaliztli) serves as ritual combat, elite competition, and public spectacle; feasting accompanies ritual and political occasions; markets function as social as well as economic spaces; pulque consumption ritualized and recreational.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: Sharp division between noble and commoner estates; warrior sodalities (like later cuauhtli and ocelotl orders) provide paths to status; merchant groups occupy an ambiguous position between commoner and noble; priests and scribes constitute a literate elite; slaves form the lowest stratum.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: Toltec state structure less well understood than later Aztec; council governance (perhaps multiple rulers or rotating authority) suggested by conflicting sources; Chichen Itza shows architectural evidence of council halls (mul-tepal "joint rule" interpretation debated); scribal bureaucracies maintain records but administrative reach remains limited compared to later periods.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: Militarism intensifies; warrior orders prominent in iconography; atlatl, obsidian-edged macuahuitl, and quilted cotton armor standard; fortifications and defensive walls appear; organized armies conduct campaigns for tribute and captives; military prowess central to elite identity.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: Warfare endemic between competing centers; Tula eventually destroyed around 1150–1200 CE amid factional conflict and outside pressure; Chichen Itza's decline by 1200 CE marks end of its hegemony; political fragmentation recurs as centralizing projects collapse; the period ends with neither highland nor lowland paramount.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: Rulers (possibly multiple at Chichen Itza) derive authority from lineage, military prowess, and priestly function; the legendary Quetzalcoatl-Topiltzin figure associated with Tula (whether historical or mythologized) becomes central to later legitimating traditions; charismatic authority blends with institutional roles.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: Legitimacy rooted in mythological charter, military success, and ritual performance; subordinate communities accept tribute obligations when backed by overwhelming force and ideological sanction; allegiance conditional on protection and redistribution.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: Expansion phases show high collective mobilization; Tula's influence extends to regions as far as northern Mexico and possibly Chichen Itza; the capacity for sustained military and construction projects indicates effective elite coordination; factional rivalries periodically fragment this will.

External Relations & Posture: Aggressive expansion characterizes both Toltec and Chichen Itza hegemonies; long-distance trade requires diplomatic relationships with distant polities; the "Toltec-Maya" connection (whether conquest, alliance, trade, or shared ideology) remains archaeologically debated but indicates significant inter-regional interaction.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: Post-collapse societies exhibit resilience and adaptation; militaristic ideology celebrates warrior valor; cosmological anxiety about world-endings and cosmic cycles shapes collective psychology; pride in ancestry and legitimating myth animates elite identity.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: The destruction of Tula around 1150–1200 CE suggests internal collapse or external conquest; Chichen Itza's abandonment indicates similar exhaustion; the period closes with no successor hegemony established, fragmenting the political landscape.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Maya hieroglyphic script continues in reduced form in northern Yucatan; Central Mexican pictographic traditions persist at Tula and related centers; literacy remains restricted to trained scribes (ah tz'ib in Maya, tlacuilo equivalents in highland traditions); oral transmission carries the bulk of cultural knowledge.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Foot messengers traverse trade routes; information follows caravan and canoe networks; royal courts and temples serve as information nodes; transmission velocity limited to speed of human travel, roughly 30–40 km per day on maintained sacbeob (raised roads) in Yucatan.

Record, Storage & Persistence: Codex production continues though no Early Postclassic originals survive; monumental inscriptions decline dramatically from Classic peaks but do not disappear entirely; genealogical and historical records likely maintained in screenfold format; architectural programs encode cosmological and political information.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: Official narratives promulgated through monuments and public ritual; competing polities maintain rival historical claims; scribes serve as propagandists for ruling lineages; iconographic programs at Chichen Itza promote militaristic and sacrificial themes.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: Public spectacles (ballgame, sacrifice, procession) broadcast elite messages to non-literate populations; painted murals and sculptural programs visible to gathered crowds; oral performance in markets and temples extends the reach of official narratives.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: The Classic-period collapse fragmented archival continuity; the Postclassic inherits partial and mythologized memories of the Classic past; Toltec legendary history already accreting by this period, blurring historical and mythological registers.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Reciprocity between humans and gods grounds moral order; tribute and sacrifice conceived as cosmic obligations maintaining world stability; warrior honor and captive-taking valorized; social hierarchy naturalized through cosmological sanction.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: Customary law governs most disputes; elite courts adjudicate matters affecting noble interests; specific codes unknown but parallels with later Aztec law suggest capital punishment for serious crimes, compensation for property offenses, and status-differentiated penalties.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: Rulers and councils serve as courts; confession under torture employed in serious cases; sanctions range from compensation and slavery (debt or criminal) to death by sacrifice, burning, or stoning; swift justice expected.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Commoners owe tribute, labor, and military service; nobles enjoy judicial privileges and land rights; slaves possess minimal protections; no formal rights doctrine but customary expectations structure obligations.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: Elite violence against commoners largely unpunished; inter-polity warfare operates outside juridical frameworks; vengeance and feud provide informal redress mechanisms; structural impunity for ruling classes.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: Astronomical observation continues, tracking Venus, Mars, eclipse cycles, and solar-lunar phenomena; mathematical traditions (vigesimal base-20 system, zero concept) maintained; medical-botanical knowledge transmitted through apprenticeship; no separation of empirical and cosmological explanation.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Metallurgical knowledge (lost-wax casting, alloy production) arrives from West Mexico and Central America; obsidian-blade production reaches high refinement; architectural techniques for corbeled vaults, hydraulic management, and monumental construction sophisticated; agricultural intensification techniques (terracing, raised fields) applied.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: Scribal and priestly training in temple-schools transmits literacy, calendrics, ritual, and astronomy to elite youth; craft knowledge transmitted through apprenticeship in workshops; commoner education informal within household and calpulli; knowledge highly stratified by class.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: Classic Maya scribal traditions contract; southern lowland sites abandoned, their archives lost; historical knowledge mythologized; the Toltec period becomes legendary even before the Aztec era, indicating rapid information loss and transformation.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: The Toltec (Tollan) becomes the archetype of civilized order, a golden-age reference point for later Mesoamerican polities; origin narratives trace lineages to Tollan; the Quetzalcoatl complex (feathered serpent deity associated with Venus, wind, priesthood, and legitimate rule) central to political mythology.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: Rulers claim descent from Toltec ancestors; military conquest justified through cosmic necessity; human sacrifice as debt-payment to gods who sacrificed themselves for humanity; the warrior ideal dominates elite ideology.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: Toltec sculptural style features atlantean warrior columns, chacmool sacrifice figures, tzompantli (skull rack) architecture; Chichen Itza combines Maya and "Toltec" elements in the Great Ballcourt, Castillo pyramid, and Temple of the Warriors; feathered-serpent imagery proliferates; turquoise mosaic, gold, and copper luxury goods signal elite status.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: Classic Maya artistic and inscriptional traditions attenuate; the elaborate historical stelae of the Classic period give way to more formulaic and militaristic imagery; meaning concentrates on legitimation and cosmic maintenance rather than the biographical-dynastic detail of Classic texts.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: The world conceived as precarious, sustained by ritual feeding of gods with human blood; cyclic time (Calendar Round, Long Count) structures expectation; the present Sun-age (Nahui Ollin) destined for eventual destruction; human agency maintains cosmic order through sacrifice and proper ritual.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: Human sacrifice intensifies, with heart extraction, decapitation, and arrow sacrifice depicted at major centers; ballgame as cosmic drama; calendar festivals structure collective devotion; pilgrimage to sacred sites and cenotes (at Chichen Itza's Sacred Cenote, offerings include human sacrifice and precious goods).

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: Temple complexes serve as priestly residences, schools, and ritual centers; priestly hierarchies maintain calendrical and divinatory knowledge; doctrine transmitted orally and through screenfold books; no pan-Mesoamerican ecclesiastical institution but shared cosmological frameworks.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: The "Toltec" stylistic and ideological complex spreads widely, appearing at Chichen Itza, suggesting religious diffusion or shared cults; Quetzalcoatl/Kukulkan veneration bridges highland and lowland traditions; local deities and cults persist beneath overarching cosmological framework.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: The collapse of major centers (Tula, then Chichen Itza) can be read as cosmological crisis, the failure of rulers to maintain divine favor; survivors must reinterpret events, attribute failure, and seek renewed sources of sacred legitimation; the search for Tollan-like authority continues into the Late Postclassic.

docs.title: 550 CE – 800 CE — Late Classic Maya Florescence
docs.text: Summary: The Maya lowlands at their apex, when dozens of competing kingdoms sustain the densest populations, most elaborate monumental architecture, and most prolific hieroglyphic record production in pre-Columbian America — a florescence whose binding constraint is the intensive agricultural system that feeds it, already pressing its ecological ceiling as inter-polity warfare intensifies and the elite scribal apparatus expands to legitimate an increasingly competitive political order.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
