Geography & Spatial Friction: The southern Maya lowlands occupy the Peten basin and adjacent zones of modern Guatemala, Belize, and southern Mexico — a limestone platform covered by seasonal tropical forest, dissected by seasonal rivers (Usumacinta, Pasion, Belize) and punctuated by bajo wetlands that flood in the wet season but hold water poorly in the dry. Travel occurs along rivers and overland causeways (sacbeob); the forest imposes friction sufficient to prevent any single polity from consolidating the region, instead fragmenting it into dozens of autonomous kingdoms within a few days' march of one another. Obsidian, jade, and cacao require long-distance exchange from highland Guatemala, the Motagua Valley, and Pacific coastal zones respectively.

Climate Regime & Volatility: The monsoon regime delivers 1,500–3,000 mm of annual rainfall concentrated in a May–December wet season, followed by a pronounced dry season when surface water becomes scarce. Interannual variability is significant; multi-year droughts appear in paleoclimate records (lake sediment and speleothem proxies) and correlate with political crises. The period 550–800 CE includes both favorable decades and drought episodes, with climate volatility tightening the margin between surplus and subsistence.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: Hurricane tracks occasionally penetrate the interior, damaging crops and structures. Volcanic eruptions in highland Guatemala deposit ash regionally. Localized flooding affects bajo margins. Fire risk in dry season constrains storage of perishables and bark-paper manuscripts. Hazard exposure is moderate but sufficient to stress a system operating near capacity.

Resource & Energy Endowment: Limestone is abundant for construction and lime plaster production (itself fuel-intensive). Flint nodules provide local tool stone. Obsidian must be imported from highland sources (Ixtepeque, El Chayal). Timber and thatch are locally available but under pressure from construction and fuel demand. Agricultural soils are thin over limestone bedrock, requiring careful management.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Deforestation for fuel, construction, and field clearance accumulates through the period; soil erosion deposits sediment in bajos and lakes. Lime production for plaster consumes enormous quantities of firewood, accelerating forest degradation. The system's waste load is approaching the point where degraded soils and thinned forests reduce agricultural returns — a slow-motion feedback not yet catastrophic but visibly accumulating.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: Endemic tropical diseases (intestinal parasites, malaria in some zones) impose a background mortality load. Dense populations in urban cores concentrate waste and increase disease transmission. Skeletal evidence shows moderate but not catastrophic pathogen burden; mortality concentrates in infancy and early childhood. No catastrophic epidemics are recorded, though localized outbreaks likely occurred.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: Maize, beans, and squash provide the dietary staple, supplemented by deer, turkey, fish, cacao, and a range of cultivated and wild plants. Skeletal analysis shows adequate nutrition for most of the population, with some evidence of periodic stress (enamel hypoplasias) reflecting seasonal or drought-related shortfalls. Elites display better nutritional status than commoners.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Healing knowledge resides with specialists versed in herbal pharmacopoeia and ritual treatment. Elite tombs contain medicinal plants and healer's kits. Recovery capacity is household- and lineage-based, with no evidence of institutional medical provision. The capacity is adequate for endemic conditions but limited against epidemic or mass-casualty events.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Marriage patterns are alliance-forming among elite lineages, documented in hieroglyphic texts recording royal marriages between polities. Commoner pairing is less visible but presumably household-based. Elite polygyny is attested. Reproductive biology operates within normal tropical parameters.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Population peaks during this period; estimates for major centers reach tens of thousands (Tikal, Calakmul, Copan), with regional populations in the low millions. Settlement surveys show densities of 200–500 persons per square kilometer in urban cores, unprecedented in pre-Columbian America. This density presses the carrying capacity and requires ever-more-intensive agriculture.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: The age structure skews young; life expectancy at birth is perhaps 25–30 years. The productive cohort supports a significant child-dependent load. Elite longevity appears somewhat greater. The system regenerates adequately but carries no surplus capacity against sustained demographic shock.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: Swidden (slash-and-burn) agriculture forms the base, supplemented by intensive methods: terracing on hillslopes, raised fields in bajos, household gardens (solares), managed forest groves of ramon (breadnut), cacao, and other tree crops. The provisioning floor is adequate in good years but tight; the system requires continuous expansion of cleared land or intensification, both approaching limits.

Energy Capture & Conversion: Human muscle provides the primary motive power; there are no draft animals. Fire (wood fuel) drives cooking, lime production, and ceramic firing. The energy budget is constrained by the labor available and the diminishing wood supply as forests thin. No technological breakthrough lifts the work ceiling.

Labor Organization & Coercion: Commoner households owe labor tribute to lords for construction, agriculture, and warfare. Corvee mobilizes thousands for pyramid and palace construction. Captive labor from warfare supplements the workforce; high-status captives are sacrificed rather than worked. The labor relation mixes tribute obligation with redistribution through feasting and ceremony.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Agricultural surplus supports a substantial non-producing elite: rulers, nobles, priests, scribes, artisans, warriors. Ceramic production, textile weaving, and craft specialization flourish. Surplus is adequate for monumental construction but fully committed; little slack remains. The system is at or near its productive ceiling.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: Maize stores in household and palace granaries; cacao beans serve as a portable value store. Elite reserves provide some buffer against single-year shortfalls. Multi-year drought would exhaust reserves. The buffering capacity is thin relative to the population load.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: Long-distance trade networks bring obsidian, jade, Spondylus shell, quetzal feathers, and cacao to lowland centers. Trade moves by canoe along rivers and by porter along overland routes. Markets exist but their scale and regularity are debated. Tribute flows from subordinate centers to capitals. External dependence on highland obsidian and jade creates vulnerability to disruption.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: Cacao beans and jade serve as value stores; no coinage exists. Tribute obligations encode deferred extraction. Elite gift exchange binds polities and lineages in reciprocal debt. Credit in the modern sense is absent.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: Tribute in labor and goods flows to royal courts, redistributed through feasting, ritual, and construction wages. Extraction is heavy but legitimated by cosmological obligation and spectacle. The elite share of surplus is large; commoner margins are narrow.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Wealth concentrates in royal and noble lineages. Elite compounds display exotic imports and elaborate craft goods. Commoners retain household goods, garden plots, and local exchange access. Social mobility is limited. Elite wealth is defended by lineage solidarity and coercive capacity.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Organic waste recycles through household gardens. Construction debris accumulates at site margins. Deforestation and soil erosion represent unrouted environmental waste. No financial mispricing accumulates in the absence of monetary abstraction.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Patrilineal descent predominates among elites; royal succession passes through males, though women transmit legitimacy and elite women marry across polities to cement alliances. Commoner kinship is less documented but presumably bilateral with patrilocal residence. Inheritance of land and goods follows lineage lines.

Association & Mutual Aid: Craft guilds and occupational specializations cluster in wards. Lineage groups provide mutual aid. Commoner communities owe collective tribute but retain internal solidarity. The fabric is dense within polities but fractured between them.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: The ballgame (pitz) serves as ritual, spectacle, and diplomatic arena; ball courts anchor public space at every major center. Feasting, music, and dance mark calendrical rituals. Elite sociability centers on court life; commoner sociability is household- and ward-based.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: A sharp elite/commoner divide structures society. The royal household (ajaw and sajal lords, royal kin, attached specialists) stands atop noble lineages, who dominate commoner farmers and laborers. Captives and slaves form the lowest tier. Boundaries are hereditary and rigid; upward mobility is rare.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: The k'uhul ajaw (divine lord) rules each polity through a palace bureaucracy of scribes, stewards, and tribute collectors. Emblem glyphs mark polity identity. Administrative reach extends to subordinate centers (under sajal lords) but rarely beyond a few days' march. Inter-polity relations are managed through diplomacy, marriage, alliance, and warfare — no overarching administrative structure unites the region.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: Each polity fields a warrior force under noble leadership. Warfare is frequent, ritualized, and aims at captive-taking for sacrifice and tribute extraction rather than territorial annihilation. Elite warriors bear obsidian-edged clubs, spears, and shields. Fortifications appear at some sites. The coercive balance is roughly even among major powers, preventing regional consolidation.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: Warfare intensifies through the period, disrupting agriculture and trade. Factional conflict within polities occasionally surfaces in the inscriptions. The system's equilibrium depends on a rough balance of power; any destabilization cascades into disorder. The apparatus shows signs of strain but has not yet collapsed.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: The k'uhul ajaw (divine lord) embodies the polity, depicted in hieroglyphic texts and monumental art performing rituals, receiving tribute, and defeating enemies. Personal charisma, military success, and ritual efficacy ground authority. Weak or defeated rulers lose legitimacy rapidly.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: Legitimacy derives from cosmological performance: the ruler as axis mundi, mediator between human and divine realms, guarantor of rain and harvest. This is lived allegiance, enacted in public ritual rather than merely claimed. The system requires continuous performance; legitimacy erodes if rains fail or wars are lost.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: Collective will mobilizes for monumental construction and warfare. The ruling lineage coheres around succession, though contested accessions appear in the record. Will is directed outward against rival polities; internal mobilization depends on external threat and ritual occasion.

External Relations & Posture: Inter-polity relations oscillate between alliance (often sealed by marriage) and warfare. Hegemonic ambitions (Tikal, Calakmul) seek regional dominance without achieving permanent consolidation. Tribute relationships mark subordination; contested borderlands generate chronic conflict. No external power threatens the region in this period.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: Elite confidence is high; monuments proclaim victory, divine descent, and cosmic centrality. Commoner sentiment is harder to read but participation in monumental construction and ritual spectacle suggests at least acquiescence. Trust extends within lineages and polities; inter-polity relations are competitive and suspicious.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: No clear evidence of mass disaffection appears in this period, though intensifying warfare and agricultural stress may generate unrecorded discontent. The system's emotional reserves appear adequate — for now.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: The elite possess a fully developed logosyllabic script capable of recording any utterance in the Maya languages. Literacy is restricted to trained scribes (aj tz'ib) attached to royal courts; commoners are illiterate. The scribal class is small — perhaps a few hundred across all polities — but the script's expressive capacity is complete.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Oral proclamation carries messages within polities; runners and diplomatic envoys carry messages between polities. Inscriptions on public monuments broadcast elite ideology to illiterate audiences who understand the imagery if not the glyphs. The channel is slow — days to weeks between centers — but adequate for the political timescale.

Record, Storage & Persistence: Hieroglyphic texts on stone monuments, stucco facades, painted ceramics, and carved bones persist for centuries. Screenfold books (codices) on bark paper (huun) are produced for calendrical, divinatory, and historical purposes; none survive from this period, though Colonial-era copies attest to their existence. Archives presumably existed in palaces; their contents are lost. The monumental record survives; the perishable record does not.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: Monumental texts glorify rulers and suppress failure; defeats are rarely recorded. Court scribes control the frame. Discourse norms privilege royal agency, cosmological regularity, and dynastic continuity. Alternative voices are absent from the surviving record.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: Public monuments are placed in plazas for collective viewing during rituals. Repeated ceremonies amplify the message. Elite ceramics circulate within the noble stratum. The audience is captive and attentive during ritual; attention outside these contexts is harder to sustain.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: The scribal tradition maintains high fidelity; texts are carefully composed and executed. Copying errors exist but are rare. The main noise source is physical destruction: burning, vandalism by rival polities, and weathering. Signal integrity is high within the surviving corpus.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Justice is hierarchical: obligations flow upward as tribute and downward as protection and redistribution. Reciprocity governs elite exchange. Cosmological order requires human sacrifice to repay divine gifts and sustain the universe. This is not arbitrary cruelty but obligatory maintenance of cosmic balance.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: Codified law in the modern sense is absent. Custom and ruler's edict govern conduct. Elite disputes may be adjudicated by paramount lords. Commoner disputes are presumably handled by local authorities. No written law codes survive.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: The ruler holds ultimate judicial authority. Sanctions include sacrifice of high-status captives, execution, and presumably lesser punishments. Evidence for routine adjudication is thin. The system relies on hierarchy and custom rather than codified procedure.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Commoners bear heavy tribute and corvee obligations. No formal rights limit extraction, though customary expectations constrain it. Elite rights derive from lineage and office. The compliance burden is high but accepted as cosmologically necessary.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: Elite impunity is substantial; rulers' actions are above challenge. Wronged commoners have little recourse. Inter-polity wrongs (defeat, captive-taking) are not redressed but avenged. The gap between justice owed and delivered is wide but not perceived as such within the cosmological frame.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: Astronomical observation reaches high sophistication: eclipse prediction, Venus cycles, lunar series calculations appear in inscriptions. Mathematics employs a vigesimal (base-20) positional system with a true zero. The Long Count calendar anchors historical chronology. Inquiry is oriented toward divinatory and calendrical ends rather than naturalistic explanation.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Architectural technique produces stable corbel-vaulted masonry structures of enormous scale. Hydraulic engineering manages water through reservoirs, canals, and terracing. Agricultural intensification applies accumulated knowledge of soils, seasons, and crop management. Scribal technique produces durable polychrome manuscripts and carved inscriptions.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: Scribal training occurs in palace contexts, likely within elite lineages. The knowledge stock — calendrical, astronomical, ritual, historical — accumulates in codices and the trained memories of specialists. Skill distribution is narrow; literacy and numeracy are elite monopolies. Craft knowledge (masonry, ceramics, weaving) transmits through apprenticeship.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: Earlier inscriptions are occasionally copied or cited; the tradition is cumulative. Some sites show erasure or alteration of earlier texts for political reasons. The main risk is loss of perishable codices and death of trained specialists — a risk that will materialize in the collapse.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: Creation narratives (later recorded in the Popol Vuh) ground Maya identity in a cyclical cosmos of creation and destruction. Dynastic histories trace royal lineages to mythic ancestors and patron deities. Memory anchors in monumental inscriptions and oral tradition. Identity is polity-specific (Tikal, Copan, etc.) but shares a common Maya cultural substrate.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: Royal ideology presents the k'uhul ajaw as divine mediator, descended from gods, responsible for cosmic maintenance. Military victory demonstrates divine favor. Hieroglyphic monuments narrate this legitimating story in stone. The narrative is totalizing; alternative ideologies are invisible in the record.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: Polychrome ceramics depict mythic scenes, courtly life, and supernatural beings. Carved stelae and lintels display rulers in elaborate regalia. Jade mosaic masks, featherwork, and painted murals (Bonampak) represent the apex of Mesoamerican visual culture. The style is baroque in its elaboration and symbolically dense.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: The forms are at their peak, not exhausted. Stylistic elaboration intensifies through the period. If anything, the proliferation of monuments suggests competitive escalation rather than staleness. Form exhaustion will come only with the collapse.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: The cosmos is a three-tiered structure: celestial realm, earthly plane, underworld (Xibalba). Time is cyclical, marked by calendrical periods requiring specific rituals. Humans owe a debt to the gods repaid through sacrifice. The existential outlook is pious and obligatory rather than fatalistic; correct performance ensures cosmic continuity.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: Royal bloodletting, human sacrifice of captives, offerings of incense, food, and precious objects mark the ritual calendar. Period-ending ceremonies (katun endings, especially) require elaborate observance. Commoner devotion is less visible but presumably involves household shrines and participation in public rituals.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: The ruler is the chief priest; specialized priesthood exists but is subordinate to royal authority. Temples atop pyramids house cult images and receive offerings. Doctrinal authority resides in the scribal-priestly class that maintains calendrical and ritual knowledge. Orthodoxy is polity-specific; no pan-Maya religious institution exists.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: Maya religion is stable within the region; external influence (from Teotihuacan, earlier) has been absorbed. No competing cosmology challenges the prevailing system. Syncretism is internal, blending local patron cults with shared Maya deities.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: No disenchantment is visible. The sacred is fully operational, enacted in every monument and ritual. The period represents the high point of Maya religious elaboration. Disenchantment will arrive only when the system fails to deliver — when rains do not come and wars are lost.

docs.title: 1200 CE – 1428 CE — Late Postclassic Transformations and Mexica Rise
docs.text: Summary: The Late Postclassic witnesses the fragmentation of earlier hegemonies and the emergence of the Mexica (Aztecs) from marginal newcomers to dominant power in the Basin of Mexico, with the formation of the Triple Alliance in 1428 CE marking the culmination of two centuries of migration, adaptation, alliance-building, and militaristic expansion; the binding constraint is the intense competition among Basin polities for land, tribute, and legitimacy in a densely populated lacustrine environment.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: The Basin of Mexico forms a closed hydrological system at 2,240 meters elevation, containing interconnected lakes (Texcoco, Xochimilco, Chalco, Xaltocan, Zumpango) whose waters enable canoe transport, chinampa agriculture, and lacustrine resource extraction; surrounding mountain ranges (Sierra Nevada, Sierra de las Cruces) channel access through passes; the Yucatan Peninsula meanwhile fragments politically after Mayapan's rise, with the northern plains supporting competing lineage states; highland Guatemala hosts the K'iche' and Kaqchikel kingdoms in defensible mountain basins.

Climate Regime & Volatility: The period falls within the Medieval Climate Anomaly's later phases and the transition toward the Little Ice Age; Basin of Mexico experiences predictable monsoonal rainfall (May–October) with periodic drought years disrupting harvests; Yucatan remains vulnerable to hurricane damage and drought; climate volatility intensifies competition for productive land.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: Volcanic activity and seismic risk persist in the Basin of Mexico; periodic flooding affects lakeside settlements, requiring hydraulic management (dikes, canals); frost risk limits highland agriculture above certain elevations; the Popocatepetl eruption of c. 1350 CE deposits ash over portions of the Basin.

Resource & Energy Endowment: Obsidian from Pachuca and Otumba sources feeds tool production; lake resources (fish, waterfowl, algae, salt) provide protein and trade goods; pine-oak forests supply timber and fuel; agricultural land at a premium in the densely settled Basin; no metal ores locally but copper and gold imported from western and southern Mexico.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Lacustrine ecosystems absorb organic waste; chinampa agriculture recycles nutrients; localized deforestation for fuel and construction degrades watershed slopes; salt accumulation in Texcoco's waters (saline versus freshwater lake zones) creates environmental gradients.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: Endemic gastrointestinal and respiratory diseases; no catastrophic epidemics in the pre-contact period; infant and child mortality elevated by Mesoamerican standards but population expanding; highland elevation reduces some tropical disease vectors.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: Maize, beans, squash, amaranth, and chia provide dietary staples; chinampa agriculture yields multiple harvests, reducing food insecurity; lake resources add protein; elite access to cacao, imported fruits, and game; commoner nutrition adequate but vulnerable to harvest failure.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Herbal medicine sophisticated, with extensive pharmacopoeia recorded in later colonial sources; ticitl (healers) treat illness through botanical, ritual, and surgical means; sweat baths, bone-setting, and wound treatment practiced; epidemic-response capacity untested in this period.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Elite polygyny produces large noble households and succession disputes; commoner monogamy normative; marriage alliances between ruling houses structure inter-polity relations; the Mexica practice strategic intermarriage with established Basin lineages to acquire legitimacy.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Basin of Mexico population grows substantially, reaching perhaps 1–2 million by 1400 CE; Tenochtitlan founded 1325 CE grows from a small island settlement; intense competition for land drives agricultural intensification; Yucatan and highland Guatemala populations stable to growing.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: Warfare casualties (including sacrifice of captives) create demographic costs; tribute labor extracted from subordinate populations; widows and orphans absorbed through kinship networks; the demographic structure remains expansionary.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: Chinampa (raised-bed) agriculture in the Basin's freshwater lakes achieves extraordinary productivity, supporting dense populations; milpa farming on surrounding slopes supplements lake-based production; household gardens and maguey cultivation diversify the subsistence base; periodic drought threatens the provisioning floor.

Energy Capture & Conversion: Human muscle remains primary; no draft animals; canoe transport on lake systems dramatically reduces energy costs of bulk movement compared to overland portage; fire for cooking, lime-processing, and craft production; charcoal production strains highland forests.

Labor Organization & Coercion: Commoner households owe tribute and corvee to their calpulli and overlords; slaves (tlacotin) from debt, crime, or war labor in households and on state projects; craft specialists increasingly detached from subsistence agriculture; tributary labor mobilized for construction, warfare, and public works.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Craft production intensifies in obsidian, ceramics, textiles, featherwork, and lapidary work; market systems expand with major markets (tianquiztli) at Tlatelolco and elsewhere; surplus extraction supports warrior elites, priests, and growing administrative classes; the Basin's agricultural productivity enables urban concentration.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: State granaries (built by Nezahualcoyotl at Texcoco in the later period) buffer against harvest failure; household storage of dried maize; tribute goods warehoused in temple-palace complexes; chinampa year-round production reduces seasonal vulnerability.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: Long-distance merchant groups (pochteca) emerge as a distinct class; trade networks link the Basin to the Gulf Coast (cotton, cacao, rubber), Oaxaca (cochineal, gold), Pacific Coast (shells, cacao), and beyond; local markets operate on a rotating schedule; canoe transport on Basin lakes moves bulk goods efficiently.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: Cacao beans, cotton mantles (quachtli), and copper axes serve as currency; no coinage; credit extended through kinship and merchant networks; debt bondage (tlacotin status) results from unpaid obligations; deferred reciprocity structures elite exchange.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: Tribute (in goods and labor) flows from subordinate polities to dominant centers; the Triple Alliance (forming 1428 CE) systematizes extraction; temples receive offerings; redistribution through feasting, ritual, and military reward; commoner tax burden significant but negotiated through calpulli structures.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Noble-commoner distinction hardens; pipiltin (nobles) control land and office; macehualtin (commoners) hold usufruct through calpulli membership; successful warriors achieve limited upward mobility; wealth concentrated in textiles, featherwork, cacao, and tribute rights rather than land alone.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Chinampa agriculture integrates organic waste as fertilizer; urban waste managed through sweeping and canal disposal; lake ecosystems process organic load; localized pollution around craft production areas.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Patrilineal noble houses (tecalli) transmit titles, land, and office; commoner calpulli units provide land access, mutual aid, and collective identity; inheritance follows male lines with provisions for widow and minor support; the Mexica royal line (claimed descent from Culhuacan via marriage alliance) legitimates sovereignty.

Association & Mutual Aid: Calpulli structure provides neighborhood-based mutual aid, collective labor, and local governance; pochteca merchant guilds organize long-distance trade with internal courts and rituals; craft groups (e.g., featherworkers, goldsmiths) cluster residentially and maintain occupational identity; temple complexes organize devotional communities.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: Ballgame continues as elite sport and cosmic drama; feasting accompanies ritual calendars, market days, and political occasions; pulque and cacao consumption mark ceremonial and recreational contexts; music, dance, and poetry cultivated among elites.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: Rigid division between pipiltin (nobles) and macehualtin (commoners) with distinct legal status, dress codes, and privileges; tlacotin (slaves) form lowest stratum; ethnic hierarchy emerges as Mexica assert superiority over other Nahua groups and non-Nahua peoples; warrior orders (cuauhtli, ocelotl) provide achievement-based status.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: Polities in the Basin operate through rulers (tlatoani) advised by councils; calpulli leaders (calpulleque) manage local affairs; tlacuilo scribes record tribute, calendrics, and histories; administrative capacity expands as the Mexica grow from small polity to regional power; the Triple Alliance (1428 CE) creates a coordinated but decentralized imperial structure.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: Warrior sodalities organized by age-grade and achievement; the macuahuitl (obsidian-edged sword), atlatl, bow, and quilted cotton armor standard; armies levy commoners alongside professional warriors; fortifications defend key sites; military success essential to political advancement and tribute acquisition.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: Endemic warfare among Basin polities; the Tepanec hegemony under Azcapotzalco dominates until 1428 CE when a coalition of Mexica (Tenochtitlan), Acolhua (Texcoco), and Tepanec dissidents (Tlacopan) overthrows it; the period is one of continuous violent competition, with major polities (Culhuacan, Azcapotzalco, Texcoco) rising and falling; internal factional conflict accompanies succession disputes.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: Tlatoani (speakers/rulers) like Itzcoatl (r. 1427–1440), who leads the Triple Alliance's formation, combine military charisma, priestly authority, and lineage legitimacy; the cihuacoatl (second ruler) shares administrative burden; leadership succession contested, requiring political skill and often violence.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: Mexica legitimacy initially fragile, derived from service as mercenaries and marriage alliances with Culhuacan's royal line; the founding of Tenochtitlan (1325 CE) at the site where the eagle perched on cactus provides divine sanction; victory over Azcapotzalco (1428 CE) transforms legitimacy from dependent to imperial.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: The Mexica demonstrate extraordinary collective mobilization, transforming from tribute-payers to tribute-collectors within a century; the willingness to accept subordinate status while building strength shows strategic patience; the 1428 CE revolt against Azcapotzalco requires coordinated uprising and sustained military effort.

External Relations & Posture: Pre-1428 CE relations defined by subordination to the Tepanec empire; marriage alliances and mercenary service build connections with established powers; rivalry with Azcapotzalco intensifies through the early fifteenth century; alliance-building with Texcoco and Tlacopan enables the overthrow; post-1428 CE posture becomes aggressively expansionist.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: Militaristic ideology celebrates warrior virtue; ethnic pride intensifies as the Mexica transform from despised immigrants (the founding myth involves their wandering and rejection) to dominant power; cosmic anxiety about maintaining world-order through sacrifice colors collective psychology; ambition and restless expansion characterize the polity's temper.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: The Tepanec ruler Maxtla's harsh treatment of subject peoples, including the murder of Chimalpopoca (Mexica tlatoani), triggers defection and rebellion; Azcapotzalco's hegemony collapses when allegiance fails; the lesson of overreach and alienation informs subsequent Aztec imperial strategy.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Nahuatl serves as lingua franca across much of central Mexico; Maya languages dominate Yucatan and Guatemala; pictographic-logographic writing systems (not fully phonetic) restricted to trained scribes; oral transmission carries most cultural knowledge; multilingual interpreters facilitate long-distance trade.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Foot messengers (paynani) traverse maintained roads; canoe transport in Basin lakes speeds local communication; information follows trade routes; royal courts and markets serve as information nodes; no faster-than-human transmission possible.

Record, Storage & Persistence: Tlacuilo scribes produce screenfold codices on bark paper (amatl) or deerskin recording tribute lists, genealogies, calendrical cycles, historical narratives, and ritual knowledge; archives maintained in temple-palace complexes; the Mixtec genealogical tradition produces elaborate screenfolds (Codex Nuttall, Codex Bodley survive as Colonial-era copies of Postclassic originals); oral performance accompanies and interprets pictorial records.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: Official histories serve ruling lineages; Itzcoatl reputedly orders the burning of old codices to rewrite history favoring the Mexica (reported in colonial sources, debated by scholars); iconographic programs on temples and public architecture broadcast power; scribal production controlled by elites.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: Public rituals, processions, and market assemblies reach non-literate populations; painted imagery on temples and monuments conveys messages to viewers; oral recitation of histories accompanies pictorial display; the screenfold format allows selective revelation.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: Competing polities maintain rival historical claims; conquest involves destruction or appropriation of defeated peoples' records; mythological and historical registers blend; the retrospective reframing of Mexica origins (from despised wanderers to chosen people) indicates deliberate signal manipulation.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Reciprocity with gods and community grounds moral order; honoring obligations (tribute, sacrifice, kinship duties) constitutes virtue; warrior honor valorizes captive-taking for sacrifice; social hierarchy naturalized as divinely ordained.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: Customary law governs most disputes; the great lawgiver Nezahualcoyotl of Texcoco (r. 1431–1472, just after this period) codifies laws that become the model for the Triple Alliance; capital crimes include treason, adultery (for women), theft, murder, and sorcery; status-differentiated penalties apply.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: Rulers and councils serve as courts; calpulli leaders adjudicate minor disputes; major cases heard at royal courts; sanctions range from compensation to death (by stoning, garroting, sacrifice); swift public execution demonstrates power; confession sometimes extracted through torture.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Nobles enjoy judicial privileges; commoners owe tribute and service but retain calpulli-mediated land rights; slaves retain certain protections (cannot be sold without consent except after repeated offenses, their children born free); compliance burden significant but customary.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: Elite violence against commoners largely unchecked; inter-polity warfare operates outside juridical frameworks; the Tepanec treatment of subject peoples illustrates the abuses unconstrained hegemony enables; the Triple Alliance formation represents in part a response to Tepanec injustice.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: Astronomical observation tracks Venus, solar zenith passages, and eclipse cycles for calendrical and divinatory purposes; mathematical traditions (vigesimal system, positional notation with zero) maintained; cosmological models explain natural phenomena through divine action; no separation of empirical and theological explanation.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Hydraulic engineering for chinampa construction, lake-level management, and dike-building reaches high sophistication; obsidian-knapping, featherwork, and lapidary techniques refined; architectural methods for monumental construction; agricultural knowledge of intensive cultivation, fertilization, and water management.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: Calmecac (noble schools) train priestly, scribal, and administrative elites in literacy, calendrics, rhetoric, and ritual; telpochcalli (commoner schools) emphasize military training and civic duty; craft knowledge transmitted through workshop apprenticeship; knowledge distribution highly stratified by status.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: Destruction of codices (whether by Itzcoatl's order or through warfare) eliminates historical records; oral traditions supplement but cannot fully preserve detailed archives; the pre-Mexica history of the Basin becomes fragmentary and contested; scribal traditions continue but with strategic revision.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: The Mexica migration narrative (the journey from Aztlan, the trials en route, the divine sign founding Tenochtitlan) structures collective identity; Huitzilopochtli (war god, sun deity) serves as patron; claimed connection to Toltec civilization through Culhuacan marriage alliance provides civilized legitimacy; the transformation from despised newcomers to imperial people constitutes the central drama.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: The Mexica present themselves as chosen by Huitzilopochtli for world-historical mission; military success proves divine favor; human sacrifice conceived as cosmic obligation maintaining the Sun's motion; the Flowery Wars (ritualized conflict for captives) institutionalize sacrificial ideology; conquest justified through sacred necessity.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: Aztec sculptural style develops from Toltec and Mixtec precedents, featuring monumental deity images, sacrificial iconography, and cosmological calendars (the famous Sun Stone dates from later, but the tradition develops here); featherwork, goldwork, and turquoise mosaic mark elite luxury production; cotton textiles with complex weaves distinguish status; architecture emphasizes twin-temple pyramids (Templo Mayor form).

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: The period is one of cultural florescence rather than exhaustion; new forms and symbols actively generated; the older Basin cultures (Culhuacan, Azcapotzalco) provide raw material for Mexica synthesis; some traditions (like earlier Toltec forms) recycled and reinterpreted rather than simply continued.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: The universe conceived as multiple layered heavens and underworlds surrounding the earth-disk; cyclic creation and destruction (the present Fifth Sun destined to end in earthquake); human existence precarious, sustained by blood-feeding of the gods; solar motion depends on continuous sacrifice; cosmic pessimism underlies religious obligation.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: Human sacrifice intensifies as ideological and state practice; heart extraction, decapitation, flaying, and burning employed; the xiuhmolpilli (New Fire ceremony every 52 years) marks calendar round completion; monthly festivals structure collective devotion; household shrines, temple ceremonies, and pilgrimage organize religious life; autosacrifice (bloodletting) practiced by priests and penitents.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: Temple-pyramid complexes serve as priestly residences, schools, and ritual centers; priestly hierarchies (tlamacazqui) maintain calendrical, divinatory, and sacrificial knowledge; no pan-Mesoamerican church but shared cosmological frameworks; doctrine transmitted through calmecac education and oral-pictorial tradition.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: The Mexica adopt and adapt deities and cults from conquered and allied peoples; Quetzalcoatl, Tlaloc, Tezcatlipoca, and local deities incorporated into expanding pantheon; religious pluralism within shared cosmological assumptions; the Mexica actively collect defeated peoples' deity images (housed in the Coateocalli, "house of foreign gods," at Tenochtitlan).

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: The period shows no evidence of secularization; religious intensity increases with imperial expansion; however, the demands of sacrificial ideology generate internal tensions (the "Flowery Wars" provide captives but also perpetuate enmity); the cosmological stakes of failure remain terrifying, driving ever-greater ritual elaboration.

docs.title: 400 BCE – 250 CE — Late Preclassic Maya and Script Development
docs.text: Summary: The Late Preclassic Maya lowlands witness the emergence of state-scale polities and, with them, a logosyllabic script that anchors dynastic authority in durable record — the binding constraint is the invention of a writing system capable of fixing spoken language in stone and stucco, transforming ephemeral claim into permanent monument and enabling the administrative continuity that state complexity demands.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: The Maya lowlands span the Yucatan Peninsula's limestone shelf, the Peten rainforest basin, and the piedmont zones linking highlands to coast, terrain that imposes high friction on overland movement through dense tropical canopy while offering navigable river corridors — the Usumacinta, Pasion, Motagua — and coastal routes that connect emerging centers. Kaminaljuyu sits in the Guatemala highlands at 1,500 meters, El Mirador and Nakbe in the low Peten interior, dispersed nodes linked by sacbe causeways where engineered and by forest trails elsewhere.

Climate Regime & Volatility: Seasonal monsoon brings wet-season abundance (May–November) alternating with dry-season stress; interannual variability in rainfall timing determines surplus margins, and the lowlands remain vulnerable to multi-year droughts that test stored reserves and strain agricultural extensification. No evidence of catastrophic climate forcing in this window, but the baseline volatility selects for buffering strategies — water management, raised fields, forest garden cultivation.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: Hurricanes strike the Caribbean coast periodically; the interior lowlands face localized flooding and drought cycles rather than seismic or volcanic risk. The porous karst geology provides cenotes and caves for water access but limits surface water storage, creating dependence on seasonal rainfall patterns and artificial reservoirs at major centers.

Resource & Energy Endowment: Limestone for construction is abundant; chert and obsidian for tools must be imported from highland sources, creating long-distance exchange dependencies. Forest resources — timber, bark paper, thatch, game — remain plentiful. Agricultural soils are thin over limestone bedrock, requiring intensive management (terracing, raised fields, household gardens) to sustain growing populations around monumental centers.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Low population densities relative to available forest allow organic waste to cycle through slash-and-burn cultivation without significant sink saturation. Monumental construction at El Mirador and Nakbe concentrates labor and resources but does not yet strain the absorptive capacity of surrounding forest ecosystems.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: Tropical lowland disease ecology includes endemic gastrointestinal parasites, malaria where present, and periodic epidemic stress, though no evidence of catastrophic mortality events in this window. Infant and child mortality remain high by modern standards, shaping demographic replacement dynamics.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: Maize-bean-squash agriculture supplemented by forest game, fish, and gathered foods provides adequate protein and caloric intake for population growth. Skeletal evidence suggests variable nutritional status by social stratum, with elite burials showing better dental health and stature than commoner populations.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Healing knowledge resides in ritual specialists who combine herbal pharmacopeia with spiritual intervention; no institutional medical apparatus exists, but kinship networks provide care for sick and injured.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Polygyny among elites documented in later inscriptions likely extends to this period; commoner households appear monogamous. Reproductive capacity is not constrained — population grows steadily through the Late Preclassic.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Population expands significantly, with El Mirador reaching an estimated 100,000 people at peak — a scale unprecedented in the lowlands. Centers grow through natural increase supplemented by in-migration from surrounding hinterlands. Density at major sites tests local carrying capacity.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: The demographic profile skews young given high fertility and mortality; the dependent load — children, elderly, infirm — is absorbed within extended household structures without evidence of systemic strain.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: Maize agriculture provides the staple foundation, intensified through raised-field cultivation in bajo (seasonal wetland) zones, forest gardens, and household plots. Provisioning floor rises with agricultural technique but remains vulnerable to multi-year drought sequences.

Energy Capture & Conversion: Human labor constitutes the sole power source; no animal traction or mechanical advantage beyond simple machines (lever, inclined plane). The energy ceiling for monumental construction — La Danta pyramid at El Mirador rises 72 meters — is set by corvee labor mobilization rather than per-capita work capacity.

Labor Organization & Coercion: Labor for monument construction and public works draws on tributary obligations organized through emerging elite hierarchies; the degree of coercion versus prestige-based recruitment is unclear but growing inequality suggests compulsion increases with state scale.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Agricultural surplus permits non-producing specialists (scribes, priests, artisans, rulers) and funds monumental construction. The scale of El Mirador's architecture implies sustained surplus extraction across generations.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: Granary storage documented archaeologically; water reservoirs engineered at major centers. Buffering capacity sufficient for single bad years but vulnerable to sequential drought.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: Long-distance exchange networks supply obsidian from Guatemala highlands, jade from the Motagua Valley, marine shell from Caribbean and Pacific coasts, cacao from Soconusco. Trade routes consolidate; elite control over prestige goods intensifies hierarchical stratification.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: Cacao beans serve as a value medium in later periods and likely emerge here; no formal credit instruments exist, but reciprocal obligations within kinship and tribute networks defer exchange across time.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: Emerging elites extract surplus through tribute and labor drafts, redistributing through feasting, public ritual, and monumental construction that legitimizes authority. The extraction-redistribution cycle intensifies as polities grow.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Inequality widens visibly: elite burials contain jade, elaborate ceramics, and sacrificial victims while commoner interments remain modest. Elite lineages consolidate control over land, labor, and trade access.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Construction debris accumulates at major sites; organic waste recycles through agricultural systems. No evidence of waste management crisis.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Patrilineal descent governs elite succession; extended households form the basic production and consumption unit. Inheritance of elite status consolidates across generations, visible in multi-generational dynastic sequences recorded once script matures.

Association & Mutual Aid: Village-level cooperation persists in agricultural work, construction labor, and ritual observance. Kinship networks extend mutual aid obligations beyond nuclear households.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: Ballgame courts appear at emerging centers, providing ritual-athletic spaces that integrate sociability with cosmological performance. Feasting occasions mark calendrical and life-cycle transitions.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: Elite-commoner distinctions sharpen: rulers emerge with divine-kingship attributes, supported by noble lineages controlling land, labor, and ritual knowledge. Craft specialists occupy intermediate positions. Stratification is not yet fully rigidified but trends toward hereditary closure.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: Emergent state apparatus coordinates labor for monumental projects, manages tribute collection, and organizes calendrical ritual. Administrative capacity rudimentary by later standards but sufficient to build La Danta. Writing emerges as an administrative and legitimating tool.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: Warfare attested iconographically; elite warriors lead conflict between polities. No standing military apparatus — forces mobilize for specific campaigns. Fortifications appear at some sites, suggesting defensive concerns.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: El Mirador's abandonment circa 150 CE marks the first major collapse in lowland Maya history — cause unclear but likely combines drought stress, political fragmentation, and warfare. The center fails to sustain its scale; population disperses to smaller sites, and the polity's administrative apparatus breaks down.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: Ajaw (ruler) figures emerge with divine-royal attributes, commanding personal authority grounded in lineage, ritual performance, and military success. Portraiture on monuments begins to individualize rulers.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: Legitimacy rests on ruler's capacity to mediate between human and divine realms, ensure agricultural fertility, and organize successful warfare. Monumental construction visibly demonstrates power and divine favor.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: The will to undertake multi-generational building projects implies sustained political coherence across successions. Factional competition between lineages and polities is endemic but does not yet fragment the major centers catastrophically until El Mirador's decline.

External Relations & Posture: Inter-polity warfare attested; long-distance trade implies diplomatic as well as commercial relations. Kaminaljuyu maintains highland-lowland connections. No evidence of imperial expansion in modern sense — competition among peer polities predominates.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: Monumental construction implies collective mobilization around shared purpose — whether through enthusiasm, obligation, or coercion is unclear. The scale of labor suggests elite capacity to command broad participation.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: El Mirador's abandonment suggests exhaustion of the political will sustaining the center — whether through elite factional collapse, commoner defection, or external conquest remains debated.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Maya language family provides the spoken substrate; dialects diverge across the lowlands but mutual intelligibility persists within regions. Writing emerges as an elite technology — accessibility restricted to trained specialists.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Information travels at walking speed along causeways and trails, by canoe along rivers and coasts. No rapid-transmission technology; news of distant events arrives slowly, limiting coordination across large polities.

Record, Storage & Persistence: The critical transition: hieroglyphic script emerges, encoding Maya language in logosyllabic signs carved in stone, molded in stucco, painted on murals. San Bartolo murals (c. 100 BCE) preserve early captions; Stela 1 at El Porton (c. 400 BCE) among earliest dated texts. The Long Count calendar system develops, enabling precise temporal reference across centuries. Writing fixes dynastic claims, ritual knowledge, and calendrical computation outside living memory — the defining manuscript-stage transition.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: Monumental texts controlled by ruling elites; content focuses on royal legitimation, military victory, ritual performance. No evidence of competing public discourse — writing serves power.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: Texts on public monuments address gathered audiences during ritual occasions; the ability to read remains restricted, but carved images accompanying texts communicate to non-literate viewers. The text as spectacle precedes the text as consulted record.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: Stone and stucco inscriptions durable over centuries; perishable media (bark paper codices) likely in use but do not survive archaeologically from this period. Information loss through monument destruction remains the primary risk.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Justice embedded in cosmological order — rulers mediate between human and divine realms, and their actions maintain balance (or disrupt it). Moral authority flows from ritual correctness and divine favor rather than abstract principle.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: No evidence of codified law; custom and elite judgment govern disputes. Writing does not yet carry legal code — its function is commemorative and divinatory rather than regulatory.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: Rulers adjudicate disputes within their domains; sanction ranges from compensation to execution and sacrifice. No formal court apparatus — judgment is personal and divine-royal.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: No concept of individual rights against the collectivity; subjects owe tribute and labor to rulers who owe protection and cosmic mediation in return. The bargain is hierarchical and unequal.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: Elite impunity is structural — rulers answer to divine judgment, not human accountability. Commoner grievances find no institutional redress beyond appeal to elite patron.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: Cosmological paradigm integrates astronomical observation, calendrical mathematics, and divine-human relations into coherent worldview. The Maya calendar — combining 260-day ritual cycle, 365-day solar year, and Long Count — represents sophisticated mathematical achievement. Astronomy serves ritual prediction rather than abstract inquiry.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Architectural engineering permits construction of massive pyramidal platforms (La Danta at 72 meters among largest pre-Columbian structures). Hydraulic engineering manages water through reservoirs and canals. Agricultural technique intensifies through raised-field and forest-garden systems.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: Knowledge transmission occurs within elite lineages and specialist schools (later documented as scribal training institutions). Literacy restricted to small specialist class; technical skills (architecture, astronomy, writing) concentrate among elite-controlled specialists.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: El Mirador's abandonment results in localized knowledge loss as scribal and architectural traditions disperse; the broader Maya tradition continues at other centers. The Long Count system and script corpus survive the transition.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: Maya identity crystallizes around shared cosmology (Popol Vuh themes documented in later sources likely ancient), ancestral claims, and divine-kingship ideology. Origin narratives connect ruling lineages to founding ancestors and cosmic events.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: Rulers justify authority through descent from founders, successful warfare, ritual performance, and cosmic mediation. Monumental inscriptions — the new manuscript technology — permanently record these claims, transforming ephemeral performance into enduring legitimation.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: Polychrome ceramics, jade working, monumental sculpture and architecture in distinctive Maya style. San Bartolo murals show sophisticated painting tradition. Iconography depicts mythological scenes, royal ritual, warfare. The visual vocabulary of power consolidates.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: No evidence of form exhaustion in this creative period — traditions are in formation rather than decline. El Mirador's collapse brings localized cultural disruption but the broader tradition continues to develop.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: Layered cosmos — thirteen heavens, nine underworlds, earth as middle plane — populated by gods, ancestors, and supernatural beings. Human action affects cosmic balance; rulers bear special responsibility for maintaining harmony through proper ritual.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: Bloodletting, sacrifice (human and animal), ballgame, calendrical ceremonies structure religious life. Elite ritual performed atop pyramidal temples. Caves and cenotes serve as portals to underworld. The ritual calendar governs agricultural and political timing.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: Priestly specialists control ritual knowledge; rulers combine political and religious authority in divine-kingship role. No separate ecclesiastical institution — religious and political power fuse in the ajaw.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: Shared cosmological framework across Maya regions with local variation; contact with highland Guatemala (Kaminaljuyu) and other Mesoamerican traditions introduces stylistic and possibly theological influences. The tradition is in expansion, incorporating rather than excluding.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: No evidence of sacred discharge — the cosmological system remains vital and elaborating. El Mirador's collapse may indicate localized loss of faith in particular dynasty's cosmic mandate, but the broader religious tradition continues undiminished.

docs.title: 1650 CE – 1750 CE — Mature Colonial Society and Baroque Culture
docs.text: Summary: A century of relative stability following demographic nadir, during which the colonial manuscript regime reaches full institutional maturity — parish registers, notarial archives, tribunal records, and indigenous community documents forming an interlocking documentary system that undergirds social hierarchy, property, and governance — while baroque cultural expression achieves distinctive American forms in architecture, literature, and religious practice, the binding constraint being silver extraction whose cycles of boom and contraction set the rhythm of colonial prosperity and whose revenues fund both secular administration and ecclesiastical splendor.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: The colonial territory maintains its fundamental division between the densely administered highland cores — the basins of Mexico, Puebla-Tlaxcala, Oaxaca, and Michoacan — and the more thinly governed peripheries of the northern mining frontier, the Yucatan Peninsula, and the Pacific and Gulf coastal plains; royal roads (caminos reales) link major centers but much territory remains accessible only by mule path or indigenous trail, maintaining spatial friction that limits administrative reach.

Climate Regime & Volatility: The Little Ice Age continues through this period, bringing somewhat cooler and more variable conditions than earlier centuries; the monsoon pattern of summer rains persists, with agricultural life organized around maize cultivation in the wet season; periodic drought years (notable cluster 1695–1697) trigger food crises and elevated mortality, though the recovering population has rebuilt some buffering capacity.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: Earthquakes continue to threaten highland settlements, with major events in 1653, 1696 (Oaxaca), and 1711; Mexico City's lacustrine setting produces chronic flooding despite ongoing drainage works (the desague project launched 1607 continues as an unfinished expense); hurricane damage affects Gulf coast ports and Yucatan settlements; volcanic quiescence provides relief from that hazard.

Resource & Energy Endowment: Silver mining remains the economic foundation, though the richest shallow deposits show depletion and operations require deeper shafts and more intensive drainage; new discoveries in the north (Real de Catorce, 1773, just beyond this period) will refresh the industry; highland forests continue to supply timber and charcoal, though deforestation pressure persists around cities and mining centers; maguey cultivation expands for pulque production.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Mercury contamination remains localized around refining sites; urban waste loads in Mexico City strain the canal system but the relatively modest population limits overall pressure; deforested hillsides show erosion; the environmental footprint remains lighter than the pre-contact period when much larger populations cultivated intensively.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: The major epidemic diseases become endemic rather than catastrophic, with periodic outbreaks of smallpox, measles, and typhus causing elevated mortality but no longer the society-destroying waves of the conquest era; the surviving population has acquired some immunity; matlazahuatl (probably typhus) in 1736–1739 causes perhaps 200,000 deaths, the worst outbreak of the century.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: The indigenous population, now recovering from its nadir, subsists primarily on maize, beans, squash, and chile, supplemented by pulque; nutritional adequacy varies by region and season; the casta populations and Spanish settlers consume more diverse diets including wheat bread, meat, and imported goods; periodic drought-induced famines (1695–97, 1749–50) demonstrate continued vulnerability.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Hospitals operate in major cities under ecclesiastical and municipal sponsorship; indigenous healing traditions continue alongside Spanish humoral medicine; curanderos and parteras (midwives) provide care in communities without physicians; the Protomedicato (medical licensing board) regulates practitioners in urban areas; care capacity reaches only a fraction of the population.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Parish marriage registration documents the formation of families across casta categories; indigenous communities maintain high fertility as population recovery proceeds; Spanish and creole families show lower but stable fertility; unions across casta lines continue despite social disapproval, feeding population mixing.

Demographic Renewal & Density: The indigenous population recovers slowly from the nadir of approximately one million around 1620–1650, reaching perhaps two million by 1750; the mestizo, mulato, and other casta populations grow more rapidly; Spanish and creole population remains small but demographically stable; total population perhaps three to four million by 1750; urban centers concentrate population.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: The age structure normalizes as recovery proceeds; dependency ratios improve from the crisis era; orphan and widow populations remain significant but manageable; the ecclesiastical network provides some safety net through cofradias and charitable institutions.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: Maize agriculture remains the dietary foundation, with indigenous communities cultivating milpas (mixed-crop fields) and haciendas producing for urban markets; wheat cultivation serves Spanish and urban demand; livestock ranching expands across northern grasslands; pulque production increases substantially, becoming a major industry; the provisioning floor is adequate in normal years but vulnerable to drought.

Energy Capture & Conversion: Animal power (horses, mules, oxen) supplements human labor across agriculture, transport, and mining; water mills process grain and run ore-crushing stamps; charcoal fuels smelting and domestic cooking; energy remains fundamentally organic but animal power raises the work ceiling above pre-contact levels.

Labor Organization & Coercion: The repartimiento system continues for public works and mining but wage labor (partly coerced through debt peonage) increasingly dominates hacienda and mining employment; indigenous communities retain internal labor organization; craft production in cities operates through guilds with regulated membership and prices; African slavery persists in sugar production, domestic service, and urban occupations.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Silver production fluctuates but remains substantial, with annual output averaging perhaps twelve to fifteen million pesos; textile obrajes (workshops) produce cloth for domestic markets; agricultural surplus flows from haciendas to urban markets; craft production supplies colonial demand for most manufactured goods; surplus capacity exceeds crisis-era levels but operates below pre-contact intensity.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: Municipal granaries (alhondigas) buffer urban grain supply; ecclesiastical institutions accumulate substantial capital reserves; haciendas hold grain stores; government treasuries maintain fiscal reserves; indigenous community chests (cajas de comunidad) continue; the buffering system remains vulnerable to sustained drought but handles ordinary fluctuations.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: The silver peso serves as the primary medium of exchange, circulating throughout the Spanish empire and into Asian and European markets; internal trade networks link producing regions to urban centers; the Manila galleon trade brings Asian silks, porcelain, and spices; the annual fleet system connects Veracruz to Spain; local tianguis (markets) continue indigenous exchange patterns.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: The Church functions as the colony's primary financial institution, holding mortgages (censos and capellanias) that provide credit to landowners, miners, and merchants; silver accumulates in ecclesiastical treasuries; merchant credit networks extend from Mexico City to provincial towns and mining centers; the monetary system remains fundamentally stable.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: The colonial state extracts through tribute, mining royalties, alcabala (sales tax), pulque taxes, and the tobacco monopoly (established 1764, end of period); ecclesiastical tithes channel substantial surplus to the Church; redistribution flows through ecclesiastical charity, public works, and patronage networks; total extraction burden is substantial but sustainable.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Wealth concentrates in hacendado, merchant, and mining families, with the Church as the single largest holder of capital and urban property; indigenous communities retain communal lands but face continued encroachment; creole families consolidate landholdings across generations; entail (mayorazgo) protects elite estates from division.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Mining generates mercury-contaminated tailings; urban waste accumulates in canals and vacant lots; organic waste is largely recycled through domestic animal husbandry; the environmental impact remains localized but cumulative.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Spanish inheritance law (partible with mejoras) governs property transmission; the Church regulates marriage, documenting unions in parish registers that become crucial identity records; compadrazgo relations cross-cut kinship networks; extended household structures accommodate relatives and dependents.

Association & Mutual Aid: Cofradias (religious confraternities) provide the primary associational structure, organizing feast sponsorship, burial insurance, and communal solidarity; guilds regulate urban crafts; indigenous communities maintain cargo systems for rotating civic and religious offices; the regular orders and secular clergy coordinate charitable activity.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: The religious calendar structures collective festivity, with major celebrations for Corpus Christi, patron saints, and the Guadalupe feast (December 12); bullfighting and horse racing provide elite entertainment; cockfighting spans classes; pulquerias serve as popular gathering places; theatrical performances occur in urban centers.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: The sistema de castas reaches full elaboration, with elaborate nomenclature (mestizo, castizo, mulato, zambo, and dozens more) classifying mixed-ancestry individuals; practical boundaries remain somewhat permeable through wealth, education, and presentation; peninsulares (Spanish-born) maintain precedence over criollos (American-born Spaniards); indigenous principales retain status within their communities.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: The viceregal administration operates with established routines; the Audiencia provides judicial oversight; corregidores and alcaldes mayores govern provincial districts with substantial autonomy; municipal cabildos manage urban affairs; indigenous cabildos administer communities under Spanish oversight; documentary procedures are comprehensive and standardized.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: A small military force maintains coastal defenses and guards against foreign incursion; internal order relies on local officials and ecclesiastical authority; the Inquisition continues to police religious orthodoxy; militia units can be mobilized for emergencies; banditry persists in peripheral areas but major rebellion is absent.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: Social friction finds release through legal process, religious ritual, and festive release; urban crime and rural banditry remain endemic but contained; major uprisings are absent in this period of relative stability; the apparatus shows some sclerosis but maintains functional integrity.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: Viceroys exercise personal authority as the king's representatives, with notable figures including the Duke of Alburquerque (1653–1660) and the Duke of Linares (1711–1716); archbishops wield parallel religious authority; individual charisma matters less than institutional position in this routinized period.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: The colonial order commands formal allegiance through the combined authority of crown and Church; indigenous acceptance remains pragmatic, rooted in legal protections and religious incorporation; creole loyalty is genuine if tinged with grievance; legitimacy rests on continuity and the absence of alternative.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: The viceregal administration maintains sufficient coherence to govern effectively; indigenous communities demonstrate collective will through legal action and community maintenance; the system operates by routine rather than energetic direction; major initiatives are absent in this period of consolidation.

External Relations & Posture: New Spain remains integrated within the Spanish imperial system, sending silver to the metropole and receiving administrative direction; the Manila galleon maintains Pacific trade; war between Spain and other European powers occasionally disrupts shipping but New Spain itself faces no serious external threat during this period.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: The colonial population exhibits resigned accommodation to established hierarchy; religious piety provides emotional anchorage; creole pride develops alongside resentment of peninsular precedence; indigenous communities maintain collective identity through documented claims and ritual practice; the mood is stable, neither enthusiastic nor rebellious.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: Creole resentment of peninsular precedence simmers without boiling over; indigenous disaffection finds outlets through legal process and communal ritual; the overall temper is one of stable accommodation rather than either enthusiasm or despair.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Spanish serves as the language of administration, commerce, and elite culture; indigenous languages (Nahuatl, Maya, Zapotec, Mixtec, others) remain primary for most of the population; Latin appears in ecclesiastical and academic contexts; literacy is restricted to perhaps ten percent of the population — clergy, officials, merchants, indigenous scribes — but this minority produces and consumes a substantial documentary flow.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Information travels by courier along royal roads, reaching distant provinces in days to weeks; communication with Spain requires months; the annual fleet and Manila galleon carry news and correspondence on set schedules; rumor networks supplement formal channels; printed gazettes do not yet exist.

Record, Storage & Persistence: The colonial archive reaches full development: parish registers (baptism, marriage, burial) document vital events; notarial archives preserve contracts, wills, and property transfers; tribunal records accumulate; indigenous community documents (titulos, maps, petitions) continue production; institutional archives provide systematic storage; survival depends on continued institutional care.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: The Inquisition reviews publications and polices religious discourse; the printing press operates under license, producing primarily religious works, devotional literature, and official documents; critical discussion of colonial rule is unacceptable; acceptable discourse operates within Catholic orthodoxy and monarchical loyalty.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: The literate minority consumes manuscript and printed materials; sermons reach wider audiences; visual media (church art, processional displays, theatrical performances) convey messages across literacy barriers; oral transmission remains the primary information channel for most.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: Institutional archives maintain good preservation within their custody; documents in indigenous communities face greater risk of loss or decay; translation and transcription introduce errors; forgery of land documents continues as a recognized problem; verification relies on comparison to archived originals and witness testimony.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Catholic natural law provides the dominant moral framework, teaching hierarchical obligation alongside universal spiritual dignity; indigenous moral traditions persist within Christian frameworks; the sense of justice accommodates extreme inequality as divinely ordained while also recognizing limits and reciprocal obligations.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: The Recopilacion de las Leyes de Indias (1680) codifies colonial law; additional cedulas and viceregal orders supplement the code; ecclesiastical law governs religious and family matters; indigenous customary law continues for community internal affairs; the legal framework is comprehensive and relatively stable.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: The Audiencia serves as supreme court; corregidores and alcaldes mayores provide provincial justice; indigenous cabildos handle minor matters; ecclesiastical courts address clergy and religious cases; the Inquisition tries heresy; multiple jurisdictions create complexity but the system provides regular process; judicial proceedings generate extensive documentation.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Indigenous peoples retain their formal status as protected vassals; these rights enable legal action against exploitation, though with variable success; compliance burden includes tribute payment, labor service, and conformity to Christian norms; the compliance load is substantial but routinized.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: Local officials often exploit their positions; powerful families evade sanctions; the justice system provides some check through appeal processes but the gap between law and practice remains significant; impunity correlates with social position.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: Scholastic philosophy dominates academic inquiry through the University of Mexico and Jesuit colegios; natural history continues with investigations of American flora, fauna, and peoples; astronomical observation maintains quality at European levels; Carlos de Siguenza y Gongora (1645–1700) exemplifies creole polymath inquiry; the questioning of received frameworks remains muted.
