Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: Camp life was intimate; mood was shared. Trust within the band was high; suspicion attached to strangers and neighboring bands with whom conflict had occurred. The temper was cautious and cooperative, shaped by mutual dependence in the forest.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: Disaffection expressed itself through departure. An individual or family unhappy with the band simply left to join relatives elsewhere. Apathy was rare; survival required active participation. Spent will was a personal, not collective, condition.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Spoken language was universal within the band; neighboring bands often shared mutually intelligible dialects. Communication was face-to-face; the deaf and mute were marginalized or excluded. No written or symbolic code extended the reach of speech.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: News traveled at the speed of walking. Drum signals and long-distance calls transmitted simple messages across forest distances; complex information required in-person speech. Transmission was slow and spatially limited.

Record, Storage & Persistence: All record was oral: genealogy, territorial knowledge, ritual, medicinal lore. Memory was the only archive. Knowledge persisted only as long as living speakers remembered and transmitted it; unspoken, it was lost.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: Speech was governed by etiquette: respect for elders, avoidance of taboo topics, circumlocution around death and danger. Censorship was social, not institutional—gossip and ridicule enforced norms. The permitted band of discourse was wide but not unlimited.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: Attention was personal; stories and news circulated through retelling. Amplification was linear—one speaker to a few listeners, who might retell to others. No mechanism for mass broadcast existed.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: Oral transmission introduced drift: each retelling could alter detail. Error correction relied on multiple independent transmissions and collective memory. Noise accumulated slowly; catastrophic loss occurred when too few speakers survived.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Justice was restorative and relational. Harm required compensation or reconciliation; unpunished wrong festered and could split the band. Fairness in sharing was fundamental—hoarding was the cardinal sin.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: No written law existed. Custom was orally transmitted and enforced through consensus. Rules governing marriage, hunting rights, and taboo were stable across generations but never codified.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: Disputes were mediated by elders or resolved through discussion. Sanction ranged from ridicule to ostracism to, in extreme cases, expulsion or execution. Liability was personal; kin might share the burden of compensation.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Rights were embedded in kinship and reciprocity, not abstract entitlement. Protection depended on kin networks; the unconnected were vulnerable. Compliance with sharing norms was constant but not burdensome—it was simply how one lived.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: Impunity was difficult in a small band where everyone knew everyone. Persistent wrongdoers were expelled. Unredressed wrong accumulated as grievance and eventually forced fission or violence. The system cleared most disputes but could not absorb serial transgression.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: Understanding of the natural world was empirical and animist: observed regularities were attributed to spirits, ancestors, and the inherent agency of forest beings. Theory was embedded in myth, not abstracted into propositions.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Botanical, zoological, and ecological knowledge was extensive and practically oriented: which plants were edible, medicinal, or poisonous; animal behavior and tracking; seasonal resource availability. Technique was refined over generations and transmitted orally.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: Learning was experiential and lifelong. Children learned by watching and doing; specialized knowledge (healing, ritual) passed from elder to apprentice. The knowledge stock was distributed across the band; no individual held all of it.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: Knowledge decayed when transmission failed—when an elder died before teaching, when a band dispersed, when a dialect went extinct. The slow pace of change meant obsolescence was rare; loss through broken transmission was the greater risk.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: Identity was rooted in the forest: origin myths told of ancestral emergence from trees, rivers, or the forest floor. The forest was not merely habitat but home, kin, and cosmos. Memory reached back only as far as oral genealogy could carry.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: No ideology of rule existed because no rule required legitimation. The order was the band, and the band justified itself through kinship and survival. Narrative authority attached to elders and skilled performers, not to offices.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: Material culture was portable and functional: bark-cloth, woven baskets, wooden and bone tools, body paint, and ornament. Artistic expression flourished in ephemeral forms—song, dance, storytelling—rather than durable objects.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: Cultural forms were stable and slowly evolving. Exhaustion was rare; the small scale of society and the integration of culture with daily life kept forms vital. Loss occurred through population decline and broken transmission, not through repetition into cliche.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: The forest was ensouled: trees, animals, rivers, and ancestors inhabited a continuous spiritual landscape. Human life was embedded in a web of obligations to non-human persons. Death was not extinction but transition to ancestral presence.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: Ritual accompanied hunting, gathering, birth, death, and initiation. Daily devotion was woven into routine: offerings to spirits, observance of taboo, invocations before hunting. The sacred was immanent, not set apart.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: No institution held religious authority. Ritual specialists—healers, diviners—held personal knowledge and charisma, not office. Doctrine was oral and localized; orthodoxy was enforced by tradition, not hierarchy.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: Spiritual practice was localized and stable. Diffusion occurred through inter-band contact and marriage; syncretism was gradual and unforced. No external cosmology displaced indigenous belief in this period.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: Disenchantment was unknown. The forest remained alive and responsive to human action. The sacred answered daily; no existential void opened. The spiritual residue was not disenchantment but the ordinary maintenance of relation with the unseen.

docs.title: 130,000 BCE – 70,000 BCE — Early Middle Stone Age Occupation of the Congo Basin
docs.text: Summary: A snapshot of the sparse human presence in the Congo Basin during the early Middle Stone Age, when small bands of anatomically modern humans occupy the forest margins and river corridors of equatorial Africa. The binding constraint is the oral substrate: whatever these people know of the forest, of each other, of the past and the possible, rides on breath and living memory — spoken or it does not exist, remembered or it is lost. The most causal factor is the forest itself, an environment so dense, so dark, so poor in large game that human occupation remains thin and marginal, clustered where rivers open the canopy and where forest meets savanna.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: The Congo Basin spreads as a vast shallow depression across equatorial Africa, drained by the Congo River and its tributaries — the Ubangi, Kasai, Lualaba — whose channels cut through dense forest and create the primary corridors of movement. The central cuvette holds seasonally flooded swamp forest, impassable and uninhabitable; the peripheral zones grade into drier forest and woodland savanna where human occupation concentrates. River margins and forest-savanna ecotones offer reduced friction for travel, hunting, and camp placement; the deep forest interior imposes near-total obstruction, its undergrowth, waterlogged terrain, and absence of game trails blocking sustained human presence.

Climate Regime & Volatility: The climate holds warm and wet through most of this span, with rainfall exceeding 1,500 mm annually across the forest core. Interglacial conditions prevail until roughly 70,000 BCE, when cooling begins; within the snapshot, the forest extends close to its maximum Pleistocene range. Seasonal variation is muted — no dry season long enough to open the canopy significantly. Interannual volatility remains low, but the forest's very stability works against the large-mammal concentrations that sustain dense human populations elsewhere.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: Acute hazards are few: no seismic or volcanic activity threatens the Basin's interior; flood pulses on the major rivers are seasonal and predictable rather than catastrophic. The forest itself is the hazard — its darkness, its disease load, its scarcity of food — but these are chronic pressures, not acute shocks. Human groups face no regime of sudden environmental disaster.

Resource & Energy Endowment: The forest offers plant foods — wild yams, fruits, nuts, palm hearts — dispersed and seasonal, requiring wide-ranging foraging. Large game is scarce; the forest elephant, the bongo antelope, and the forest buffalo exist but at low densities, difficult to locate and pursue in dense vegetation. Rivers provide fish and shellfish, the most reliable protein sources. Stone for toolmaking must often be carried from distant outcrops; raw material scarcity shapes lithic traditions. No concentrated energy endowment exists — no herds, no grain fields, no easily exploited mineral deposits — only the diffuse, low-density resources of the tropical forest.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Human populations are too sparse to saturate any sink. Organic waste decomposes rapidly in the warm, wet conditions; fire is localized and quickly absorbed by the surrounding humidity. The forest's absorptive capacity vastly exceeds the minimal human load. No accumulating residue; the sink remains open.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: The forest is a pathogen reservoir — malaria (Plasmodium falciparum), trypanosomiasis, filariasis, intestinal parasites, and a suite of viral hemorrhagic fevers endemic to the region. Infant and child mortality is high; adult life expectancy short. Those who survive carry acquired immunities, but the disease load imposes a constant attrition that caps population growth.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: Nutritional adequacy depends on mobility and knowledge — the ability to locate ripe fruits, to dig wild yams, to fish productive stretches of river. Bodies are lean, adapted to caloric scarcity and high activity. Protein intake is irregular, spiking with a successful hunt or fish catch, falling during lean periods. Chronic mild undernutrition is the baseline; acute famine is rare given low population density and the forest's year-round productivity, but plenty is equally rare.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Healing relies on plant knowledge passed orally — which bark reduces fever, which leaf poultices wounds, which roots ease childbirth. No specialized healers are archaeologically attested; the knowledge is diffused through the band. Recovery from serious injury or illness is uncertain; those who cannot keep up are likely abandoned or die. The healing capacity is minimal, adequate only for the small population it serves.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Reproductive patterns are shaped by high infant mortality and the energetic demands of forest foraging. Birth spacing is likely wide, enforced by prolonged breastfeeding and the caloric cost of carrying infants through difficult terrain. Pair-bonding patterns are unknown but presumably flexible, given the small band sizes. Selective pressures favor those who survive the disease gauntlet of childhood.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Population density is extremely low — perhaps a few hundred individuals scattered across a region the size of Western Europe. Birth and death roughly balance; any surplus is absorbed by high mortality rather than expansion. Migration flows are minimal, limited to the slow drift of bands along river corridors and forest edges. The carrying ceiling is set by food scarcity and disease, and the population sits well below it, constrained by the difficulty of extracting a living from the forest.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: The dependent load is small because few survive to old age and orphaned children are unlikely to outlive their providers. The productive cohort bears a light burden of dependency; the harsh conditions clear the residue of attrition quickly. No overhang accumulates.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: Subsistence is immediate-return foraging — what is found today is eaten today or within days. Wild yams, forest fruits, palm products, honey, insects, and small game form the plant and invertebrate base; fishing and occasional large-game hunting provide protein spikes. The provisioning floor sits just above bare survival; any interruption in foraging — illness, injury, displacement — drops a band to the edge of hunger.

Energy Capture & Conversion: Human muscle is the sole power source; fire is used for cooking and perhaps for driving game, but no animal or water power is harnessed. The energy ceiling is set by human endurance and the caloric return on foraging effort. The conversion is inefficient — much labor for modest return — but the low population density keeps the system in equilibrium.

Labor Organization & Coercion: Labor is organized by gender and age within small bands: men hunt and fish, women gather plant foods and process materials, children assist as they mature. No coercion exists beyond the social pressure of reciprocity and the necessity of contribution for inclusion. Division is cooperative, not hierarchical.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Production matches consumption; no surplus accumulates. Stone tools — scrapers, points, blades — are produced as needed from transported cores or local river cobbles. There is no slack, no expansion, no storage of excess beyond a few days' food. The system is at equilibrium, not in growth.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: No storage infrastructure exists; food spoils rapidly in tropical conditions, and mobility precludes carrying reserves. The buffer is the forest itself — the knowledge that food can be found if one keeps moving. Debt and pre-committed claims do not exist; there is nothing to borrow against.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: Exchange is internal to the band — the sharing of a kill, the distribution of gathered foods — with no evidence of inter-band trade networks. Movement is local, following seasonal resources; no logistics beyond what individuals can carry. External dependence does not apply.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: No value storage exists beyond the reciprocity obligations that bind band members: share now, expect sharing later. There is no medium of exchange, no accumulation, no wealth. Deferred reciprocity is the only credit.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: No surplus exists to extract; redistribution is the immediate sharing of food within the band. No tribute, no tax, no rent. The system has no revenue to raise.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Wealth is absent; all possess roughly the same few tools and ornaments. No defense of holdings is needed because there are no holdings. Concentration cannot occur where accumulation does not exist.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Organic waste is left at campsites and rapidly decomposed; lithic debitage scatters at knapping sites. No toxic output; no lasting detritus. The residue is nil.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Kinship structures are unknown in detail, but band society likely organizes around bilateral kin ties with fluid group membership. Marriage, if formalized, links bands and permits movement between them. Inheritance is minimal — tools, ornaments, perhaps knowledge — passed within families. The scaffold is flexible, adapted to small-group mobility.

Association & Mutual Aid: The band is the unit of mutual aid — sharing food, caring for the sick to the extent possible, defending against predators. No associations beyond kin and camp exist. The fabric is thin but strong within its small radius; beyond the band, no reliable cooperation.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: Non-work time is filled with talk, storytelling, grooming, and play — the social activities that bind small groups. Shared festive space is the campfire, the only light in the forest dark. Sociability is constant and necessary; isolation is death.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: No class or caste exists; status distinctions are minimal and earned — the skilled hunter, the knowledgeable elder, the productive gatherer. Stratification cannot develop where surplus does not accumulate. Group boundaries are permeable; individuals move between bands.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: No administration exists; decisions are made by consensus or by the informal authority of experienced individuals. No offices, no bureaucracy, no record-keeping. The apparatus is the spoken word and the face-to-face agreement.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: No organized coercive capacity exists beyond individual violence and collective shunning. Weapons are hunting tools — spears, perhaps throwing sticks. Conflict is resolved by avoidance, by fission, by moving away. The means of force are personal, not institutional.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: Social friction is discharged through mobility — those who quarrel can separate. Grievance does not accumulate where people can simply leave. No crime beyond the interpersonal, no apparatus to decay. The residue is nil.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: Leadership is situational and personal — the experienced hunter leads the hunt, the knowledgeable elder is consulted on camp placement or plant use. No permanent authority; no office to inherit. Influence follows demonstrated competence.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: Legitimacy is direct and face-to-face: one follows those whose judgment has proved sound. No abstract right of rule; allegiance is earned daily. Disaffection means departure, not revolt.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: Collective will is limited to the band's immediate concerns — where to camp, when to move, how to distribute a kill. There is no political struggle beyond interpersonal negotiation, no contest for power where power does not concentrate. Resolve is measured in the group's willingness to move or to stay.

External Relations & Posture: Relations with other bands are occasional and probably cautious — exchanging individuals, sharing information, perhaps trading ornaments or raw materials. No rivalry, no expansion, no posture of power. The stance is coexistence at a distance.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: The prevailing temper is cautious, attuned to the forest's dangers and rewards. Trust within the band is high — survival depends on it; trust beyond the band is limited to known individuals from neighboring groups. Risk perception is acute; the forest punishes carelessness.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: Disaffection is discharged through mobility; those who are unhappy leave. Apathy cannot persist where daily effort is required for survival. The residue does not accumulate.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Speech is the medium — fully grammatical language enabling discussion of the absent, the past, the future, the abstract. The code is shared within the band and probably intelligible to neighboring groups speaking related languages. No script, no symbol system beyond the spoken word. Exclusion is by foreignness or by absence — those not present cannot receive the message.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Information moves at the speed of human travel and the reach of the human voice. The channel is face-to-face speech, supplemented perhaps by calls and signals across distances. Reach is limited to the band and the occasional inter-band meeting; beyond that, information travels only when people do.

Record, Storage & Persistence: Memory is the only archive. Genealogies, territorial knowledge, plant lore, hunting techniques, and the stories that bind the group are held in human minds and transmitted through speech. Nothing is written; nothing persists beyond the chain of oral transmission. The record is fragile — one generation's failure to transmit is permanent loss.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: No formal censorship, but discourse norms govern what is said and when — who may speak in council, what topics are taboo, how elders are addressed. The permitted band is set by custom, enforced by social pressure.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: Audiences are small — the band gathered around the fire. Attention is direct; there is no competition for it. Amplification is repetition — the story told again, the lesson repeated to children. Virality does not apply; propagation is slow and personal.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: In small face-to-face groups, signal integrity is high — misunderstanding is caught and corrected, lies are difficult to sustain among those who know each other intimately. Noise is minimal. The only surveillance is mutual; privacy is impossible in the band.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Right and wrong are grounded in reciprocity, kinship obligation, and the needs of the group. Fairness means sharing; justice means proportionate response to harm. The conscience is communal, enforced by shame and the threat of exclusion.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: No written law, but customary rules govern conduct — the distribution of meat, the resolution of disputes, the treatment of the dead. These rules are orally transmitted and adapt slowly through practice and consensus.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: Disputes are adjudicated by group discussion, mediated by elders; liability is personal and communal — a wrong against one is a wrong against kin. Sanctions range from verbal rebuke to exclusion from sharing to banishment. Severe wrongdoing may invite collective violence.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Rights are embedded in kinship and band membership — the right to share in food, to be defended, to be included. No abstract individual rights; protections are relational. Compliance burden is light; the rules are few and internalized.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: In small groups, impunity is difficult — wrongdoing is visible and sanctioned. But where bands are isolated, wrongs between groups may go unredressed; there is no external authority to appeal to. The residue is minimal within the band, uncertain beyond it.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: Explanation is embedded in oral tradition — the world is as the ancestors described it, animated by spirits and governed by custom. There is no formal inquiry, no testing of hypotheses, but there is acute empirical observation: which plants are edible, where game is found, how the river rises. The paradigm is mythic-practical, not theoretical.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Tool-making techniques are transmitted orally and by demonstration — how to knap stone, how to haft a point, how to weave a fish trap. The methods are refined over generations but remain stable within the snapshot; innovation is incremental and conservative.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: Education is apprenticeship — children learn by watching and doing, by listening to elders. The knowledge stock is distributed across the band, specialized by gender and age but held communally. Literacy does not exist; the stock is entirely oral.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: Knowledge is lost when the knower dies without transmitting it; obsolescence is not driven by new theory but by broken transmission. In stable conditions, the rate of decay is low; the oral chain holds. But a demographic shock — disease, disaster — could erase entire domains of knowledge in a generation.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: Identity is rooted in kinship, territory, and the stories that explain origins — how the first people came, why the forest is as it is, what the spirits demand. Deep memory is carried in oral tradition; foundational identity is the band, the lineage, the place.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: The order needs no elaborate justification; it is simply how things are and have always been. The legitimating narrative is the continuity of custom — we do as our ancestors did. No ideology contests this; there is no alternative to propose.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: Material culture is minimal — stone tools, perhaps wooden implements (unpreserved), body ornaments (beads, pigment), the use of ochre for decoration or ritual. Artistic expression is likely vocal and performative — song, dance, storytelling — leaving no archaeological trace. The visual and material surface is sparse, functional, and perishable.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: In a stable tradition, forms do not exhaust; they are renewed through each performance. But the potential for decay is present — if the tradition is disrupted, if the singers die, if the stories are forgotten, the meaning is lost. Within the snapshot, no exhaustion is evident; the residue is nil.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: The world is animated by spirits — in the forest, the river, the animals, the ancestors. Human life is embedded in this spiritual ecology, subject to forces that must be respected and propitiated. The existential outlook is fatalistic but engaged; one cannot control the spirits, but one can seek their favor.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: Ritual is likely embedded in daily life — offerings before a hunt, observances at death, seasonal ceremonies (if any seasonality is marked). The sacred is enacted through action and speech, not through permanent structures or written liturgy. Devotion is communal and practical.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: No separate religious institution exists; the spiritual is not distinguished from the social. Elders or individuals with spiritual gifts may mediate with the unseen, but there is no priesthood, no doctrine, no hierarchy. Authority is diffuse and personal.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: In the isolation of the forest, no external spiritual system presses; there is no diffusion, no syncretism, no displacement. The cosmology is stable, unchallenged, and unreflective.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: No disenchantment occurs; the sacred is not questioned. The spiritual need is met by the existing cosmology. The residue is nil — the world remains enchanted, the spirits present, the rituals efficacious in the minds of those who perform them.

docs.title: 1,000 BCE – 500 CE — Iron Age Consolidation and Village Society Formation
docs.text: Summary: The spread of iron smelting and nucleated village settlement across the Congo Basin over fifteen centuries, transforming dispersed Bantu-speaking cultivator communities into stable agricultural societies with differentiated crafts and formalized kinship structures. The binding constraint remains oral: all technical knowledge of smelting, all land tenure, all genealogical authority passes through speech and memory alone, anchoring the village order in living recall rather than written record.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: The Congo Basin's dense equatorial forest imposes high friction on movement and communication; river corridors—the Congo, Ubangi, Kasai, and their tributaries—serve as primary transit arteries, while interfluves remain difficult terrain where travel proceeds by foot along narrow trails cleared through undergrowth.

Climate Regime & Volatility: A stable equatorial regime prevails, with high annual rainfall (1,500–2,000 mm), year-round warmth, and two wet seasons; interannual variability is modest, though localized droughts affect forest margins and gallery forests periodically.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: Acute hazards are limited—no significant seismic or volcanic exposure in the basin core—but seasonal flooding along river corridors periodically inundates settlements, while forest fires during dry spells threaten cleared agricultural plots.

Resource & Energy Endowment: Iron ore occurs in lateritic deposits and bog iron across the basin; charcoal fuel is abundant given the forest biomass; soils are generally poor in nutrients, acidic, and rapidly leached, making shifting cultivation necessary to maintain yields.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: At low population densities, forest regeneration absorbs cleared land within decades; ash from smelting and domestic fires disperses into the soil without accumulation; no significant sink saturation occurs during this period.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: The tropical forest disease environment is severe: endemic malaria (Plasmodium falciparum), sleeping sickness (trypanosomiasis), yaws, and intestinal parasites impose a high background mortality, particularly among children; sickle-cell trait provides partial malaria resistance among Bantu-descended populations.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: Dietary staples include yams, plantains, oil palm products, forest game, and fish; protein intake is adequate where hunting and fishing remain productive, though seasonal variation affects nutritional status; stature is moderate, reflecting the disease burden.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Healing rests on herbalists and ritual specialists who apply forest pharmacopoeia orally transmitted across generations; knowledge of wound treatment, childbirth assistance, and fever remedies is held by lineage elders and specialist healers; capacity meets endemic loads but is overwhelmed by epidemic outbreaks.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Polygyny is common among lineage heads and successful men; fertility is high but offset by infant and child mortality from disease; marriage alliances between villages reinforce trade and kinship networks.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Population grows slowly across the period as iron tools enable more efficient forest clearance and agricultural expansion; densities remain low (perhaps 1–5 persons per km2 in forest core), with higher concentrations along rivers and at favorable ecotones.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: High child mortality means many births do not survive to adulthood; elderly dependents are few given life expectancy limits; the productive cohort absorbs the dependency load without strain at these densities.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: Shifting cultivation (slash-and-burn) of yams, plantains, and later bananas provides the carbohydrate base; hunting, fishing, and gathering supplement; the forest offers a reliable if modest provisioning floor, and famine is rare except after exceptional droughts or pest outbreaks.

Energy Capture & Conversion: Human muscle provides nearly all labor; fire is used for land clearance, cooking, and smelting; no animal traction is employed due to tsetse fly presence and lack of suitable domesticates; per-capita energy throughput is limited to what human effort can sustain.

Labor Organization & Coercion: Labor is organized by kinship; household members work fields under lineage-head direction; corvee-like communal labor clears land and builds structures; specialized smiths enjoy elevated status but remain embedded in kinship reciprocity; coercion is minimal and social rather than political.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Surplus above subsistence is modest—iron tools, palm oil, dried fish, smoked game—and serves exchange and social obligations rather than accumulation; the production ceiling is constrained by labor availability and soil exhaustion cycles.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: Yams and plantains store poorly; palm oil keeps longer; smoked fish and game provide some reserves; there is no granary system comparable to savanna societies; buffering against crop failure relies on forest fallback foods and inter-village reciprocity.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: Trade networks relay forest products (ivory, skins, palm oil) toward savanna margins in exchange for salt, copper, and iron where local ores are scarce; canoe transport along rivers is efficient; overland porterage is slow and costly; oral agreements and memory of past exchanges govern credit and obligation.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: No standardized currency; value is stored in iron tools, copper ornaments, and livestock where feasible; deferred reciprocity—bridewealth obligations, meat-sharing debts—functions as credit, all tracked orally within kinship networks.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: Village headmen and lineage elders collect tribute in labor and kind for communal projects and redistribution at feasts; extraction is light and embedded in reciprocity norms; no state-level taxation exists.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Wealth differences exist between lineage heads and junior members, successful hunters and others, but accumulation is limited by perishability of goods and social pressure for redistribution; iron tools and copper ornaments mark status without creating sharp stratification.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Slag from iron smelting accumulates at furnace sites; organic waste returns to forest soils; no toxic accumulation occurs; the conversion cycle remains largely closed at low intensity.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Matrilineal or patrilineal descent (varying by group) organizes inheritance, residence, and authority; the lineage is the primary social unit above the household; cross-cousin marriage and bridewealth payments cement inter-lineage alliances.

Association & Mutual Aid: Age-grades, hunting associations, and initiation societies provide cross-cutting ties beyond kinship; communal labor for clearing and building is organized through these structures; the village as a whole cooperates in defense and ritual.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: Communal gatherings, storytelling, music, and dance mark seasonal transitions, initiations, and funerals; the evening fire is the primary social space where oral tradition is performed and transmitted.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: Status distinctions exist between lineage heads and dependents, smiths and non-smiths, elders and youth, but no rigid caste or class system; slavery exists at low levels, typically captives or debtors integrated into households over time.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: Political organization is village-scale; the headman (chief) mediates disputes, allocates land, and organizes ritual; authority is personal and charismatic, not bureaucratic; inter-village councils meet occasionally for trade or defense but lack permanent structure.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: No standing military; adult men bear spears, bows, and iron-tipped weapons for hunting and defense; village defense is collective; raiding between groups occurs but is limited by forest terrain and low population densities.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: Disputes over land, inheritance, and marriage are mediated by elders and settled through compensation or ritual; unresolved grievances may lead to fission, with disaffected lineages founding new settlements; violence is contained but simmering feuds persist across generations.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: Headmen lead through persuasion, generosity, and ritual competence rather than coercion; charismatic hunters, smiths, and healers command respect; authority is earned and can be lost if reciprocity obligations are neglected.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: Allegiance flows to elders and ancestors who guarantee fertility, health, and prosperity; legitimacy is performative—demonstrated through successful harvests, hunts, and the absence of misfortune—and erodes when calamity strikes.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: Collective action mobilizes for communal labor, defense, and ritual; will is strong for immediate, visible goals but difficult to sustain for long-term or distant objectives; inter-village coordination is episodic.

External Relations & Posture: Relations with neighboring villages range from alliance through intermarriage to wary neutrality to occasional raiding; forest-forager populations (ancestral "Pygmy" groups) are integrated through exchange relationships and ritual interdependence, though with asymmetric status.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: The mood is cautious and cooperative within the village, wary toward outsiders; trust extends reliably to kin and village-mates, less so to strangers; forest spirits and ancestor displeasure are constant background anxieties shaping behavior.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: Disaffection surfaces when headmen fail to redistribute or when misfortune is attributed to sorcery; the remedy is fission—departure to found a new settlement—rather than internal reform; apathy is rare given the intimacy of village life.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Spoken Bantu languages provide the shared code; each village or cluster speaks a mutually intelligible dialect; forest-forager populations maintain their own languages but many are bilingual; no script exists—all information is oral.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Information travels at the speed of foot and canoe; drum signaling (slit-drum telegraphy) transmits simple messages rapidly across forest distances; detailed information requires face-to-face speech or trusted messengers.

Record, Storage & Persistence: All record is human memory: genealogies, land boundaries, ritual procedures, technical knowledge of smelting and healing are memorized and transmitted orally; persistence depends on living recall and is lost when transmission chains break.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: Elders control authoritative speech; certain knowledge (ritual secrets, smelting techniques) is restricted by gender, age, or initiation status; public discourse respects hierarchy and avoids direct confrontation.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: Stories, songs, and proverbs are the primary vehicles for transmitting values and knowledge; repetition and performance at communal gatherings reinforce retention; memorable formulations survive, forgettable ones do not.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: Oral transmission introduces variation with each retelling; consensus among elders serves as verification; signal integrity is high for frequently-rehearsed content (genealogies, rituals) and lower for rarely-accessed information.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Justice centers on reciprocity, kinship obligation, and harmony with ancestors and spirits; wrongs are defined as violations of these relationships; compensation restores balance more often than punishment.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: No written law; customary rules are orally transmitted and interpreted by elders; the corpus evolves slowly through precedent and consensus, with regional variation across village clusters.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: Disputes are adjudicated by headmen and elder councils; ordeals and divination may determine guilt in ambiguous cases; sanctions include compensation, exile, and in extreme cases execution or sale into slavery.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Individual autonomy is limited by kinship obligations; land is held collectively by lineages; compliance with customary norms is enforced by social pressure and fear of spiritual sanction; the compliance burden is embedded in daily life rather than formalized.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: Powerful lineage heads may escape sanction; sorcery accusations can target the vulnerable unjustly; when redress fails, the wronged party may depart to found a new settlement rather than endure unresolved grievance.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: Explanation is animist and ancestral: events are caused by spirits, ancestors, and sorcery; empirical observation of plants, animals, and materials is acute but embedded in spiritual interpretation; no naturalistic paradigm exists.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Iron smelting represents sophisticated pyrometallurgical technique—ore selection, furnace construction, charcoal preparation, temperature control—transmitted orally through apprenticeship; agricultural methods, hunting strategies, and forest pharmacopoeia are similarly transmitted.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: Knowledge passes from elders to youth through observation, participation, and oral instruction; initiation societies transmit specialized knowledge; skill distribution is broad for subsistence tasks, narrow for specialized crafts like smithing.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: When transmission chains break—through death, migration, or population decline—knowledge is lost; regional variation in smelting techniques suggests both innovation and loss over time; no external record preserves what is forgotten.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: Origin myths trace descent from founding ancestors who cleared the forest and established the village; migration narratives connect present communities to ancestral homelands; identity is rooted in lineage, village, and language group.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: The authority of elders and headmen is legitimated by their proximity to ancestors and knowledge of tradition; innovation is framed as recovery of ancestral practice rather than novelty; the narrative of continuity sustains the order.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: Woodcarving, raffia weaving, pottery, and body decoration express group identity and status; iron tools and weapons are both functional and prestige goods; masks and figurines embody spirits and ancestors and are used in ritual; the aesthetic is geometric, symbolic, and linked to cosmology.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: Forms remain vital within their oral transmission context; no evidence of widespread meaning decay during this period; the ritual and artistic repertoire renews with each generation through living performance.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: The cosmos is populated by spirits of forest, water, and ancestors; the boundary between living and dead is permeable; human welfare depends on maintaining harmony with these forces through proper conduct and ritual.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: Rituals mark life transitions (birth, initiation, marriage, death), agricultural cycles, and responses to misfortune; offerings, sacrifices, and dances propitiate spirits and ancestors; ritual specialists (diviners, healers) mediate between worlds.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: No separate priestly hierarchy; ritual authority is embedded in lineage eldership and specialized roles (smiths, healers, diviners); doctrine is customary rather than codified, varying by locality.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: Beliefs diffuse through intermarriage and trade contact; local cults adopt and adapt elements from neighbors; no external missionary pressure during this period; the spiritual landscape is plural and locally anchored.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: Disenchantment is absent; the sacred pervades daily life; misfortune is explained within the spiritual framework (sorcery, ancestral displeasure) rather than provoking doubt; the cosmology remains fully inhabited.

docs.title: 70,000 BCE – 12,000 BCE — Late Pleistocene Forest Contraction and Human Persistence
docs.text: Summary: A long-term trend spanning the Late Pleistocene, during which global cooling drives the contraction of the Congo Basin rainforest into fragmented refugia while human populations adapt, persist, and perhaps differentiate in isolation. The binding constraint is the oral substrate: all knowledge of how to survive the changing forest — which refugia hold food, which routes connect them, which techniques work in new conditions — is spoken, remembered, and transmitted mouth to ear across generations, or it is lost forever. The most causal factor is climate: the glacial drying that shrinks the forest to its refugial minimum forces human populations into smaller, more isolated patches, shaping the genetic and cultural divergence of the ancestral forest peoples.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: The Congo Basin's geography remains constant — the central cuvette, the peripheral highlands, the great river system — but the character of the land cover shifts dramatically. As the forest contracts, savanna and woodland expand into former forest zones, opening new corridors while closing others. River valleys and the eastern highlands become refugia where dense forest persists; the central cuvette may remain forested but increasingly isolated. Spatial friction intensifies where forest fragments: crossing open savanna exposes forest-adapted peoples to unfamiliar terrain, predators, and competitors. The refugia become islands; movement between them requires crossing hostile ground.

Climate Regime & Volatility: Global cooling intensifies from 70,000 BCE, culminating in the Last Glacial Maximum (approximately 26,500–19,000 BCE). Reduced temperatures lower evaporation and precipitation; the Congo Basin dries. Rainfall drops by perhaps 30–50% in some areas; the dry season lengthens and deepens. Forest gives way to savanna in zones that were formerly closed canopy. Volatility increases — drier years stress the refugia, wetter years permit temporary forest expansion. The climate regime shifts from warm-wet stability to cool-dry instability with a sustained trend toward aridity.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: The primary hazard is the drying itself — not an acute shock but a chronic constriction of the habitable zone. Drought becomes more frequent; fire spreads through dry vegetation. Forest fragmentation exposes populations to edge effects and to the fauna of the expanding savanna. The hazard regime shifts from the chronic challenges of dense forest to the compound pressures of a contracting, drying, burning landscape.

Resource & Energy Endowment: Within the refugia, the forest's resources persist — wild yams, fruits, fish, forest game — but in smaller, more intensively exploited patches. Competition for resources within refugia intensifies; the endowment per capita may hold or even rise as populations decline. In the expanding savanna, different resources become available — grassland game, different plant foods — but forest-adapted peoples may lack the knowledge and techniques to exploit them. The endowment is spatially reorganized: concentrated in refugia, unfamiliar elsewhere.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Human populations remain sparse; even concentrated in refugia, they do not saturate local sinks. The drier conditions may slow decomposition in some areas, but the overall human load remains negligible. No accumulating residue; the sink remains open even as it contracts.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: The pathogen load may shift as climate changes — some vectors contract with the forest, others expand with the savanna. Malaria may intensify where populations concentrate near water; other diseases may recede or arrive. The mortality baseline remains high, perhaps rising in crowded refugia and falling where populations thin out. The trend is uncertain but the load remains severe.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: Nutritional status depends on the refugium — those in productive river valleys may maintain adequacy; those in marginal zones face chronic scarcity. Bodies remain lean; physiological stress may increase with the contraction of foraging range. The trend is toward increased nutritional pressure as the forest shrinks, partially offset by reduced population density and intensified exploitation of surviving resources.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Healing knowledge persists through oral transmission, but the plant pharmacopoeia may shift as the forest contracts — some medicinal plants become scarce, others remain available. The healing capacity is strained by the same pressures that strain subsistence; smaller, more isolated groups may lose specialized knowledge. Recovery capacity holds but does not expand.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Reproductive patterns adapt to conditions: in stressed populations, fertility may decline and birth spacing widen further. Isolation in refugia may constrain mate choice, leading to increased inbreeding in small populations. Conversely, contact between refugia during wetter phases may permit genetic exchange. Pairing dynamics are shaped by the geography of refugia — who can reach whom determines who mates with whom.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Population density declines overall as the habitable area shrinks; birth and death continue to roughly balance at lower absolute numbers. Refugial populations may be small — dozens to a few hundred — and isolated for millennia. The demographic structure is fragmented: multiple small populations with limited exchange rather than one dispersed population. Renewal is local; migration between refugia is rare and consequential.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: The dependency load remains light; harsh conditions continue to clear those who cannot contribute. The trend is toward a leaner population structure with few surviving to old age, few orphans surviving without providers. No overhang accumulates; attrition is discharged rapidly.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: Subsistence remains immediate-return foraging, but the foraging range contracts with the forest. Groups in refugia intensify their exploitation of smaller territories; knowledge of local resources becomes more critical. The provisioning floor holds where refugia are productive, drops where they are marginal. Vulnerability to local shortfalls increases as the buffer of extensive range disappears.

Energy Capture & Conversion: Human muscle remains the sole power source; fire is used for cooking and increasingly for modifying vegetation — burning clearings, perhaps driving game. The energy ceiling does not change, but the efficiency of conversion may vary: forest game is harder to take than savanna game, but forest peoples lack the techniques for open-country hunting. Energy capture per capita may decline with the forest.

Labor Organization & Coercion: Labor organization remains cooperative, gendered, and kin-based within bands. No new coercion emerges; the system does not change in structure, only in the intensity of effort required. Groups work harder for the same return as the forest shrinks.

Production & Surplus Capacity: No surplus accumulates; production matches consumption as before. Stone tools are produced from available materials — perhaps with more difficulty as raw material sources are cut off by changing vegetation. The system remains at equilibrium, but the equilibrium is tighter, with less margin.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: No storage infrastructure develops; the buffer is still the forest's year-round productivity, now reduced. The knowledge of multiple refugia and the routes between them may function as a distributed buffer — if one area fails, another may hold. But this buffer is oral: remembered maps, spoken directions, knowledge that one generation fails to transmit is lost.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: Exchange remains internal to the band; inter-band contact may become rarer as populations contract into isolated refugia. Where refugia are close enough to permit contact, exchange may intensify — the sharing of mates, information, perhaps raw materials. Logistics remain limited to what individuals carry. Isolation is the trend, punctuated by occasional contact.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: Reciprocity obligations persist within bands; no other value storage emerges. Deferred exchange between bands — remembered debts, promised returns — may become more important where contact is rare and valuable. But these obligations are oral, held in memory, lost if the parties do not meet again.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: No surplus exists to extract; redistribution remains the immediate sharing of food within the band. The trend is toward more even sharing under conditions of scarcity, or toward conflict if sharing breaks down. No tribute, tax, or rent develops.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Wealth remains absent; concentration cannot occur. The trend is toward uniformity of poverty in contracted refugia. No defense of holdings is needed.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Waste output remains minimal and rapidly absorbed. The trend introduces no change; the residue is nil.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Kinship structures persist, but the isolation of refugia may lead to the divergence of kinship terminologies and practices. Smaller populations mean closer kin ties within groups and potentially greater importance of kin links between groups for maintaining genetic viability. Inheritance remains minimal — tools, ornaments, knowledge — but the knowledge of how to survive in a specific refugium becomes a crucial inheritance.

Association & Mutual Aid: The band remains the unit of mutual aid, but the stakes of mutual aid rise as conditions tighten. Sharing within the band intensifies where possible; failure to share leads to exclusion when survival is marginal. Associations beyond the band become rarer and more valuable — remembered ties to other refugia, kinship links that permit movement.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: Leisure continues around the fire, but the content of sociability may shift — more talk of the ancestors, of the old forests, of the routes between refugia. Play and sociability remain essential for group cohesion; isolation increases their importance as external contacts diminish.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: Stratification remains minimal; status is still earned through competence. But in isolated, stressed groups, the authority of those who know — the elders who remember, the skilled hunters who provide — may intensify. The trend is toward somewhat greater differentiation within the flattened structure, driven by the premium on scarce knowledge and skill.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: No administration develops; decisions continue to be made by consensus and informal authority. The trend introduces no institutional change. The apparatus remains the spoken word.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: No organized coercive capacity emerges; weapons remain hunting tools. Conflict may become more common where groups compete for the same refugia, but there is no trend toward organized warfare. Avoidance and fission remain the primary conflict resolution mechanisms.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: Social friction is still discharged through mobility, but mobility is constrained by the contracted habitable zone. Where groups cannot simply move apart, tension may rise; grievance may accumulate. The residue of undischarged friction may be higher than in earlier periods, but evidence is absent. The trend is toward a tighter social order with less room for exit.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: Leadership remains situational and personal, but the premium on memory and knowledge may give elders greater authority — those who remember the old forests, the routes, the techniques, carry irreplaceable information. Personal authority is knowledge-based; the wise are followed.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: Legitimacy remains direct and face-to-face; allegiance is given to those who provide and protect. The trend is toward intensified dependence on competent leaders as conditions stress the group.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: Collective will is tested by the contracting environment: the group must decide whether to stay or move, whether to share or hoard, whether to accept outsiders or exclude them. Resolve is measured in the group's ability to hold together under pressure. Fission is always possible, but smaller splinter groups face greater risks.

External Relations & Posture: Relations with other groups become rarer but potentially more fraught. Competition for refugia may generate hostility; alternatively, the rarity of contact may increase the value of exchange — mates, information, alliance. The posture is ambivalent: cautious, potentially hostile, but also potentially open to cooperation where benefit is clear.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: The prevailing temper is likely one of heightened caution and stress as conditions tighten. Trust within the band remains high, essential for survival; trust beyond the band may narrow as contact becomes rarer. The behavioral temper is shaped by scarcity: vigilance, conservation, wariness of strangers from unknown refugia.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: Disaffection may rise where conditions are desperate and leadership fails; apathy is a luxury that scarcity does not permit. The residue of exhausted will may accumulate in groups that are failing — the last generations of populations that do not survive the glacial maximum. But for those who persist, will is renewed by necessity. The trend is toward the survival of those with sufficient collective resolve.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Speech remains the medium; the code is shared within the band and probably intelligible to related groups in nearby refugia. Isolation may lead to linguistic divergence — the ancestors of the diverse "Pygmy" languages may begin to differentiate in this period. The trend is toward reduced mutual intelligibility across refugia as contact diminishes.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Information moves at the speed of human travel; the channels contract with the habitable zone. Where groups are isolated for generations, information from outside does not arrive. Velocity within the band remains high; velocity between refugia drops toward zero.

Record, Storage & Persistence: Memory remains the only archive, and the stakes of memory rise. The knowledge of how to survive in a specific refugium, of the routes that connect refugia, of the techniques that work — all must be orally transmitted or lost. The trend is toward the intensification of oral tradition: more deliberate teaching, more repeated telling, more careful preservation of critical knowledge. But the potential for catastrophic loss also rises — a disease that kills the elders, a disaster that breaks the chain of transmission, ends a lineage of knowledge.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: Discourse norms persist within groups; no external authority imposes censorship. The trend may be toward more rigid preservation of traditional knowledge — what the ancestors said becomes more authoritative as innovation becomes more dangerous.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: Audiences remain small; attention is focused. The content of what is amplified may shift toward survival knowledge, genealogical memory, and the stories that explain the changing world. Amplification is still repetition; the rate of repetition may increase as the stakes of transmission rise.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: Within isolated groups, signal integrity remains high; lies are difficult where everyone knows everything. Noise may enter the system through broken transmission — the garbled memory, the half-remembered technique, the story whose meaning has been lost. The trend is toward the accumulation of small errors in isolated transmission chains, offset by the correction that occurs when groups occasionally meet and compare traditions.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: The moral foundations of reciprocity and kinship obligation persist; justice remains a matter of proportionate response and community sanction. The trend may be toward stricter enforcement of sharing norms as scarcity intensifies — hoarding becomes a graver wrong when survival depends on pooling.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: Customary rules persist through oral transmission; no codification occurs. The rules may become more rigid as the margin for error narrows — deviation from proven practice is more dangerous when conditions are tight.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: Adjudication remains communal; sanctions remain social — rebuke, exclusion, banishment. The severity of sanctions may rise with scarcity: exclusion from a refugial band may be a death sentence where there is nowhere else to go.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Rights remain embedded in kinship and band membership; no abstract rights emerge. The trend is toward more intensive mutual obligation — the right to share is matched by the duty to share.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: Impunity within the band remains difficult; wrongdoing is visible. Between isolated groups, wrongs may go unredressed for generations if contact does not occur. The residue may accumulate at the inter-group level, remembered in oral tradition, shaping hostility when groups eventually meet.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: Explanation remains embedded in oral tradition; the paradigm remains mythic-practical. The changing environment may prompt new explanations — why the forest is shrinking, why the ancestors' world is no longer present — but these explanations are incorporated into myth, not tested empirically. Acute observation of the new environment is necessary for survival; theory adapts slowly through narrative.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Tool-making techniques persist; methods may adapt to new materials and conditions. Forest peoples encountering savanna-edge conditions may develop or acquire new techniques — different hunting methods, different plant processing. The trend is toward the diversification of technique in response to varied refugial environments, but also toward the loss of techniques that no longer apply.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: Education remains apprenticeship; the knowledge stock is distributed within the band. The trend is toward the intensification of knowledge transmission — more deliberate teaching, more emphasis on critical survival skills. But isolation also means that innovations in one refugium do not spread; the knowledge stock fragments across refugia.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: Obsolescence is driven by environmental change — techniques suited to dense forest become less useful as savanna expands — and by broken transmission in isolated, shrinking populations. The rate of knowledge decay may rise during demographic stress; entire domains of knowledge may be lost with their last practitioners. The residue is lost technique, forgotten lore, traditions whose meaning is no longer understood. Some refugial populations preserve more; others preserve less. The trend is toward uneven decay across isolated groups.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: Identity remains rooted in kinship, territory, and oral tradition, but the territory is now a refugium — a shrunken remnant of the ancestral range. Memory of the old forests, the larger world, may persist in tradition, becoming mythic: the time when the forest was vast, when the ancestors walked everywhere. Foundational identity may crystallize around the refugium and the struggle to survive in it.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: The legitimating narrative is continuity with the ancestors, now colored by loss — we persist as they persisted, in hard times as in good. The order is justified by survival itself; those who have survived validate the way of life that enabled it.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: Material culture remains minimal and functional; artistic expression remains performative — song, dance, story. The content of the art may shift to include the new conditions, the changed landscape, the memory of what was lost. Archaeological evidence is sparse; the trend is invisible but likely toward the incorporation of the glacial experience into oral tradition.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: In isolated groups, forms may exhaust — stories retold so many times they lose meaning, rituals performed without understanding. But renewal also occurs through the incorporation of new experiences into old forms. The trend is ambivalent: some traditions deepen through repetition, others hollow out. The residue of exhausted form may be present in groups that are failing, absent in those that are renewing.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: The cosmology of spirit-animated nature persists, but the spirits may be understood as having withdrawn as the forest retreats. The existential outlook may darken — the world is harder, the spirits less generous, the future less certain. Fatalism may deepen; piety may intensify as people seek to propitiate angry or distant powers.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: Ritual practice persists and may intensify as people seek spiritual explanation and remedy for their hardship. New rituals may emerge to address the new conditions; old rituals may be preserved with greater care as links to the ancestral world. Devotion is communal and practical, oriented toward survival.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: No separate religious institution exists; the spiritual remains embedded in the social. Individuals with spiritual gifts — those who interpret dreams, who communicate with spirits — may gain greater authority as the community seeks guidance. But there is no priesthood, no doctrine, no hierarchy.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: Isolation precludes diffusion from outside; there is no external spiritual system to syncretize with or be displaced by. Within refugia, spiritual traditions may diverge as groups develop separate interpretations of their separate experiences. The trend is toward differentiation, not syncretism.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: No disenchantment occurs; the world remains enchanted, the spirits present. But the character of the enchantment may shift — from a generous world to a harsh one, from friendly spirits to demanding ones. The sacred remains operative but is experienced as more demanding, less comforting. The residue is not disenchantment but a darkened enchantment, a spiritual world that explains hardship as well as abundance.

docs.title: 500 CE – 1,500 CE — Mature Forest Village Society Before Atlantic Contact
docs.text: Summary: The Congo Basin's village-based agricultural society at its pre-Atlantic equilibrium—a millennium of relative stability in which iron-using, Bantu-speaking communities occupy the forest through networks of autonomous villages linked by kinship, trade, and shared ritual, while forest-forager populations persist in the deep interior and at the margins of cultivator settlement. The binding constraint remains oral: without script, all coordination—land tenure, genealogy, alliance, technical knowledge, sacred tradition—passes through speech and living memory, giving the social order its intimacy, flexibility, and fragility.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: The Congo Basin's equatorial forest blankets some two million square kilometers, penetrated by the Congo River and its vast tributary network; rivers are the highways, enabling canoe travel at speeds far exceeding forest porterage; the forest interior remains friction-heavy, with movement constrained to cleared paths and stream courses.

Climate Regime & Volatility: The equatorial climate delivers 1,500–2,200 mm of annual rainfall in two wet seasons; temperatures are warm and stable year-round; interannual variability is low, providing a predictable agricultural calendar; multi-decadal droughts affect forest margins but rarely penetrate the humid core.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: Acute hazards remain limited; seasonal floods along major rivers are predictable and settlements adapt through siting and construction; lightning fires during dry spells affect forest edges; no significant seismic or volcanic threat exists in the basin proper.

Resource & Energy Endowment: Iron ore remains available in lateritic soils and alluvial deposits; forest biomass provides inexhaustible charcoal fuel; soils are poor but adequate for shifting cultivation; copper, salt, and certain clays require trade from peripheral zones.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Population densities remain low enough that forest regeneration absorbs agricultural fallows within decades; smelting slag and domestic ash disperse without accumulation; the system operates well within its absorptive limits.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: The disease environment is stable and severe: endemic malaria, sleeping sickness in river valleys, yaws, and intestinal parasites impose high infant and child mortality; adult survivors carry acquired immunity to many endemic pathogens; epidemic outbreaks occasionally spike mortality but populations recover.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: The dietary base of plantains, yams, cassava (arriving late in the period), palm oil, fish, and forest game provides adequate calories and reasonable protein; seasonal variation affects nutritional status; stature is moderate, reflecting chronic disease burden.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Herbalists and ritual healers maintain extensive pharmacopoeia—bark, leaves, roots—transmitted orally; wound care, childbirth assistance, and fever treatment are competent within endemic disease loads; epidemic crises exceed capacity.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Polygyny concentrates reproductive success among senior men and lineage heads; fertility is high; bridewealth payments (in iron, copper, or labor) structure marriage alliances between lineages and villages; marriage is a political as much as reproductive institution.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Population grows slowly, filling favorable riverine and ecotone zones while the deep forest interior remains sparsely occupied; densities range from under 1 per km2 in dense forest to 5–10 per km2 in favorable areas; the demographic regime is stable, neither expanding nor contracting sharply.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: High child mortality means many births do not reach adulthood; few survive to extreme old age; the dependency load is modest and absorbed within household and lineage structures without strain.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: Shifting cultivation of plantains, yams, and oil palm, supplemented by hunting, fishing, and gathering, provides a reliable subsistence floor; the forest offers fallback foods during crop shortfalls; outright famine is rare and localized.

Energy Capture & Conversion: Human muscle remains the primary energy source; fire serves cooking, land clearance, and smelting; no animal traction is available; per-capita energy throughput is low but sufficient for the village-scale economy.

Labor Organization & Coercion: Labor is organized through kinship: household members cultivate under lineage-head direction; communal labor parties clear land, build structures, and smelt iron; specialized smiths command elevated status; slavery exists—captives and debt-pawns integrated into households—but is not the dominant labor form.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Surplus above subsistence is modest: iron tools, palm oil, dried and smoked fish, forest products (ivory, skins, resins) are traded; the production ceiling is constrained by labor, soil exhaustion cycles, and transport friction; no large-scale accumulation occurs.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: Plantains and yams store poorly; palm oil keeps longer; smoked fish and game provide limited reserves; forest fallback foods and inter-village reciprocity buffer against crop failure; no granary system exists comparable to savanna societies.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: Long-distance trade networks relay forest products toward the savanna periphery and coast: ivory, skins, palm oil, and slaves move outward; salt, copper (from Katanga and the Niari), iron (where local ores are poor), and prestige goods move inward; river canoes enable efficient bulk transport; porterage handles overland segments; oral agreements and memory govern credit.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: Value is stored in durable goods—copper crosses, iron bars, prestige textiles (raffia)—and in social claims: bridewealth debts, meat-sharing obligations, deferred reciprocity tracked orally within kinship networks; no monetary system exists but copper and iron serve quasi-currency functions in some areas.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: Village headmen collect tribute in labor and kind for communal projects, ritual feasts, and redistribution; extraction is light and embedded in reciprocity norms; no state-level taxation; chiefly wealth is redistributed to maintain legitimacy.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Wealth differences exist between lineage heads and dependents, successful traders and subsistence cultivators, but accumulation is limited by perishability, redistribution pressure, and the absence of defensible stores; stratification is real but not rigid.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Slag accumulates at smelting sites; organic waste returns to forest soils; no toxic accumulation; the material cycle remains largely closed.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Descent is reckoned matrilineally in western regions (among Kongo-related peoples) and patrilineally in eastern areas; the lineage organizes inheritance, land access, and political succession; cross-cousin marriage and bridewealth cement alliances; the household nests within the lineage within the village.

Association & Mutual Aid: Age-grades, initiation societies, and craft associations (smiths, hunters) provide cross-cutting ties; mutual aid for clearing, building, and crisis response operates through these structures and through kinship; the village functions as a cooperative unit.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: Communal gatherings at evening fires, seasonal festivals, initiation ceremonies, funerals, and market days structure sociability; storytelling, music (drums, xylophones, thumb pianos), and dance transmit culture and reinforce bonds.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: Status distinctions separate lineage heads from dependents, elders from youth, free from slave, initiated from uninitiated; smiths occupy an ambiguous position—powerful but often ritually set apart; forest-forager ("Pygmy") populations occupy a subordinate but interdependent position, exchanging forest products and ritual services for agricultural goods.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: Political scale remains village-level in most of the forest; headmen mediate disputes, allocate land, and lead ritual; authority is personal, not bureaucratic; inter-village councils meet for trade, alliance, and defense but lack permanent structure; the Kongo Kingdom on the Atlantic margin represents the largest polity, but its reach does not penetrate the forest interior.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: No standing armies; adult men bear iron-tipped spears, bows, and knives for hunting and defense; village defense is collective; raiding for slaves and plunder occurs but is limited by terrain and the costs of forest warfare.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: Disputes over land, inheritance, and marriage are mediated by elders and settled through compensation or ritual; unresolved grievances may lead to fission, with disaffected lineages founding new settlements; violence is contained at low levels; sorcery accusations provide an outlet for tensions but also generate new conflicts.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: Headmen and lineage elders lead through persuasion, generosity, ritual competence, and demonstrated success; charismatic figures—great hunters, renowned smiths, effective healers—command personal followings; authority is earned and can be lost.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: Allegiance flows to leaders who deliver: successful harvests, protection from enemies, effective mediation, proper ritual; legitimacy is performative and contingent; failure invites defection or replacement.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: Collective action mobilizes effectively for communal labor, defense, and ritual; sustained coordination beyond the village is difficult; inter-village alliances form for specific purposes and dissolve when goals are met or disputes arise.

External Relations & Posture: Relations with neighboring villages range from alliance (often through intermarriage) to rivalry and raiding; trade partnerships extend over long distances through relay networks; forest-forager populations are integrated through exchange and ritual interdependence but occupy subordinate status.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: The prevailing mood within villages is cautious cooperation; trust extends reliably to kin and village-mates, less so to outsiders; anxiety about sorcery and spiritual displeasure colors daily life; confidence rises with successful harvests and hunts, falls with misfortune.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: Disaffection surfaces when leaders fail or when sorcery fears spread; the remedy is typically exit—departure to found a new settlement—rather than reform; apathy is rare in the intimate village setting; spent will manifests as fission rather than collapse.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
