Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: Ritual centers on hunting success, death, and seasonal transitions; offerings, invocations, and purification are performed orally and enacted bodily; no permanent ritual infrastructure.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: No religious institutions exist; shamanic or elder figures may mediate with spirits, but authority is personal and situational; no doctrine beyond orally transmitted myth and practice.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: Spiritual beliefs are localized to band and language group; diffusion occurs through intermarriage and contact; no evidence of displacement or large-scale syncretism at this scale.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: No disenchantment is detectable; the sacred pervades daily life; spiritual need is continuously re-anchored through oral repetition and ritual practice; no standing residue of unmet transcendence.

docs.title: 900 BCE – 400 BCE — La Venta Succession and Olmec Transformation
docs.text: Summary: The five centuries following San Lorenzo's decline see the Olmec center of gravity shift to La Venta, where monumental construction, long-distance exchange, and elite ritual reach their apex before the Olmec heartland loses its primacy and regional polities absorb its legacy. The binding constraint is oral transmission: La Venta's authority rests on spoken tradition, chanted cosmology, and face-to-face negotiation; no written archive records its genealogies or commands, and when the spoken chain breaks, the center's grip dissolves.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: La Venta sits on a salt-dome island amid the coastal swamps of Tabasco, its elevation slight but critical for permanent settlement in a landscape of seasonal floods. Rivers provide canoe corridors linking the site to the Gulf littoral and interior piedmont; the levee system channels movement but also fragments overland travel, making watercraft essential for bulk transport. Distance to the basalt sources in the Tuxtla Mountains remains roughly 80 km, unchanged from the San Lorenzo phase.

Climate Regime & Volatility: The tropical wet-dry regime delivers heavy summer rains and a pronounced dry season; interannual variability tied to Pacific sea-surface anomalies can swing rainfall by a third, stressing maize yields. No secular trend dominates the window, but episodic droughts toward 500 BCE may correlate with political instability in the heartland.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: Hurricanes and flooding constitute the primary acute hazards; the low-lying site floods when rivers overtop natural levees. No seismic or volcanic threat affects the coastal plain directly, though ashfall from distant eruptions occasionally reaches the region.

Resource & Energy Endowment: The immediate hinterland supplies cacao, rubber, and tropical hardwoods; aquatic protein from rivers and lagoons supplements maize. Basalt, jade, serpentine, and obsidian arrive only through exchange, making La Venta dependent on networks it must maintain through persuasion and prestige rather than coercion alone.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Population density remains low relative to carrying capacity; organic refuse decomposes rapidly in the humid climate. Monumental construction concentrates earth movement but does not exhaust local soils. No saturation signal is evident.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: Tropical pathogens—malaria, intestinal parasites, vector-borne fevers—impose a steady attrition; skeletal evidence from comparable lowland sites shows elevated childhood mortality and moderate adult lifespans averaging 30–35 years. Endemic load remains stable; no epidemic signature appears in the record.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: Maize, beans, squash, fish, and game provide adequate macronutrients; dental caries increase with maize dependence, and porotic hyperostosis in some burials suggests periodic iron deficiency. Overall nutritional status supports population growth.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Healing relies on herbalism, bone-setting, and ritual intervention; no institutional medicine exists. Recovery capacity is limited by knowledge transmission through oral apprenticeship; loss of a healer means loss of technique until another is trained.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Marriage patterns remain kin-regulated; polygyny likely among elites given burial evidence of status differentiation. Physiological fertility is adequate; no reproductive crisis appears.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Population in the heartland grows slowly; La Venta's resident population may reach several thousand, with a larger hinterland population in dispersed hamlets. Migration into the center for labor drafts and ceremonies supplements local births.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: The dependent load—children, elderly, infirm—is absorbed within extended kin groups; no institutional support exists. The load does not outpace productive capacity during this window.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: Maize-based agriculture supplemented by fishing, hunting, and gathering sustains the population; no famine signature appears in the archaeological record. Household pooling buffers seasonal variation.

Energy Capture & Conversion: Human muscle remains the sole power source; no animal traction is used. Canoe transport leverages river current, reducing friction on bulk goods. Per-capita work output suffices for monumental construction through corvee mobilization.

Labor Organization & Coercion: Labor for monuments and ritual construction is mobilized through obligatory tribute or corvee, organized by kin and community obligation rather than formal slavery. Coercion is embedded in social expectation and ritual duty.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Agricultural surplus supports a non-producing elite and specialist artisans (jade carvers, sculptors). Surplus flow is adequate for sustained monument building but not for territorial expansion requiring standing forces.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: Granary-level storage buffers single-season shortfalls; no evidence of multi-year reserves. Risk pooling operates through kin networks and reciprocal obligation with neighboring communities.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: Long-distance exchange networks bring jade from Guatemala, obsidian from highland Mexico, serpentine from Oaxaca, and basalt from the Tuxtlas. La Venta sits at a node controlling access to Gulf routes; its prestige goods circulate widely, but the network depends on voluntary participation sustained by ideology and gift exchange, not military enforcement.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: No coinage exists; value is stored in durable prestige goods (jade celts, carved mirrors) and deferred through reciprocal obligation. Credit operates as social debt remembered and recited, not recorded.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: Elites extract surplus through tribute in labor and goods, redistributing a portion in feasts and ceremonies that reinforce their authority. The extraction rate is sustainable but leaves little margin for expansion.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Wealth concentrates in elite hands as jade caches, elaborate burials, and monumental tombs; commoners possess utilitarian goods. Defense relies on burial concealment and the sacredness of offerings rather than armed guards.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Organic waste is absorbed locally; construction spoil is incorporated into platform fill. No financial mispricing accumulates; the economy is pre-monetary.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Patrilineal descent likely governs elite succession; kin groups organize labor and ritual participation. Inheritance of status and sacra passes through lineage, validated by oral genealogy recited at ceremonies.

Association & Mutual Aid: Craft specialists (jade carvers, sculptors) may form loose associations; village communities maintain reciprocal aid networks. No formal guilds exist.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: Ball courts do not appear at La Venta, but ritual gatherings, feasting, and probable ball games provide sociable contexts. Ceremonies at the Great Pyramid and associated plazas mark seasonal and political cycles.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: Society is stratified: a hereditary elite controls ritual and exchange, a specialist class produces prestige goods, and commoners farm and labor. Status boundaries are firm but not caste-rigid; display and ritual performance reinforce hierarchy.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: Administration is minimal and personal; no bureaucracy or written record exists. Authority inheres in named individuals whose commands are transmitted orally and enforced through kin and client networks. Succession depends on oral genealogy and ritual validation.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: No standing army exists; force is mobilized through kin obligation when needed. Weapons are utilitarian (spears, atlatls); no specialized warrior class is evident. La Venta's influence rests on prestige, not conquest.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: Social friction is discharged through feasting, ritual, and the legitimation of hierarchy. By 500–400 BCE, La Venta's monuments are ritually defaced and buried, signaling either internal succession crisis or external pressure; the apparatus decays as authority fragments among successor centers.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: Leadership is personal and charismatic; rulers are likely priest-kings whose authority fuses religious and political power. Colossal heads may depict specific rulers, memorializing personal authority in stone.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: Allegiance is enacted through ritual participation, labor tribute, and acceptance of elite cosmology. Legitimacy depends on successful mediation with the supernatural; failure—crop failure, flood, defeat—erodes it.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: Collective will is directed toward monument construction, long-distance exchange, and ritual elaboration. No evidence of military campaigns; the will to expand territorially is absent or frustrated.

External Relations & Posture: La Venta projects influence through prestige and ideology, not conquest. Relations with distant regions (Oaxaca, highlands) are diplomatic and commercial; no subordination is imposed. Rivalry with emerging centers (San Jose Mogote, Chalcatzingo) may increase toward the window's end.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: Sentiment during La Venta's apogee is confident; monumental construction proceeds for centuries. Trust extends within kin networks and to the elite center. As decline sets in, sentiment likely darkens; the defacement of monuments suggests contested legitimacy.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: The terminal defacement of La Venta's monuments—heads buried, altars mutilated—indicates spent legitimacy or active repudiation. Whether internal disaffection or external attack, the affective bond to the center breaks by 400 BCE.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Spoken language—likely a proto-Mixe-Zoquean tongue—is the universal medium; mutual intelligibility extends throughout the heartland. Iconography (were-jaguar, serpent, maize deity) encodes meaning but requires oral explication.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Information travels at walking and canoe speed; messengers carry oral commands and news. Transmission velocity is slow; rumors and reports take days or weeks to reach distant communities.

Record, Storage & Persistence: No writing exists; all record is oral. Genealogies, ritual formulae, and cosmological narratives persist in specialist memory—priests, elders, bards. Loss of a memory-keeper risks loss of the tradition.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: Elite control of ritual performance frames permissible discourse; cosmological narratives justify hierarchy. No formal censorship exists, but deviation from orthodoxy risks exclusion from ritual community.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: Attention is captured at mass ceremonies; monumental architecture amplifies the message of elite power. Oral repetition in households and villages sustains the narrative between ceremonies.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: Without writing, signal integrity depends on fidelity of oral transmission; drift is inevitable over generations. Conflicting traditions and misremembered genealogies accumulate as noise, visible archaeologically in iconographic variation across sites.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Justice is embedded in kin obligation, reciprocity, and cosmic order; offenses against persons and gods are handled within kin groups or by elite adjudication. The sense of fairness is relational, not abstract.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: No codified law exists; norms are customary and orally transmitted. Elite pronouncements carry binding force within their sphere but are not recorded.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: Disputes are adjudicated by kin elders or elite figures; liability is collective (kin group responsible for member's acts). Sanctions include compensation, exile, or ritual execution; no prison system exists.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Individual rights are embedded in kin status; commoners owe labor and tribute, elites owe protection and ritual mediation. Compliance burden is customary and predictable.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: Elite impunity is likely; wrongs by elites against commoners may go unredressed. The gap between justice owed and delivered is managed by ideology legitimating hierarchy.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: Inquiry is cosmological, not empirical; the paradigm is mythic, explaining the world through supernatural agency. Astronomical observation for calendrical purposes may exist but is not recorded.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Techniques include basalt carving, jade polishing, earthwork construction, and hydraulic management. Methods are transmitted orally through apprenticeship; no written manuals exist.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: Knowledge is held by specialists—priests, artisans, healers—and transmitted within lineages. Literacy is absent; skill distribution is narrow, concentrated in the heartland.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: When La Venta declines, its specialist knowledge disperses; some techniques (colossal-head carving) are lost, others absorbed by successor cultures. Oral transmission is fragile; a generation's lapse can break the chain.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: Olmec identity centers on the were-jaguar, the feathered serpent, the maize deity, and the supernatural realm accessed through trance and ritual. Memory of San Lorenzo ancestors may persist in oral genealogy.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: The elite's right to rule is grounded in descent from supernatural beings and successful mediation with cosmic forces. Monumental art proclaims this narrative visually; oral recitation fills in the story.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: Material culture includes colossal basalt heads, altar-thrones, jade celts, serpentine mosaics, and ceramic figurines. Style emphasizes naturalism in portraiture, abstraction in supernatural imagery, and bilateral symmetry in layout.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: By the window's end, Olmec iconography spreads so widely that its original potency dilutes; successor cultures adopt motifs without the heartland's ritual authority. The defacement of La Venta's monuments signals exhaustion of the form's legitimating power.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: The cosmos is animated by supernatural forces—jaguar spirits, maize gods, ancestors—accessible through ritual and trance. Human existence is embedded in cycles of death and renewal mirroring agricultural seasons.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: Ritual includes offerings of jade, serpentine, and human sacrifice (probable but debated); bloodletting may accompany elite ceremonies. The Great Pyramid at La Venta is the axis mundi; ceremonies align with solstices and equinoxes.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: No formal priesthood is documented, but elite figures combine political and religious roles. Doctrinal authority is personal, transmitted orally, and validated by successful ritual performance.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: Olmec religious motifs spread to Oaxaca, the highlands, and beyond, but local traditions absorb rather than replace them. By 400 BCE, heartland cosmology is one tradition among several, no longer dominant.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: The deliberate destruction of La Venta's sacred monuments—heads buried face-down, offerings smashed—indicates either ritual termination or repudiation of the sacred. The heartland's spiritual authority is discharged; successor centers must generate their own.

docs.title: 4,000 BCE – 2,500 BCE — Late Archaic Intensification and Early Village Life
docs.text: Summary: Across the Mexican highlands and emerging lowland clearings, scattered foraging bands shift toward semi-sedentary hamlets as fully domesticated maize, squash, and beans anchor a mixed subsistence regime; speech carries the planting calendar, seed-selection knowledge, and kin-reciprocity obligations that coordinate labor and redistribute harvests, yet no durable record exists beyond living memory — the binding constraint that limits community scale and institutional continuity to what elders can recall and retell.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: The Mexican highlands — the Basin of Mexico, Valley of Oaxaca, Tehuacan Valley — provide temperate basins ringed by volcanic uplands, with alluvial soils replenished by seasonal flooding; the Gulf Coast and Yucatan lowlands remain heavily forested, traversable along rivers and coastal margins but resisting permanent clearance without metal tools. Movement between ecological zones follows footpaths along ridges and river corridors, with travel times measured in days; no draft animals shorten distance.

Climate Regime & Volatility: The mid-Holocene dry phase eases toward wetter conditions by 3,000 BCE, extending the monsoon season and improving maize yields in the highlands; interannual rainfall variability remains significant, with drought years still common enough to require mobile fallback strategies. Temperature gradients between highland and lowland zones drive vertical transhumance patterns among groups that exploit both.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: Volcanic activity in the Transmexican Belt poses localized risks — ashfall can enrich soils over time but destroy crops in the short term; flooding in lowland rivers threatens stored harvests; drought remains the most frequent hazard, pushing groups back toward wild-plant refugia when rains fail. Settlement avoids floodplains and active volcanic slopes where oral memory recalls past disasters.

Resource & Energy Endowment: Obsidian sources in the highlands (Otumba, Zinapecuaro) provide high-quality lithic material for tools and nascent exchange networks; clay for pottery emerges as a valued resource as ceramic technology appears late in the period. Forests supply fuel and construction wood; wild game remains available but thinning as human density increases. Energy derives entirely from human muscle and fire.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Population density is low enough that organic refuse, fire ash, and human waste disperse without accumulating; middens form near hamlets but do not foul water sources. The landscape absorbs the modest load without degradation; no feedback from environmental saturation affects the system.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: Endemic tropical diseases — intestinal parasites, insect-borne fevers — affect lowland populations more heavily; highland groups experience seasonal respiratory illness in cool, dry months. Infant mortality remains high from gastrointestinal infection and malnutrition during lean seasons; adult mortality from accident, violence, and untreated infection keeps life expectancy around 25–30 years.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: Maize agriculture improves caloric security compared to full dependence on foraging, but dietary diversity narrows as cultivation intensifies; protein comes from deer, rabbit, turkey, fish, and occasional large game, supplemented by beans where adopted. Skeletal evidence from the period shows some dental caries from carbohydrate-heavy diets but generally adequate stature.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Healing knowledge is held by specialists — proto-shamans who combine herbal remedies with ritual invocation — transmitted orally from practitioner to apprentice. Childbirth attended by experienced women; wound treatment relies on plant poultices and fire-cautery. Healing capacity is local and cannot be scaled; loss of a knowledgeable healer leaves a gap until another is trained.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Monogamous or mildly polygynous pair bonds structure reproduction; fertility regulated informally by prolonged breastfeeding and spacing. Sedentism increases fertility by reducing the caloric cost of infant transport; population begins a slow upward trend correlated with agricultural adoption.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Population remains thin — perhaps a few thousand across the highlands — but localized clusters form where agricultural productivity permits. Birth rates rise modestly as sedentism reduces mobility burdens; replacement is positive where harvests succeed and negative where drought triggers dispersal.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: The elderly who carry oral tradition are valued but also represent a dependency load the productive cohort must feed; orphans absorbed by kin networks. The dependency ratio remains manageable given low life expectancy and high labor participation across ages.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: A mixed economy combining maize-squash-bean cultivation with hunting, fishing, and wild-plant gathering ensures against single-source failure; the milpa polyculture emerges as the integrating strategy, with nitrogen-fixing beans enriching soils depleted by maize. Provisioning sits above bare survival in good years but remains vulnerable to drought.

Energy Capture & Conversion: Human labor is the sole power source; fire for cooking, heating, and land clearance. The energy ceiling limits field size, construction scale, and surplus accumulation. No animal traction or mechanical advantage beyond simple tools.

Labor Organization & Coercion: Labor is organized through kinship — household members work fields together, with extended kin mobilized for clearing, planting, and harvest through reciprocal obligations encoded in oral agreements. No coerced labor; participation is kin-obligated and socially enforced through reputation and reciprocity.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Surplus is modest — a few months' stored maize in pit-lined caches — sufficient to buffer a short bad season but not to support craft specialists or non-producers. Production expands as more land is cleared; contraction follows drought or pest outbreaks.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: Maize stored in underground pits or raised granaries where rodents are a threat; beans and squash dried for preservation. Storage technology is adequate for annual cycles but insufficient for multi-year drought; no formal pooling institutions beyond kin-group sharing.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: Obsidian moves tens of kilometers from highland sources to lowland communities; exchange networks remain informal, based on kin ties, marriage alliances, and seasonal gatherings. No markets or standardized exchange protocols; goods move as gifts establishing reciprocal obligations.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: Value is stored in durable goods (obsidian, shells, feathers) and in social credit — obligations owed and remembered. No currency or formal accounting; debt and credit exist as oral agreements witnessed by kin.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: No formal taxation or tribute; surplus redistributed through feasting, kin sharing, and ceremonial gifting. Emerging big-men may accumulate and redistribute to build prestige, but extraction is voluntary and reputation-based.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Wealth differences are minimal — access to better land, larger kin networks, or more stored seed. No fortifications or defended stores; theft deterred by social sanction and kin retaliation.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Organic waste composted into fields or deposited in middens; no toxic byproducts. Material waste (broken tools, used hearths) accumulates near settlements but does not degrade the environment at current densities.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Bilateral or patrilineal kinship organizes households and defines marriage eligibility; inheritance of stored seed, land-use rights, and ritual knowledge passes through remembered genealogies. Household composition is nuclear or extended, depending on labor needs and land availability.

Association & Mutual Aid: Beyond the household, hamlet-level cooperation for land clearance, harvest, and defense organizes through orally contracted reciprocity — labor exchanged for labor, food shared in expectation of return. No formalized associations; mutual aid is kin-obligated.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: Seasonal gatherings at resource-rich locations bring together dispersed kin groups for collective hunts, feasting, courtship, and ritual; games and contests build bonds across households. Sociability reinforces the oral networks through which information and obligation flow.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: Status differences emerge based on age, ritual knowledge, hunting prowess, and accumulated social credit; no hereditary stratification. Big-men who can mobilize kin and redistribute surplus gain influence but hold no formal office. Boundaries between groups are permeable through marriage and adoption.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: No formal administration; coordination depends on oral consensus-building among household heads and recognized elders. Decision-making is face-to-face and deliberative; the hamlet is the largest unit of coordinated action. No bureaucracy, record-keeping, or offices.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: No standing warriors or organized force; adult males are part-time defenders and hunters. Weapons are hunting tools — atlatl-thrown darts, knives, clubs. Violence is interpersonal or inter-hamlet, managed through blood feud, compensation, and mediation by respected figures.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: Conflict over land, theft, and personal grievance is mediated through kin negotiation and ritual resolution; unresolved feuds occasionally flare into violence. The system lacks formal mechanisms to compel compliance; social order depends on reputation and the threat of kin retaliation. Disorder remains episodic and localized.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: Leadership is personal and informal — elders whose memory is trusted, hunters whose skill is proven, healers whose rituals succeed. Authority depends on demonstrated competence and generosity; no inherited or appointed offices.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: Allegiance is to kin and hamlet, not to institutions or titles; legitimacy accrues to individuals who fulfill obligations and maintain relationships. Disaffection manifests as withdrawal from cooperation or departure from the group.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: Collective action is mobilized through oral persuasion and appeals to shared interest; resolve is high for immediate threats (raids, drought response) but difficult to sustain for long-term projects. Succession is not contested because formal offices do not exist; influence passes informally to the next capable figure.

External Relations & Posture: Relations with neighboring groups range from cooperative (intermarriage, trade) to competitive (raiding, territorial disputes); no permanent alliances or enmities. Posture is defensive and opportunistic; expansion occurs by fission and migration rather than conquest.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: The prevailing mood is cautious optimism tempered by awareness of environmental fragility; trust extends reliably within kin networks and provisionally to affines and neighbors. Anxiety spikes during drought years; collective relief accompanies successful harvests. The radius of trust is narrow — the hamlet and its immediate kin connections.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: Failed harvests or leadership disputes produce disaffection expressed through withdrawal, fission, or migration; the small scale of communities allows exit as a pressure valve. Apathy is rare given the labor demands of subsistence; spent will is restored through seasonal renewal rituals.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Speech is the universal medium; all community members share the local language and can participate in deliberation. No writing or symbolic recording; information exists only in utterance and memory. Geographic isolation produces dialect divergence over generations.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Information travels at the speed of a walking messenger; the channel is face-to-face speech or relayed word-of-mouth. Reach is limited to a few days' travel; news from distant regions arrives sporadically through visiting kin or traders.

Record, Storage & Persistence: Memory is the sole archive; knowledge persists only as long as those who know it live and teach. Ritual mnemonics — songs, chants, formulaic recitations — aid retention of critical information (planting calendars, genealogies, healing formulas). Loss of an elder before transmission means permanent knowledge extinction.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: Discourse norms are set by custom; certain topics (sacred knowledge, shamanic technique) are restricted to initiates. No formal censorship; framing depends on the speaker's authority and audience reception.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: Attention is highest at communal gatherings — feasts, rituals, seasonal assemblies — where important information is announced and repeated. Amplification depends on repetition and the speaker's reputation; false claims are checked against community memory.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: In small communities, verification is possible through direct inquiry; conflicting accounts are resolved through consensus or appeal to recognized authorities. Noise increases with distance and relay; information from distant sources is less reliable. Obsolete knowledge is shed informally as practices change.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Justice is conceived as balance — harm requires compensation, generosity earns reciprocity, taboo violation demands ritual restoration. The moral universe is kin-centered; obligations are strongest within the household and weaken with social distance.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: No written law; behavioral norms are customary, transmitted through storytelling, proverb, and direct instruction. Taboos (incest, certain food prohibitions, sacred-space violations) are enforced by supernatural sanction and community shunning.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: Disputes are adjudicated by informal mediation — respected elders or ritual specialists arbitrate, proposing compensation (goods, labor, marriage) to restore balance. Liability is collective (kin groups responsible for members' actions); sanction ranges from compensation to ostracism to blood feud.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Individual rights are embedded in kin status; protection comes from kin backing. Compliance burden is light — norms are internalized through socialization — but violation costs are high (social exclusion, supernatural penalty).

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: Where kin groups are unequal in size or influence, weaker parties may receive inadequate redress; powerful figures may escape full sanction. The gap between justice owed and delivered is managed through grudge-holding and eventual retaliation or dispersal of the wronged party.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: Inquiry is practical and observational — which plants thrive where, when rains come, how animals behave. The reigning paradigm is animist: natural phenomena are inhabited by spirits whose moods affect outcomes. Explanation is narrative and mythological rather than systematic.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Technical knowledge is sophisticated within its domain: seed selection, soil assessment, tool-knapping, pottery (emerging late in the period), construction, hunting techniques. Method is empirical but transmitted as custom rather than explicit theory; innovation occurs through trial and is preserved if successful.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: Knowledge is transmitted through apprenticeship and participation — children learn by doing alongside adults. Specialized knowledge (healing, ritual, obsidian knapping) is concentrated in practitioners who select and train successors. Literacy does not exist; the knowledge stock is distributed across living memories.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: Knowledge decays when practitioners die without successors or when environmental change renders old techniques irrelevant. Obsolete practices are shed informally; no archive preserves superseded methods. Error and untested tradition persist where no verification challenges them.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: Identity is rooted in kin lineage and place — the valley where ancestors lived, the stories of first planting, the origin accounts connecting people to landscape and supernatural patrons. Mythic time is continuous with the present; ancestors remain active as spirits.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: The order is legitimated by custom and cosmological sanction — this is how ancestors lived, how spirits require. No ideology of conquest or progress; continuity is valued over change.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: Material culture includes ground-stone tools, woven textiles and basketry, emerging pottery with simple geometric decoration, clay figurines (often female, possibly fertility-related), shell and feather ornaments. Architecture is modest — pole-and-thatch houses, cleared plazas for communal gathering. The aesthetic is functional with emergent symbolic elaboration.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: Forms are vital and evolving; the period represents cultural elaboration rather than exhaustion. Symbols remain potent; rituals are efficacious to participants. No anomie or meaning erosion evident.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: The cosmos is animate and layered — an underworld of the dead, an earthly realm of humans and spirits, a celestial realm of powerful forces. Human existence is precarious, dependent on maintaining relationships with supernatural beings through offering and correct behavior. Fatalism and piety coexist; human agency is real but constrained by spirit will.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: Ritual marks agricultural and life-cycle transitions — planting, harvest, birth, death, puberty. Offerings (food, incense, blood) propitiate spirits and ancestors. Shamanic practitioners enter trance states to communicate with spirits, heal illness, and divine outcomes. Ritual is communal and reinforces social bonds.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: No formal institutions; ritual specialists hold knowledge but not institutional office. Doctrine is oral tradition, varied across communities, enforced by consensus rather than hierarchy. Sacred sites (caves, springs, hilltops) are recognized but not monumentalized.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: Beliefs are local and kin-transmitted; gradual diffusion occurs through intermarriage and trade contact. No missionary pressure or doctrinal competition; syncretism is the normal mode as groups exchange practices.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: The sacred remains vivid and present; no disenchantment or secularizing drift. Spiritual need is met through functioning ritual practice; no existential void opens in this period.

docs.title: 600 BCE – 400 BCE — Mesoamerican Interaction Sphere at the Oral Threshold
docs.text: Summary: A snapshot of the pan-Mesoamerican interaction sphere at the close of the oral era, capturing the simultaneous florescence of multiple regional centers—La Venta in the Olmec heartland, San José Mogote and nascent Monte Alban in Oaxaca, Cuicuilco in the Basin of Mexico, and emerging Maya polities in the lowlands—linked by exchange, shared iconography, and common ceremonial calendars, yet each developing distinct trajectories. The binding constraint is oral culture: all institutional memory, calendrical knowledge, ritual authority, and political coordination depend on speech and recall; the earliest glyphic notations (~600–500 BCE) remain isolated calendrical or name signs, not full writing; what is not spoken and remembered is lost. The most causal factor is the density and reach of the interaction network itself, which circulated prestige goods, iconographic conventions, and oral traditions across ecological zones, enabling parallel complexity without political unification.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: The interaction sphere spans three ecological bands: the Gulf Coast lowlands (tropical, riverine, Olmec heartland), the highland valleys (temperate, volcanic, Basin of Mexico and Oaxaca), and the Maya lowlands (tropical karst, seasonal wetlands). Movement between zones required crossing mountain passes or traversing coastal and riverine routes; friction was high, but established trade corridors (Tehuantepec, Pacific piedmont, Gulf coast) enabled regular exchange.

Climate Regime & Volatility: Regional climates varied: humid tropical in the lowlands with wet-dry seasonality; temperate with summer monsoon in the highlands. ENSO variability affected coastal and lowland rainfall; highland agriculture was more stable. Climate differences drove complementary exchange (tropical products upward, obsidian and highland goods downward).

Hazard Regime & Exposure: Volcanic activity threatened highland centers; flood and hurricane affected lowland coasts. Drought risk was higher in the Maya lowlands and drier highland valleys. Hazard regimes were regional; no single shock threatened the entire sphere, distributing risk across polities.

Resource & Energy Endowment: Resources were distributed unevenly, driving exchange: obsidian from highland Mexico, jade from Guatemala, cacao and rubber from Gulf and Pacific lowlands, marine shell from coasts, salt from coastal and highland sources. No single polity controlled all critical resources; interdependence structured the network.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Population densities remained low enough across all regions that sink saturation was not a constraint. Organic waste was absorbed by tropical and volcanic soils; no evidence of pollution or degradation limiting activity.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: Endemic parasitic and gastrointestinal infections prevailed throughout the sphere. Lowland populations faced higher mosquito-borne disease loads. Mortality was highest in infancy and childhood; survivors reached moderate life expectancy. No pandemics are attested; population was growing across regions.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: Maize-bean-squash agriculture provided the nutritional base, supplemented by regional proteins (fish, game, domesticated turkey and dog). Lowland populations added cacao and tropical fruits; highland populations relied more on lake resources. Skeletal evidence indicates adequate nutrition for elites; commoner health varied.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Healing was oral-traditional: herbal pharmacopoeia, ritual curing, and shamanic intervention. Knowledge was transmitted through specialist lineages. No institutional medicine existed; care was household- and kin-based with specialist consultation.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Monogamous or mildly polygynous households predominated. Elite polygyny concentrated reproduction; kin exogamy structured marriage alliances across communities. Birth rates were high where nutrition sufficed.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Population grew across all regions during the window. La Venta may have reached 10,000 or more; San José Mogote and Cuicuilco approached similar scales. Total Mesoamerican population in the sphere likely numbered in the hundreds of thousands. Density remained well below carrying capacity.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: Dependent loads were absorbed by extended households and communal networks. No evidence of demographic stress or abandonment; surplus supported dependents without strain.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: Maize agriculture, supplemented by beans, squash, and regional resources, provided reliable subsistence across all zones. Household storage buffered seasonal variation; communal granaries supported larger centers. Famine was rare and localized.

Energy Capture & Conversion: Human muscle remained the sole power source; no draft animals existed. Fire processed food and materials. The per-capita energy ceiling constrained monumental construction to seasonal labor mobilization; the pyramids and platforms at La Venta and Cuicuilco represented substantial but achievable labor investments.

Labor Organization & Coercion: Labor was organized through kinship, communal obligation, and corvée mobilized by chiefs. No evidence of large-scale slavery; coercion was limited to raiding and captive-taking at regional margins. Laborers were kin and clients, not a servile class.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Agricultural surplus supported non-farming specialists: craft producers (obsidian, jade, ceramics), ritual practitioners, and emerging elites. Production centers specialized by resource endowment: Pachuca obsidian, Motagua jade, Gulf Coast rubber. Surplus flowed through exchange networks and elite redistribution.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: Granaries at household and center scale stored maize. Prestige goods (jade, obsidian, shell) served as stored value for elites. No centralized treasury or monetary reserves existed; buffering was distributed across households and kin networks.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: Long-distance exchange linked all regions: obsidian from highland Mexico reached the Gulf Coast and Maya lowlands; jade from Guatemala circulated northward; cacao, rubber, and shell moved inland. Exchange was embedded in alliance, kinship, and ritual obligation rather than impersonal markets. Canoe transport along coasts and rivers; overland porterage through mountain passes.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: No monetary medium existed. Value was stored in prestige goods (jade, obsidian, shell, feathers) and deferred-reciprocity obligations. Credit and debt operated through kinship and alliance networks, not formal instruments.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: Chiefs extracted surplus through corvée, tribute in kind, and control of prestige goods. Redistribution at feasts and ceremonial events reinforced authority. Extraction was moderate; no evidence of coercive over-taxation.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Elites accumulated prestige goods visible in burials (La Venta tombs, San José Mogote graves). Wealth concentration was real but limited; no landed aristocracy with alienable estates. Defense of assets relied on social position and alliance rather than fortification.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Organic and craft waste was disposed locally; obsidian debitage accumulated at workshops. No toxic byproducts; waste loads remained within ecological absorption capacity.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Kinship organized society across all regions. Descent reckoning varied (patrilineal, bilateral, possibly matrilineal elements); inheritance passed through lineages. Marriage alliances linked elite families across polities, creating inter-regional kinship networks.

Association & Mutual Aid: Village solidarity and communal labor provided mutual aid. Craft specialization created emergent occupational groups, but formal guilds did not exist. Reciprocity and kinship obligation governed cooperation.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: Feasting, dance, and communal ritual provided leisure. Ball courts appear in some centers (La Venta); the ballgame carried ritual and social significance. Communal spaces around platforms served sociable functions.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: Ranked societies existed across all centers: elites distinguished by burial goods, residence near ceremonial architecture, and access to prestige items. Status was partly hereditary, partly achieved through ritual prowess and alliance-building. No rigid caste; boundaries remained permeable. Regional identities (Olmec, Zapotec, highland Mexican, early Maya) were crystallizing but not exclusionary.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: Chiefs and ritual specialists administered centers; no bureaucracy or formal offices existed. Authority was personal, validated by genealogy, oratory, and ritual performance. Oral tradition carried precedent; no written records. Inter-polity relations were managed through kinship, alliance, and periodic ceremonial gatherings.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: No standing armies existed. Warfare was small-scale and raiding-based; atlatl darts with obsidian points, clubs, and shields were standard. Captive-taking for sacrifice and labor occurred. Defensive architecture was limited; La Venta and Monte Alban show some fortification or strategic siting.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: Social friction was absorbed through feasting, ritual, and mediation. Excluded individuals could migrate or join rival centers. Factional competition was normal but rarely escalated to collapse. The sphere remained stable; no center collapsed during the window (La Venta declined ~400 BCE, at the window's end).

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: Chiefs derived authority from genealogical claims, ritual performance, oratorical skill, and success in exchange and warfare. Leadership was personal and charismatic; the colossal heads at La Venta and San Lorenzo memorialized individual rulers. Succession passed within elite lineages but required public validation.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: Allegiance to rulers was grounded in reciprocity: leaders who provided feasting, protection, and ritual access commanded loyalty. Disaffection arose when reciprocity failed; followers could migrate or support rivals. Legitimacy was personal and performative, not institutional.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: Collective will was mobilized for monumental construction (La Venta pyramid, Monte Alban terracing), long-distance exchange expeditions, and defense. Competing centers maintained rivalry while sharing ceremonial calendars and iconographic conventions; competition and cooperation coexisted.

External Relations & Posture: Relations among centers were primarily commercial and ceremonial, not military-imperial. No single center dominated the sphere; influence radiated through prestige, exchange, and cultural emulation rather than conquest. The Olmec heartland exerted cultural influence but not political control.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: Confidence and ambition characterized the period: population growth, ceremonial elaboration, and expanding exchange networks indicate collective energy. Inter-center rivalry coexisted with cooperation; trust extended through kinship and alliance; distrust marked relations with outsiders.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: No evidence of widespread disaffection; the expanding networks and ceremonial investment indicate collective energy remained high. La Venta's decline ~400 BCE may reflect local succession failure or resource shifts, not sphere-wide exhaustion.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Multiple language families coexisted: Mixe-Zoquean (Olmec heartland), Otomanguean (Oaxaca), proto-Mayan (lowlands), Uto-Aztecan ancestors (highlands). Bilingualism and lingua francas enabled inter-regional communication; iconographic conventions (Olmec-style symbols) provided limited cross-linguistic meaning-transmission.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Information traveled at the speed of human movement along trade routes. No couriers or formal message systems existed. News spread through trade caravans, pilgrimages, and kinship visits over weeks or months. The interaction sphere's extent (~1,000+ km) meant information took weeks to traverse.

Record, Storage & Persistence: No full writing existed. The earliest glyphic notations (~600–500 BCE, San José Mogote Monument 3, possibly Gulf Coast) were isolated calendrical or name signs, not connected discourse. All institutional memory—genealogy, ritual calendar, precedent, history—was stored in living minds and transmitted orally. Memory loss at death was irreversible unless transmitted beforehand.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: Chiefs and ritual specialists controlled authoritative speech. Iconography encoded religious and political messages but required oral interpretation. Taboos governed speech about the sacred; transgressive speech risked sanction. No institutional censorship existed beyond social pressure.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: Reception was face-to-face and communal at feasts and rituals. Amplification occurred through prestige of speakers and repetition. Successful narratives spread through the exchange network; unsuccessful ones faded.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: Oral transmission introduced drift across regions and generations. Ritual formulae and mnemonic devices reduced noise; iconography provided visual anchors. No verification mechanism existed beyond consensus. The sphere's linguistic diversity increased noise at inter-regional boundaries.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Reciprocity, kinship obligation, and cosmic balance grounded the moral order across the sphere. Generosity, hospitality, and ritual propriety defined virtue. Betrayal of reciprocity, sacrilege, and kinship violation were condemned.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: No written law existed anywhere in the sphere. Custom, transmitted orally and enforced by chiefs and elders, governed conduct. Taboos surrounding the sacred, the dead, and exchange obligation were binding. The earliest calendrical glyphs (~600 BCE) may have marked ritual obligations, not legal code.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: Chiefs and elders adjudicated disputes through mediation and oral precedent. Inter-polity disputes were managed through negotiation, alliance, or warfare. Sanction ranged from compensation and shaming to exile and sacrifice. Blood feud remained possible for unresolved grievances.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: No formal rights existed; protection derived from kinship, village membership, and elite patronage. Compliance burden was low; conduct was governed by face-to-face accountability and reputational pressure.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: Powerful elites could evade sanction for minor wrongs, but dependence on followers limited impunity. Inter-polity wrongs (raiding, captive-taking) were addressed through retaliation or negotiated compensation. No backlog of unresolved cases accumulated; justice was immediate or abandoned.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: Knowledge was practical and ritual-oriented: astronomical observation for calendrical and agricultural timing, herbal medicine, craft techniques. Explanation was mythological; no formal natural philosophy existed. The 260-day and 365-day calendrical cycles, coordinated across the sphere, represented accumulated astronomical knowledge transmitted orally.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Techniques for jade carving, obsidian knapping, ceramic production, monumental construction, and agricultural intensification were sophisticated. Knowledge was embodied in practice and transmitted through apprenticeship. Inter-regional exchange spread techniques (e.g., mirror-making, figurine styles).

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: Education was informal, within households and specialist lineages. Ritual and calendrical knowledge was restricted to specialists; craft skills were transmitted through lineages. The knowledge stock was distributed unevenly across and within polities.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: Techniques that lost utility faded. Oral transmission risked loss when lineages died without successors. The sphere's connectivity mitigated loss: knowledge could be recovered through exchange if it survived elsewhere. No mechanism preserved superseded theory; what was not taught was lost.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: Regional identities crystallized around founding myths, ancestral migrations, and supernatural patrons. Olmec iconography (were-jaguar, feathered serpent, maize deity) provided shared symbolic vocabulary; local traditions interpreted and elaborated these motifs. Memory was anchored in place (sacred mountains, caves, springs) and lineage.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: Rulers legitimated authority through genealogical claims, ritual performance, and association with supernatural power. The ideology of reciprocal obligation—leaders who mediated with the sacred and provided for followers were owed service—sustained hierarchy. Olmec iconographic prestige lent authority to elites who displayed it.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: The sphere's visual culture was recognizably Mesoamerican: jade celts and earspools, obsidian mirrors, ceramic effigy vessels, were-jaguar motifs, colossal sculpture (Olmec heads), platform architecture. Regional styles differentiated (Zapotec urns, Maya incised pottery, highland figurines), but shared conventions marked participation in the sphere. Color palette: earth tones, red, black, jade green.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: No form exhaustion is evident; iconographic and ritual forms remained vital and elaborating. La Venta's decline ~400 BCE may reflect political failure, not cultural exhaustion. Local traditions were ascending; the sphere was diversifying, not decaying.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: The cosmos was animate, layered (sky, earth, underworld), and cyclical. Supernatural beings (maize god, rain deity, were-jaguar, feathered serpent) inhabited natural features and required propitiation. Human life was embedded in cosmic obligation; ritual maintained balance. Fatalism and piety coexisted; proper ritual ensured favorable outcomes.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: Ritual centered on agricultural cycles, solar events, bloodletting, and offering. Jade and greenstone, associated with water and fertility, held supreme sacred value. Elite burials (La Venta tombs) included massive jade offerings. Sacrifice (human and animal) is attested. Ceremonial platforms and plazas provided ritual stages.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: No formal priesthood or temple institution existed. Ritual specialists (shamans, diviners, healers) held authority derived from personal power and lineage. Doctrine was fluid, transmitted orally, and varied by region. No orthodoxy was enforced; local traditions coexisted.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: Olmec-derived iconography and cosmological concepts had diffused across the sphere, blending with local traditions. Syncretism was ongoing; regional variants (Zapotec, highland Mexican, early Maya) elaborated shared themes. No displacement or conversion; accretion and blending predominated.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: No disenchantment is evident; the sacred remained vital. Ceremonial elaboration across all regions indicates spiritual investment was increasing. The threshold of literacy (~600–500 BCE) introduced calendrical notation that would eventually codify sacred knowledge, but within the window, the sacred remained fully oral and expanding.

docs.title: 6,000 BCE – 4,000 BCE — Middle Archaic and the Teosinte-Maize Transition
docs.text: Summary: The binding constraint is spoken language as the sole medium through which cultivation knowledge passes — seed selection, planting timing, and processing technique exist only in oral instruction and are lost if not transmitted. Within this two-millennium window, forager communities in highland Mexico complete the domestication of maize from its wild teosinte ancestor, a discrete macro-event that will transform Mesoamerican subsistence; the transition is accomplished through incremental selection guided by accumulated oral knowledge, with Guilá Naquitz and the Tehuacán Valley caves documenting the shift from wild teosinte to recognizably domestic maize cobs.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: The domestication event concentrates in highland valleys: the Valley of Oaxaca (Guilá Naquitz at 1,500 m), the Tehuacán Valley (~1,500 m), and the Balsas River drainage where wild teosinte grows natively. These intermontane basins offer temperate climate, seasonal rainfall, and alluvial soils suited to early cultivation. Movement between highland valleys and lowland zones continues but the highlands become the center of agricultural innovation, their isolation encouraging local experimentation.

Climate Regime & Volatility: The Mid-Holocene (6,000–4,000 BCE) brings a drier interval in some regions, pushing foragers toward more reliable water sources and encouraging intensified plant manipulation. Seasonal monsoon rains define the agricultural calendar: plant in May-June, harvest in October-November. This rainfall regime makes maize cultivation viable but imposes a narrow planting window that must be tracked orally and transmitted across generations.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: Volcanic activity continues in the Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt; ash deposits periodically fertilize highland soils. Drought stress is more pronounced than in the Early Archaic, creating selection pressure for drought-tolerant maize varieties. Flash floods in highland arroyos threaten camps and early plantings. Bands buffer hazard through mobility and site selection transmitted as oral knowledge of safe locations.

Resource & Energy Endowment: Wild teosinte (Zea mays ssp. parviglumis) grows in the Balsas drainage and adjacent highlands — the genetic ancestor of domestic maize. Squash, beans, chili, and avocado continue under manipulation. Obsidian remains the premier toolstone; sources at Otumba and Pachuca are increasingly exploited. Animal resources (deer, rabbit, turkey) supplement the growing plant component of diet. The endowment is transitional: wild resources still dominant but cultivated plants rising in importance.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Population remains sparse enough that waste load is negligible. Midden deposits at rockshelters contain ash, bone, maize cob fragments, and lithic debitage but do not accumulate to problematic levels. Sink capacity remains unlimited for practical purposes.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: Disease burden remains low. Sedentism is increasing but population density is still insufficient for epidemic transmission. Parasitic infections from water and stored food may increase slightly as people spend longer periods at cultivation sites. Mortality baseline is unchanged from the Early Archaic: injury, childbirth, and occasional food stress dominate.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: The dietary transition introduces new nutritional patterns. Maize provides carbohydrate calories but is deficient in niacin and certain amino acids unless processed with alkali (nixtamalization, which may develop later). Skeletal evidence is sparse but does not indicate nutritional decline; the mixed diet of cultivated plants, wild foods, and game maintains adequate nutrition.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Healing knowledge continues to pass orally. Medicinal plant use expands as foragers become more sedentary and familiar with local flora. No specialized healer class exists, but certain individuals accumulate expertise transmitted through apprenticeship. Recovery capacity remains limited by lack of surgical knowledge.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Pairing remains exogamous across bands. Increasing sedentism may begin to alter pairing patterns as bands spend more time at fixed locations. Physiological fertility is unimpaired. Child-carrying costs decrease slightly as mobility decreases, potentially allowing shorter birth intervals.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Population density increases modestly, perhaps doubling over the window to 0.1–0.2 persons per square kilometer in favorable highland valleys. Maize cultivation supports more people per unit area than foraging alone. Growth remains slow; the agricultural transition is gradual, not a sudden transformation.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: Dependency patterns shift slightly as sedentism increases. Elders can remain at base camps while productive adults forage or tend plots. The elderly become more valuable as repositories of accumulated cultivation knowledge — their extended survival serves the group's interest. Overall dependency load remains light.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: Subsistence transitions from foraging-dominant to mixed foraging-cultivation. Maize, squash, and beans provide an increasing share of calories; hunting and gathering continue to supply protein and dietary variety. The provisioning floor rises as cultivation reduces subsistence risk, but dependence on rainfall timing introduces new vulnerabilities. Oral knowledge of planting calendars becomes critical.

Energy Capture & Conversion: Human muscle remains the sole power source. Fire is used for cooking, land clearing (possibly slash-and-burn), and processing. No animal traction exists. Energy conversion improves as cultivated plants yield more calories per unit labor than wild gathering — the fundamental logic of the agricultural transition.

Labor Organization & Coercion: Labor organization remains kin-based but becomes more differentiated. Cultivation introduces new tasks: plot clearing, planting, weeding, harvesting. Gender and age divisions may sharpen: women's gathering expertise transfers to plant cultivation; men continue hunting. Coercion remains absent; cooperation is enforced by kinship and reciprocity.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Surplus capacity begins to increase. A successful maize harvest can be stored longer than wild seeds, extending the food supply into the dry season. However, surplus is still modest — enough to buffer seasonal variation, not to support non-producing specialists. The transition enables surplus but does not yet generate stratification.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: Storage technology improves as cultivation incentivizes preservation. Pit caches, ceramic containers (appearing late in the window), and woven granaries hold maize, beans, and squash seeds. Reserves extend to several months' consumption, reducing reliance on mobility as a buffer. The shift from movement to storage marks a fundamental economic transition.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: Exchange patterns continue down-the-line trade in obsidian, shell, and exotic goods. New trade in seeds, cuttings, and agricultural knowledge may occur between bands, though evidence is indirect. Logistics remain foot-based. Trade networks expand slightly as population density increases and more groups participate in regional exchange.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: No formal value medium exists. Stored grain functions as a form of wealth — surplus maize can be traded or gifted for social advantage. Deferred reciprocity continues: obligations are remembered and enforced through oral agreement and reputation. Credit remains purely social.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: No extraction institutions exist. Redistribution operates through sharing norms applied to harvests as to hunts: successful producers share with kin and band members. The transition introduces a new basis for potential inequality — differential access to stored surplus — but this potential is not yet realized.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Wealth inequality remains minimal. Stored grain and productive plots represent new forms of wealth, but sharing norms constrain accumulation. Defense of assets is social — reputation and kinship deter theft — rather than physical. The concept of land ownership does not yet crystallize.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Organic waste (cob fragments, chaff, husks) accumulates at processing sites. Maize waste may be fed to dogs or burned. No persistent pollution develops. Financial waste concepts remain inapplicable.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Kinship remains the organizing principle. As cultivation increases, land-use rights may become more formalized — a family's plot passes to descendants, creating incipient lineage property. Inheritance of material goods remains minimal, but inheritance of cultivation knowledge (which plots, which varieties, which timing) becomes crucial and passes orally through family lines.

Association & Mutual Aid: Mutual aid extends to agricultural labor — planting and harvesting may require more hands than a nuclear family provides. Work parties draw on kin and neighbors, reinforcing social bonds. Seasonal aggregations continue for ritual and exchange. The agricultural transition strengthens mutual-aid networks by creating new opportunities for cooperation.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: Leisure patterns shift with the agricultural cycle. Intensive work during planting and harvest is balanced by slack periods. Evening sociability around fires continues; storytelling and song transmit cultivation knowledge alongside myth. Sociability reinforces the oral tradition on which agricultural success depends.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: Stratification remains minimal but new bases for status emerge. A family with abundant stored surplus gains prestige through generosity. Cultivation knowledge becomes a form of social capital — those who know when to plant, which seeds to select, how to process and store gain authority. Status is still achieved, not ascribed, but the seeds of differentiation are planted.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: No formal administration exists. Decision-making remains consensual and oral. The agricultural transition does not yet require coordination beyond the band level. Scheduling is embedded in oral tradition, not administrative apparatus.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: No specialized coercive apparatus exists. Conflict over resources may increase as cultivation makes locations more valuable, but violence remains interpersonal and managed through kinship. Weapons are still subsistence tools (atlatl, spear) that double for conflict.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: Social friction remains low. Increased sedentism may create new tensions over plot access, but kinship mediation and fission remain available. No excluded class or standing grievance accumulates. Apparatus decay is inapplicable.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: Leadership remains informal. Agricultural expertise becomes a new source of authority: the elder who remembers drought-resistant varieties or optimal planting times commands attention. Oratorical skill matters — leaders must persuade through speech, explaining and justifying decisions to skeptical band members.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: Legitimacy remains personal. Successful cultivation enhances a leader's standing; crop failure undermines it. Allegiance attaches to those who provide security and knowledge. Exit remains the primary check on authority — dissatisfied individuals or families can leave and join other groups.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: Collective action expands to include communal agricultural tasks. Will is mobilized through discussion at band gatherings. Coordination across bands remains limited to seasonal aggregations for ritual, exchange, and intermarriage. No supra-band political units exist.

External Relations & Posture: Relations with other groups remain governed by kinship and trade. The agricultural transition may reduce territorial fluidity — groups become more attached to productive land. Posture remains cautious and reciprocal, but defense of cultivation sites may become more salient than in the purely foraging past.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: Sentiment remains intimate and kin-based. Confidence may increase as stored surplus reduces subsistence anxiety. The behavioral temper is increasingly oriented toward the agricultural cycle — attention to rainfall, planting timing, and harvest success. Trust networks expand slightly as sedentism increases face-to-face interaction with neighbors.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: Disaffection is managed through exit and fission. The agricultural transition creates new stakes — leaving means abandoning cultivated plots — but mobility remains viable. Apathy is rare; the demands of cultivation require active engagement. Exhaustion of will does not accumulate at this scale.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Speech remains universal. The agricultural transition adds new vocabulary for plants, cultivation techniques, and seasonal timing. Regional dialects continue to differentiate. No script exists; all agricultural knowledge is encoded in oral form. Gestural and pictorial communication continues to supplement speech.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Channels remain face-to-face and oral. Information about cultivation techniques spreads through kinship networks and inter-band contact at seasonal gatherings. Velocity is slow but adequate — agricultural knowledge accumulates over generations, not seasons. A useful innovation may take decades to spread across the region.

Record, Storage & Persistence: Memory remains the sole storage medium. Cultivation knowledge — which seeds to save, when to plant, how to process — is encoded in oral instruction, song, and myth. Persistence depends on transmission; the loss of knowledgeable elders can set a group back generations. The stakes of transmission failure rise as cultivation becomes more important.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: Discourse norms continue to privilege elder authority. Agricultural knowledge may be treated as family patrimony, shared within lineages but guarded from outsiders. Certain cultivation secrets (the best seed varieties, optimal processing techniques) may be restricted, creating incipient knowledge asymmetries.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: Attention focuses on agricultural matters during critical seasons. Stories encode planting calendars and processing techniques; songs mark seasonal transitions. Amplification occurs through retelling; successful techniques spread as groups observe their neighbors' success and ask how it was achieved.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: Signal integrity depends on repeated practice. Agricultural knowledge is tested against outcome: techniques that produce good harvests are reinforced; those that fail are discarded. Verification is empirical, built into the cultivation cycle. Noise is low; information volume remains manageable for oral tradition.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Justice continues to center on reciprocity. New questions arise: who has right to use a cleared plot? What claims does shared labor create? The moral foundation expands to encompass agricultural property relations, though these remain embedded in kinship rather than formalized in law. Generosity with surplus remains a core virtue.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: No formal law exists. Customary norms expand to cover agricultural situations: rights to cleared land, obligations of labor sharing, claims on stored surplus. These norms evolve through precedent held in collective memory. Taboos continue to carry supernatural sanction.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: Disputes over land use and surplus are adjudicated through kinship mediation. Liability may extend across generations — a family's claim to land derives from ancestors who cleared it. Sanction remains informal: shaming, compensation, ostracism. Violence over resources may increase but is constrained by kinship networks.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Rights crystallize around land use: the family that clears and cultivates a plot has claims on it. These rights are not formalized but socially recognized. Protection derives from kinship and reputation. Compliance burden remains light; rules are familiar and internalized.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: Impunity remains limited by social proximity. As sedentism increases, disputes are harder to escape — parties must continue to interact. This creates pressure for resolution but also risk of chronic grievance. Redress through compensation or mediation remains the norm; unredressed wrong accumulates slowly if at all.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: The domestication of maize represents a major intellectual achievement: sustained, multi-generational observation and selection that transforms a wild grass into a productive crop. Inquiry is practical — which plants to favor, which conditions produce better yields — but its accumulation constitutes applied botany. Paradigm remains animist; spirits are propitiated for good harvests.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Technique expands dramatically. Seed selection (choosing the largest, most productive cobs for replanting) is the core method, transmitted orally from parent to child. Plot preparation, planting depth, weeding, and harvest timing all constitute technical knowledge. Processing techniques (grinding, possibly early nixtamalization) are developed and refined. All are transmitted through oral instruction and demonstration.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: Education remains embedded in practice. Children learn cultivation by working alongside adults. The knowledge stock expands significantly — each generation adds to the accumulated understanding of maize and associated crops. Skill distribution broadens as more families practice cultivation, but specialized expertise (the best seed-savers, the most knowledgeable processors) confers status.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: Some foraging knowledge may begin to decay as cultivation absorbs more attention. However, mixed subsistence maintains most foraging skills. Knowledge decay remains the primary risk — an epidemic that kills elders, a family line that dies out, could erase generations of accumulated cultivation expertise. Transmission is the fragile link.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: Maize begins to enter mythos. The plant that feeds becomes sacred; origin stories may start to incorporate maize as a gift from spirits or ancestors. Place-names and memory attach to productive sites. Identity begins to include "those who grow maize" alongside kinship and locality markers. The transformation is gradual but foundational.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: The prevailing order remains simple and needs little justification. However, the agricultural transition introduces new claims: families that clear and plant have rights to harvest. Legitimation of these claims derives from labor invested, transmitted as oral precedent. No elaborate ideology is required at this scale.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: Expression continues in rock art, personal ornament, and perishable forms. Maize imagery may begin to appear, though evidence is sparse for this early period. Material culture expands with cultivation tools: planting sticks, storage baskets, grinding implements. Architecture remains minimal — brush shelters and rockshelters — but more permanent camps emerge at cultivation sites.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: Form exhaustion does not occur. Expressive tradition adapts to incorporate agricultural themes. Symbols remain potent and actively used. Anomie does not develop; shared agricultural practice reinforces community meaning-making.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: The cosmos remains animate. Plants, including cultivated ones, possess spirit and require propitiation. The agricultural cycle reinforces cyclical cosmology: planting, growth, harvest, death, renewal. Existential outlook expands to include gratitude and obligation to the plants that sustain life — reciprocity extends from human relations to the plant world.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: Ritual expands to accompany cultivation: planting ceremonies, harvest thanks, first-fruits offerings. Practice remains collective and oral — prayers and songs transmitted across generations. Sacred sites may include especially productive plots or locations where maize was first successfully grown. Devotion is embedded in agricultural labor itself.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: No specialized religious institutions exist. Ritual specialists may hold knowledge of agricultural rites, but they are not a separate class. Authority remains distributed among elders. Orthodoxy is tradition, enforced by consensus and the empirical test of harvest success.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: Cultivation spreads with its spiritual accompaniments. Groups that adopt maize also adopt associated rites and beliefs. Syncretism is natural — new plant spirits join existing pantheons. No displacement or conversion occurs; spiritual change is gradual and additive.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: Disenchantment does not occur. The agricultural transition reinforces enchantment: the mysterious productivity of plants, the dependence on unseen forces (rain, fertility), all demand spiritual interpretation. The sacred remains fully engaged in daily life. No residue of unfulfilled transcendence accumulates.

docs.title: 900 BCE – 400 BCE — Oaxacan Complexity and Early Monte Alban
