docs.text: Summary: By the mid-first millennium BCE a mature Iron Age village society spans the West African savanna from the Niger Bend to the Jos Plateau, where Nok culture produces the region's first monumental sculpture and demonstrates sophisticated ironworking, all sustained by grain agriculture and coordinated through oral tradition alone, with no writing and no centralized state, leaving authority dispersed among kinship networks and ritual specialists whose knowledge is spoken, performed, and remembered rather than inscribed.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: The savanna corridor extends from the Niger Inland Delta through the Volta basin to the Jos Plateau and Benue valley, a mosaic of grassland, gallery forest, and granite inselbergs; rivers provide water, fish, and alluvial soils; the Jos Plateau's elevation and laterite outcrops support the Nok heartland; spatial friction is moderate, with travel constrained by seasonal flooding and bush.

Climate Regime & Volatility: The monsoon delivers 600–1,200 mm of rainfall annually across the belt; the wet season supports grain cultivation while the dry season permits smelting and craft work; interannual variability causes episodic drought and flood; the climate is stable relative to the preceding millennium but still unpredictable.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: Seasonal flooding affects riverine settlements; bushfire clears fields but threatens granaries; locust swarms periodically devastate crops; disease exposure heightens near standing water; no evidence of catastrophic hazard events in this window.

Resource & Energy Endowment: Laterite nodules yield abundant iron ore; the Jos Plateau's geology provides tin, though large-scale tin working is later; hardwood forests supply charcoal; clay deposits support the terracotta tradition; the endowment is sufficient for local self-sufficiency in tools and craft.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Smelting deposits slag heaps near furnace sites; woodland clearance for charcoal and agriculture opens vegetation; the landscape absorbs the load without evidence of degradation; localized scarring around intensive smelting sites is the only residue.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: Endemic malaria, guinea worm, and intestinal parasites sustain background mortality; trypanosomiasis limits livestock in the southern margins; childhood mortality high; adult life expectancy perhaps 35–40 years; no epidemic die-offs documented.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: Grain staples provide caloric stability; fish, game, and legumes supplement protein; seasonal hunger occurs before harvest; skeletal evidence suggests adequate but not robust nutrition; dental wear from grit in grain processing is common.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Healing remains kin-embedded; herbalism, bonesetting, midwifery, and ritual healing transmitted orally; no specialized institutions; recovery depends on household resources and kin support.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Sedentary agriculture supports stable households and relatively high fertility; polygyny common among wealthier households; marriage arranged through kinship networks with bridewealth negotiated orally; reproductive success tied to grain and livestock wealth.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Population density rises modestly as agriculture matures; villages of 100–500 people cluster on defensible terrain and near water; the Jos Plateau supports denser settlement than surrounding lowlands; migration and intermarriage connect communities.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: High childhood mortality and short adult lifespans limit the dependency ratio; the aged and infirm remain within kin compounds; orphans absorbed by extended kin; no institutional dependency management.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: Pearl millet, sorghum, and yams anchor the diet; cowpea and shea butter provide protein and fat; cattle, sheep, goats, and fishing supplement grain; the granary buffers seasonal scarcity; subsistence is secure in normal years.

Energy Capture & Conversion: Human muscle powers all production; livestock provide transport and limited traction; fire is essential for cooking, clearing, smelting, and firing terracotta; per-capita energy remains low but supports craft specialization.

Labor Organization & Coercion: Labor organized by household and kin; seasonal work parties mobilize through reciprocal obligation; craft specialists (smiths, potters, sculptors) freed partially from farming by surplus; no evidence of slavery or large-scale coercion in this period.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Grain surplus supports dry-season reserves, craft production, and ritual feasting; ironworking and terracotta sculpture represent surplus-dependent specialization; production is local and village-scale; no large-scale manufacture or export.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: Clay granaries and underground pits store grain for one to two years; livestock serve as mobile wealth; no monetary instruments; buffering depends on kin-network reciprocity and intra-village sharing.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: Local exchange of grain, livestock, pots, iron tools, and ornaments at village and regional scale; long-distance exchange of copper, salt, and prestige goods exists but is limited; all conducted face-to-face and orally negotiated; no markets or written records.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: Cattle, grain, and iron implements function as stored value; bridewealth and tribute obligations create deferred reciprocity; no coinage; credit embedded in kinship and verbal agreement.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: Surplus circulates through kinship obligation, bridewealth, and ritual feasting; no centralized tribute or taxation; redistribution governed by oral custom and elder authority; no evidence of extractive hierarchy.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Wealth differentiates households modestly; cattle and iron tools mark status; land held by lineage; no fortifications; wealth protected by kin solidarity and reciprocal obligation.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Agricultural waste feeds livestock or composts; metallurgical slag accumulates at smelting sites; broken terracotta fragments scatter near production areas; waste is minimal and locally absorbed.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Patrilineal descent predominates; the extended family compound is the basic social unit; inheritance follows oral custom mediated by elders; marriage links lineages through bridewealth and alliance.

Association & Mutual Aid: Age grades, work parties, and ritual sodalities crosscut kinship; mutual aid in farming, building, and defense is obligatory; village cohesion maintained through face-to-face interaction and oral custom.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: Seasonal festivals mark planting, harvest, and initiation; drumming, dance, and oral performance structure communal time; terracotta figures may be associated with ritual occasions; sociability embedded in work and ritual.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: Status distinctions emerge between farmers, herders, and craft specialists; smiths and sculptors occupy ambiguous positions, respected but set apart; no formal class or caste; boundaries remain permeable; Nok society shows no evidence of hereditary aristocracy.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: No bureaucracy or formal administration; village affairs decided by council of elders; lineage heads coordinate labor and ritual; all governance oral and consensual; no writing, no record-keeping, no centralized authority.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: No standing military; iron weapons (spears, axes, arrowheads) available but dispersed among households; raiding and feuding occur between communities; no fortifications beyond natural terrain; collective defense mobilizes kin and village.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: Disputes settled by elder mediation, divination, and ritual reconciliation; feuds occasionally persist across generations; violence is episodic, not endemic; friction absorbed through kinship channels; no evidence of systemic breakdown or state collapse, as no state exists to collapse.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: Elders and lineage heads hold authority through seniority, oratorical skill, and ritual knowledge; smiths and diviners command respect through craft mastery and spiritual mediation; no paramount chiefs or kings; leadership is situational, personal, and earned.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: Allegiance attaches to kin, village, and ancestral cult; legitimacy rests on oral tradition, genealogical precedent, and ritual performance; no abstract political loyalty; authority must be continuously performed and validated.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: Collective action mobilizes for defense, labor, and ritual within the village; no regional coordination or centralized command; will is diffuse and locally bounded; no evidence of expansionist ambition.

External Relations & Posture: Relations with neighboring villages and pastoral groups negotiated orally through trade, intermarriage, and alliance; hostility is episodic; no standing alliances or enmities; no external imperial threat in this period.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: The mood is pragmatic and attuned to agricultural and ritual cycles; trust extends within kin and village; intergroup relations are negotiated cautiously; anxiety rises during drought or conflict.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: No evidence of widespread disaffection; the system is small-scale and kin-embedded; frustration absorbed through kinship and ritual; exhaustion is seasonal, tied to agricultural labor.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Speech is the sole medium of coordination; local languages mutually intelligible within regional clusters; no writing; all knowledge transmitted orally; strangers are linguistically opaque until relationships form.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Information travels at walking speed via messenger, traveler, and seasonal gathering; news diffuses through trade networks and ritual occasions; reach is limited to the regional kin and trade network.

Record, Storage & Persistence: Memory is the only archive; genealogies, craft techniques, and ritual knowledge preserved in specialist lineages and elders' minds; the terracotta sculptures themselves may encode meaning but carry no script; loss occurs with death and migration.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: Elders control ritual and authoritative speech; taboos govern discussion of the sacred and the secrets of craft; metallurgical and sculptural techniques guarded within specialist lineages; discourse shaped by respect protocols and oral etiquette.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: Reception occurs in face-to-face settings; amplification through repetition, performance, and the prestige of speakers; no broadcast medium; attention governed by social rank and ritual context.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: Oral transmission is vulnerable to drift, distortion, and loss; correction occurs through redundancy, repetition, and collective memory; no verification beyond consensus and performance; noise accumulates slowly across generations.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Justice is kinship-based, balancing reciprocity, honor, and compensation; fairness assessed by oral custom and elder judgment; the collective good prioritized over individual autonomy; supernatural sanction reinforces moral order.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: No written law; oral custom governs property, marriage, injury, and inheritance; taboos enforced by ritual sanction and social pressure; rules evolve slowly through precedent and elder interpretation.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: Elders and diviners adjudicate disputes; liability assessed through oral testimony, oath, and divination; sanctions include compensation, ostracism, and ritual purification; no imprisonment; serious offenses may invoke supernatural punishment.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Individual rights embedded in kin status; protection derives from lineage membership; compliance burden low in normal times; rule-breaking risks ostracism, compensation demands, and spiritual consequences.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: Powerful lineages may escape full sanction; feuds sometimes persist unresolved; the gap between justice owed and delivered is managed through kinship pressure and ritual but never fully closed; the system tolerates some impunity.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: Understanding is empirical and practical, embedded in oral tradition; causation attributed to spirits, ancestors, and observable regularities; no formal inquiry or theory separate from craft and ritual; knowledge is technique, not abstraction.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Ironworking is mature: ore selection, charcoal production, furnace construction, smelting, and forging are sophisticated, transmitted orally within smith lineages. Terracotta sculpture requires clay preparation, coil building, surface treatment, and controlled firing, techniques passed master to apprentice. Agricultural methods include seed selection, soil management, and crop rotation. All technique is embodied and spoken, never written.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: Knowledge transmitted through apprenticeship and initiation; metallurgical and sculptural skill restricted to specialist lineages; agricultural knowledge general; literacy nonexistent; the knowledge stock grows through oral accumulation and is vulnerable to lineage extinction.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: Stone tool techniques largely obsolete; lost skills irrecoverable without written record; knowledge decay occurs when lineages die out or disperse; the Nok sculptural tradition itself eventually declines after 300 CE, its techniques lost until archaeological recovery.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: Identity anchors in lineage, village, and ancestral cult; origin myths explain the first settlers, the discovery of fire and iron, and the covenant with the land; memory is genealogical and oral; no written history.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: Authority legitimated by seniority, ancestral precedent, and ritual purity; smiths and sculptors derive prestige from mastery of transformative craft; no abstract ideology; legitimation is enacted in performance, genealogical recitation, and the visual power of terracotta figures.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: Nok terracotta sculptures are the signature achievement: life-sized and miniature human and animal figures with elaborate coiffures, jewelry, and expressive faces; function debated (ancestor figures, ritual objects, status markers); pottery, ironwork, and personal ornament display regional styles; architecture is impermanent (mud, thatch, wood); the visual world is ritually charged and status-marked.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: Forms are stable and slowly evolving in this period; no evidence of symbolic exhaustion; meaning remains anchored in kin, craft, and ritual; the system renews through initiation and seasonal performance; the decline of Nok sculpture after 300 CE may indicate later form exhaustion or population shift.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: The world is animated by spirits, ancestors, and forces immanent in landscape, craft, and body; human life is embedded in a web of obligation to the dead and the land; fate is negotiable through ritual; the outlook is practical, relational, and this-worldly.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: Ancestor veneration structures daily and seasonal life; sacrifice, libation, and divination maintain cosmic balance; ironworking and perhaps sculpture are ritualized, mediating between human and spirit worlds; initiation rites mark life transitions; the terracotta figures may serve as ritual objects or ancestral representations.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: No formal clergy, temple, or doctrine; ritual authority diffused among elders, diviners, smiths, and perhaps sculptors; no orthodoxy; practice varies by lineage and locality; authority is personal, situational, and orally transmitted.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: No external religious contact documented in this period; practice is local and internally generated; syncretism occurs as communities interact; no displacement; the spiritual system is self-contained.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: The sacred remains vital and uncontested; no secularizing drift; the cosmology absorbs all experience; disenchantment is absent; the system is spiritually self-sufficient, with the terracotta tradition embodying spiritual investment in material form.

docs.title: 60,000 BCE – 12,000 BCE — Later Stone Age Adaptation and Climatic Oscillation
docs.text: Summary: A long-term trend spanning the Later Stone Age in the West African Sahel and Niger Basin, during which human populations adapted to dramatic climatic oscillations—from the extreme aridity of the Last Glacial Maximum through early post-glacial warming—through microlithic technologies, diversified subsistence strategies, and flexible band organization, all coordinated entirely through oral tradition; the glacial-interglacial climate cycle serves as the binding constraint, repeatedly contracting populations into riverine and lacustrine refugia during arid phases and permitting expansion during wetter intervals.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: The region spans from the Senegal valley through the Niger Bend and inland delta to the Chad Basin, with terrain alternating between sandy ergs, laterite plateaus, and river valleys that concentrate movement and settlement; during arid phases, sand seas expand and friction increases dramatically, confining viable routes to river corridors; during wetter intervals, lakeshores and seasonal wetlands open additional habitable zones, reducing spatial friction and permitting wider-ranging mobility across the savanna belt.

Climate Regime & Volatility: The trend period encompasses the most extreme climate swings of the Quaternary: from relatively warm conditions at 60,000 BP through progressive cooling to the Last Glacial Maximum (~26,500–19,000 BP), when global temperatures dropped 4–7 degrees Celsius, the Sahara expanded southward to its greatest extent, and monsoon rains retreated far to the south; post-glacial warming began after 19,000 BP, with gradual monsoon intensification, though the full "Green Sahara" phase lies beyond this window; interannual variability was high throughout, with multi-decadal droughts punctuating longer cycles.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: Chronic drought is the dominant hazard, especially during the LGM, when even major rivers shrank to seasonal flows and Lake Chad may have dried entirely; seasonal flooding along rivers during wetter intervals poses secondary risk; exposure to heat, dust storms, and fire is persistent; margin against crop failure is irrelevant (no agriculture), but margin against game and water scarcity is the limiting factor on survival.

Resource & Energy Endowment: During warmer, wetter intervals, savanna and riverine environments support diverse fauna (elephant, hippo, antelope, fish) and flora (tubers, seeds, fruits); lithic raw materials (quartz, quartzite, chert) remain available in river gravels and outcrops; firewood scarce in hyper-arid phases; during the LGM, resources contract to refugia around perennial water—Niger Inland Delta, Lake Chad remnants, Senegal valley—and competition intensifies; post-glacial recovery gradually restores resource abundance.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Anthropogenic impact remains negligible; population densities too low to burden any sink; organic refuse decomposes, lithic debitage accumulates at favored sites without consequence; the physical environment absorbs all discharge effortlessly.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: Malaria remains endemic in wetter zones; during arid phases, reduced standing water may lower mosquito-borne disease load, though waterborne and respiratory infections persist; mortality baseline is high, with life expectancy under thirty years; infant mortality severe; the direction of change oscillates with climate—wetter phases may increase malaria burden while improving nutrition.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: Nutritional status varies with climate: during wetter intervals, broad-spectrum diet (fish, game, plants) supports adequate nutrition; during the LGM, caloric stress likely increased, reflected in reduced population density and possible skeletal stress markers; post-glacial warming gradually improves nutritional access; physiological vitality tracks resource availability closely.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Healing remains limited to oral-transmitted herbal knowledge, wound care, and kin support; no specialized healers beyond those recognized for plant lore or spiritual power; recovery depends on band cohesion and mobility—the injured who cannot travel face abandonment or death; capacity is constant across the period, with no technological improvement.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Fertility constrained by nutritional stress during arid phases; birth spacing remains wide due to extended lactation and high infant mortality; pair-bonding and exogamous marriage between bands continue to require oral coordination of kinship and alliance; no evidence of changing mating systems across the period.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Population density fluctuates dramatically: during wetter intervals, expansion into savanna and lakeshores may raise regional population to several thousand; during the LGM, population contracts to refugia, potentially collapsing to hundreds of individuals in the region; replacement ratios are barely positive during favorable periods, negative during extreme contractions; post-glacial recovery initiates demographic expansion that accelerates beyond this window.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: Dependency load remains light: few survive to old age, and mobility limits dependent carrying; the LGM may have intensified dependency stress, forcing bands to abandon those unable to travel; post-glacial easing permits slightly larger dependency overhang, but the residue remains minimal.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: Economy remains immediate-return foraging, but Later Stone Age technology introduces microlithic tools—backed blades, composite hafted implements—that enable more efficient processing of a wider range of resources; provisioning floor fluctuates with climate: during wetter intervals, fish, shellfish, and game support stable caloric intake; during the LGM, the floor drops to survival margins in refugia, with population decline reflecting inadequate provisioning.

Energy Capture & Conversion: Energy capture still relies on human muscle and controlled fire; microlithic technology slightly increases efficiency of hunting (composite projectiles, traps) and plant processing (grinding stones, later in the period), but the per-capita work ceiling remains low; no animal traction or mechanical power.

Labor Organization & Coercion: Labor remains organized within kin bands, probably numbering 20–50 individuals during favorable periods, contracting to smaller units during crisis; division by age and sex persists; no coerced labor; all coordination oral; flexibility in band composition allows adaptation to fluctuating resource availability.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Surplus capacity remains negligible: microlithic technology improves efficiency but does not enable storage or surplus accumulation; during favorable periods, occasional gluts (a large kill, a fish run) are shared and consumed quickly; no mechanism for long-term storage.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: No durable storage technology emerges during this period; reserves remain body fat and knowledge of alternative sites; buffering against shortage depends on mobility—moving to wetter refugia—and on reciprocal sharing mediated orally; the trend toward microlithic technology may slightly improve foraging efficiency, providing marginally greater buffer.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: Exchange remains limited to inter-band gifting of raw materials, ornaments, and mates; during the LGM, population contraction may reduce inter-band contact, limiting exchange networks; post-glacial expansion restores wider networks; logistics are entirely pedestrian, with no boats or wheeled transport; external dependence is low, but isolation during arid phases increases vulnerability.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: No currency; value stored in oral obligations and remembered reciprocity; deferred exchange operates through kinship networks—debts remembered and called in through speech; no change across the period.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: No extraction apparatus; all production consumed or shared within the band; redistribution through immediate sharing; no taxation or tribute.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Personal property limited to tools and ornaments; no significant wealth differentiation; asset defense consists of personal possession during mobility; theft deterred by oral reputation and band transparency.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Organic waste discarded and decomposed; lithic debitage accumulates at workshop sites; no financial waste; residue negligible.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Kinship remains the primary social structure: oral genealogies define marriage partners, inheritance of status and knowledge, and alliance networks; inheritance of material property minimal; bilateral or unilineal reckoning continues without change.

Association & Mutual Aid: Bands remain the sole associational unit, with fluid membership based on kinship and affinity; mutual aid obligatory within the band; inter-band relations maintained through marriage exchange, periodic aggregation, and reciprocal visiting, all coordinated orally; during the LGM, reduced population density may attenuate inter-band networks, weakening the associational fabric.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: Leisure time persists: storytelling, singing, and dancing around fires continue as primary sociability; microlithic technology may slightly reduce foraging time during favorable phases, increasing leisure; children learn through play and imitation.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: Stratification remains minimal: age and skill confer respect, but no hereditary hierarchy emerges; status accrues to skilled hunters, knowledgeable elders, and those with spiritual power; no caste or class; band identity is the primary group boundary.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: No formal administration: decisions by consensus or elder deference; no bureaucracy or record-keeping; oral deliberation suffices for band-scale coordination; institutional capacity does not increase across the period.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: No organized military; violence interpersonal and rare; weaponry consists of hunting tools (microlithic-tipped spears, later bows and arrows toward the end of the period); conflict between bands occasional and limited; no fortification or standing defense.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: Friction discharged through band fission, mobility, and oral mediation; during the LGM, stress may increase inter-band conflict over refugia, but population density is too low for sustained warfare; disorder is minimal; institutional decay does not occur because institutions are informal and regenerate orally.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: Leadership remains situational: best hunters, most knowledgeable elders, and those with spiritual power lead in relevant domains; no permanent chiefs; personal authority is earned and ratified through oral acknowledgment; charisma and competence remain the basis of influence.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: Allegiance flows from kinship and demonstrated competence; no abstract legitimacy; leaders obeyed because they are respected kin who deliver results; erosion occurs when leaders fail and lose oral reputation.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: Collective will mobilized for hunts, camp moves, and defense, organized orally; during the LGM, survival pressure may heighten collective resolve; no political contest or succession struggle at band scale; will is episodic, not institutional.

External Relations & Posture: Relations with other bands oscillate between alliance and avoidance; during resource contraction, competition over refugia may sharpen, increasing wariness; no diplomatic apparatus; posture remains defensive—bands prefer mobility over conflict; leverage minimal.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: Prevailing mood fluctuates with climate and resources: anxiety and caution during arid contractions, confidence and expansion during wetter phases; trust remains high within bands, lower toward strangers; behavioral temper is adaptive—cooperation intensifies when survival is threatened, relaxes during abundance.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: Disaffection rare within kin groups; when it arises, fission resolves it; apathy limited by survival imperative; spent will (exhaustion, despair) may occur during prolonged drought, contributing to band dissolution; post-glacial recovery restores collective energy; residue light.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Communication remains entirely oral and gestural; language fully grammatical, permitting abstract discourse; all band members share the linguistic code; inter-band intelligibility may decrease during the LGM as populations fragment into isolated refugia, potentially allowing dialect divergence.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Channels remain face-to-face speech and song; transmission velocity limited to walking speed; during population contraction, inter-band communication attenuates, slowing regional information flow; post-glacial expansion restores wider transmission networks.

Record, Storage & Persistence: All record held in living memory; oral tradition preserves technical knowledge (microlithic manufacture, fire-making, tracking), territorial knowledge, and kin memory; persistence depends on intergenerational transmission; the LGM population bottleneck may have caused significant knowledge loss as transmission chains broke.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: Discourse regulated by oral custom; certain topics restricted by age, gender, or initiation; censorship informal, enforced by social disapproval; framing shaped by storytellers and communal validation; no change across the period.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: Reception communal; stories heard around fires with audience participation; amplification through retelling; attention governed by survival relevance; entertainment value also matters.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: Oral transmission prone to drift; verification depends on communal memory and elder cross-checking; noise low but signal degradation over generations inherent; the LGM bottleneck may have amplified drift by reducing the pool of transmitters.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Morality embedded in kinship obligations: fairness means sharing with kin, justice means reciprocity and proportional retaliation; strangers remain outside or ambiguous to the moral circle; oral reasoning contextual and case-by-case; no change across the period.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: No written law; oral custom governs marriage, sharing, violence, and resource access; change occurs slowly through accumulated precedent; microlithic technology may introduce new norms around tool ownership and exchange, but evidence is lacking.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: Disputes adjudicated through oral deliberation among elders; liability personal and familial; sanctions include gossip, shaming, ostracism, and violence; no formal courts or codified penalties.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Rights relational: band members have claims on food, protection, and mates by kinship; compliance burden light because norms internalized; predictability high within the band, uncertain in inter-band relations.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: Impunity limited by band transparency; wrongdoing observed and remembered orally; persistent offenders ostracized or expelled; unredressed wrongs simmer as grievances, potentially erupting in violence or fission; residue light.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: Inquiry remains empirical but non-systematic; knowledge of animal behavior, plant properties, weather, and terrain accumulated through observation; explanatory paradigms animistic and mythological; no formal science.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: The trend period sees significant technological change: Later Stone Age microlithic technology emerges, featuring backed blades, composite hafted tools, and eventually bow-and-arrow technology (toward the end of the period); these innovations are transmitted orally through demonstration and apprenticeship; fire management, plant processing (grinding stones appear in some regions), and trapping techniques also advance.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: Education remains informal: observation, imitation, and oral instruction from kin; knowledge stock held in collective memory; skill distribution relatively egalitarian; the LGM bottleneck may have contracted the knowledge stock, with recovery and innovation accelerating in post-glacial warming.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: Middle Stone Age technologies (Aterian tanged points, large bifaces) become obsolete, replaced by microlithic industries; knowledge loss occurs when transmission fails, especially during population crashes; error and myth may persist uncorrected; the residue of lost knowledge is invisible.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: Identity remains band-based; origin myths, ancestor stories, and territorial claims define belonging; memory extends a few generations in oral genealogy; the LGM population bottleneck may have severed some memory chains, creating discontinuities in oral tradition; post-glacial expansion permits new mythos formation around survival and migration.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: Legitimacy derives from kinship and precedent; elders invoke ancestor practice to authorize norms; no ideological apparatus beyond oral tradition; climatic stress may generate narratives of survival and endurance that become foundational for successor populations.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: Material culture evolves: microlithic tools replace earlier forms; body ornamentation (beads, ochre, shells) continues; rock art may emerge in the later part of this period in some Saharan regions (though fully dated examples are later); artistic expression is oral—song, dance, storytelling—and ephemeral; visual style changes slowly.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: Form exhaustion minimal: oral traditions renewed through performance; meaning decays only when transmission fails; the LGM may have caused loss of some narrative and ritual forms; post-glacial renewal generates new forms.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: Cosmology remains animistic: spirits inhabit the natural world; human life embedded in a community of non-human agents; death is transition; existential outlook is fatalistic—misfortune attributed to spiritual causes and addressed through ritual; climatic hardship may intensify spiritual explanations and ritual activity.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: Ritual accompanies transitions, hunts, and seasonal events; sacred practice communal, performed orally and physically; burials (where documented) suggest belief in afterlife or spiritual continuity; during the LGM, ritual may intensify as populations seek spiritual intervention against drought.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: No formal institutions: spiritual authority rests with individuals recognized for special power—shamans, healers, elders with dream access; doctrine oral and flexible; orthodoxy enforced by communal memory and performance.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: Spiritual beliefs local and band-specific; diffusion through inter-band contact and marriage; syncretism the norm; during the LGM, isolation may permit divergence; post-glacial reconnection enables renewed diffusion and blending.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: Disenchantment absent: the world remains enchanted; no secularizing drift; spiritual failure generates new rituals and explanations rather than existential void; the residue is not disenchantment but the need for renewed spiritual response to persistent hardship.

docs.title: 1200 CE – 1500 CE — Mali Empire and the Mande Expansion
docs.text: Summary: A discrete macro-event bracketing the rise, apogee, and gradual contraction of the Mali Empire, from Sundiata Keita's defeat of the Sosso at Kirina around 1235 CE to the loss of Timbuktu and Gao to Songhai by 1468 CE. The binding constraint is oral transmission: court administration, legal judgment, diplomatic protocol, and the legitimating epic of Sundiata are stored and performed through the spoken word, carried by the jeli (griots) whose hereditary memory sustains the state. Arabic literacy serves commerce and Islamic scholarship in Timbuktu and Djenno, but the Mande heartland governs through speech, and the Epic of Sundiata circulates as oral performance, not written text. The single most causal factor is the institutional apparatus of the mansa's court — the balance of tribute extraction, trade monopoly, and griot-preserved legitimacy that allowed a savanna polity to project power across the Sahel and into the Sahara, accumulating gold wealth sufficient to reshape Mediterranean bullion markets.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: The Mali Empire controls the upper Niger from its Mande heartland west of the Niger Bend, extending northwest to the Saharan salt mines of Taghaza and east to the trading cities of Timbuktu, Djenne, and Gao. The Niger River provides a navigable corridor linking interior grain production to riverine towns; the Niger Inland Delta supports flood-retreat agriculture and dense fishing populations. Overland routes cross the savanna to the Gambia and Senegal rivers, while trans-Saharan caravan trails connect to North African entrepots. Spatial friction is seasonal: the summer rains render low-lying routes impassable, compressing caravan traffic into the dry season.

Climate Regime & Volatility: The semi-arid Sahel receives 250–750 mm of summer monsoon rainfall, declining northward into the Sahara. Interannual variability is high; multi-year droughts stress pastoral populations and reduce Niger floodplain yields. The medieval period (c. 1000–1300 CE) is relatively favorable compared to later centuries, permitting agricultural expansion and population growth that underwrites state formation.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: Drought is the primary environmental hazard, triggering famine, pastoral displacement, and political instability. Locust swarms periodically devastate crops. The empire's savanna core is less exposed than its Sahelian and Saharan peripheries, where marginal rainfall makes agriculture precarious.

Resource & Energy Endowment: Gold from the Bambuk and Bure fields in the upper Senegal and Niger tributaries provides the empire's primary export commodity. Iron ore is locally abundant; smelting supports tool and weapon production. Salt, imported from Saharan mines at Taghaza and Taoudeni, is essential for human and animal metabolism and commands high exchange value in the savanna. Fuelwood and charcoal sustain metallurgy and cooking.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Population densities remain low enough that environmental sinks absorb agricultural and urban waste without saturation. Deforestation around smelting centers and urban areas is localized. The Niger floodplain flushes annually, clearing organic accumulation. The physical residue is minimal; the landscape bears the load.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: Endemic malaria, sleeping sickness in tsetse zones, and gastrointestinal infections maintain elevated childhood mortality. The savanna's lower tsetse density compared to forest zones permits cattle keeping, but trypanosomiasis still limits livestock in southern reaches. Mortality is chronic rather than epidemic during the window; no documented plague or smallpox outbreak transforms demography.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: Pearl millet, sorghum, and African rice provide carbohydrate staples; cowpeas and groundnuts add protein. Fish from the Niger supplement interior diets. Cattle, sheep, and goats provide milk, meat, and hides, though concentrated among pastoralist groups and elite households. Nutritional status is adequate for the majority in good rainfall years; drought pushes marginal populations into deficiency.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Healing rests on herbalist knowledge, spiritual intervention, and household care. No centralized medical institution exists; each village maintains its own practitioners. Islamic medicine reaches elite circles in Timbuktu and Djenne but does not penetrate rural practice. Capacity is thin but evenly distributed.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Polygyny is normative among elites and those with cattle wealth; most households are effectively monogamous due to resource constraints. Bridewealth in cattle or goods regulates marriage. Fertility is high but offset by childhood mortality; net reproduction maintains slow population growth during favorable decades.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Population is concentrated along the Niger and its tributaries, with lower densities in the drier Sahel and empty desert to the north. Total population within the empire's effective control is estimated at several million, though figures are speculative. Growth is slow but positive during the thirteenth and early fourteenth centuries.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: High childhood mortality limits the aged population; dependency ratios favor the productive cohort. Orphans are absorbed by extended kin; widows remarry or return to natal families. The dependency load does not strain the productive base.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: Rainfed millet and sorghum cultivation anchors the savanna economy; flood-retreat agriculture in the Niger Inland Delta produces African rice and supports dense fishing communities. Pastoralists raise cattle, sheep, and goats in the northern reaches, exchanging animal products for grain. The provisioning floor is secure in average years; the Niger Delta provides a buffer against regional drought.

Energy Capture & Conversion: Human and animal muscle power drive all production. Oxen and donkeys carry loads; human labor tills fields, paddles canoes, and hauls goods. Fuelwood and charcoal power metallurgy and cooking. The energy ceiling is biologically fixed, limiting the scale of construction and manufacture.

Labor Organization & Coercion: Slavery is institutionalized: captives taken in war or purchased through trade perform agricultural, domestic, and artisanal labor. Hereditary occupational castes — smiths, leatherworkers, griots — are socially distinct though not enslaved. Free farmers owe tribute and occasional corvee to local chiefs and, through them, to the mansa. Coercion is moderate; most labor is organized through kinship and clientage.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Agricultural surplus supports urban populations in Timbuktu, Djenne, Niani, and lesser towns. Artisanal production — textiles, leatherwork, metalwork — serves local and export markets. Gold mining and collection in the Bambuk and Bure fields generates the surplus that funds trans-Saharan trade; the empire controls production indirectly, taxing exports rather than operating mines.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: Grain is stored in household and village granaries; no centralized imperial reserve is attested. Merchants hold inventories of salt, cloth, and gold in urban warehouses. Livestock serve as mobile wealth reserves. Buffer depth is limited; a multi-year drought strains reserves across the system.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: Trans-Saharan caravans link the empire to North Africa, exchanging gold, slaves, and ivory for salt, copper, textiles, and horses. The Niger River carries bulk goods between interior production zones and riverine towns. Djenne and Timbuktu are the principal entrepots; Niani is the political capital. Trade routes are maintained through tributary arrangements with desert Tuareg and savanna chiefs.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: Gold dust and salt bars serve as media of exchange; cowrie shells circulate for smaller transactions. Credit arrangements among merchants are oral, witnessed and remembered; Islamic law provides a framework for commercial contracts in urban centers. No coinage is minted; value is weighed, not counted.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: The mansa levies tribute on subordinate chiefs, who extract from villages in their domains. Customs duties at trade chokepoints — river crossings, caravan nodes — generate imperial revenue. Gold exports are taxed or monopolized; the mansa reportedly controlled gold nuggets, leaving dust to traders. Redistribution flows through the court as gifts, feasts, and support for military retinues.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Wealth concentrates among the mansa, provincial governors, and merchant elites. Land is held communally by lineages; movable wealth — gold, slaves, cattle — is personally owned. Defense against seizure relies on concealment, dispersal among kin, and the protection of powerful patrons.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Agricultural waste is recycled as fodder, fuel, or fertilizer. Urban waste accumulates in middens; organic matter decomposes in the tropical climate. Metallurgical slag is dumped at smelting sites. No waste stream overwhelms local sinks; the physical residue clears or settles without feedback.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Mande society is organized by patrilineages (jamuw) that structure marriage, inheritance, and political obligation. Clans trace descent from mythic ancestors; the Keita lineage claims Sundiata and dominates the imperial succession. Inheritance passes patrilineally; land is held by lineages, movable wealth by individuals. Marriage creates alliances between lineages; bridewealth flows from groom's to bride's kin.

Association & Mutual Aid: Age-grade associations (ton) organize labor, socialization, and military service in Mande villages. Hunter associations (donso-ton) provide a cross-cutting network linking men across lineage boundaries. Merchant communities (jula) maintain internal solidarity and credit networks. Mutual aid operates through kin obligation, age-grade solidarity, and patron-client ties.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: Festivals mark agricultural cycles, royal events, and religious observances. Music, dance, and oral performance by griots entertain and instruct. Hunting expeditions serve social as well as subsistence purposes. The court of the mansa is the apex of elite sociability, where feasting, gift-giving, and display reinforce hierarchy.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: Society divides into freeborn (horonw), occupational castes (nyamakalaw), and slaves (jonw). Within the freeborn, nobles and commoners are distinguished by lineage, wealth, and connection to the mansa. Occupational castes — smiths, griots, leatherworkers — are endogamous and socially distinct, neither high nor low but set apart. Slaves range from war captives to household dependents to plantation laborers. Stratification is pronounced but permeable; individual slaves may rise through service, and free lineages may fall through misfortune.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: The mansa rules through provincial governors (farba) appointed over conquered regions and through tribute relationships with subordinate chiefs who retain local authority. The court at Niani is the administrative center; the mansa's council includes generals, jurists, and senior griots. Administration is personal, not bureaucratic: orders are spoken, tribute is collected by delegates, justice is rendered by the mansa or his representatives. Reach weakens with distance; peripheral regions are loosely held.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: The mansa commands a standing cavalry force equipped with horses imported from North Africa; cavalry is the premier arm for savanna warfare. Infantry levies are raised from tributary populations. Iron weapons — swords, spears, javelins — are locally produced. Fortification is minimal; power projects through mobile force rather than fixed defense. The military apparatus suffices for tribute enforcement and raiding but struggles to hold distant conquests against resurgent rivals.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: Succession disputes recur, as the Keita lineage produces multiple claimants and no fixed rule determines priority. Peripheral regions — Songhai in the east, Wolof in the west — break away when central power weakens. Tuareg raids threaten Sahelian towns. The apparatus strains after the mid-fourteenth century; Timbuktu and Gao are lost by 1468 CE, and the empire contracts toward its Mande core. The residue is fragmentation and successor states.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: The mansa is the apex of political authority, commanding loyalty through lineage prestige, military success, and generous redistribution. Mansa Musa (r. c. 1312–1337 CE) epitomizes effective leadership: his pilgrimage to Mecca (1324–1325 CE) displays wealth on a scale that disrupts Egyptian gold markets and brings Mali to Mediterranean attention. Subsequent mansaa struggle to match his stature; personal authority declines with imperial fortunes.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: Legitimacy rests on three pillars: Keita descent from Sundiata, whose oral epic is performed at coronations; Islamic piety, demonstrated through pilgrimage, mosque construction, and patronage of scholars; and the material benefits of peace and trade. Allegiance holds while all three are credible; succession disputes and military failures erode belief in the mansa's divine favor.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: The empire's will to expand peaks under Sundiata and Mansa Musa; subsequent rulers maintain rather than extend. Collective resolve fractures along lineage and regional lines; no mechanism aggregates preferences beyond the mansa's council. Succession crises reveal the limits of cohesion.

External Relations & Posture: Mali projects power northward, securing the trans-Saharan routes through tributary arrangements with Tuareg groups and control of Timbuktu. Relations with North African states are commercial and diplomatic; Mansa Musa's pilgrimage is both religious obligation and diplomatic display. Relations with Songhai to the east shift from suzerainty to rivalry. The posture is extractive and hegemonic, not expansionist for territory but for trade control.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: The empire enjoys prestige and legitimacy at its height; the mansa's authority is accepted as divinely sanctioned and ancestrally grounded. Trust extends along kinship and trade networks; strangers are treated according to their lineage connections and merchant credentials. Temper is confident during the thirteenth and early fourteenth centuries, anxious as decline sets in.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: Decline in the fifteenth century generates disaffection: provincial governors defect, tribute payments cease, and peripheral peoples reject Keita authority. The will to reconquer flags; the mansa's reach contracts. The residue is resignation in the Mande heartland and opportunism on the margins.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Spoken Manding (Mandinka, Bambara dialects) is the lingua franca of the empire's core; Soninke, Songhai, Fulfulde, and other languages circulate among tributary peoples. Arabic is the language of Islamic scholarship and long-distance commerce, known to ulama and literate merchants but not to the general population. The binding constraint holds: governance, law, and legitimation are conducted orally; the Epic of Sundiata is performed, not read.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Information travels by messenger on horseback, by river canoe, and by caravan. The mansa's commands reach provincial governors within days or weeks depending on distance. Griots carry news and royal praise across the empire. Transmission velocity is slow by later standards but adequate for pre-modern administration.

Record, Storage & Persistence: Arabic manuscript culture flourishes in Timbuktu and Djenne: Quranic texts, legal treatises, and commercial records are copied and preserved. But the Mande political tradition stores its memory in living griots: the Epic of Sundiata, genealogies, and court history are transmitted orally, memorized across generations. The record is embodied, not inscribed; its persistence depends on the continuity of griot lineages.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: Griots control the narrative of lineage and state: their praise songs elevate patrons, their genealogies legitimate rule, their satire shames transgressors. Access to the mansa is mediated by court protocol; only griots may speak freely to power. Arabic scholars maintain their own discourse norms within Islamic jurisprudence. Censorship is informal but effective: to be excluded from griot praise is social death.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: The audience for griot performance includes the court, gathered villagers at festivals, and patron households at life-cycle events. Amplification is human: a compelling performance is repeated, adapted, and spread through the griot network. Arabic manuscripts circulate among a narrow literate elite in urban centers.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: Oral transmission introduces variation: each performance differs, epithets shift, episodes expand or contract. But formulaic structure and memorization discipline preserve core content across generations. The noise is absorbed as variant tradition, not signal loss. Arabic manuscript copying maintains higher fidelity within its narrower domain.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Mande moral order rests on layered foundations: ancestral custom (laada), which governs kin obligations, marriage, and inheritance; Islamic law (sharia), which applies to matters of commerce, marriage, and public morality in Muslim communities; and the mansa's decree (sariya), which overrides both in matters of state. Justice is restorative: compensation, reconciliation, and reintegration are preferred to punishment. Hospitality, honesty, and generosity are praised; theft, treachery, and cowardice are shamed.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: The Kouroukan Fouga, traditionally attributed to Sundiata's founding assembly, establishes constitutional principles: the division of society into castes, the allocation of offices to lineages, the rights of slaves and women. Whether historical or legendary, it is transmitted orally and cited as precedent. Islamic qadis in urban centers adjudicate according to Maliki fiqh. Codification is oral or, where Arabic is used, manuscript-based; no printed law exists.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: Disputes are settled by lineage elders, village chiefs, or the mansa's court depending on scale. Islamic qadis adjudicate among Muslims. Liability falls on lineages as well as individuals; kin are responsible for each other's debts and wrongs. Sanction ranges from compensation and restitution to corporal punishment, enslavement, or death for serious crimes. Backlog is light; adjudication is prompt and personal.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Rights are embedded in status: freeborn have different claims than slaves; men different from women; nobles different from commoners. Protection comes from kin, patron, and community membership. Strangers invoke guest-friendship or merchant credentials. Compliance burden is moderate: tribute obligations are seasonal, corvee demands occasional, daily conduct governed by custom rather than regulation.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: The powerful enjoy effective impunity; a mansa who seizes property or enslaves free persons may face divine sanction in the next world but rarely human sanction in this one. Peripheral peoples suffer wrongs — raiding, enslavement, tribute extraction — without recourse. The residue is grievance carried orally, erupting when central power weakens.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: Islamic scholarship in Timbuktu and Djenne engages Quranic exegesis, hadith, jurisprudence, grammar, and Sufi mysticism. Scholars correspond with North African centers; manuscripts circulate. But inquiry is textual and theological, not empirical; the paradigm is Islamic learning (ilm), not natural philosophy. Outside Islamic circles, knowledge is practical and embedded in oral tradition.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Iron smelting, gold extraction, leatherworking, weaving, boat-building, and construction techniques are transmitted through apprenticeship in occupational castes. Agricultural knowledge — planting calendars, soil management, flood-retreat timing — is held by farming lineages. Medical and ritual knowledge is the domain of healers and diviners. All applied knowledge is oral; technique is embodied, not written.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: Quranic schools (makarantas) teach Arabic literacy and Islamic fundamentals in urban centers; students who advance travel to Timbuktu or beyond for higher learning. The majority remain illiterate, educated through family apprenticeship, griot performance, and initiation societies. Skill distribution follows caste: smiths' children learn smithing, griots' children learn performance. The knowledge stock is deep within specializations, shallow across them.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: Oral transmission is vulnerable to lineage extinction: if a griot line ends without heirs or apprentices, its repertoire is lost. Arabic manuscripts decay in the Sahelian climate; copying preserves some, but many are lost. The residue is gaps in the record, variant traditions where the original is irrecoverable, and forgotten techniques where caste lines failed.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: The Epic of Sundiata is the foundational narrative: the exiled prince who overcame sorcery and oppression to defeat the tyrant Sumanguru and establish the Mali Empire. Performed at coronations and festivals, it defines Mande identity, legitimates Keita rule, and models heroic virtue — courage, generosity, cunning, filial piety. The epic is living tradition, adapted by each griot generation but anchored in core episodes.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: The mansa's legitimacy draws on three narratives: descent from Sundiata, affirmed by griot genealogy; Islamic piety, demonstrated by pilgrimage and mosque patronage; and military prowess and generous redistribution, which fulfill the heroic model. These narratives circulate orally, reinforced at court rituals and public performances. No written ideology competes; the oral tradition monopolizes political discourse.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: Mande material culture includes woven cotton textiles (bògòlanfini mud-cloth), indigo-dyed garments, gold and copper jewelry, and leatherwork. Architecture is mud-brick Sudano-Sahelian style, exemplified by the Great Mosque of Djenne (rebuilt in its current form later, but rooted in this period's tradition). Sculpture is limited; Islam discourages figural representation. Music — the balafon, kora, ngoni — accompanies griot performance. The aesthetic is functional, geometric, and restrained, with status displayed through quantity and quality of cloth, gold, and horses.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: The epic tradition remains vital throughout the window; formulaic structure prevents exhaustion by allowing infinite variation within fixed parameters. Islamic forms — calligraphy, mosque architecture — are imported and adapted, not exhausted. The residue is minimal: meaning is refreshed through performance, not depleted through repetition.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: Mande cosmology blends indigenous and Islamic elements. The creator god (Maa Ngala or variants) stands behind a world animated by spiritual forces (nyama) concentrated in certain objects, places, and persons. Islam provides the framework of submission to Allah, prayer, almsgiving, and pilgrimage. The two coexist: most Mande are Muslim, but local spirits, ancestor veneration, and divination persist. Existential outlook accepts divine will while seeking to navigate spiritual forces through proper conduct and ritual.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: Islamic ritual — the five daily prayers, Ramadan fasting, Friday mosque attendance — structures pious life in urban centers and among committed Muslims. Alongside it, initiation societies (Komo, Kore, Poro in southern reaches) conduct secret rituals, sacrifices, and spirit mediation. Divination (geomancy, consultation of spirits) guides major decisions. The sacred is enacted daily in household prayer and annually in communal festivals.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: The ulama of Timbuktu and Djenne hold doctrinal authority in Islamic matters; their fatwas guide conduct and commerce. The mansa patronizes mosques and scholars but does not control doctrine. Indigenous religious authority rests with lineage heads, diviners, and initiation society elders — decentralized and localized. No single institution monopolizes the sacred.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: Islam spreads along trade routes: merchants, scholars, and clerics carry the faith into new communities. Conversion is often superficial at first, with Islamic practice layered over indigenous belief. Full displacement of local religion occurs only in urban centers and among scholarly lineages. The balance tips toward Islam over the window but does not complete the transition.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: No disenchantment occurs; the sacred saturates Mande life. The residue is not doubt but syncretism — the negotiation between Islamic orthodoxy and indigenous practice, a tension managed through compartmentalization and selective observance. The cosmological frame holds; the spirits remain real, Allah is great, and the ancestors watch.

docs.title: 130,000 BCE – 60,000 BCE — Middle Stone Age Occupation of the Sahel
docs.text: Summary: A static snapshot of sparse, mobile human populations occupying the West African Sahel during the Middle Stone Age, when wetter climatic phases permitted seasonal exploitation of lakeside and riverine environments across what is now the southern Sahara and northern savanna; climate oscillation between humid and arid phases serves as the binding constraint, opening and closing habitable corridors and concentrating all human presence around water sources during interglacial wet intervals.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: The Sahel forms a transitional belt between the Sahara to the north and the Guinea forest to the south, stretching from the Senegal valley through the Niger Bend to the Chad Basin; terrain consists of flat sandy plains, laterite plateaus, and incised river valleys that channel movement and concentrate settlement near water; the Niger, Senegal, and paleo-Chad drainage systems provide the principal corridors, while intervening sand seas and rocky plateaus impose friction on cross-country travel that confines mobility to known routes along seasonal watercourses.

Climate Regime & Volatility: During interglacial phases, including the Last Interglacial (~130,000–115,000 BP), the monsoon belt shifted northward, bringing summer rains deep into the Sahara and transforming portions of the desert into savanna with lakes and wetlands; these humid intervals alternated with arid phases when the monsoon retreated southward and the Sahara expanded, pushing habitable zones toward the Niger and Chad basins; within the snapshot window, orbital forcing drove multi-millennial oscillations that repeatedly opened and closed northern territories to human occupation.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: Principal hazards include drought during arid phases, seasonal flooding along major rivers during wet phases, and exposure to intense dry-season heat and dust; catastrophic risk is low (no significant seismic or volcanic activity), but chronic drought during arid intervals poses the primary threat, forcing population retreat or local extinction when wet refugia contract.

Resource & Energy Endowment: During humid phases, lakeside and riverine environments provide fish, hippopotamus, crocodile, and aquatic plants, while adjacent grasslands support large herbivores (elephant, giraffe, antelope, and extinct megafauna); lithic raw materials (quartzite, chert, silcrete) available in outcrops and gravel beds along rivers; firewood abundant in wooded savanna; during arid phases, resources contract severely and only perennial water sources remain viable.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Human population densities are so low and technology so simple that anthropogenic waste is negligible; organic refuse decomposes rapidly in the tropical heat; stone tool debitage accumulates at favored sites but poses no environmental burden; the sink is effectively unlimited relative to the load.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: Endemic tropical diseases include malaria (Plasmodium falciparum) in wetter zones, waterborne parasites, and gastrointestinal infections; mortality baseline is high by modern standards but comparable to other Middle Stone Age populations; infant and child mortality particularly severe; life expectancy at birth probably under thirty years.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: Diet is broad-spectrum: fish, shellfish, game, tubers, seeds, and seasonal fruits during wet phases; nutritional adequacy depends on access to water and game; during arid contractions, nutritional stress likely increases, reflected in skeletal indicators where remains survive; body size and robusticity typical of archaic Homo sapiens or early anatomically modern humans.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Healing capacity limited to direct wound care, herbal remedies transmitted orally, and communal support within small bands; no evidence of specialized medical practice; recovery from serious injury or illness depends on kin support and mobility; the severely injured or chronically ill are a drag on mobile bands and likely experience elevated mortality.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Pair-bonding and kin-based reproductive cooperation presumed; fertility limited by nutritional status and disease; birth spacing probably wide due to extended lactation and high infant mortality; no evidence of complex mating systems, but oral coordination of kinship and alliance is necessary for exogamy between bands.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Population density extremely low—perhaps one person per 10–100 square kilometers during favorable phases; total regional population may number in the low thousands at best; during arid phases, populations contract to refugia around perennial water, potentially dropping to a few hundred individuals; replacement ratios are barely positive, with high mortality offset by high fertility within surviving bands.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: Dependency load minimal: few survive to old age, and band mobility limits the viability of carrying infirm dependents; orphaned children absorbed into kin networks or lost; the residue of dependency is light because the demographic pyramid is sharply truncated at both ends.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: Economy is immediate-return foraging: daily hunting, fishing, and gathering supply food without significant storage; during wet phases, lakeside camps exploit fish and aquatic resources intensively, while dry-season camps shift to game hunting and plant collection; the provisioning floor rises and falls with water availability and game density.

Energy Capture & Conversion: Energy capture relies entirely on human muscle and controlled fire; fire provides cooking, warmth, light, and protection from predators; no animal traction or mechanical power; the per-capita work ceiling is set by human endurance and caloric intake, limiting surplus generation to near zero.

Labor Organization & Coercion: Labor is organized within kin bands, probably numbering 20–50 individuals; division of labor by age and sex (hunting by adult males, gathering by females and mixed groups, childcare communal); no coerced labor, slavery, or tribute; all coordination oral and relational.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Surplus capacity is negligible: food spoils quickly, mobility discourages accumulation, and group size limits collective output; during favorable periods, caloric intake may exceed immediate needs briefly, but no mechanism exists for long-term storage or redistribution beyond the band.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: No durable storage technology; reserves consist of body fat and knowledge of alternative foraging sites; buffering against shortage depends on mobility—moving to better-watered areas—and on reciprocal sharing within and between bands, mediated orally.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: Exchange limited to inter-band gifting of lithic raw materials, ochre, and possibly mates; no formal markets or long-distance trade networks; logistics governed by foot travel and seasonal camp relocation; external dependence is low because bands are self-sufficient, but isolation exposes them to local resource failures.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: No currency or accounting; value stored in social obligations and reciprocal debts remembered orally; deferred exchange operates through kinship and alliance obligations—gifts given now create claims redeemable later through remembered oral agreements.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: No extraction apparatus: all production is consumed or shared within the band; redistribution occurs through immediate sharing of large kills and communal access to gathered foods; no taxation, tribute, or rent.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Personal property limited to tools, ornaments, and clothing; no significant wealth differentiation; asset defense consists of keeping possessions on one's person during mobility; theft is rare because group size and oral reputation constrain defection.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Organic waste discarded at camp peripheries and rapidly decomposed; stone debitage left in place; no accumulation of financial or accounting detritus; waste residue negligible.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Kinship is the primary social structure: bilateral or unilineal descent traced orally, defining marriage partners, alliance networks, and inheritance of status and knowledge; inheritance is minimal because material property is limited; oral genealogies preserve kin memory across generations.

Association & Mutual Aid: Bands are the sole associational unit: membership fluid, based on kinship and affinal ties; mutual aid obligatory within the band, including food sharing, cooperative childcare, and collective defense; inter-band relations maintained through marriage exchange and periodic aggregation at resource-rich locations.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: Leisure time significant in immediate-return economies: storytelling, singing, dancing, and play occupy evening hours around fires; sociability reinforces cohesion and transmits oral tradition; children learn through imitation and play.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: Stratification minimal: age and skill confer respect, but no hereditary hierarchy; status accrues to successful hunters and knowledgeable elders; no caste, class, or ethnic stratification beyond band identity; factional conflict limited by band fission—dissenters simply leave.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: No formal administration: decisions made by consensus or deference to respected elders; no bureaucracy, record-keeping, or diplomatic apparatus; oral deliberation suffices for band-scale coordination; institutional integrity depends on personal authority and oral reputation.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: No organized military or police; violence is interpersonal, regulated by kinship obligations and oral norms; weaponry consists of hunting tools (spears, possibly atlatls) that double as weapons; conflict between bands is occasional and limited, resolved by avoidance, negotiation, or skirmish rather than organized warfare.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: Friction is discharged through band fission, mobility, and oral mediation; grievances are aired in communal discussion; the excluded are rare (band membership is inclusive for kin), and disorder is minimal at this scale; sclerosis does not occur because institutions are informal and regenerate with each generation through oral transmission.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: Leadership is situational: the best hunter leads the hunt, the elder with most knowledge leads discussions; no permanent chiefs or hereditary authority; personal charisma and demonstrated competence confer temporary influence, ratified through oral acknowledgment.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: Allegiance flows from kinship and reciprocity, not abstract legitimacy; leaders are obeyed because they are respected kin, not because they hold office; erosion of legitimacy occurs when leaders fail to deliver and lose oral reputation.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: Collective will is ad hoc: mobilization occurs for hunts, camp moves, and defense, organized orally; no standing political contest or succession struggle because leadership is informal and revocable; resolve is high when survival is at stake, diffuse otherwise.

External Relations & Posture: Relations with other bands range from alliance (through marriage exchange and joint foraging) to avoidance or occasional conflict over resources; no diplomatic apparatus; posture is defensive—bands prefer to move away from conflict rather than fight; leverage is minimal because bands are self-sufficient and mobile.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: Prevailing mood is probably cautious optimism during favorable phases, anxiety during drought; trust is high within bands (tight kinship), lower toward strangers; behavioral temper is cooperative within the group, wary toward outsiders; interpersonal conflict is managed through oral mediation and social pressure.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: Disaffection is rare within small, kin-based groups; when it arises, individuals or families leave and join other bands; apathy is limited by the survival imperative; spent will (exhaustion, despair) may occur during prolonged drought, contributing to band dissolution or extinction.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Communication is entirely oral and gestural; language is grammatically complex, permitting discussion of absent referents, past events, and hypothetical futures; all band members share the same linguistic code; mutual intelligibility is high within the band, uncertain between bands speaking different dialects or languages.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Channels are face-to-face speech and song; transmission velocity is limited to the speed of walking messengers or chance encounter; information spreads slowly across bands, rapidly within them; no written or symbolic channels.

Record, Storage & Persistence: All record is held in living memory; oral tradition preserves knowledge of territory, kin relations, resource locations, and technical skills; persistence depends on intergenerational transmission through storytelling and apprenticeship; memory loss occurs when elders die before transmitting knowledge.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: Discourse is regulated by oral custom: certain topics may be restricted by age, gender, or initiation status; censorship is informal, enforced by social disapproval; framing of events occurs through oral narrative, shaped by the storyteller's perspective and communal validation.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: Reception is communal: stories are heard around fires, with audience participation; amplification occurs through retelling; attention is governed by survival relevance—knowledge of food sources and dangers spreads fastest; entertainment value also drives amplification.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: Oral transmission is prone to drift: each retelling introduces variation; verification depends on communal memory and cross-checking among elders; noise is low (no competing media), but signal degradation over generations is inherent to oral culture.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Morality is embedded in kinship obligations: fairness means sharing with kin, justice means reciprocity and retaliation; harm to kin is the paradigmatic wrong; strangers fall outside the moral circle or occupy an ambiguous status; all moral reasoning is oral and contextual.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: No written law; norms are oral custom: rules governing marriage, food sharing, violence, and resource access transmitted through example and oral instruction; change occurs slowly through accumulated precedent and oral consensus.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: Disputes are adjudicated through oral deliberation among elders and respected kin; liability is personal and familial; sanctions include gossip, shaming, ostracism, and, in extreme cases, expulsion or violence; no formal courts or codified penalties.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Rights are relational: band members have claims on food, protection, and mates by virtue of kinship; compliance burden is light because norms are internalized through upbringing and oral reinforcement; predictability is high within the band, uncertain in inter-band relations.
