Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: Adjudication conducted by elders and lineage heads in council; disputes resolved through mediation seeking consensus; liability determined by witness testimony and oath; sanctions range from compensation to exile to death; in emerging proto-states, the ruler serves as final arbiter, judging in public audience.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Rights derive from status: free persons have protections slaves lack; women hold property rights in some systems; strangers protected by hospitality norms; compliance burden light where customary rules are internalized — external enforcement needed mainly for disputes and deviance.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: Impunity exists for the powerful: dominant lineages can raid weaker groups for slaves with no external sanction; internal wrongs may go unredressed when perpetrators are too powerful to confront; vendetta and feud constitute rough justice where formal adjudication fails; the enslaved have no recognized standing to seek redress.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: Inquiry remains embedded in practical knowledge and cosmological understanding; no differentiated natural philosophy — causation attributed to spirits, ancestors, and powers manipulable through ritual; empirical observation of seasons, soils, and materials supports agriculture and metallurgy without theoretical elaboration; all held orally.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Technical knowledge is highly developed within craft traditions: iron smelting and smithing, gold extraction, pottery, weaving, leatherwork, construction, and animal husbandry all embody accumulated expertise transmitted through apprenticeship; the camel and its management represent imported technique adapted to local conditions.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: Education occurs entirely through oral transmission: children learn from parents and kin; specialized skills pass through apprenticeship; initiatory societies transmit restricted knowledge; griots train successors in genealogy and performance; no writing, no schools — the knowledge stock exists only in living minds.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: Knowledge decays when transmission fails: techniques lost if practitioners die without apprentices; genealogies forgotten if griot lineages end; yet the oral tradition proves remarkably durable where institutionalized through griots and initiatory societies — loss occurs at the margins rather than catastrophically.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: Foundational identity rests on origin narratives linking lineages to founding ancestors and specific territories; ethnic identities (Soninke, Mande, Songhai) crystallize around shared language, origin claims, and distinctive practices; memory of migration from the desiccating Sahara persists in some traditions; the land and its spirits ground collective identity.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: Ruling lineages legitimate their position through superior descent from founding ancestors, often with supernatural associations; successful military and commercial leadership reinforces claims; griots produce and perform legitimating narratives that celebrate patrons and their genealogies; no universalist ideology — legitimacy remains particularist and genealogical.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: Artistic expression flourishes in oral performance (epic, praise poetry, song), music (drums, stringed instruments, voice), and visual arts (terracotta, metalwork, textiles, architecture); material culture reflects trade connections — imported goods mark elite status; architectural traditions develop in mud-brick construction; body decoration and dress signal identity and status.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: Forms remain vital as oral tradition adapts to changing circumstances; the arrival of new goods, the rise of new lineages, and the expansion of trade provide new material for cultural expression; no exhaustion visible — the culture is expansive and absorptive within the window.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: Cosmology posits a world animated by spirits inhabiting natural features, ancestors who intervene in descendants' lives, and a high god who remains distant; human fortune depends on maintaining proper relations with spirits and ancestors through sacrifice and ritual; divination reveals hidden causes and guides action.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: Ritual pervades daily life: sacrifices at shrines, libations to ancestors, protective amulets, initiatory rites marking life transitions; seasonal ceremonies ensure agricultural fertility; healing rituals address illness attributed to spiritual causes; specialists (priests, diviners, healers) conduct elaborate rites.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: Religious authority dispersed among lineage heads (who maintain ancestor shrines), earth priests (who propitiate land spirits), initiatory societies (which guard restricted knowledge), and individual specialists; no centralized religious institution — authority remains local and specialized.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: Trans-Saharan contact brings first awareness of Islam through Berber and Arab traders, though conversion remains minimal within the window; traditional religion dominates; syncretism has not yet begun in earnest — the spiritual landscape remains indigenous, though the seeds of future transformation are present at trade nodes.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: No disenchantment occurs — the spiritual worldview remains intact and functional, providing meaning and explanation; the sacred pervades experience; where rituals fail, the response is to perform different rituals rather than to doubt the spiritual framework; existential security rests on maintained spiritual relations.

docs.title: Oral Stage in The Yellow and Yangtze River Basins — 50,000 BCE – 1,200 BCE
- 50,000 BCE – 25,000 BCE — Upper Paleolithic Settlement of East Asia
- 25,000 BCE – 15,000 BCE — Last Glacial Maximum and Refugia
- 15,000 BCE – 9,000 BCE — Terminal Pleistocene and Early Pottery
- 9,000 BCE – 6,500 BCE — Neolithic Revolution and Rice Domestication
- 9,000 BCE – 6,000 BCE — Millet Domestication and Yellow River Neolithic
- 6,500 BCE – 5,000 BCE — Early Yangshao and Hemudu Cultures
- 5,000 BCE – 3,500 BCE — Middle Neolithic Regional Diversification
- 3,500 BCE – 2,500 BCE — Late Neolithic Complexity and Liangzhu
- 2,500 BCE – 2,000 BCE — Longshan Horizon and Proto-Urban Development
- 2,000 BCE – 1,700 BCE — Erlitou and the Emergence of Bronze Age Polity
- 1,700 BCE – 1,500 BCE — Early Shang and Erligang Expansion
- 1,500 BCE – 1,300 BCE — Middle Shang and Anyang Foundation
- 1,300 BCE – 1,200 BCE — Late Shang Oracle Bone Florescence and Oral Threshold
1,700 BCE – 1,500 BCE — Early Shang and Erligang Expansion
docs.text: Summary: The Erligang phase marks the Shang polity's explosive territorial and economic expansion from its center at Zhengzhou, extending bronze-casting networks, elite material culture, and political influence across much of the Yellow and Yangtze River basins; the single most causal factor is the monopolized bronze production system, which fused ritual authority with economic control and enabled unprecedented coordination of labor, tribute, and long-distance exchange—all still governed through oral command, memory, and face-to-face delegation rather than written record.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: The Erligang heartland occupies the middle Yellow River valley where the Yiluo and Ying rivers meet loess uplands—fertile, defensible, and positioned at the junction of north-south and east-west transit corridors; expansion follows river routes and accessible passes, with outposts reaching the middle Yangtze (Panlongcheng), Shandong, and the Wei River valley, though mountain barriers and monsoon-swollen rivers impose seasonal friction on movement and supply.

Climate Regime & Volatility: The late Holocene climate remains warm and humid relative to later periods, with reliable monsoon rainfall supporting millet in the north and rice in the south; interannual variability is moderate, though flood events periodically disrupt lowland agriculture, and drought can stress marginal zones—conditions that reward centralized storage and redistribution but do not yet impose catastrophic strain.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: The Yellow River's tendency to shift course and flood the North China Plain represents the primary hazard, with earthquake risk along the Wei River graben; Erligang settlements on elevated ground or terraces buffer against flood damage, but outlying populations remain exposed, and no engineered flood control exists beyond local dikes and channel management.

Resource & Energy Endowment: Copper and tin ores are not locally abundant in the Zhengzhou region, requiring long-distance acquisition from sources in the Yangtze basin, the Zhongtiao Mountains, and possibly further afield; this scarcity makes bronze a state-controlled commodity and drives the expansion of the exchange network, while timber, clay, and agricultural land remain locally sufficient.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Bronze smelting and casting generate slag, charcoal ash, and smoke, concentrated at workshop zones near the capital; the sink is not yet saturated, and waste disposal consists of local dumping without long-range environmental feedback—the residue is negligible at this scale, absorbed into the surrounding landscape.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: Endemic diseases include intestinal parasites, malaria in southern outposts, and respiratory infections in crowded workshop quarters; infant and child mortality remain high, though no evidence of catastrophic epidemic appears in the archaeological record for this phase—mortality is chronic rather than acute, and the population is growing.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: Millet, rice, pigs, cattle, and sheep provide a diversified diet for elites, while commoners rely on grain porridge supplemented by legumes and occasional meat; skeletal evidence suggests moderate nutritional stress among laborers, with elite individuals exhibiting better stature and fewer deficiency markers.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Healing relies on herbal remedies, bone-setting, and ritual intervention transmitted orally through specialist lineages; no institutional medicine exists, and wound treatment remains rudimentary—capacity is household-level, with elite access to diviners and specialists improving outcomes at the top of the hierarchy.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Marriage patterns involve lineage-based alliances consolidating political ties, with polygyny practiced among elites; fertility is sufficient for population growth, though high child mortality limits effective family size, and labor demands for bronze production and construction may intensify during peak work seasons.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Population at Zhengzhou may reach 30,000–50,000, with satellite centers and villages adding tens of thousands more across the network; density is highest around the capital and regional centers, tapering into agricultural hinterlands—the overall trajectory is expansionary, with new settlements established in the Yangtze region.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: The young dominate the population structure; elderly and infirm are supported within lineage households, and the productive cohort absorbs the dependent load without visible strain—no evidence of demographic crisis or unmanageable dependency accumulation.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: Millet agriculture in the north and rice in the southern outposts provide the caloric base, supplemented by livestock, fishing, and gathered foods; household granaries and state-controlled reserves buffer against local shortfalls, keeping the population above subsistence margin in normal years.

Energy Capture & Conversion: Human and animal muscle provide nearly all productive power; charcoal fuels bronze smelting, and fire heats kilns for pottery—the energy ceiling is low but sufficient for the scale of production, and deforestation pressure around major centers may already require timber procurement from greater distances.

Labor Organization & Coercion: Corvée labor mobilizes commoners for construction, bronze casting, and agricultural intensification under elite direction; specialists in bronze metallurgy occupy a privileged intermediate status, while unfree laborers (war captives, debt bondsmen) perform the most dangerous foundry and mining work—coercion is embedded in the system, enforced through oral command and physical supervision.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Bronze production reaches unprecedented scale, with Zhengzhou workshops casting ritual vessels, weapons, and tools for elite distribution; agricultural surplus supports the non-farming population of artisans, soldiers, and administrators—capacity is expanding, though dependent on continuous ore supply and labor mobilization.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: Palatial granaries and bronze stockpiles serve as state reserves, buffering against harvest failure and ensuring materials for ritual and warfare; elite households maintain their own stores—reserve depth is adequate for short-term shocks but would strain under prolonged disruption of tribute flows.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: Long-distance exchange networks move copper, tin, and lead ores from southern and western sources to the capital, returning bronze goods, prestige items, and probably grain or livestock; Panlongcheng on the Yangtze functions as a colonial outpost securing southern resources—logistics rely on river transport and overland portage, with seasonal constraints.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: Bronze vessels and jade serve as wealth stores and prestige markers, circulating through elite exchange and burial; no coinage exists, and value transfer occurs through gift-giving, tribute, and reciprocal obligation—all recorded in memory and oral agreement rather than written ledger.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: Tribute flows from dependent communities to the capital in grain, labor, and raw materials; elites redistribute bronze goods, feasts, and protection downward, binding subordinates through patronage—the extraction system is oral and personal, enforced through presence and reputation rather than written record.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Wealth concentrates sharply at the top, with elite burials containing bronze vessels, jade, and sacrificial victims while commoners receive simple interments; elites defend holdings through lineage solidarity, fortified compounds, and the coercive apparatus—concentration is increasing as the bronze monopoly tightens.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Slag heaps, broken molds, and foundry debris accumulate at workshop sites; organic waste is composted or discarded locally—no significant waste crisis, and the material residue is absorbed without systemic strain.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Patrilineal descent organizes elite lineages, with inheritance passing through the male line and reinforced by ancestral veneration; marriage alliances consolidate inter-lineage ties, and the royal clan sits atop a hierarchy of aristocratic lineages—kinship is the scaffolding of political authority, transmitted orally through genealogical recitation.

Association & Mutual Aid: Lineage and village solidarities provide mutual aid below the state level; craft guilds or proto-guilds organize bronze workers, potters, and other specialists—informal networks thicken around the capital, while outlying communities maintain kin-based reciprocity as their primary safety net.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: Elite feasting, music, and ritual gatherings reinforce social bonds and display status; common people participate in seasonal festivals, communal labor celebrations, and local rites—sociability is face-to-face and oral, with feasts serving as occasions for alliance renewal and dispute resolution.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: A sharp hierarchy separates the royal house, aristocratic lineages, commoners, and unfree laborers; status is marked by access to bronze, jade, chariots, and sacrificial animals—boundaries are hardening as the bronze monopoly consolidates elite privilege, though mobility through military or craft achievement remains possible.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: Administration operates through oral delegation, with royal kinsmen and trusted retainers governing outlying centers; no bureaucratic apparatus or written record exists—capacity depends on personal loyalty, memory, and the physical presence of representatives, limiting the span of effective control.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: The military consists of chariot-borne aristocrats, infantry levies, and possibly specialized warriors; bronze weapons (ge dagger-axes, spears, arrowheads) equip the elite, while commoners carry stone or bone arms—fortifications at Zhengzhou include rammed-earth walls enclosing the palace zone, and the apparatus is sufficient to project power across the network.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: Friction is managed through lineage mediation, ritual, and the patron-client bond; outlying populations may resist tribute demands, and war captives bear the cost of coercive labor—no evidence of widespread rebellion, but the residue of grievance among subordinate groups and unfree laborers accumulates beneath the surface.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: Royal authority is personal and charismatic, reinforced by monopoly over divination, bronze, and ancestral rites; the king and his kinsmen command through presence, reputation, and the spoken word—leadership succession is contested among royal lineages, and personal authority must be continuously demonstrated.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: Legitimacy rests on ancestral sanction, ritual efficacy, and the ability to provide protection and redistribution; allegiance is strongest among kin and clients who benefit directly, attenuating with distance—lived belief in the ruler's right to command is reinforced by the spectacle of bronze ritual and successful expansion.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: The ruling elite displays strong collective will for expansion, conquest, and resource acquisition; internal factional competition is managed through ritual and redistribution—resolve is high during the expansionary phase, with succession disputes the primary source of potential fracture.

External Relations & Posture: The Shang project power outward through colonial outposts, punitive expeditions, and prestige exchange; neighboring polities are subordinated, absorbed, or held at arm's length as tribute payers—rivalry with unconquered groups (labeled "fang" enemies in later texts) structures external relations, and the posture is assertive and acquisitive.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: Confidence and expansionary momentum characterize the elite mood; commoners experience the system as demanding but orderly, with loyalty reinforced by ritual participation and redistribution—trust extends within lineage and locality, narrowing toward outsiders and subordinate groups.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: Disaffection is latent among subordinate populations and unfree laborers, but overt resistance is suppressed; elite confidence remains high—no exhaustion of will is visible, though the demands of expansion and production place cumulative strain on the system.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Spoken language—an ancestor of later Sinitic tongues—is the sole medium of coordination; elite registers and ritual formulae exist alongside vernacular speech, and mutual intelligibility extends across the core Shang territory, fragmenting at the periphery where non-Sinitic populations are encountered.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Messages travel by runner, chariot, or boat, with royal commands dispatched through trusted agents who memorize and recite instructions; speed is limited by terrain and season—urgent news can cross the network in days or weeks, but detailed coordination requires physical presence.

Record, Storage & Persistence: No writing system operates for administrative or archival purposes; proto-writing marks on pottery may indicate ownership or workshop identity but do not constitute script—all institutional memory resides in trained human minds, transmitted through oral recitation, genealogy, and ritual formula.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: Ritual speech, ancestral invocation, and royal proclamation frame public discourse; taboos govern the naming of ancestors and sacred matters—discourse norms are enforced through social sanction and the authority of ritual specialists, not written code.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: Messages are received face-to-face in assemblies, feasts, and ritual gatherings; amplification occurs through repetition, rumor, and the prestige of the speaker—attention is concentrated on the king and his agents, whose words carry binding force.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: Memory degradation and transmission error accumulate over distance and time; oral checks (repetition, genealogical cross-reference, ritual formula) partially correct drift—noise increases at the network's edges, and no external record exists to verify or correct.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Justice is conceived in terms of reciprocity, ancestral duty, and hierarchical obligation; wrongs against kin or patron demand redress, and violation of ritual propriety invites supernatural sanction—the moral order is embedded in oral tradition and reinforced through divination.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: No written law exists; binding norms are transmitted orally through customary practice, royal decree (spoken and remembered), and lineage precedent—regulation evolves through case-by-case adjudication and the memory of elders.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: Disputes are resolved by lineage heads, local elders, or royal agents; divination may determine guilt or innocence in uncertain cases—sanctions include compensation, corporal punishment, enslavement, or death, applied according to status and offense.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Rights inhere in lineage membership and status rather than individual personhood; commoners owe labor and tribute, receiving protection and subsistence in return—compliance is enforced through social pressure, patron authority, and coercive sanction.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: Elites enjoy broad impunity for wrongs against commoners and captives; justice is more reliably delivered within kin groups than across status lines—the residue of unredressed grievance accumulates among the subordinate and unfree, latent but unspoken.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: Inquiry is embedded in divination practice, which interprets cracks in heated bones to discern ancestral and spiritual will; no separation of empirical from ritual knowledge exists—the paradigm is cosmological, with ancestors and spirits as active agents in worldly affairs.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Metallurgical technique reaches high sophistication, with piece-mold casting producing complex bronze vessels and weapons; potters, jade workers, and builders apply refined craft methods transmitted orally and through apprenticeship—technique is practical and cumulative, not theorized.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: Skill transmission occurs within lineages and craft groups through oral instruction and hands-on training; elite children learn ritual, genealogy, and governance from elders—literacy is absent, and the knowledge stock resides entirely in human memory and practice.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: Techniques lost through lineage extinction or disrupted apprenticeship cannot be recovered; no written record preserves method—decay is invisible but real, and the bronze network's integrity depends on continuous transmission within specialist communities.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: Identity centers on descent from founding ancestors, whose deeds are recited in ritual and feast; the Shang conceive themselves as the favored people of their high god and ancestors—memory is genealogical, reaching back through oral chains to legendary founders.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: The ruling house justifies its authority through ancestral mandate, ritual efficacy, and military success; the narrative is performed in bronze ritual, sacrifice, and public ceremony—legitimacy is spoken, sung, and enacted, not written.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: Bronze vessels display taotie masks, zoomorphic motifs, and intricate surface patterns encoding cosmological meaning; jade, ceramics, and architecture follow standardized elite styles—material culture marks status, lineage, and participation in the Shang ritual order.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: Forms remain vital and innovative, with bronze styles evolving and regional variants incorporated—no exhaustion is visible; the cultural idiom is expanding and confident, absorbing influences from incorporated territories.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: The cosmos is populated by ancestors, nature spirits, and a high god (Di or Shangdi) who intervenes in human affairs; the living owe offerings to the dead, and fortune depends on maintaining ancestral favor—the outlook is pious and anxious, oriented toward securing supernatural support.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: Divination (scapulimancy and plastromancy) is the central ritual technology, with specialists heating animal bones and turtle shells to produce cracks read as yes-no answers; animal and human sacrifice accompanies major rites—devotion is collective, performative, and costly.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: The royal house controls access to the ancestors and the high god; divination specialists serve the king, and lineage heads conduct ancestral rites for their own dead—authority is centralized but not yet codified, with orthodoxy maintained through oral tradition and royal oversight.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: Shang spiritual practices spread with expansion, overlaying or absorbing local cults; peripheral peoples adopt Shang ritual goods and possibly beliefs—the dominant cosmology is extending, though local spirits and practices persist beneath the Shang overlay.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: No disenchantment is visible; the sacred remains potent and central to political authority—ritual efficacy is believed, and the residue of spiritual doubt is undetectable in the material or textual record.

docs.title: 6,500 BCE – 5,000 BCE — Early Yangshao and Hemudu Cultures
docs.text: Summary: A snapshot of the two principal regional Neolithic cultures flourishing in the Yellow and Yangtze basins during the sixth millennium BCE—Yangshao in the middle Yellow River loess plateau with its painted pottery and millet agriculture, and Hemudu in the lower Yangtze wetlands with its pile dwellings, rice paddies, and lacquerware—representing parallel but distinct adaptations to northern dry-farming and southern wet-rice environments, both organized entirely through oral tradition without writing; the single most causal factor is the divergent ecological adaptation, as millet-based Yangshao and rice-based Hemudu develop different settlement patterns, material cultures, and social organizations shaped by their contrasting environments.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: The Yangshao heartland occupies the middle Yellow River region where the loess plateau meets the North China Plain, characterized by deeply dissected loess hills, river terraces suitable for settlement, and friable soils ideal for millet cultivation without heavy tillage; spatial friction is moderate, as river valleys channel movement while hills impede cross-country travel. The Hemudu zone lies in the lower Yangtze delta, a flat, waterlogged landscape of lakes, marshes, and seasonally flooded plains; movement here favors watercraft along channels and lakes, with terrestrial travel impeded by wetlands. The two culture zones are separated by several hundred kilometers of hill country and the Huai River basin, limiting direct contact.

Climate Regime & Volatility: The Holocene Climatic Optimum prevails, bringing warmer and wetter conditions than today across both regions. The Yangshao zone experiences a semi-arid continental climate with hot summers, cold winters, and monsoon-concentrated rainfall; interannual variability is significant, with drought a recurring threat. The Hemudu zone has a subtropical monsoon climate with mild winters, hot humid summers, and abundant rainfall; flooding rather than drought poses the greater risk. Both regions are climatically favorable for their respective crops.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: In the Yangshao region, Yellow River flooding and loess erosion constitute the primary hazards; drought threatens millet harvests in dry years. In the Hemudu region, seasonal flooding is endemic and expected, but extreme flood events can destroy crops and settlements; typhoons occasionally reach the coastal zone. Neither region faces significant seismic or volcanic hazard during this period.

Resource & Energy Endowment: Yangshao communities draw on loess soils for agriculture, river water for irrigation and domestic use, timber from mixed forests for construction and fuel, and stone from piedmont zones for tools. Hemudu communities exploit the rich aquatic resources of the delta—fish, shellfish, waterfowl—alongside wetland plants and timber, with clay for pottery and water for rice paddies abundantly available. Neither region exploits metals; stone, bone, and wood supply tool materials.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Population densities remain low enough that anthropogenic waste places no significant pressure on either environment; organic refuse decomposes or is recycled into fields; fire clearance regenerates within years; no accumulating environmental degradation is evident.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: Sedentary village life and pig domestication increase potential pathogen exposure compared to mobile foraging, but low population density limits epidemic transmission. Hemudu's wetland environment likely carries higher parasitic and waterborne disease loads than the drier Yangshao zone. Childhood mortality remains high in both cultures from nutritional stress and infectious disease; adult life expectancy at maturity probably reaches the mid-thirties to early forties.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: Yangshao populations subsist primarily on millet supplemented by pig, dog, wild game, fish, and gathered plants; dietary breadth narrows compared to foraging but caloric security improves. Hemudu populations rely on rice as the staple, with a protein-rich diet from abundant aquatic resources; nutritional status is likely comparable or slightly superior to Yangshao given the richer local fauna. Skeletal evidence from comparable populations shows moderate stature and occasional signs of nutritional stress.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Healing knowledge in both cultures is oral and kinship-transmitted, comprising herbal remedies, wound treatment, and midwifery; settlement permanence allows sustained care of the ill; no institutional medical capacity exists.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: In both cultures, pair-bonding occurs within community-regulated frameworks, with exogamy rules articulated through oral kinship reckonings. Sedentism and supplementary weaning foods permit shorter birth intervals than mobile foraging; fertility is not artificially suppressed; population growth is gradual.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Yangshao villages range from small hamlets to communities of several hundred, such as Banpo and Jiangzhai, with populations of 100–500. Hemudu settlements are somewhat smaller, constrained by the wetland environment. Birth rates exceed death rates in both zones, producing slow population growth and gradual expansion into new territories over the millennium.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: Dependents—children, elderly, and infirm—are supported within household and lineage structures; surplus grain storage buffers non-productive members; the dependency load does not yet strain carrying capacity in either culture.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: Yangshao subsistence centers on foxtail and broomcorn millet cultivation, supplemented by pig and dog husbandry, hunting (deer, small mammals), fishing, and gathering (nuts, fruits, tubers); households are largely autarkic. Hemudu subsistence centers on wet-rice cultivation in managed paddies, with extensive exploitation of aquatic fauna (fish, turtle, crocodile), waterfowl, wild boar, deer, and gathered plants including acorns and water chestnuts. Both cultures have raised the provisioning floor above foraging levels through agriculture.

Energy Capture & Conversion: Human muscle power and fire constitute the energy portfolio in both cultures; no draft animals are used; canoes and rafts extend movement capacity in the Hemudu zone. The caloric return from rice cultivation may slightly exceed millet, but both operate near similar per-capita energy ceilings.

Labor Organization & Coercion: Labor is organized through the household and extended kin group in both cultures; gendered division of labor assigns men to hunting, fishing, land clearance, and heavy construction while women tend crops, process grain, produce pottery, and weave textiles. No coerced labor or slavery is evident; reciprocal labor exchange among households occurs for major tasks.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Both cultures produce storable surplus in good years—dried millet in Yangshao, dried rice in Hemudu—enabling buffering against crop failure and supporting gradual population growth; surplus is not yet large enough to support significant non-food-producing specialization, though part-time craft production (pottery, weaving, jade working at Hemudu) is emerging.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: Yangshao communities store grain in semi-subterranean pits and pottery vessels. Hemudu communities store rice in raised granaries suited to the damp environment, evidenced by pile-dwelling architecture. Both systems buffer single-year failures; multi-year drought or flood sequences would strain reserves.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: Exchange is primarily local and reciprocal in both cultures, embedded in kinship and ceremonial gifting. Some long-distance movement of exotic materials—shells, jade, unusual stone—indicates intermittent contact networks, but no regular markets or trade routes exist. Hemudu's waterways facilitate canoe-borne exchange within the delta region.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: No medium of exchange exists; value is stored in durable goods (pottery, jade ornaments) and deferred through reciprocal obligations tracked orally; credit operates through kinship debt and social memory.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: No institutionalized surplus extraction occurs; redistribution operates through kinship sharing, feasting, and ritual obligations; no political authority appropriates household production.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Material wealth differentiation is minimal in both cultures; burial goods show little systematic stratification, though some individuals are interred with more pottery or ornaments than others; land is likely held by lineage or village; no fortifications exist.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Agricultural waste is burned, composted, or used as fuel; organic refuse accumulates in middens; pottery sherds and broken tools enter settlement deposits; no problematic waste accumulation occurs.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Both cultures are organized through kinship, probably patrilineal with patrilocal residence in Yangshao and possibly matrilineal or more flexible arrangements in Hemudu, based on later regional patterns and archaeological ambiguity. Extended family households occupy multi-room structures (Yangshao) or pile dwellings (Hemudu); inheritance of cultivation rights and portable property passes within the lineage; marriage rules regulate exogamy and alliance.

Association & Mutual Aid: The village is the primary social unit in both cultures; mutual aid networks extend to neighboring villages linked by kinship and marriage; no formal institutions exist above the village level, though seasonal gatherings may bring multiple communities together for ritual or exchange.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: Seasonal festivals accompany agricultural cycles in both cultures; communal feasting, music (bone flutes, drums), and dance mark life transitions and ritual occasions; children's play and intergenerational storytelling fill non-work time; leisure is embedded in communal life.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: Society in both cultures is largely egalitarian or only mildly ranked; status varies by age, sex, personal achievement, and perhaps lineage seniority; no hereditary elites or marked class distinctions are evident in burial patterns; boundary permeability is high.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: No formal administrative apparatus exists in either culture; village affairs are managed through oral consensus among senior household heads; decisions are reached in face-to-face gatherings; no written records, bureaucracy, or formal offices; inter-village coordination is episodic.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: No specialized military organization exists; adult males form a militia for defense using weapons that double for hunting (bows, spears, axes); conflict likely occurs occasionally over resources, insult, or revenge but does not escalate to sustained warfare; no fortifications appear in this period.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: Social friction is discharged through kinship mediation, elder arbitration, and village fission when conflicts cannot be resolved; no standing disorder or institutional decay is evident in these flourishing mid-Neolithic communities.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: Leadership is informal and achieved rather than ascribed, resting on age, wisdom, hunting prowess, ritual knowledge, or personal charisma; respected elders guide decisions through persuasion; no hereditary chiefs or formal officeholders exist in either culture.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: Authority derives from kinship seniority, personal reputation, and ancestral connection; allegiance is relational rather than institutional; legitimacy is embedded in fulfilled obligations and demonstrated competence.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: Collective will mobilizes for seasonal labor, communal construction, defense, and ritual; unity depends on kinship solidarity and oral exhortation; no political will extends beyond the village cluster; inter-regional coordination does not exist.

External Relations & Posture: Relations with neighboring communities are shaped by kinship alliance, marriage exchange, and occasional reciprocal visiting; conflict over resources or personal grievance occurs but does not define intergroup relations; no external polities or powers impose on these communities; posture is defensive and localized.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: Communities in both cultures are bound by face-to-face familiarity and dense kinship ties; interpersonal trust extends to the village and marriage-linked settlements; strangers are approached cautiously; the prevailing temper is confident adaptation to established agricultural lifeways.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: The mid-Neolithic is a period of expansion and confidence in both cultures; disaffection is minimal; those who cannot integrate may depart to found new settlements; no widespread apathy or exhaustion is evident.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Spoken language is the sole medium of communication; all villagers share a common tongue, with dialectal variation increasing across distance; no writing, notation, or symbolic recording system exists in either culture; mutual intelligibility may fail between distant Yangshao and Hemudu communities.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Information travels at walking speed or, in the Hemudu zone, at canoe speed along waterways; messages pass through kinship networks, seasonal gatherings, and deliberate messengers; transmission radius is limited to a few days' travel for timely information.

Record, Storage & Persistence: All knowledge resides in human memory; genealogies, agricultural calendars, craft techniques, ritual procedures, and community histories are stored orally and transmitted through repetition, song, apprenticeship, and storytelling; persistence depends on continuous teaching; the Jiahu symbols (~6,600 BCE, slightly earlier) are isolated marks, not a writing system.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: Elders control authoritative speech; certain knowledge (ritual secrets, healing lore, lineage history) may be restricted to initiated adults; no formal censorship exists, but social norms and taboos constrain discourse.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: Audiences gather for storytelling, ritual, and communal decisions; the rarity and social weight of such occasions concentrate attention; authoritative speakers' words are repeated and remembered; amplification is personal and social.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: Small community size and face-to-face interaction minimize signal degradation within the village; oral transmission across generations introduces drift, but redundancy (multiple transmitters, social correction) limits corruption; no surveillance exists; rumor and gossip circulate freely but are checked by dense social knowledge.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Reciprocity governs moral life in both cultures—debts must be repaid, gifts returned, wrongs redressed; fairness is relational, measured by balance over time; harm to kin or community is the fundamental wrong; ancestral approval validates conduct.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: No written law exists; norms are oral custom, ancestral precedent, and communal consensus; taboos regulate food, sex, ritual, and death; rules evolve slowly through reinterpretation within oral tradition.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: Disputes are settled by elder arbitration through oral hearings; liability is collective, falling on the household or lineage of the offender; sanctions include compensation, public shaming, and exile for serious offenses; physical punishment or death may apply to grave transgressions.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Individual rights as a concept do not exist; protection and obligation derive from kinship membership; compliance burden is the weight of custom, which is stable and internalized from childhood.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: In small communities, wrongdoing is difficult to conceal; social memory is long; impunity is rare because kinship accountability is strong; unredressed wrongs may fester into feuds resolved through compensation or fission.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: Systematic inquiry is practical and embedded—experimentation with crop varieties, tool designs, construction techniques, firing temperatures for pottery; no abstract theorizing exists; explanation proceeds through narrative, analogy, and ancestral wisdom rather than empirical investigation.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Both cultures command sophisticated applied knowledge: Yangshao produces distinctive painted pottery with red and black geometric designs, ground stone tools, and semi-subterranean architecture with timber frames. Hemudu produces remarkable lacquerware (the world's earliest known), jade ornaments, sophisticated joinery in pile dwellings, and rice paddy management. All techniques are transmitted through oral instruction and hands-on apprenticeship.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: Children learn by observation and participation; skill distribution follows gender and lineage lines; the knowledge stock expands as techniques improve; literacy is absent, so all knowledge is oral; craft skills may concentrate in particular lineages.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: Techniques evolve gradually; earlier styles give way to new forms (pottery designs, tool types); knowledge lost through premature death of skilled practitioners is a constant risk; some foraging knowledge fades as agriculture dominates.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: Identity is rooted in kinship, place, and ancestry; Yangshao communities identify with their village, their lineage, and the ancestors buried in the communal cemetery; Hemudu communities similarly anchor identity in the pile-dwelling settlement and surrounding waters. Origin narratives likely explain the provenance of crops (millet, rice), the founding of lineages, and the spirits of the landscape; memory extends several generations through oral genealogy.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: The social order is legitimated by ancestral precedent—custom is sanctified by the claim that ancestors established it; no abstract political ideology exists; the narrative is one of continuity, proper conduct, and fulfillment of inherited obligation.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: Yangshao is famous for painted pottery: bowls, jars, and amphorae decorated with red and black geometric designs (spirals, triangles, fish motifs) expressing regional identity and possibly cosmological symbolism; houses are semi-subterranean with timber posts and thatched roofs; personal ornaments include bone hairpins and stone pendants. Hemudu material culture features pile dwellings with sophisticated mortise-and-tenon joinery, lacquered wooden bowls and vessels, carved bone and ivory implements, jade pendants and beads, and paddle-impressed pottery; the aesthetic emphasizes organic forms and mastery of wood and water. Both cultures lack monumental architecture.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: Cultural forms are vital and evolving in this mid-Neolithic florescence; painted pottery styles diversify regionally within Yangshao; Hemudu craft traditions elaborate; no exhaustion or hollowing of symbols is evident.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: Both cultures inhabit an animated cosmos where spirits dwell in the landscape—rivers, mountains, trees, and animals are numinous; ancestors remain active presences requiring propitiation and respect; human welfare depends on maintaining proper relations with these powers; no systematic theology exists, only oral tradition encoding belief.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: Seasonal rituals mark agricultural cycles—planting, harvest—and life transitions—birth, coming of age, marriage, death; offerings to ancestors and spirits ensure fertility and protection; Yangshao burials in communal cemeteries express continuing bonds with the dead; Hemudu may practice water-related rituals given its lacustrine environment. Ritual specialists may emerge within kinship structures, but no priestly class exists; practice is communal and oral.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: No religious institutions exist; doctrine is oral tradition transmitted through elders and ritual practitioners; authority rests on claimed ancestral connection and demonstrated ritual efficacy rather than formal office.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: Spiritual traditions are localized; limited contact between Yangshao and Hemudu zones means little direct diffusion; within each culture area, shared traditions spread through kinship networks and marriage exchange; no missionary activity or systematic displacement occurs.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: The sacred is fully woven into daily life; agriculture, craft, and social life are permeated by spiritual meaning; no disenchantment or secularizing drift is evident; spiritual need is met through continuous practice and ancestral connection.

docs.title: 2,000 BCE – 1,700 BCE — Erlitou and the Emergence of Bronze Age Polity
docs.text: Summary: A Discrete Event in the Yiluo River valley as Erlitou crystallizes from the Longshan substrate into the first archaeologically attested Bronze Age polity in East Asia, marked by palatial architecture, bronze ritual vessels, turquoise workshops, and a hinterland of subordinate settlements—yet still governed entirely through oral command, with no writing system to fix law, record, or decree. The single most causal factor is the mastery of bronze casting for ritual vessels, which concentrated symbolic and material power in elite hands and created the template for Shang and Zhou statecraft.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: Erlitou sits at the confluence of the Yi and Luo rivers, a node where the loess plateau meets the North China Plain; the site commands fertile alluvium and transit routes linking the middle Yellow River to the eastern plains and the southern highlands; spatial friction is moderate—river transport eases movement, but overland travel through the surrounding hills remains slow.

Climate Regime & Volatility: The late Holocene cooling continues; monsoon variability produces alternating flood and drought years; the Yiluo valley is better watered than the loess plateau to the west but subject to the Yellow River's unpredictable floods; climate stress rewards the concentrated storage and redistribution that Erlitou's elites command.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: Flooding is the principal hazard; the site is elevated above the floodplain but its hinterland is not; seismic risk is moderate; the palace compound's rammed-earth foundations represent investment vulnerable to earthquake and flood, but the site's three-century occupation suggests hazards were manageable.

Resource & Energy Endowment: Alluvial soils support millet and rice; copper ore is imported from sources in the Zhongtiao Mountains and beyond; tin is rarer, imported over longer distances; jade comes from the Yangtze region and possibly further; turquoise is sourced from the northwest; the resource base is no longer purely local but depends on long-distance procurement networks.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: The settlement generates substantial waste—ash, pottery shards, bronze slag, food refuse—which accumulates in pits and middens; the sink capacity of the surrounding alluvium is adequate; bronze-working leaves slag deposits, but the scale is not yet industrially polluting; the physical residue is contained.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: Aggregation of 20,000–30,000 people raises pathogen exposure; fecal contamination of water sources is likely; skeletal evidence shows infectious disease alongside trauma; mortality remains high but compatible with demographic growth; no epidemic collapse is documented.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: Millet, rice, pigs, and cattle provide the dietary base; elite burials contain more diverse grave goods, suggesting better provisioning; some skeletal evidence of nutritional stress in non-elite individuals; overall vitality is adequate for sustained labor and reproduction.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Healing is embedded in household and ritual practice; shamanic specialists likely perform healing rites alongside divination; no institutional medicine exists; recovery depends on kin care and the herbs and techniques transmitted orally through generations.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Kinship and marriage are organized through oral genealogies and residence rules; elite polygyny is likely, concentrating reproduction among high-status males; biological fertility is unconstrained; the demographic base is expanding.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Erlitou is the largest settlement of its era, with population estimates of 20,000–30,000; the age structure is young; high fertility offsets high mortality; migration into the center from surrounding villages concentrates population and labor.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: The dependent load is absorbed by extended kin groups; elite households support larger retinues including servants, artisans, and possibly slaves; no institutional care for dependents exists; the productive base sustains the load.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: Agriculture provides the subsistence base; the Yiluo valley is fertile and well-watered; the provisioning floor sits above bare survival for most, with elite households far above; storage in granaries and pits buffers against poor harvests.

Energy Capture & Conversion: Human and animal muscle remain dominant; fire is essential for bronze smelting and casting, pottery firing, and cooking; charcoal production for metallurgy begins to draw on forest resources; the per-capita work ceiling rises slightly with bronze tools but remains muscle-bound.

Labor Organization & Coercion: Labor is organized through kinship, residence, and corvée; the construction of palatial compounds and the operation of bronze workshops require coordinated labor on a scale implying command rather than voluntary cooperation; the presence of apparent sacrificial victims in some contexts suggests captive labor and extreme coercion.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Agricultural surplus supports a non-farming elite, craft specialists, and workers; bronze production is the premier specialized industry, consuming imported ores and producing ritual vessels for elite use; the surplus flow is sufficient to sustain the palatial establishment and its workshops.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: Granaries concentrate reserves under elite control; bronze and jade objects represent stored wealth; the treasury is the palace itself; buffering capacity is substantial but depends on continued surplus extraction from the hinterland.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: Long-distance exchange networks bring copper, tin, jade, turquoise, and cowrie shells to Erlitou; the center redistributes bronze vessels and prestige goods to subordinate settlements; logistics depend on human porters, boats, and carts; no evidence of market exchange—trade is elite-administered and embedded in political relations.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: Bronze vessels, jade, and turquoise serve as stores of value and media of elite exchange; cowrie shells may function as proto-currency or prestige objects; no monetary system exists; obligations are tracked orally and materially through gift and counter-gift.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: Elites extract surplus through tribute, corvée, and control of prestige goods; redistribution occurs through feasting, burial gifts, and ritual display; the extraction load is sustainable, as the system persists for three centuries without evident productive collapse.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Wealth is highly concentrated; elite burials contain bronze, jade, turquoise, and lacquer, while non-elite burials are sparse; the palace compound itself is a statement of concentrated wealth; the distribution is steeply unequal and hardening.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Bronze slag, broken molds, and ceramic waste accumulate in workshop areas; organic refuse is discarded in pits; the material waste load is locally significant but not systemically problematic; no monetary system generates financial residue.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Kinship is organized through patrilineal descent, with inheritance of status and property passing through male lines; elite lineages distinguish themselves through access to bronze, jade, and palatial residence; oral genealogies anchor identity and succession rights.

Association & Mutual Aid: Village communities and workshop groups provide mutual aid; the palace compound organizes craft production and labor mobilization; no autonomous guilds or associations are attested; mutual aid is embedded in kinship and political hierarchy.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: Feasts and rituals mark agricultural cycles and political events; music (drums, chimes, flutes) accompanies ceremonies; leisure is not separated from kinship and ritual obligation; sociability is structured by hierarchy.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: Society is sharply stratified; the palace compound separates elites from commoners; elite burials contain bronze and jade, while non-elite burials are impoverished; status boundaries are hardening toward hereditary distinction; factional blocs organized around rival lineages likely contest succession.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: Administration is oral and personal; no bureaucracy or written records exist; the palace compound serves as the administrative center, concentrating command in the person of the ruler and his household; the state's reach is coterminous with the ruler's personal network; institutional capacity is thin but effective within its range.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: Bronze weapons (ge halberds, axes) begin to appear, though stone and bone weapons remain common; the palatial compound and its workshops imply a retinue capable of defending the center and enforcing commands; walls are not prominent at Erlitou, suggesting security through hinterland control rather than fortification; the apparatus is sufficient to dominate the Yiluo valley and project influence into surrounding regions.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: Violence is attested by weapons and possible sacrificial victims; disorder is contained by elite authority; the system persists for three centuries without visible collapse, suggesting effective management of friction; the eventual transition to Erligang represents displacement rather than decay.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: Leadership is concentrated in the palace, exercised through command of ritual, bronze, and force; the ruler's personal authority is enacted orally through pronouncement and demonstrated materially through palatial display; charisma and lineage credential together underwrite command.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: Legitimacy rests on ancestral sanction, demonstrated by divination and ritual efficacy; the ruler's right to rule is performed through feasts, sacrifices, and the display of bronze vessels that only he can commission; allegiance is held through a mix of awe, obligation, and coercion.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: The will to build palaces, cast bronze, and administer a regional polity demonstrates strong collective resolve, directed by elite leadership; the ruling group's cohesion is demonstrated by the continuity of the site over three centuries; succession is managed, though likely contested.

External Relations & Posture: Erlitou dominates its immediate region but coexists with other centers; exchange networks imply cooperation alongside competition; no single rival is strong enough to challenge Erlitou during its peak; the posture is expansive but not yet imperial.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: The mood is one of confident expansion; the scale of palatial construction and bronze production suggests elite élan; the radius of trust extends within the elite lineage and its retinue but not far beyond; commoners are subjects rather than citizens, their sentiment unrecorded.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: The site's eventual abandonment and the rise of Erligang at Zhengzhou suggest a transfer of power, possibly through conquest or elite displacement; disaffection may have accumulated among subordinate populations or rival lineages, contributing to the transition; spent will is re-anchored at the successor center.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Speech is the sole high-bandwidth medium; the languages spoken are ancestral to later Sinitic tongues; mutual intelligibility extends across the Erlitou polity but not necessarily to distant regions; no writing exists; all commands, contracts, and records are oral.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Information travels at the speed of messengers; the palace concentrates information through its role as the ritual and administrative center; commands radiate outward through retainers and subordinate elites; feedback is slow but sufficient for the scale of the polity.

Record, Storage & Persistence: Memory is the sole record; oral tradition preserves genealogies, ritual formulas, and technical knowledge (including bronze-casting recipes); the death of a specialist risks knowledge loss; no durable external record exists except in the mute form of artifacts.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: Discourse is shaped by hierarchy and ritual propriety; taboos govern speech about the ruler, ancestors, and the sacred; censorship is personal and situational, enforced by fear of punishment and supernatural sanction.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: The palace commands attention through architectural monumentality and ritual spectacle; feasts and ceremonies amplify messages to assembled audiences; the dynamics of amplification are limited by the size of the gathering.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: Oral transmission introduces drift; ritual repetition and the authority of specialists constrain error; verification is limited to consensus and demonstrated efficacy; noise accumulates slowly in the absence of external correction.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Justice is conceived as reciprocity within the lineage and obedience to the ruler; the ancestors sanction conduct; the sacrifice of captives and the concentration of wealth suggest a morality that sharply distinguishes insiders from outsiders, permitting extreme exploitation of the latter.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: No written law exists; all rules are oral custom, enforced by the ruler and his agents; taboos govern conduct toward the sacred and the powerful; the regulatory corpus is embedded in ritual and pronouncement, evolving through oral decree.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: The ruler or his delegates adjudicate disputes; divination provides supernatural warrant; sanctions include punishment, exile, and death; the caseload is small enough for personal adjudication; justice is summary and unchecked by external appeal.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Rights are group rights, vested in lineage and status; commoners have no rights against the elite except what custom provides; the compliance burden is heavy for those subject to corvée and tribute, light for those who command.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: Elite impunity is extensive; the ruler can sacrifice, punish, and extract without institutional check; the wronged have no recourse except flight or revenge; impunity accumulates within the elite but is periodically discharged through succession struggles or external conquest.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: Inquiry is practical and ritual; knowledge of metallurgy, agriculture, and construction is empirically grounded; the reigning paradigm is cosmological, explaining events through ancestral will and cosmic forces accessed via divination.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Piece-mold bronze casting is the technical breakthrough of the era—a uniquely Chinese invention that produces ritual vessels of unprecedented complexity; turquoise inlay, jade carving, and lacquerwork reach new levels of sophistication; techniques are transmitted orally from master to apprentice within palace workshops.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: Education is apprenticeship; literacy is zero; the knowledge stock is held in living memory; skill distribution is uneven, concentrated in the palace workshops; the bronze-casting lineages are the most valuable knowledge-holders of the polity.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: The bronze-casting tradition is robust, transmitted successfully to Erligang successors; other techniques (jade carving, turquoise work) are also preserved; no major knowledge decay is documented, though the oral channel remains vulnerable to generational breaks.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: Identity is rooted in lineage and the Erlitou center itself; origin narratives and ancestor cults define belonging; the memory of Erlitou would echo in later texts that may remember it as the Xia dynasty, though no contemporary record survives to anchor that identification.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: Legitimacy is narrated through ancestral sanction and ritual efficacy; the ruler's right is demonstrated by successful divination, abundant harvests, and the possession of bronze vessels that channel ancestral power; no written ideology exists—legitimation is performed and enacted.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: Bronze vessels with animal-mask (taotie-like) designs, jade ge blades, turquoise-inlaid plaques, and lacquerware constitute the visual vocabulary; the aesthetic is austere, geometric, and ritually charged; palatial architecture emphasizes rammed-earth platforms and axial layout; the material culture sets the template for Shang and Zhou elite expression.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: The bronze-vessel complex is new and vital; forms are evolving rather than exhausting; no evidence of anomie or meaning decay—the symbolic vocabulary is generative and expanding into successor cultures.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: The cosmos is populated by ancestors, spirits, and cosmic forces; human fate depends on ancestral favor, accessible through divination; the existential outlook combines fatalism about the cosmic order with activism about ritual intervention—the proper rite can secure blessings.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: Scapulimancy remains central, though still without inscription; bronze vessels are cast for ritual use, likely to hold offerings to ancestors; feasts, sacrifices (including human sacrifice), and music enact the sacred; devotion is collective and commanded by the ruler.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: No separate priesthood exists; ritual authority is fused with political authority in the person of the ruler; doctrine is oral tradition; institutional reach extends as far as the palace's network; the ruler is simultaneously king and chief ritualist.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: Erlitou synthesizes spiritual elements from the Longshan substrate and adds new forms (bronze vessels as ritual media); the jade complex continues; no single orthodoxy exists, but Erlitou's ritual vocabulary diffuses to successor cultures; the direction is toward consolidation.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: The sacred remains potent; there is no evidence of disenchantment; the bronze vessels intensify rather than diminish the sacred charge; the spiritual need is fully anchored in the ancestral cult and the ritual apparatus the polity commands; the eventual transition to Erligang represents succession, not secularization.

docs.title: 25,000 BCE – 15,000 BCE — Last Glacial Maximum and Refugia
docs.text: Summary: At the height of the last Ice Age, cold and aridity compress human populations into scattered refugia—the middle Yangtze valleys, southwestern karst basins, and sheltered coastal pockets—where small bands persist through broad-spectrum foraging, their survival knowledge and social bonds transmitted entirely through speech and memory against environmental conditions that leave little margin for error.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: The Yellow River basin is largely depopulated or very thinly occupied; loess deposition accelerates, burying older surfaces; the North China Plain is cold, windswept steppe; the Yangtze basin remains more habitable, with the middle reaches (modern Hubei, Hunan) and southwestern karst country (Guizhou, Yunnan) offering sheltered valleys and limestone caves; coastal areas are exposed by lower sea levels, but cold and dry; spatial friction is extreme—mountain barriers, seasonal flooding, and resource scarcity confine populations to isolated pockets.

Climate Regime & Volatility: Global temperatures are 4–7 degrees Celsius below Holocene averages; the East Asian monsoon weakens drastically, reducing summer rainfall; winters are severe in the north, with permafrost extending into northern China; even the south is cooler and drier than today; interannual volatility remains high, with cold snaps and multi-year droughts capable of collapsing local resources; the climate regime is at its harshest sustained level of the Pleistocene.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: Dust storms intensify as loess accumulates; flood hazard is reduced by lower precipitation but flash floods remain possible in mountain valleys; cold exposure is the primary hazard—hypothermia, frostbite, and resource failure during cold spells; fire in dry vegetation is possible; populations in refugia face less hazard than those on exposed plains, but margin is thin everywhere.

Resource & Energy Endowment: Large fauna (mammoth, woolly rhinoceros, horses, deer) persist in the north but at lower densities; in southern refugia, subtropical fauna (deer, wild pigs, monkeys, small mammals) and diverse plant foods (tubers, nuts, wild rice in favorable microhabitats) sustain foraging; stone for toolmaking is available in most regions; firewood is critical and may be scarce in degraded or cold environments; the energy endowment is contracted relative to earlier and later periods.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Population density is so low that human waste output is negligible; abandoned sites are rapidly buried by loess in the north or overgrown in the south; no sink saturation; environmental feedback is from climate, not human impact.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: Infectious disease pressure remains low in small, isolated populations; zoonotic exposure from game processing poses some risk; cold exposure, injury, and resource failure are the leading causes of death; infant and childhood mortality is high; life expectancy at birth is likely 25–30 years; mortality spikes during resource crashes.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: Diet is constrained by reduced plant diversity and game availability; broad-spectrum foraging (small game, fish, shellfish, roots, nuts) buffers against single-resource failure but overall nutritional margins are thin; skeletal evidence suggests periodic nutritional stress; physiological robustness is maintained in survivors, but population health is precarious.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Healing knowledge is oral and limited: wound tending, fracture setting, herbal remedies known within the band; no specialist healers; care for the sick and injured is constrained by band resources and mobility needs; in extremis, the vulnerable may be abandoned.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Fertility is constrained by nutritional stress and prolonged lactation; pair-bonding persists, likely with kin-regulated mating rules; exogamous mate exchange between refugial bands maintains genetic diversity but is limited by isolation and low encounter rates.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Population density is at its Pleistocene nadir in this region; total population may number in the hundreds to low thousands across both basins combined; birth rates are low, death rates high; net growth is near zero or negative; refugial populations are fragmented and vulnerable to local extinction.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: The dependent load (young, old, infirm) is proportionally significant in small bands; attrition is high during resource stress; the capacity to carry dependents is limited; this is a survival regime, not a growth regime.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: The provisioning floor is immediate-return foraging with no storage capacity beyond a few days; hunting, fishing, and plant gathering must succeed continuously; the floor is close to carrying capacity limits, with little margin; household pooling distributes risk within the band.

Energy Capture & Conversion: Human muscle and fire are the only energy sources; fire is critical for warmth, cooking, and possibly game drive; no animal traction; per-capita energy throughput is low; the energy ceiling constrains all activity to what hands and fire can achieve.

Labor Organization & Coercion: Labor is organized by age and sex within the band; hunting, gathering, and processing tasks are coordinated orally; no coercion beyond social pressure; task allocation is flexible and consensus-based.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Production is for immediate consumption; surplus is rare and fleeting—a successful hunt is shared and consumed quickly; no durable surplus accumulates; productive capacity is limited to band labor.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: Reserves are minimal: dried meat, cached plant foods may last days or weeks; no granaries, no formal pooling institutions; buffering depends on mobility and fallback resources; reserves are inadequate against prolonged resource failure.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: Exchange occurs when bands encounter each other—probably seasonally and infrequently in this period; raw materials (stone, shell, ochre) and ornaments circulate; logistics are limited to personal carrying; no trade routes; isolation reduces exchange frequency.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: No currency; reciprocal obligation is the mechanism of deferred exchange, enforced by memory and reputation; prestige goods exist but are not systematically convertible; credit is personal and oral.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: No extraction apparatus; redistribution is egalitarian sharing within the band; no chiefs, tribute, or rent; surplus, when it occurs, is consumed collectively.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Wealth differences are minimal; portable tools, weapons, and ornaments are personal property; land is not owned; accumulation is impossible; asset defense is unnecessary.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Waste (butchering debris, ash, knapping refuse) is left at campsites; no routing decisions; no accumulation of refuse or mispricing.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Kinship organizes all social relations: descent, marriage, residence, and cooperation; inheritance is of knowledge and portable goods, transmitted orally; no property in land.

Association & Mutual Aid: The band (perhaps 20–40 individuals in stressed conditions) is the unit of association; mutual aid is obligatory among kin; no institutions beyond kinship; reciprocity and reputation enforce cooperation.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: Leisure is constrained by survival demands but not absent: fireside gathering, storytelling, song, and play persist as the medium of sociability and cultural transmission.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: Stratification is minimal; status accrues to skilled hunters and knowledgeable elders but confers no coercive power; group structure is fluid; bands may shrink, merge, or fragment in response to conditions.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: No administration; decision-making is collective and oral; leadership is situational; no offices, bureaucracy, or formalized external relations.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: No standing force; all able-bodied adults can fight; weapons are hunting tools; violence is interpersonal, not organized; no fortifications; interband conflict is probably rare given low population density and isolation.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: Friction is discharged through mobility, mediation, and band fission; unresolved disputes lead to separation; no accumulated disorder or decaying apparatus; social structure is simple and resilient.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: Leadership is personal: the competent hunter, the wise elder, the persuasive speaker; authority cannot be inherited or formalized; influence depends on demonstrated skill and generosity.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: Legitimacy is embedded in kinship and reciprocity; no separate political order exists; allegiance is to kin and band; dissent is expressed by departure.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: Collective action requires consensus; will is mobilized for hunts, moves, and survival tasks; resolve is tested by repeated hardship; sustained collective effort depends on shared necessity.

External Relations & Posture: Relations with other bands are rare due to isolation; posture is wary; no expansion or conquest; occasional encounters may be for mate exchange or resource information sharing.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: Sentiment is shaped by survival anxiety; trust is high within the band, guarded toward outsiders; mood tracks resource availability; behavioral temper is cautious, risk-averse.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: Prolonged hardship may produce despair, but band structure keeps apathy contained; disaffection leads to departure; spent will after resource crashes may contribute to group dissolution, particularly if leadership fails.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Fully grammatical spoken language is the medium; mutual intelligibility extends to neighboring bands but contact is rare; no writing, no notation; exclusion is by isolation or deafness.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Channels are face-to-face; transmission velocity is limited to human travel; news of distant conditions arrives slowly if at all; no amplification.

Record, Storage & Persistence: Memory is the only record; knowledge persists through oral repetition—songs, stories, instructional routines—but is vulnerable to transmission failure; loss of elders means loss of knowledge; isolation threatens cultural persistence.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: Discourse is governed by kinship respect, age deference, and taboo; no formal censorship; framing is embedded in myth and convention.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: Reception is limited to those present; amplification is through retelling; isolation limits the spread of information between bands; each refugial population may diverge culturally.
