Signal Integrity & Noise Load: Signal integrity depends on individual memory; noise accumulates through forgetting and embellishment; no external verification; within-band consensus is the only check.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Justice is embedded in reciprocity and kinship obligation; sharing is mandatory; hoarding and deception are wrong; revenge for wrongs is legitimate; the moral sense is enforced by gossip and exclusion.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: No written law; norms are customary and oral; taboos govern sacred matters, mating, and food distribution; regulation is informal.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: Disputes are adjudicated by elders or consensus; liability is personal and kin-based; sanction ranges from rebuke to expulsion; no formal courts.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Rights are implicit in kinship status; protections depend on kin advocacy; compliance burden is low—norms are internalized.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: Impunity is limited by small group size; unredressed wrongs may fuel feuds; the gap between justice owed and delivered is small but present when enforcement fails.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: Inquiry is empirical but embedded in myth; observation of environment, weather, and animal behavior guides action; theory is narrative, not abstract; survival knowledge is the frontier.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Technical knowledge is critical: stone toolmaking, fire-making, tracking, plant identification, shelter construction, cold-weather survival techniques; methods are transmitted orally and by demonstration.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: Education is lifelong and informal; children learn by observation and participation; the knowledge stock is held in elder memories; skill distribution is broad; specialization is limited to individual aptitude.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: Obsolescence is slow; knowledge decay is a serious risk in isolated populations—loss of skilled elders can mean loss of techniques; error correction depends on practical testing; isolation threatens intellectual persistence.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: Identity is rooted in kinship, landscape, and origin myth; foundational narratives explain the world and the band's place in it; memory is oral and vulnerable to loss.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: The legitimating narrative is mythological: ancestors established the way; spirits sanction the norms; no separate ideology; tradition is authority.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: Material culture is portable and functional: stone tools, bone implements, shell and tooth ornaments, ochre; artistic expression is in personal adornment and perishable media; no monumental art; cave sites may preserve some traces, but evidence is sparse in this region compared to Europe.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: Forms are stable; no exhaustion in the modern sense; meaning is renewed through ritual and storytelling; anomie is rare in small, integrated groups; the threat is cultural extinction, not exhaustion.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: The cosmos is animate: spirits inhabit animals, plants, landforms, and the dead; the world is layered and interconnected; human existence is embedded in this larger order; outlook is shaped by survival anxiety but also by trust in spiritual guidance.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: Ritual marks life transitions, seasonal events, and critical moments (successful hunts, deaths, crises); practices include offerings, taboo observance, and probably trance or shamanic performance; devotion is collective.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: No institutional religion; shamans or ritual specialists hold knowledge but not coercive authority; doctrine is oral and locally variable; no orthodoxy.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: Isolation limits diffusion; each refugial population may develop distinctive spiritual traditions; syncretism occurs when bands merge; no displacement by conquest; spiritual evolution is local and continuous.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: Disenchantment is absent; the world remains enchanted; the sacred suffuses daily life; no secular sphere exists; spiritual need is continuously met; the threat is extinction of the tradition-bearing group, not erosion of belief.

docs.title: 3,500 BCE – 2,500 BCE — Late Neolithic Complexity and Liangzhu
docs.text: Summary: By the mid-fourth millennium BCE the lower Yangtze delta supports the Liangzhu culture—massive earthen platforms, elite burials laden with jade cong and bi, and probable palatial structures suggesting chiefly or proto-state hierarchy—while the Yellow River region sees Longshan precursors with wheel-thrown black pottery and the first walled towns; the chief causal factor is intensified surplus extraction enabling hereditary elites to monopolize ritual authority, prestige goods, and coercive capacity, yet all administration, record-keeping, and ideological legitimation remain oral, resting on spoken command, memorized genealogy, and performed rite rather than written archive.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: The lower Yangtze delta is a mosaic of lakes, rivers, and low mounds amid waterlogged plains; Liangzhu centers cluster on elevated ground at Mojiaoshan and surrounding sites, using waterways as highways and marshes as barriers; the middle Yellow River remains loess-terraced, while Shandong's coastal plain hosts Dawenkou successors edging toward Longshan.

Climate Regime & Volatility: The Holocene Climatic Optimum is waning; conditions remain warm and wet but show increased variability; sea-level stabilization allows sustained occupation of low-lying delta sites; occasional flooding is managed through raised platforms, but catastrophic flood events will eventually contribute to Liangzhu's collapse around 2,300 BCE, just beyond this window.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: Flood risk is endemic in the Yangtze delta; Liangzhu's monumental earthworks may serve partly as flood-proofing; seismic risk is moderate; drought is less threatening in the wet south than in the north, where harvest failure can trigger localized crisis.

Resource & Energy Endowment: Alluvial soils sustain intensive rice agriculture; timber from surrounding forests supplies construction; jade sources—Tremolite from Xiuyan or other locales—are accessed through long-distance exchange networks, their control a key to elite power; stone, clay, and lacquer are locally available.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: The dense populations around Liangzhu centers generate concentrated waste; midden layers thicken; waterlogged conditions preserve organic refuse archaeologically but may have created sanitary challenges; no evidence of regional degradation, though local exhaustion may prompt settlement shifts.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: Dense nucleated populations and waterlogged conditions increase exposure to parasitic and waterborne diseases; malaria and schistosomiasis are plausible in the delta; infant and child mortality remain high; adult skeletal evidence suggests moderate lifespans without catastrophic epidemic.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: Rice dominates the diet, supplemented by fish, aquatic plants, pork, and hunted game; nutritional adequacy is high for elites, less certain for laborers mobilized for monument construction; dental pathology and skeletal stress markers are present but not extreme.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Shamanic practitioners likely mediate healing; herbal remedies and wound care are transmitted orally; elite burials suggest access to finer foods and care; no specialized medical institution; healing capacity remains kin- and community-scale.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Patrilineal or cognatic lineages structure marriage and inheritance; elite polygyny is possible given burial evidence of differential status; fertility supports population growth sufficient to sustain large labor pools.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Population peaks in the Liangzhu heartland; estimates suggest tens of thousands within the site complex and surrounding villages; density is among the highest in Neolithic East Asia; in-migration and natural increase both contribute; labor mobilization for monumental construction depends on this density.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: The dependent load—infants, aged, infirm—is absorbed by extended kin networks and surplus production; elite households may command labor to buffer dependency; no evidence of crisis-level attrition within this window.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: Intensive wet-rice cultivation, supported by paddy management and water control, raises the provisioning floor above earlier Neolithic levels; fish, shellfish, and pork round out the diet; famine risk is reduced by storage and surplus, though not eliminated.

Energy Capture & Conversion: Human labor remains the sole motive force; fire is used for pottery kilns, cooking, and land clearance; the labor mobilization for Liangzhu's earthworks—millions of cubic meters—represents massive energy expenditure organized through social compulsion rather than mechanical advantage.

Labor Organization & Coercion: Monumental construction implies corvée-like labor mobilization; elites command labor beyond household scale, suggesting coercive extraction or debt-bondage relations; craft specialists—jade-workers, potters—may be attached to elite households; wage labor does not exist.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Surplus is substantial, enabling full-time craft specialists and monumental construction; jade workshops produce standardized cong and bi for elite consumption and burial; the surplus is extracted upward, not merely stored at household level.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: Granaries and raised-floor structures store rice reserves; elite control over storage concentrates buffering capacity; multi-year reserves are plausible given the scale of construction; household reserves are subordinate to communal or elite-controlled stocks.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: Jade moves from distant sources through elite-controlled exchange networks; Liangzhu jade objects appear in distant cultures, suggesting prestige exchange or tribute; waterborne logistics along rivers and lakes facilitate bulk transport; no market or currency.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: Jade cong, bi, and ornaments serve as concentrated stores of value and prestige; deferred exchange operates through oral obligation and gift reciprocity; elite burials convert surplus into permanent display; no currency or accounting system.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: Elites extract surplus through tribute, corvée, and control of prestige goods; redistribution flows downward through feasting, gift-giving, and patronage, legitimating extraction; the circuit is oral, personal, and ritualized.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Extreme concentration is visible in burial: elite tombs at Fanshan and Yaoshan contain hundreds of jade objects, while commoner graves hold few or none; wealth is defended by kinship, ritual authority, and probable retainer forces; no fortification yet, but differentiation is stark.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Craft production generates debitage (jade, stone) and kiln waste; organic refuse accumulates in middens; waste routing is local; no toxic byproducts; the economic residue is material accumulation, not financial imbalance.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Elite lineages dominate; inheritance of status, land, and ritual prerogative likely follows patrilineal descent; commoner kinship remains important but subordinate; marriage alliances probably cement inter-lineage relations.

Association & Mutual Aid: Kin-based reciprocity persists, but it is now overlaid by hierarchical obligation; craft guilds or specialist households may form proto-associations; communal labor is mobilized by elite command, not solely by mutual aid.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: Elite feasting and ritual performance are visible in artifact assemblages (musical instruments, fine ceramics); communal festivals likely continue; leisure is now stratified—elites consume differently from commoners.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: Clear hierarchical stratification: a paramount elite (possibly a chief or king), subsidiary elites, craft specialists, and commoner agriculturalists; status is likely inherited; social mobility is constrained; ethnic or regional boundaries distinguish Liangzhu from surrounding cultures.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: No formal bureaucracy or written records; administration is oral, exercised through personal command, retinue, and face-to-face oversight; the scale of construction implies significant organizational capacity, but it rests on memory, oral decree, and personal loyalty, not archive.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: Stone and bone weapons; elite retainers may serve as armed guards; no standing army, but labor mobilization implies coercive capacity; human sacrifice (attested at some Longshan sites) may be emerging; coercion is personal and ritualized.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: Social friction is discharged through ritual, feasting, and perhaps scapegoating or sacrifice; no evidence of rebellion within this window; disorder residue is low but the structures of extraction create latent grievance; the apparatus is not yet sclerotic—it is still forming.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: Paramount leaders at Liangzhu centers command through charisma, ritual authority, and control of jade and feasting; authority is personal, possibly hereditary, and enacted through oral performance and display; no impersonal office.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: Allegiance flows to the paramount through kinship, ritual awe, and material dependence; legitimacy is enacted in ceremony, not inscribed in charter; it must be renewed through each generation's performance.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: The paramount can mobilize collective labor for massive projects, indicating concentrated will; succession is oral and potentially contested; cohesion depends on continued ritual efficacy and material flow.

External Relations & Posture: Relations with other cultures (Dawenkou, Songze successors, early Longshan) are mediated through prestige exchange and probably intermarriage; no evidence of conquest or empire; competition is channeled through display and exchange, not warfare on a grand scale.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: The mood is probably a mix of awe and resentment—awe at elite ritual power and monumental display, resentment at extraction; trust extends within kin groups but is mediated by hierarchy across them; the temper is deferential but not servile.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: No evidence of widespread disaffection within this window; extraction is heavy but legitimated by ritual; the eventual collapse (~2,300 BCE) may involve spent will, but it lies beyond the snapshot.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Spoken language is universal; Liangzhu elites may use specialized registers or ritual speech; regional dialects persist; no writing—Liangzhu symbols on pottery and jade are marks or emblems, not phonetic script.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Information travels by messenger, seasonal gathering, and exchange network; waterways accelerate travel within the delta; oral orders from the paramount reach subordinates within days; velocity is adequate for regional coordination but not instantaneous.

Record, Storage & Persistence: Memory is the only archive; genealogies, ritual protocols, tribute schedules, and craft recipes are stored in trained minds; jade symbols may serve as mnemonic or ownership marks but do not encode language; nothing survives the death of the knower without oral transmission.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: Ritual speech is formulaic and controlled; taboos govern discussion of the sacred and the paramount; censorship is social, not institutional; discourse norms are shaped by hierarchy—commoners speak differently to elites.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: Ritual performances, feasts, and monumental display command attention and amplify elite messages; oral proclamation in assembly reaches hundreds; no mass media; amplification is architectural and performative.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: Oral transmission introduces drift; elite control of ritual speech may impose conservatism; competing oral traditions may exist among commoners; noise accumulates but is disciplined by repetition and hierarchy.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Justice is hierarchical—elites owe protection and ritual efficacy, commoners owe labor and tribute; fairness is reciprocity within rank, not equality; transgression against the sacred or the paramount is grave.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: No codified law; norms are oral, transmitted as ancestral precedent and elite decree; evolution occurs through reinterpretation by living authorities, not legislation.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: Elites or ritual specialists adjudicate disputes; liability may be collective (kin-group responsibility); sanctions include compensation, exile, sacrifice, or death; no court or written record.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Rights are embedded in status, not personhood; elites enjoy prerogatives; commoners have obligations; compliance is habitual, enforced by surveillance and sanction within small-scale hierarchy; the burden increases with extraction.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: Elites may enjoy impunity for acts that would sanction commoners; wrongs against commoners by elites are redressed only if they threaten stability; the gap between justice owed and delivered widens with stratification.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: Empirical knowledge of hydraulics, agriculture, jade-working, and construction accumulates; theory remains embedded in animist and ancestral cosmology; no distinction between technical and ritual knowledge; the paradigm is practical-sacral.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Jade-working reaches high refinement—precision drilling, polishing, and standardized forms (cong, bi, yue axes); wheel-thrown pottery appears in Longshan contexts; water management for rice paddies implies hydraulic technique; all transmitted orally.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: Apprenticeship within specialist households transmits craft knowledge; elite families may monopolize ritual and prestige-craft skills; no formal schooling; literacy is absent; the stock is distributed unequally.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: Techniques lost with lineage extinction; regional specialization may insulate against total loss; jade-working skills are concentrated and vulnerable; innovation and loss proceed together; no archive buffers decay.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: Liangzhu identity is expressed through jade iconography—the cong tube, the bi disk, the taotie-like mask motif—encoding cosmological meaning now lost; origin narratives and ancestral heroes are oral and unrecoverable; identity is lineage-bound and hierarchical.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: Elite authority is legitimated by descent from powerful ancestors, command of ritual, and monopoly of jade symbolism; the narrative is that elites mediate between human and spirit worlds, and their prosperity ensures communal welfare.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: Jade cong and bi are the supreme artistic achievement—abstract geometric forms with incised designs of faces and eyes; fine black pottery, lacquerware, and silk (possibly) complement the material repertoire; monumental platforms and mound-burials shape the built landscape.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: Forms remain potent within this window; jade symbolism is vital, not hollow; standardization indicates codification, not exhaustion; the eventual collapse may involve meaning-crisis, but it lies beyond the snapshot.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: The cosmos is layered and animated; the cong may symbolize earth, the bi heaven, mediating cosmic realms; ancestors and spirits inhabit the world and must be propitiated; human life is embedded in this sacred order.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: Elaborate burial rites, foundation deposits, and probably seasonal ceremonies enact the sacred; jade placement in burials follows precise protocols; shamanic figures or priest-chiefs mediate ritual; practice is oral and performative.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: The paramount may combine political and religious authority; no separate clergy visible, but ritual specialists exist; doctrine is oral tradition, guarded by lineage heads; authority is charismatic and hereditary.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: Liangzhu jade symbolism spreads to other cultures through exchange, suggesting diffusion of cosmological ideas; syncretism with neighboring traditions is probable; no missionary expansion or doctrinal conflict is visible.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: No evidence of disenchantment; the sacred is vividly present in jade, ritual, and monument; spiritual need is fully engaged; no residue of emptied cosmology; the void, if it comes, follows collapse.

docs.title: 1,300 BCE – 1,200 BCE — Late Shang Oracle Bone Florescence and Oral Threshold
docs.text: Summary: The Late Shang capital at Anyang witnesses the institutionalization of oracle bone divination with incised inscriptions, marking the threshold where external written record begins to supplement oral memory as the medium through which royal decisions are authorized and preserved. The single most causal factor is the routinization of pyro-scapulimancy into a bureaucratic archive — cracks interpreted, questions inscribed, outcomes recorded — which binds divination to durable media and inaugurates Chinese literacy even as speech remains the substrate of daily governance, ritual recitation, and popular memory.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: Yinxu sits on the northern bank of the Huan River, a tributary of the Yellow River, on the North China Plain where flat terrain and loess soils ease movement and cultivation. The capital's location at the junction of alluvial plain and piedmont gives access to both agricultural surplus and metal-bearing uplands to the west. Transit to bronze-producing regions in the Zhongtiao Mountains and jade sources in distant Xinjiang depends on overland routes across open terrain punctuated by river crossings — friction low by Bronze Age standards but still measured in weeks of ox-cart travel.

Climate Regime & Volatility: The warm, moist phase of the mid-Holocene has given way to a cooler, more variable climate by the late second millennium BCE. Monsoon rains remain adequate for millet and some rice, but interannual variability is rising, and droughts and floods appear in oracle bone queries — divinations asking whether rain will come, whether the Huan will overflow. The climate remains within the band that sustains intensive agriculture, but the margin of error is narrowing.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: Flooding from the Yellow River and its tributaries poses the chief acute hazard; oracle bones record royal concern with river behavior. Drought triggers famine risk; locust swarms occasionally devastate crops. Seismic activity is low in this region. The palace precinct and elite tombs are sited above the floodplain, suggesting awareness of flood risk, but the broader settlement sprawls onto vulnerable lowland.

Resource & Energy Endowment: Copper and tin for bronze come from mines in the Zhongtiao Mountains, the middle Yangtze, and possibly further afield — Yinxu is a consumer, not a producer. Local endowment consists of fertile loess, clay for pottery and molds, timber for construction and fuel, and reliable water. Energy is entirely organic: human and animal muscle, firewood, and charcoal for smelting. The bronze supply chain is extended and vulnerable to disruption.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Craft production at Yinxu generates bronze slag, ceramic waste, and bone refuse from butchering and divination. Workshop debris accumulates in pits and middens. Organic waste decomposes readily in the temperate monsoon climate. The sink is far from saturated; landscape degradation from deforestation and soil erosion is locally noticeable but not yet critical.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: Endemic malaria is present in the warmer southern periphery; the North China Plain is relatively healthier but not disease-free. Parasitic infections from irrigation waters, intestinal diseases from crowded settlement, and periodic epidemics impose a steady background mortality. Elite tombs show individuals dying at various ages; infant mortality remains high. Life expectancy at birth is probably in the mid-twenties; those surviving childhood may reach fifty or beyond.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: Millet, supplemented by wheat, soybeans, vegetables, and meat from pigs, cattle, sheep, and dogs, forms the staple diet. Elites enjoy better nutrition, as evidenced by larger stature and fewer skeletal stress markers. Commoners show signs of periodic nutritional stress. Overall, the population is adequately fed in normal years; famine follows drought or flood.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Healing knowledge is embedded in oral tradition and shamanic practice; diviners ask ancestral spirits about illness and its causes. Herbal remedies, acupuncture precursors, and ritual healing coexist. No institutionalized medical profession exists; care falls to kin and ritual specialists. Recovery capacity is limited; serious injury or infection often proves fatal.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Elite polygyny is documented in oracle bone references to multiple royal consorts. Commoner marriage patterns are less visible but probably monogamous or mildly polygynous. Fertility is high; the population is growing. Lineage and descent organize access to resources and status; reproductive success correlates with social position.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Yinxu's population is estimated at 50,000–150,000 at its peak, making it one of the largest settlements in the Bronze Age world. The broader Shang polity encompasses hundreds of thousands. Birth rates exceed death rates; the population is expanding. Migration into the capital from surrounding regions supplies labor for monumental construction and craft production.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: Human sacrifice — attested in royal tombs and oracle bone inscriptions — removes war captives and sometimes domestic dependents from the population. The elderly and infirm rely on kin support. Widows and orphans appear in the archaeological record; their absorption depends on lineage solidarity. The dependency load is substantial but managed within kin networks.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: Millet agriculture, supplemented by animal husbandry, hunting, and fishing, provides the subsistence base. Oracle bones record royal concern with harvests; the provisioning floor is adequate in normal years but vulnerable to climatic disruption. Royal granaries buffer against shortage; commoners depend on kin and village reserves.

Energy Capture & Conversion: Human and animal muscle power all production. Bronze tools — axes, knives, chisels — enhance woodworking and craft efficiency but remain elite goods; stone and bone tools persist among commoners. Charcoal-fired furnaces smelt copper and tin; wood fires power ceramics and cooking. Energy throughput is rising with population and bronze output but remains within organic limits.

Labor Organization & Coercion: Labor is organized by lineage, corvee obligation, and enslavement. Craft specialists — bronze workers, bone carvers, potters — work in royal workshops under elite supervision. Corvee mobilizes commoners for construction and agriculture. War captives supply sacrificial victims and some forced labor. Coercion is overt and institutionalized; labor is not free.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Bronze production is the prestige sector; ritual vessels, weapons, and chariot fittings flow from Yinxu workshops. Agricultural surplus supports a non-farming elite and craft-specialist population. The surplus is substantial but concentrated; most flows to the royal lineage and allied clans. Production is expanding during this window.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: Royal granaries store millet against famine; bronze and jade accumulate in elite treasuries. The oracle bones themselves become an archive — a store of decisions and precedents. Debt and credit mechanisms are invisible in the record but probably exist in oral form. Reserves are adequate for normal shocks but would strain under prolonged drought or military defeat.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: Long-distance exchange moves bronze, jade, cowrie shells, and exotic goods across hundreds of kilometers. Cowrie shells from the southern coast serve as prestige currency. Ox-carts and human porters transport goods; rivers provide cheaper bulk transport where available. Trade is embedded in tribute and gift exchange rather than impersonal markets.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: Cowrie shells, bronze, and jade store value; no coinage exists. Deferred exchange operates through kinship obligation and tributary relationships. Oracle bones record gifts and tribute but not commercial transactions. Credit, if it exists, is oral and personal.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: The king and royal lineage extract surplus through tribute, corvee, and direct control of craft production. Allied lineages share in redistribution through ritual feasting and gift exchange. The extraction rate is high; the royal precinct absorbs a disproportionate share of bronze, jade, and labor. Room to extract more is limited by the loyalty of subordinate lineages.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Wealth concentrates sharply: royal tombs contain tons of bronze, thousands of jade objects, and hundreds of sacrificed humans; commoner burials are sparse. Lineage membership defends access to resources. Theft is presumably punished; the walls of the elite precinct mark a physical defense of wealth.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Bronze slag, broken molds, bone refuse, and ceramic shards accumulate in workshop areas and are dumped in pits. Organic waste decomposes. No evidence of recycling beyond the re-melting of scrap bronze. Financial waste in the modern sense is absent; surplus is consumed in ritual and prestige display.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Patrilineal descent organizes society. Royal succession passes through the male line, though the exact rule (primogeniture vs. fraternal succession) varies. Lineages — named zu — control land, labor, and ritual obligations. Marriage is exogamous at the clan level; affinal alliances bind lineages. Inheritance of land and rank follows patrilineal rules recorded nowhere but in oral memory and now, partially, in oracle bone references.

Association & Mutual Aid: Lineage solidarity provides the primary safety net. Village communities share labor for agriculture and construction. No guilds or voluntary associations exist; all organization is kin-based or state-imposed. Mutual aid is embedded in kinship obligation, not formal institution.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: Ritual feasting accompanies sacrifice and seasonal ceremonies; music, dance, and intoxication (millet wine) mark elite gatherings. Hunting is a royal pastime and a ritual act. Commoner leisure is less visible; seasonal festivals probably punctuate the agricultural calendar. Sociability is organized around lineage and locality.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: Society is sharply stratified: the royal lineage at the apex, allied and subordinate lineages below, commoners beneath, and slaves and war captives at the bottom. Status is ascribed by birth; mobility is limited. The elite is marked by bronze, jade, chariots, and elaborate burial. Status boundaries are rigid and reinforced by ritual and violence.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: The oracle bone archive represents a new administrative capacity: decisions are inscribed, outcomes recorded, and precedents accumulated. Scribes — diviners who carve inscriptions — form an emerging bureaucratic stratum. The king consults ancestors and officials; divination formalizes decision-making. Administrative reach extends over a core domain of perhaps 30,000 square kilometers, with tributary influence beyond. Corruption is invisible in the record; institutional integrity depends on the king's personal authority.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: The Shang military fields chariots, bronze weapons (dagger-axes, spears, bows), and infantry. Chariots are elite prestige weapons; mass infantry provides the bulk of force. Fortifications are minimal at Yinxu; defense relies on mobile armies. The army campaigns against peripheral enemies (Qiang, Gui-fang, Ren-fang) named in oracle bones. Coercive capacity is substantial but stretched across a wide perimeter.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: Human sacrifice discharges captives and perhaps surplus dependents into death. Ritual violence — the killing of hundreds for royal funerals — absorbs social tension by dramatizing royal power. Disorder is not absent: oracle bones record rebellions, defections, and military setbacks. The apparatus functions but shows signs of strain; peripheral enemies resist, and subordinate lineages require constant ritual and coercive maintenance.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: The king (wang) is the supreme leader, mediating between the living and the ancestors through divination. His personal authority rests on ritual efficacy, military success, and lineage prestige. Oracle bones record kings by name (Wu Ding, the most prolific, reigns in the early part of this window); their personalities shape policy. Charisma is enacted through sacrifice, warfare, and successful divination.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: Legitimacy rests on the king's unique access to ancestors and his role as ritual leader. Allegiance is enacted through participation in sacrifice and tribute. Disaffection exists — oracle bones mention rebellious subordinates — but the ritual-military nexus sustains the royal claim. Legitimacy is eroding slowly as peripheral enemies press and subordinate lineages negotiate autonomy.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: Royal will is focused on maintaining ancestral favor, defeating enemies, and securing succession. The king decides with advice from ancestors (via divination) and officials. Succession is contested at times; oracle bones record concern with heirs. Collective resolve is mobilized through ritual and war; the elite is cohesive around royal sacrifice, but subordinate lineages pursue their own interests.

External Relations & Posture: The Shang face hostile neighbors on multiple fronts: Qiang pastoralists to the northwest, various fang (enemy polities) to the north and west, and less-visible southern competitors. Posture is defensive-aggressive: campaigns to punish raiders and extract captives, punctuated by periods of peace. Oracle bones record warfare as a recurring concern. Diplomatic relations with subordinate allies involve tribute, marriage, and ritual obligation.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: Elite sentiment is dominated by ancestral piety and ritual anxiety — the need to please ancestors and secure their blessing. Fear of divine displeasure and enemy attack colors royal divination. Trust radiates outward from lineage; inter-lineage relations are cautious. The behavioral temper is ritualized, hierarchical, and violence-ready. Commoner sentiment is invisible but presumably shaped by the same ancestral piety and local loyalties.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: The oracle bone archive itself registers royal anxiety — constant questioning of ancestors about outcomes, enemies, and harvests. Disaffection among subordinates appears as rebellion and defection. Apathy is not visible, but the sheer volume of divination suggests a ruling elite seeking reassurance. Will is not yet spent but is under strain from external pressure and internal competition.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Spoken Chinese is the universal medium; all orders, negotiations, ritual recitations, and daily communication pass through speech. The oracle bone script is accessible only to a tiny scribal elite — perhaps a few dozen diviners and their apprentices at court. Literacy is not a tool of general administration but a specialized ritual technology. The gap between oral and literate is opening but remains narrow; most information still travels by voice.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Messengers on foot or horseback transmit royal commands across the Shang domain; speed is limited to roughly 50–100 kilometers per day. Oracle bone queries suggest information lags: the king asks about events at the frontier without knowing outcomes. Channels are personal and hierarchical; no postal system exists. Information flows faster within the capital than across distance.

Record, Storage & Persistence: The oracle bone archive is the transformative innovation. Inscribed turtle plastrons and cattle scapulae record the question, the diviner's name, and sometimes the outcome. Bones are stored in pits — the archive. This is the first durable record-keeping system in Chinese history, supplementing memory with material trace. Most information, however, still resides in oral memory: genealogies, ritual procedures, legal precedents, technical knowledge — all transmitted by speech.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: Oracle bone inscriptions frame divination as royal prerogative; the king asks, the ancestors answer. The scribal record is official and formulaic; dissent does not appear. Oral discourse presumably allows more latitude, but commoner speech leaves no trace. Censorship in the modern sense is absent, but the discourse is constrained by ritual propriety and hierarchical deference.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: The audience for oracle bone inscriptions is tiny: the king, his diviners, and perhaps a few officials. The archive is not for public reading but for ritual validation and royal memory. Oral proclamations amplify royal will through messenger networks. Attention is focused on the king and the ancestors; no competing channels exist.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: The oracle bone script is a high-fidelity medium: inscriptions are durable, legible, and standardized. Oral transmission introduces variation; genealogies and rituals drift over generations. The archive preserves signal against noise, but its scope is narrow — only divination is inscribed. Surveillance is personal: the king's agents observe and report, but no systematic intelligence apparatus exists.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: The moral order rests on filial piety, ancestral obligation, and hierarchical loyalty. Justice is not abstract but relational: right conduct consists in fulfilling obligations to ancestors, kin, and superiors. The king's justice is enacted through punishment and reward; offenses are relational (rebellion, impiety) rather than individual (theft, murder, though these too are punished).

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: No law code survives from the Shang; law is oral, customary, and royal. Oracle bones record punishments (execution, mutilation) but not the rules that warrant them. The king's word is law in matters brought before him. Customary rules govern lineage affairs, land tenure, and marriage, but these are unwritten and enforced by kin and community.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: The king adjudicates disputes among elites; lineage heads handle local matters. Divination serves as adjudication: the ancestors are asked to judge guilt and determine outcomes. Sanctions are severe — death, mutilation, enslavement — and public. Liability is collective as well as individual; a lineage may suffer for its head's offense.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Rights in the modern sense do not exist; individuals hold status and obligations, not rights. Elites are protected by lineage solidarity and royal favor; commoners have no recourse against superiors. Compliance is enforced by kinship pressure, community sanction, and royal violence. The compliance burden is heavy; hierarchy pervades all conduct.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: The king and high elites enjoy substantial impunity; subordinates bear the weight of sanction. Wrongs done by superiors to inferiors are not redressed; the hierarchy itself defines justice. Unredressed wrong accumulates among captives, slaves, and defeated enemies — visible in the thousands of sacrificed bodies in royal tombs. Justice is partial and unequal.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: The dominant paradigm is divinatory: knowledge is sought through consultation with ancestors and spirits. The oracle bone system formalizes this inquiry — question, crack, interpretation, record. Empirical inquiry in the modern sense is absent; observation serves ritual rather than theory. The paradigm is performative: knowledge is revealed, not discovered.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Bronze metallurgy represents the highest technical achievement: piece-mold casting, alloying, and finishing reach sophisticated levels. Ceramic technology, jade carving, chariot construction, and agricultural technique embody accumulated practical knowledge. Method is transmitted orally and by apprenticeship; no technical manuals exist.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: Education is lineage-based and oral. Scribal training — the ability to read and write oracle bone script — is restricted to a tiny elite. Technical skills are transmitted through craft lineages. The knowledge stock is rich but unevenly distributed: elites control ritual and scribal knowledge; commoners hold practical agricultural and craft skills. Literacy is not yet a general tool; the threshold is just being crossed.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: Technical knowledge is stable; bronze-casting methods persist across generations. Ritual knowledge may drift; genealogies and precedents are vulnerable to memory failure. The oracle bone archive introduces a check on decay: inscribed decisions can be retrieved and compared. But most knowledge remains oral and subject to transmission loss.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: The Shang identity is rooted in ancestral mythology: the royal lineage traces descent from divine progenitors (the high god Di and the semi-divine ancestors). Memory is genealogical; the past is inhabited by named ancestors whose favor must be maintained. Identity is lineage-based: to be Shang is to belong to the network of lineages that acknowledge the king and share in sacrifice.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: The legitimating narrative is ancestral mandate: the king rules because his ancestors ordained it, and he maintains their favor through correct ritual. The oracle bone system dramatizes this narrative — every inscription enacts the king's unique access to ancestral wisdom. Ideology is ritual, not discursive; it is performed rather than argued.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: Bronze ritual vessels — ding, gui, jue — are the supreme artistic achievement: massive, intricately decorated with taotie masks and zoomorphic motifs, cast in piece-molds with technical virtuosity. Jade carving reaches new heights; white nephrite is worked into bi disks, cong tubes, and figural ornaments. Chariot fittings, bone carvings, and ceramics display the same aesthetic of controlled, powerful form. The color palette is dominated by bronze green and jade white; the visual rhetoric is one of ancestral power and cosmic order.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: The bronze aesthetic is at its peak, not yet exhausted. Taotie imagery is potent and central to ritual meaning. No sign of form exhaustion appears; the iconography is intensifying, not hollowing. Meaning is actively renewed through constant sacrifice and inscription. The forms will persist into the Western Zhou, evolving rather than decaying.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: The cosmos is populated by ancestors, spirits, and the high god Di. The living and the dead interpenetrate; ancestors influence harvests, wars, and health. The existential outlook is one of anxious piety: the world is responsive to ritual, and disaster follows neglect. Fatalism coexists with agency — the king can influence outcomes through correct divination and sacrifice, but the ancestors' will is ultimately sovereign.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: Divination is the central sacred practice: pyro-scapulimancy, in which heat-cracked bones reveal ancestral responses to royal queries. Sacrifice accompanies divination: animals, grain, and wine are offered; on major occasions, human victims are killed. Ritual is frequent, elaborate, and expensive; the sacred pervades governance. Devotion is enacted through participation in sacrifice; piety is a communal performance.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: The king is the supreme religious officiant, mediating between the human and ancestral realms. Diviners serve the king; priests tend ancestral shrines. No separate religious institution exists apart from the royal cult; doctrinal authority is vested in the king and the ancestral tradition he embodies. Orthodoxy is not contested; the ritual order is stable.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: The Shang cult is dominant in the core domain but coexists with local cults in subordinate territories. Peripheral peoples (Qiang, fang) have their own spiritual practices, incompletely absorbed. No external religion challenges the Shang cosmology; syncretism is localized and subordinate. The trajectory is consolidation, not diffusion.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: No disenchantment is visible. The sacred is intensifying: oracle bone inscriptions multiply, sacrifice escalates, and royal ritual becomes more elaborate. The spiritual need is fully anchored in the ancestral cult. If anything, the threshold being crossed — the inscription of divination — strengthens the sacred by giving it material permanence. The residue of disenchantment has not yet begun to accumulate; that will come in later centuries when the mandate passes to the Zhou and the Shang ancestors lose their cosmic centrality.

docs.title: 2,500 BCE – 2,000 BCE — Longshan Horizon and Proto-Urban Development
docs.text: Summary: A Long-Term Trend across the Yellow and Yangtze River Basins as the Longshan cultural horizon integrates regional populations into walled proto-urban centers with marked social stratification, elite control of jade and divination, and incipient political confederations—all coordinated through oral command rather than written record. The single most causal factor is the concentration of surplus and coercive capacity within walled enclosures, which enabled ranked elites to emerge and persist across generations without any literate administration.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: The loess plateau of the middle Yellow River, the alluvial North China Plain, and the lower Yangtze delta remain the principal settlement zones, with the Shandong highlands and the Yiluo River corridor emerging as secondary nodes; movement across the terrain depends on river corridors and overland paths through the loess, which channel interaction and concentrate populations at river confluences and defensible promontories.

Climate Regime & Volatility: The late Holocene cooling trend intensifies, ending the Climatic Optimum; monsoon variability increases, with flood events recorded in alluvial sediments and droughts suggested by lake-core proxies; this heightened unpredictability rewards storage and coordination, favoring those communities able to buffer against failed harvests.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: Flooding along the Yellow and Yangtze rivers poses the primary acute hazard, with alluvial deposits documenting major events; seismic activity affects the northwest; the walled towns of the period represent a new investment in fixed defenses, increasing exposure to local hazards while reducing exposure to raiding and war.

Resource & Energy Endowment: Loess soils remain fertile under millet cultivation; the Yangtze delta supports intensive rice paddies; jade from Liaoning and the Yangtze region is actively mined and traded; copper and tin sources are not yet systematically exploited, keeping the material base Neolithic; fuel wood is locally abundant but subject to deforestation around major centers.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Ash pits, refuse middens, and discarded pottery accumulate within and around walled settlements; the larger centers (Taosi, Shimao) generate substantial organic and ceramic waste, but the absorptive capacity of the surrounding loess and alluvium remains adequate; no evidence of systemic pollution or sink saturation.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: Aggregation into larger settlements raises exposure to fecal-oral pathogens; skeletal evidence from Taosi and Shimao shows trauma from violence alongside infectious disease markers; background mortality remains high but compatible with population growth.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: Millet in the north and rice in the south provide the caloric base; pigs and dogs contribute protein; dietary breadth narrows compared to earlier foraging phases, with some skeletal evidence of nutritional stress during poor harvests; elite burials suggest better nutrition for the privileged few.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Healing remains a household and ritual function; shamanic specialists—whose oral invocations accompany scapulimancy—likely double as healers; no institutional medical capacity exists; recovery from injury depends on kin care and communal support.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Pairing practices are inferred from burial patterns, which show paired and group interments; kinship structures are organized through oral genealogies and residence rules; the biological capacity to reproduce is unconstrained, with demographic growth evident in settlement expansion.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Population density rises as walled centers draw in surrounding populations; Taosi may have housed 10,000–20,000 people at its peak; the age structure skews young, with high fertility offsetting high child mortality; migration from smaller villages into proto-urban centers is demographically significant.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: The dependent load of the aged, infirm, and orphaned is absorbed by kin groups; elite households may support larger retinues; no institutional mechanisms for caring for dependents exist; the productive cohort sustains the load without visible strain.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: Millet and rice agriculture, supplemented by pig husbandry, provide the subsistence base; the provisioning floor sits above bare survival for most, with storage in pits and granaries buffering against seasonal shortfalls; the walled centers concentrate surplus, raising their floor above that of outlying villages.

Energy Capture & Conversion: Human and animal muscle remain the sole power sources; fire is used for cooking, pottery production, and limited metallurgy (copper smelting is emerging but not yet dominant); the per-capita work ceiling is constrained by the limits of muscle power and simple tools.

Labor Organization & Coercion: Labor is organized by kinship and residence, with corvée-like mobilization evident in the construction of massive rammed-earth walls (Shimao's walls required hundreds of thousands of person-days); the degree of coercion is unclear, but the scale of construction implies coordinated command over labor, possibly including captives.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Agricultural surplus is generated above subsistence, enabling craft specialization in jade carving, pottery production, and nascent copper working; the surplus flow is expanding, supporting larger populations and more elaborate elite consumption.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: Granaries and storage pits proliferate; the walled centers concentrate reserves, giving elites control over buffering capacity; the accumulated stock is sufficient to weather one or two failed harvests, but multi-year drought would strain even the best-provisioned centers.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: Long-distance exchange networks move jade from Liaoning and the Yangtze to Longshan centers in Shandong and the Yellow River valley; pottery styles circulate regionally; no evidence of market exchange—all trade is embedded in kinship and ritual networks, coordinated orally.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: Jade objects, fine pottery, and possibly pig feasts serve as stores of value and media of deferred reciprocity; no currency or standardized unit of account exists; obligations are tracked in memory and oral agreement, creating dense webs of social debt.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: Elites extract surplus through tribute, corvée, and control of storage; redistribution occurs through feasting and ritual display; the extraction load is unclear but sustainable, as the productive base continues to grow rather than contract.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Wealth is concentrated in elite burials at Taosi, Fanshan, and Shimao, which contain hundreds of jade objects; the non-elite majority possesses little beyond household goods; the distribution is widening as the period progresses, with sumptuary distinctions hardening.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Pottery shards, food refuse, and ash are discarded in middens; the material waste load is locally significant but not systemically problematic; no evidence of financial mispricing or debt accumulation in the absence of a monetary system.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Kinship is organized through patrilineal or bilateral descent groups, with inheritance rules passed down orally; elite lineages distinguish themselves through access to jade, burial rites, and oral genealogies linking them to ancestors; marriage alliances connect lineages across settlements.

Association & Mutual Aid: Village communities provide mutual aid for agriculture, construction, and defense; the walled centers formalize this cooperation under elite direction; guilds or craft associations are not yet evident, but specialized jade carvers and potters work within elite households.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: Feasts mark agricultural cycles, funerals, and political gatherings; ritual music (drums, bone flutes) accompanies ceremonies; sociability is embedded in kinship and residence rather than autonomous leisure institutions.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: Social stratification is marked and growing; elite burials at Taosi contain hundreds of jade objects and evidence of human sacrifice, while non-elite burials are sparse; status boundaries are hardening, though not yet into rigid castes; factional blocs organized around rival lineages are likely.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: No bureaucracy or written records exist; all administration is oral and personal, exercised through the authority of chiefs, elders, and ritual specialists; the "state" exists only as the personal reach of the leader and the memory of the community; administrative capacity is thin and dependent on the leader's presence.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: Walled settlements imply organized defense; the construction of walls and the evidence of violence (skulls embedded in Shimao's walls) suggest coercive capacity sufficient to wage war and execute captives; weaponry is stone (axes, maces) and bone, with bronze not yet militarily significant; the apparatus is sufficient to dominate surrounding villages but not to project power far beyond the center's hinterland.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: Violence between centers is endemic, as evidenced by burnt settlements and sacrificial victims; disorder is contained within the walls by elite authority but not eliminated; the friction between lineages and between centers is managed through ritual, marriage alliance, and occasional warfare rather than institutional adjudication.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: Leadership is personal and charismatic, exercised through command of ritual, surplus, and force; the chiefs of Taosi and Shimao are figures of concentrated authority, their legitimacy enacted through oral pronouncement and ritual performance rather than written law.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: Legitimacy rests on ancestral blessing, demonstrated by divination (scapulimancy without inscriptions), and on the leader's capacity to provide and protect; allegiance is held so long as the chief delivers; disaffection is expressed through migration or rebellion rather than legal challenge.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: The will to build walls, wage war, and conduct mass sacrifice demonstrates strong collective resolve, directed by elite leadership; the ruling groups cohere around lineage loyalty; succession is contested, as evidenced by the violent destruction of some elite compounds.

External Relations & Posture: Relations among Longshan centers are competitive; jade exchange networks imply some cooperation, but the walled settlements and evidence of warfare indicate a baseline of rivalry; no single center dominates the horizon; alignment is fluid and situational.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: The mood is one of competitive expansion; elites display confidence through elaborate burials and monumental construction; the radius of trust extends within the lineage and the walled center but not much beyond; intergroup relations are marked by wariness and rivalry.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: Some centers are abandoned or destroyed during the period, suggesting episodes of disaffection or defeat; the collapse of Liangzhu around 2,300 BCE, possibly due to flooding and social breakdown, illustrates the fragility of proto-urban authority when will and legitimacy fail; spent will is re-anchored in successor centers rather than accumulating as systemic despair.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Speech is the sole medium of high-bandwidth communication; the Sino-Tibetan languages of the Yellow River populations and the unattested languages of the Yangtze region provide mutual intelligibility within communities but barriers between regions; no writing exists; all coordination is oral.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Information travels at the speed of messengers on foot or by boat; the walled centers concentrate information within their walls; rumors, commands, and news pass through kinship networks; no amplification beyond the reach of voice and memory.

Record, Storage & Persistence: Memory is the sole record; oral tradition preserves genealogies, ritual formulas, and technical knowledge; the death of a specialist can mean the loss of knowledge; no durable external record exists except in the mute form of artifacts and architecture.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: Discourse is shaped by ritual propriety and the authority of elders and chiefs; taboos govern speech about the dead and the sacred; censorship is personal and situational, enforced by social pressure rather than institutional apparatus.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: Attention is commanded by the chief and the ritual specialist; feasts and ceremonies amplify messages to assembled audiences; the dynamics of virality are limited by the size of the gathering and the reach of voice.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: Oral transmission introduces drift and distortion across generations; the mechanisms for clearing error are ritual repetition and the authority of elders; verification is limited to consensus and internal coherence; noise accumulates slowly but inexorably.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Justice is conceived as reciprocity within kinship and revenge against outsiders; the ancestors sanction right conduct; the sacrifice of captives and the display of severed heads at Shimao suggest a morality that permits extreme violence against enemies while demanding loyalty within the group.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: No written law exists; all rules are oral custom, enforced by elders and chiefs; taboos govern conduct toward ancestors, the dead, and the sacred; the regulatory corpus is embedded in memory and practice, evolving through oral negotiation.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: Disputes are adjudicated by elders, chiefs, or ritual specialists; divination (scapulimancy) provides supernatural warrant for decisions; sanctions range from shaming to exile to execution; the caseload is small enough for personal adjudication to keep pace.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Rights are group rights, vested in lineage and residence; individual autonomy is constrained by kinship obligation; the compliance burden is high for those subject to corvée and tribute, lower for elites who command rather than obey.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: Elite impunity is substantial; the powerful can sacrifice captives, extract labor, and punish the disobedient without external check; the wronged may seek revenge through kinship or migration, but institutional redress is absent; impunity accumulates within elite circles but is periodically discharged through violent succession or center collapse.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: Inquiry is practical and ritual rather than theoretical; knowledge of agriculture, jade carving, and construction is empirically grounded; the reigning paradigm is cosmological, explaining events through ancestral will and cosmic forces accessible only to diviners.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Rammed-earth wall construction, jade carving with abrasive techniques, wheel-made pottery, and incipient copper smelting represent the technical frontier; methods are transmitted orally from master to apprentice; no written manuals exist.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: Education is apprenticeship within the household or craft group; literacy is zero; the knowledge stock is held in living memory and transmitted orally; skill distribution is uneven, with specialized crafts concentrated in elite households at major centers.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: Techniques lost with the death of masters are not recoverable; the collapse of Liangzhu likely resulted in knowledge loss (its jade-carving tradition did not fully transfer to successor cultures); obsolescence is slow but irreversible without external record.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: Identity is rooted in lineage and place; origin narratives, ancestor cults, and oral genealogies define who belongs; the trauma of Liangzhu's collapse and the triumphs of Taosi's construction are remembered in oral tradition, shaping collective memory.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: Legitimacy is narrated through ancestral blessing and ritual efficacy; the chief's right to rule is demonstrated by successful divination, abundant harvests, and victory in war; no written ideology exists—legitimation is performed orally and enacted ritually.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: Black burnished pottery, jade cong and bi, turquoise inlay, and painted designs constitute the visual vocabulary; elite burials display sumptuary distinction; architecture emphasizes rammed-earth platforms and walls; the aesthetic is austere, geometric, and ritually charged.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: The jade complex inherited from Liangzhu is absorbed and transformed rather than exhausted; new forms (Longshan black pottery) emerge alongside older ones; no evidence of form exhaustion or anomie—the symbolic vocabulary remains vital and generative.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: The cosmos is populated by ancestors, spirits, and forces accessible through divination; human fate is tied to ancestral favor; the existential outlook is fatalistic regarding natural hazards but activist regarding ritual intervention—the proper rite can secure blessings and avert disaster.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: Scapulimancy (oracle bone divination without inscription) is the premier ritual technology; the diviner heats animal bones and interprets cracks as ancestral messages; feasts, burials, and sacrifices (including human sacrifice at Shimao) enact the sacred; devotion is collective and commanded rather than individual and voluntary.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: No separate priesthood exists; ritual authority is vested in chiefs and lineage heads who also hold political power; doctrine is oral tradition, not codified scripture; institutional reach extends only as far as the chief's personal network.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: The jade complex (cong, bi) diffuses from the lower Yangtze across the Longshan horizon, indicating spiritual borrowing; regional cosmologies interact and blend; no single orthodoxy dominates; the direction is toward greater integration without uniformity.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: The sacred remains potent; there is no evidence of secularizing drift or disenchantment; the collapse of Liangzhu may have been interpreted as ancestral disfavor, but the response was to seek new sacred centers rather than abandon the cosmology; the spiritual need is re-anchored at Taosi, Shimao, and successor sites.

docs.title: 5,000 BCE – 3,500 BCE — Middle Neolithic Regional Diversification
docs.text: Summary: Across fifteen centuries the farming villages of the Yellow and Yangtze basins multiply, diverge, and knit themselves into distinct regional traditions—Yangshao painted pottery in the middle Yellow River, Dawenkou jade and elaborate mortuary rites in Shandong, Majiabang and Songze wet-rice communities in the lower Yangtze—while exchange corridors move goods, styles, and probably spoken lore across hundreds of kilometers; the chief causal factor is demographic growth on a now-secure agricultural base, which drives village fission and territorial expansion until regional cultural boundaries crystallize, all governed through spoken tradition alone.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: The middle Yellow River cuts through loess terraces that yield easily to digging sticks and hoes, while the lower Yangtze spreads across alluvial plains and lake-margin wetlands suited to paddy rice; corridors along tributary valleys and the Huai River drainage connect these zones, though ridges and marshes impose friction that encourages local clustering rather than continuous settlement.

Climate Regime & Volatility: The Holocene Climatic Optimum continues: monsoon rainfall is strong and reliable, winters milder than in preceding millennia, and the northern millet zone receives sufficient summer precipitation while the southern rice zone enjoys long, warm growing seasons; interannual variability remains, but no sustained droughts or floods punctuate the archaeological record severely enough to collapse settlement.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: Localized flooding along river courses is endemic, prompting villages to occupy terrace edges or elevated ground; earthquake risk exists along fault systems but leaves no catastrophic horizon in the stratigraphy; wildfire threatens the forested margins of expanding farmland, and slash-and-burn clearance is itself a controlled hazard.

Resource & Energy Endowment: Loess soils in the north replenish nutrients through wind-borne deposition, while alluvial silts in the south renew fertility with seasonal floods; timber for construction and fuel is locally abundant though receding as clearance advances; stone for grinding tools is quarried regionally, and jade sources—Liaoning, Jiangsu, and points farther—supply prestige goods through exchange.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Midden accumulation around villages grows with population, but settlements are small enough and turnover frequent enough that abandoned sites revegetate; river systems carry organic waste downstream; no evidence of regional degradation, though localized soil depletion may prompt village relocation after decades of cultivation.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: Endemic gastrointestinal and parasitic infections persist wherever humans cluster near stagnant water and animal pens; childhood mortality remains high, but adult skeletal evidence suggests moderate lifespans without epidemic spikes; malaria may be present in the southern wetlands.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: Millet in the north and rice in the south now provide staple carbohydrates; supplementary protein comes from pigs, dogs, fish, and hunted game; dental caries appear in rice-dependent populations, but stature is stable or improving relative to Late Pleistocene foragers; vitamin deficiencies remain possible where diets narrow.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Wound care, herbal remedies, and midwifery are transmitted orally within kin groups; shamanic practitioners likely mediate healing rituals; skeletal evidence of healed fractures indicates survival through injury; no specialized medical caste is visible, and care capacity is limited to village-scale reciprocity.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Monogamous or mildly polygynous pair-bonding is inferred from house sizes and burial pairing; exogamous marriage between villages is probable given genetic diversity; fertility is high enough to drive population growth, constrained mainly by infant mortality and resource limits.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Population expands from nucleated villages of a few hundred into networks of dozens of settlements per regional culture; birth-to-death ratios favor growth, and migration flows outward as daughter villages hive off from parent sites; density remains low by later standards—perhaps 5–20 persons per square kilometer in core areas.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: The aged and infirm are visible in burials but not in numbers that strain productive capacity; infant mortality absorbs a large fraction of births; communal storage and kinship obligations buffer the dependent load without evidence of crisis.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: Millet agriculture in the north and rice paddies in the south secure the caloric floor; gardens provide vegetables; pigs and dogs supply protein; foraging supplements the cultivated base; famine risk is reduced but not eliminated when harvests fail.

Energy Capture & Conversion: Human labor remains the primary motive force, supplemented by fire for land clearance, cooking, and pottery kilns; no draft animals yet harness muscle power for plowing; per-capita work output is modest, gating the scale of construction and craft production.

Labor Organization & Coercion: Households organize their own cultivation; communal labor for larger tasks—house-raising, ditch-digging, perhaps kiln-firing—is coordinated through kinship obligation and oral agreement rather than coercion; no evidence of slave-taking or corvée.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Surplus is modest but sufficient to support part-time craft specialists—potters, jade-workers, basket-weavers—and to provision communal feasts; granary pits indicate multi-season storage; the surplus remains village-scale, not aggregated into regional treasuries.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: Subterranean storage pits preserve grain against spoilage and rodents; household and communal reserves buffer against single-season shortfalls; multi-year famines would exhaust reserves, but no such collapse is recorded in the archaeology.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: Long-distance exchange moves jade from northeastern and southeastern sources, marine shell from the coast, and distinctive pottery styles along river corridors; exchange is embedded in reciprocity and gift-giving, not market trade; no standardized value medium exists.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: Jade objects, fine ceramics, and ornaments serve as stores of prestige and potential reciprocity obligations; deferred exchange operates through oral memory of who owes whom; no currency or accounting beyond remembered claims.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: Village leaders or lineage heads likely coordinate feasting and redistribution, extracting contributions through social pressure rather than formal taxation; no palatial storehouses or bureaucratic apparatus; redistribution is oral, personal, and bounded by face-to-face relations.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Burial goods show modest differentiation—some graves richer in pottery, jade, or pig mandibles—but no extreme concentration; wealth is defended by kinship solidarity and communal reputation rather than fortification or armed retainers.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Broken pottery, food refuse, and ash accumulate in middens; organic waste decomposes or is scattered on fields; no toxic byproducts; settlement relocation after decades may be partly a response to midden saturation and local soil exhaustion.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Clan and lineage structure, organized through oral genealogy, determines residence, marriage eligibility, and access to land; inheritance likely follows patrilineal or cognatic descent depending on region; household clusters in village layouts suggest extended-family compounds.

Association & Mutual Aid: Reciprocal labor exchange, communal storage, and collective ritual bind households within villages; inter-village exchange alliances extend mutual aid across the landscape; no formal associations beyond kinship and locality are visible.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: Communal feasting, musical instruments (bone flutes, pottery drums), and decorative arts suggest organized sociability; ceramic styles may mark group identity; play and festival punctuate the agricultural calendar, reinforcing bonds through shared pleasure.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: Status differentiation is emerging but not rigid—richer burials, larger houses, finer goods—yet no hereditary elite is archaeologically certain; elders, skilled craft-workers, and shamanic figures likely hold prestige; boundaries between villages and regions are cultural, not caste-based.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: No formal administration exists; village affairs are managed through oral deliberation, elder authority, and consensus; inter-village relations are negotiated face-to-face or through kin networks; no bureaucracy, no archive, no permanent office.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: Weapons include bows, stone axes, and bone or stone-tipped spears; violence is attested by occasional skeletal trauma, but no standing military or fortification appears in this window; coercion remains interpersonal, not institutionalized.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: Village fission and migration discharge social friction by allowing discontented lineages to depart; no evidence of endemic warfare or widespread violence; the social fabric is loose enough that exit, not rebellion, resolves grievance; disorder residue is low.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: Leaders are likely lineage heads or charismatic individuals skilled in ritual, oratory, or craft; authority is personal, not official, and must be renewed through persuasion, generosity, and demonstrated competence; no hereditary chieftainship is certain.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: Allegiance flows to kin, ancestors, and local spirits rather than to abstract institutions; loyalty is face-to-face, conditional, and reinforced by reciprocity; no concept of sovereignty or state commands obedience.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: Collective action is achievable for village-scale projects—house construction, ritual feasting, perhaps defense—but coordination beyond the village is episodic and negotiated; no permanent polity concentrates will.

External Relations & Posture: Relations among regional cultures are mediated by exchange, intermarriage, and probably oral diplomacy; no evidence of conquest or tributary relations; competition exists but is channeled through prestige rather than warfare.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: The mood is expansive—population growing, land available, harvests reliable—fostering confidence and willingness to colonize new ground; trust extends through kin and exchange partners but not beyond; intergroup suspicion remains a check on cooperation.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: No evidence of widespread disaffection; the outlet of migration absorbs malcontents; anomie and exhaustion are not archaeologically visible; will remains localized and renewable.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Spoken language is universal within communities; regional dialects likely diverge as populations spread, but mutual intelligibility persists within cultural zones; no writing; all complex communication is oral.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Information travels at walking pace along river corridors and trade routes; oral messengers, seasonal gatherings, and exchange visits move news and innovation; transmission velocity is slow but sufficient for regional style diffusion over generations.

Record, Storage & Persistence: Memory is the sole archive; genealogies, mythic narratives, and technical know-how are stored in trained minds and transmitted through speech and demonstration; nothing is retrievable once the knower dies without teaching a successor.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: Discourse is face-to-face and regulated by kinship etiquette; taboos govern speech about the dead, the sacred, and possibly clan secrets; no formal censorship, but social pressure shapes what may be said and to whom.
