Leadership & Personal Authority: Editors (Nekrasov, Chernyshevsky, Mikhailovsky, Struve) become intellectual leaders whose opinions shape movements. Critics (Belinsky, Dobrolyubov, Pisarev) wield immense influence.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: The thick journal earns legitimacy by speaking truths the state suppresses; readers feel allegiance to "their" journal as to a cause.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: Journals articulate and mobilize will—campaigns for emancipation, against famine relief corruption, for constitutional reform. The word precedes the deed.

External Relations & Posture: Russian journals engage Western ideas—French, German, English—translating and adapting them. Émigré publications (Herzen's Kolokol) feed into domestic discourse.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: Reading a particular journal signals political and moral identity; subscription lists are communities of sentiment. Enthusiasm or despair flows through lead articles.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: Repeated suppression breeds cynicism; the "superfluous man" of 1840s fiction embodies educated paralysis. By 1930, the thick journal tradition is absorbed into party organs, and independent will is extinguished.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Literacy is the threshold; until the 1890s, only 10–20% can read Russian. Journals address the educated elite—perhaps 1–2 million readers by 1900.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Monthly publication cycles mean news is old by arrival; journals compensate with analysis, criticism, and serialized fiction that reward slower reading.

Record, Storage & Persistence: Bound volumes accumulate in libraries; back issues are cited, quoted, and reprinted. The journal record becomes the intelligentsia's collective memory.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: "Aesopian language"—allusion, allegory, historical parallel—evades censors. Literary criticism encodes political commentary (Belinsky on Gogol, Dobrolyubov on Turgenev). Censors often miss the subtext.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: Lead articles circulate beyond subscribers; excerpts are copied, read aloud, and debated. A single review (Belinsky's 1847 letter to Gogol) can define a generation's sensibility.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: Factional polemics generate heat as well as light; accusations of apostasy, careerism, and government service inject noise. Authenticity is precious and contested.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: The intelligentsia defines itself by moral seriousness; the journal is a pulpit for secular preaching. Justice, truth, and the people's welfare are constant themes.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: Censorship statutes (1804, 1826, 1865) define what may be published; editors learn the boundaries and push them. The 1865 reform replaces preventive with punitive censorship for capitals, shifting risk to publishers.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: Editors face fines, suspension, and closure; contributors risk exile. The law is unpredictable—severity depends on political climate and personal connections.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: No right to publish exists; everything is privilege. Compliance with censorship is mandatory for legal operation.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: Censors and officials face no accountability; arbitrary suppression is normal. After 1917, Bolshevik monopoly replaces tsarist arbitrariness with party discipline.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: Thick journals transmit European philosophy (Hegel, Comte, Marx) and generate Russian syntheses (Slavophilism, Populism, legal Marxism). The critic as thinker dominates.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Printing technology advances; stereotyping, lithography, and rotary presses increase output. Typewriters accelerate manuscript production after 1880.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: Universities and gymnasia produce the authors and readers; the journal completes education by providing ongoing intellectual engagement.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: Ideas supersede rapidly: Hegelianism yields to materialism, Populism to Marxism. Older journals seem dated; new ones launch to capture new currents.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: The thick journal constructs a canon—Pushkin, Gogol, Turgenev, Dostoevsky, Tolstoy—serialized, reviewed, and consecrated. The journal is the church of Russian letters.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: Each journal advances a worldview: Westernizer liberalism (Vestnik Evropy), radical democracy (Sovremennik), Populism (Otechestvennye Zapiski), legal Marxism (Nachalo). The narrative justifies the opposition.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: Journal aesthetics evolve from austere typography (1800s) to illustrated covers (1880s). Serialized novels shape literary form—the "thick" format demands length.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: By 1900, the thick-journal model is challenged by daily newspapers and cheap illustrated weeklies. After 1917, party journals (Novyi Mir, Krasnaia Nov) inherit the form but not the independence; by 1930, the intelligentsia as autonomous stratum is liquidated.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: The intelligentsia oscillates between religious doubt and secular faith; journals host debates over materialism, spiritualism, and the "accursed questions" of God and immortality.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: Reading the monthly issue is a ritual; the literary anniversary (Pushkin 1880, Gogol 1909) becomes a secular feast day.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: The Orthodox Church is largely absent from thick-journal culture, which is lay and often anticlerical. Tolstoyan and mystical currents find expression, but institutional religion does not.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: Western secularism, German idealism, and later Marxism displace Orthodox piety among the educated; the journal is the vector of displacement.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: The thick journal's sacralization of literature and criticism creates its own disenchantment: by 1930, the Bolshevik state has made literature a party instrument, and the independent sacred voice is silenced.

docs.title: 1914 CE – 1921 CE — War, Revolution, and Civil War
docs.text: The binding constraint is institutional collapse under compound shock: four years of industrial war drain the empire's reserves, shatter the army's cohesion, and delegitimize the autocracy; the February Revolution unseats the tsar but the Provisional Government cannot stabilize authority or end the war; the October Revolution installs a Bolshevik dictatorship that imposes press monopoly, expropriates property, and fights a civil war whose violence, blockade, and requisitioning push the population to the edge of subsistence. Print — newspapers, decrees, broadsides, pamphlets — saturates the revolutionary rupture as the primary channel for mobilization, agitation, and command, even as paper shortages and censorship constrict all other publishing.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: The East European Plain extends from the Baltic to the Black Sea, traversed by rivers and, since the 1860s, by a rail network radiating from Moscow and Petrograd. The front line runs through western borderlands — Poland, the Baltic, Galicia, then Ukraine and the Caucasus — while interior distances complicate supply. Rail is the critical artery; its seizure determines which faction controls provisioning, troop movement, and communications.

Climate Regime & Volatility: Harsh winters impose logistical constraints on campaigns; the 1916–1917 winter sees fuel and food shortages compound urban misery. Harvests in 1916 and 1920 are adequate, but procurement failures and blockade turn sufficiency into famine.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: Typhus, cholera, and influenza (1918–1919 pandemic) sweep through populations weakened by malnutrition, crowded refugee columns, and collapsed sanitation. The Civil War zone experiences epidemic mortality exceeding combat deaths.

Resource & Energy Endowment: The empire possesses coal (Donbas), oil (Baku), iron (Urals), and vast grain-producing regions, but war and civil conflict sever access. Baku changes hands repeatedly; the Donbas lies in contested territory; grain regions fall to Whites, Greens, and foreign intervention before Red reconquest. The energy base is present but inaccessible.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Urban sanitation collapses; corpses accumulate unburied during worst epidemics; industrial effluent ceases as factories close. Environmental pressure is low because production itself has stopped.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: Typhus spreads explosively, killing millions during 1918–1921. The 1918 influenza pandemic adds to mortality. Endemic tuberculosis worsens with overcrowding and malnutrition. Military and civilian death rates spike far above the prewar baseline.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: Urban populations starve as grain requisitioning and transport breakdown cut rations. Petrograd's population falls from 2.4 million (1917) to under 700,000 (1920) through death, flight, and mobilization. Peasants hoard grain against requisition squads. Caloric intake falls well below subsistence in cities and contested zones.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Military medical services strain beyond capacity; civilian hospitals lose staff and supplies. Doctors and nurses flee, emigrate, or are conscripted. The Red Army prioritizes its own wounded; civilian care collapses outside party channels.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Wartime separation and mortality depress fertility; marriages postpone; births fall sharply. The demographic gap persists into the 1920s.

Demographic Renewal & Density: The empire enters the war with 170 million; by 1921, the Soviet territory holds perhaps 135 million — losses from combat, disease, famine, emigration, and territorial cession (Poland, Finland, Baltic states). Cities empty; rural areas absorb refugees.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: War orphans, widows, crippled veterans, and displaced refugees overwhelm relief capacity. The 1921 famine in the Volga region adds five million deaths and millions more orphaned children.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: By 1918, the provisioning floor collapses in cities. War Communism (1918–1921) requisitions grain at gunpoint, leaving peasants with seed grain or less. Urban workers subsist on rations distributed through workplace canteens. Barter displaces money; the ruble hyperinflates into worthlessness. Survival depends on access to party channels or the black market.

Energy Capture & Conversion: Coal production falls by 80%; oil output plummets as Baku is contested. Factories close for lack of fuel. Petrograd's electrical supply intermittently fails. Wood replaces coal where possible; furniture and books are burned for heat.

Labor Organization & Coercion: The Bolshevik state militarizes labor; Trotsky proposes labor armies. Workers are tied to enterprises by ration cards. Peasants are subject to grain requisitioning enforced by armed detachments. Coercion replaces wages as the primary labor mobilization mechanism.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Industrial output falls to perhaps 10–20% of prewar levels. Agricultural production declines as peasants plant only for subsistence, anticipating confiscation. There is no surplus; the system consumes its capital stock.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: Reserves exhaust by 1918. The treasury is empty; gold reserves are seized and spent. There is no buffer against the 1921 drought.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: The market economy collapses under War Communism's prohibitions. Internal trade is illegal (though pervasive on the black market). External trade is blockaded by the Allies until 1920. Rail transport, the only efficient logistics, is monopolized by military needs.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: The ruble hyperinflates; by 1921 it has lost essentially all purchasing power. Barter, in-kind payment, and ration distribution replace monetary exchange. Credit ceases to exist.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: The state extracts through prodrazvyorstka (grain requisitioning), seizing peasant output. Redistribution occurs through ration tiers — workers and soldiers prioritized, former bourgeois ("lishentsy") last. The extraction regime fuels peasant revolts.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: The October Revolution expropriates property — land, factories, banks, buildings. Former owners lose all. Concealment of valuables, emigration with portable wealth, and barter hoarding are the only asset-defense strategies. By 1921, wealth is nearly leveled — at subsistence.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Industrial waste ceases with production. Urban refuse accumulates uncollected. Financial debris — worthless bonds, canceled contracts, unredeemable deposits — is simply voided by revolutionary decree.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Revolutionary legislation abolishes estate-based inheritance and introduces civil marriage and easy divorce. Family structure strains under separation, death, and displacement. Orphanages fill.

Association & Mutual Aid: Pre-revolutionary associations — zemstvos, cooperatives, professional societies — are dissolved or absorbed into Soviet structures. The party, soviets, and trade unions monopolize associational life. Informal mutual aid persists in villages and among neighbors.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: Organized leisure collapses; fuel shortages close theaters and cinemas. The party sponsors agitprop performances and mass festivals. Street life diminishes under curfew and fear.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: Revolutionary upheaval inverts the old hierarchy. Former nobles, officials, and bourgeois become disenfranchised "former people" (byvshie), subject to discrimination in rations, housing, and employment. Workers and poor peasants are rhetorically valorized, though party cadres form a new elite. Class origin becomes the primary status marker.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: The tsarist bureaucracy disintegrates; the Provisional Government fails to build a replacement. The Bolsheviks construct a new party-state apparatus — the Cheka (secret police), the Red Army, local soviets — but capacity is low, staffed by inexperienced cadres and forced to coerce compliance. Corruption, arbitrariness, and incompetence are endemic.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: The old army dissolves in 1917; the Provisional Government cannot rebuild it. The Bolsheviks create the Red Army (1918) under Trotsky, using conscription, military specialists (former tsarist officers), and commissar supervision. The Cheka conducts Red Terror — summary executions, hostage-taking, concentration camps — against class enemies and opponents. White armies, foreign interventionists, and peasant insurgents (Greens) contest Bolshevik control. The Civil War is won by 1921 through superior organization, central position, and ruthlessness.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: The period is maximal disorder — revolution, civil war, banditry, pogroms (especially in Ukraine, 1919–1920), peasant uprisings (Tambov, 1920–1921), worker strikes (Kronstadt, 1921). The state responds with terror; order is imposed by force, not consent.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: Lenin commands Bolshevik allegiance through ideological authority and tactical acumen. Trotsky builds the Red Army and inspires through oratory. Local commanders and commissars exercise personal authority in the chaos. Kerensky fails to command allegiance; White generals lack unified leadership.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: The tsarist regime loses legitimacy by February 1917; the Provisional Government never acquires it. The Bolsheviks claim legitimacy through soviets and class mission, but rely on coercion. Peasants accept Bolshevik land decrees but resist requisitioning.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: The Bolshevik party exhibits concentrated will — disciplined, centralized, willing to use unlimited force. Opponents are divided: Whites lack political vision; Greens are local and defensive. The Red victory reflects superior political will as much as material advantage.

External Relations & Posture: The regime signs the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk (March 1918), ceding vast territory to exit the war. Allied intervention supports the Whites but commits insufficiently. The Comintern (1919) promotes world revolution, but no revolution succeeds abroad. By 1921, the regime is isolated but surviving.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: The initial revolutionary moment produces euphoria and utopian expectation; by 1920, exhaustion, fear, and disillusionment predominate. Peasants resent requisitioning; workers strike against hunger; soldiers desert. Trust is confined to immediate circles.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: By 1921, all factions are exhausted. The Kronstadt rebellion expresses disillusionment even among revolutionary sailors. The shift to NEP acknowledges that coercion has reached its limit.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Russian is the dominant language; literacy is perhaps 40% by 1920, rising through Bolshevik campaigns. Ukrainian, Polish, and other languages persist in borderlands. The party communicates through Russian; local agitation uses vernaculars.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Telegraph and rail-borne press remain the primary channels. The party controls telegraph traffic. Newspapers are printed in Petrograd and Moscow and distributed by rail to provincial centers. Oral agitation supplements print where literacy is low.

Record, Storage & Persistence: Archives are seized, reorganized, and partially destroyed in revolutionary transitions. The party builds new record-keeping systems — personnel files, denunciations, surveillance reports — but institutional memory is fragmented. Many pre-revolutionary records survive by accident.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: The Provisional Government briefly permits press freedom; hundreds of newspapers appear across the political spectrum. The Bolsheviks close opposition newspapers (November 1917), establish Glavlit (1922), and impose party control on all publishing. By 1921, only party-approved publications circulate legally. Agitprop dominates; dissent is silenced.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: Newspapers are read aloud in factories and barracks; posters, broadsides, and illustrated placards (ROSTA windows) reach the illiterate. Attention is captured by crisis; amplification is controlled by the party.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: Rumor, misinformation, and propaganda saturate the information environment. Competing factions spread contradictory claims. The party monopoly reduces noise by silencing alternatives, not by establishing truth.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Revolutionary justice replaces tsarist law: class origin determines guilt. "Bourgeois legality" is rejected; revolutionary necessity justifies any action. Peasant moral economy — the right to land and harvest — conflicts with requisitioning.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: Tsarist law is abolished; the Bolsheviks govern by decree. Legal codes are drafted but not yet consolidated. The Cheka operates outside any legal constraint. Revolutionary tribunals dispense summary justice.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: Courts are replaced by tribunals; procedure is minimal. The Cheka conducts extrajudicial executions. Hostage-taking and collective punishment are routine. Liability is determined by class, not act.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Pre-revolutionary rights are void. The 1918 Soviet Constitution proclaims worker rights but provides no enforcement against the state. Compliance with party directives is absolute or fatal.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: Impunity is total for party and Cheka agents; wrong is unredressable for victims. Pogroms in Ukraine kill tens of thousands of Jews with no sanction. The moral residue is vast: mass death, dispossession, and injustice accumulate without reckoning.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: Marxism-Leninism becomes the official paradigm, displacing liberal and conservative thought. Scientific inquiry is disrupted by emigration, closure of institutions, and subordination to ideology. Some scientists remain and adapt.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Technical knowledge is critical for the Red Army and remaining industry. Former specialists (spetsy) are employed under political supervision. Practical method continues; theoretical advance pauses.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: The Bolsheviks prioritize literacy campaigns (likbez) to create a literate proletariat. Schools reopen under Soviet control with new curricula. Universities are disrupted; many professors emigrate. The knowledge stock survives but transmission is interrupted.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: Pre-revolutionary humanistic and religious education is declared obsolete and suppressed. Technical knowledge is preserved; classical learning atrophies. The break in transmission creates gaps that persist.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: The Revolution becomes instant myth — October as the decisive rupture, the proletariat as world-historical agent, Lenin as prophet. Tsarist memory is suppressed; revolutionary martyrology replaces it. National identities (Ukrainian, Georgian) complicate the Russian-centered narrative.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: Marxism-Leninism provides the legitimating narrative: the dictatorship of the proletariat, the transition to socialism, the withering of the state. The narrative justifies terror as historical necessity.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: Revolutionary art flourishes briefly — Constructivism, avant-garde poster design, agitprop theater. Mayakovsky, Meyerhold, Rodchenko. The material culture is impoverished — ragged clothing, repurposed buildings, requisitioned goods — but revolutionary aesthetics embrace the austere.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: Traditional forms are declared exhausted and bourgeois. New revolutionary forms are created but not yet canonized. The transition is generative rather than exhausted; meaning is actively contested.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: Official atheism replaces Orthodox Christianity. Dialectical materialism provides the cosmology: history has direction, class struggle is its engine, communism its terminus. For many, the revolutionary moment carries quasi-religious intensity.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: Revolutionary rituals replace religious ones — red funerals, revolutionary holidays, oath-taking ceremonies. Church services continue but under pressure; clergy are persecuted.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: The Orthodox Church is disestablished, its property confiscated, its hierarchy fractured. The Patriarch Tikhon resists, then accommodates. Sectarians and Old Believers face similar pressure. Religious authority collapses under state assault.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: Atheism is promoted; religious practice recedes in public and persists in private. The revolutionary cause absorbs spiritual energy for many participants.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: The sacred is officially discharged — secularization by decree. For believers, the loss is traumatic. For revolutionaries, the cause provides transcendence. The spiritual residue accumulates: the void is filled by ideology, or left empty.

docs.title: Print Stage in The Iberian Peninsula and Western Mediterranean — 1500 CE – 1930 CE
- 1500 CE – 1598 CE — Habsburg Zenith and Counter-Reformation Print
- 1598 CE – 1700 CE — Habsburg Decline and Baroque Culture
- 1700 CE – 1808 CE — Bourbon Reforms and Enlightened Press
- 1808 CE – 1833 CE — Napoleonic Invasion and Liberal Constitution
- 1833 CE – 1874 CE — Liberal Revolution and Carlist Conflicts
- 1874 CE – 1898 CE — Restoration System and Colonial Collapse
- 1898 CE – 1923 CE — Crisis of Restoration and Mass Politics
- 1923 CE – 1930 CE — Primo de Rivera Dictatorship and Censorship
- 1500 CE – 1930 CE — Inquisition, Index, and Spanish Censorship
- 1500 CE – 1930 CE — Portuguese Print and Atlantic Networks
1700 CE – 1808 CE — Bourbon Reforms and Enlightened Press
docs.text: The Bourbon century transforms print from Counter-Reformation instrument into Enlightenment vehicle, yet the binding constraint remains the Crown's insistence on administrative centralization without political liberalization: periodicals, academies, and economic societies propagate useful knowledge while Inquisitorial censorship persists, so that the public sphere expands within channels the state controls rather than against it, and the reformist press cultivates a readership dependent on royal patronage whose autonomy collapses when invasion shatters the Bourbon order.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: Madrid consolidates as administrative center; the central meseta remains poorly connected to peripheral coastal zones. Roads improve under Charles III but overland transit stays slow compared to maritime routes. Atlantic orientation intensifies as American trade expands, while Mediterranean commerce declines relative to northern Atlantic powers. The Pyrenean barrier channels French influence through limited passes.

Climate Regime & Volatility: The Little Ice Age persists into the early eighteenth century, with harsh winters and variable harvests. Droughts in the meseta and Andalusia periodically stress grain supply. Warmer decades mid-century ease agrarian pressure, though interannual volatility remains significant.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: The 1755 Lisbon earthquake devastates Portuguese printing infrastructure and sends shockwaves through Seville and Cadiz. Periodic floods affect the Guadalquivir and Ebro valleys. Epidemic outbreaks remain localized but disruptive.

Resource & Energy Endowment: American silver continues to flow, though declining from Habsburg-era peaks. The peninsula lacks coal deposits comparable to northern Europe; charcoal and wood remain primary fuels. Water power in Catalonia supports early textile mechanization.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Urban expansion in Madrid, Seville, and Barcelona strains rudimentary sanitation. Rivers carry industrial and domestic waste; sink capacity adequate for the scale of activity, though localized pollution increases near tanneries and dye works.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: Endemic typhus, malaria in lowland Andalusia, and periodic smallpox outbreaks maintain high infant mortality. Urban death rates exceed birth rates; cities depend on rural migration. The mortality baseline improves slightly through the century but remains elevated by northwestern European standards.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: Grain dependency exposes the population to harvest failure. Maize and potatoes spread slowly. Average stature remains low; nutritional deficiency affects working capacity. Slight improvements late century as New World crops diffuse.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Hospital infrastructure expands under Bourbon reforms; royal hospitals in Madrid improve. Medical education advances through anatomical theaters and surgical colleges. Church-run charity hospitals serve the poor; capacity remains uneven between cities and countryside.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Marriage patterns follow western European norms: relatively late marriage age, nuclear household formation. Ecclesiastical control over marriage persists. Fertility rates remain moderately high within marriage.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Population grows from approximately 7.5 million (1717) to 10.5 million (1797). Recovery from seventeenth-century decline proceeds unevenly; coastal regions and Catalonia grow faster than the meseta. Internal migration feeds urban growth.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: High infant mortality reduces the dependency ratio among youth; adult mortality leaves widows and orphans supported through church charity and kinship networks. The dependency load remains manageable as population growth accelerates.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: Grain supply remains precarious; the meseta depends on wheat, the periphery on mixed cropping. The 1766 Esquilache riots reveal urban food insecurity. Liberalization of grain trade under Charles III improves supply flexibility but intensifies price volatility.

Energy Capture & Conversion: Human and animal muscle dominate; water mills power textile production in Catalonia. Charcoal serves metallurgy. Per-capita energy remains low; the agrarian base limits surplus for non-agricultural activity.

Labor Organization & Coercion: Guild structures persist in urban crafts; rural labor varies from smallholding peasants in the north to landless jornaleros in Andalusian latifundia. Wage labor expands in Catalan textiles. Serfdom is absent but labor coercion through debt and custom remains significant in the south.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Catalan textile production grows, supplying American markets. Castilian wool declines as the Mesta loses privileges. Agricultural output rises with population but productivity gains lag. The surplus flows to landlords, church, and Crown rather than reinvestment.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: Municipal granaries (positos) buffer grain supply but prove inadequate in major crises. Royal treasuries depend on American remittances and loans; Bourbon fiscal reforms increase revenue but expenses consistently exceed income. Debt accumulates through each war.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: Cadiz monopolizes American trade until 1778 liberalization opens additional ports. The Consulado system organizes merchant guilds. Internal customs barriers (eliminated 1714 in Crown of Aragon) facilitate Castilian integration. Road improvements under Charles III enhance internal circulation but the network remains thin.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: The Bank of San Carlos (1782) attempts to stabilize credit; royal debt instruments (vales reales) circulate but depreciate. Merchant credit networks operate through family and guild ties. Monetary instability and repeated devaluations erode savings.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: Crown and Church extract through tithes, alcabalas, and ecclesiastical levies. Bourbon reforms attempt to increase royal revenue at Church expense but face resistance. American remittances remain crucial; their decline strains the treasury.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Landownership concentrates among nobility and Church; entailment (mayorazgo) protects aristocratic estates. Urban commercial wealth grows in Barcelona and Cadiz. Inequality intensifies; the propertied defend holdings through legal privilege and ecclesiastical sanctuary.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Urban waste management improves marginally; Madrid's street cleaning advances under Charles III. Industrial waste from Catalan textiles enters rivers with minimal treatment. Financial mispricing accumulates in state debt obligations.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Primogeniture and mayorazgo preserve noble estates; middling groups divide property among heirs. Regional variation persists: stem families in the Basque Country and Catalonia, nuclear households in Castile. Church control over marriage and inheritance law remains firm.

Association & Mutual Aid: Guilds organize urban crafts; cofradias (religious brotherhoods) provide mutual aid and burial. Economic Societies of Friends of the Country (Sociedades Economicas de Amigos del Pais), founded from 1765, create new associational space for provincial elites to discuss agricultural improvement and useful knowledge.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: The tertulia (salon conversation) emerges as a sociable form among urban elites; cafes appear in Madrid and Barcelona. Bullfighting consolidates as spectacle. Carnival and religious festivals structure popular leisure.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: The traditional hierarchy persists: nobility (grandees, hidalgos), clergy, commoners. Limpieza de sangre (blood purity) requirements decline but do not disappear. A nascent bourgeoisie emerges in commercial and textile centers. The gap between propertied and landless widens.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: The Nueva Planta decrees (1707-1716) eliminate Aragonese, Catalan, Valencian, and Majorcan fueros, imposing Castilian administrative uniformity. Bourbon centralization creates intendancies, reorganizes colonial administration. Corruption remains endemic but bureaucratic capacity increases. The Council of Castile oversees censorship and licensing.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: The standing army expands; Bourbon military reforms modernize training and equipment. The navy rebuilds after Habsburg decline, supporting Atlantic trade and colonial defense. Internal order depends on urban police (created 1782 in Madrid) and rural constabulary. The Inquisition retains arrest powers but uses them less frequently.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: The 1766 Esquilache riots demonstrate urban volatility; rural banditry persists in Andalusia and Catalonia. The apparatus contains disorder without eliminating its sources. Regional grievances from abolished fueros simmer in Catalonia and Aragon.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: Charles III (r. 1759-1788) embodies enlightened absolutism; his personal authority enables reform. Ministers Aranda, Floridablanca, and Campomanes drive policy. Under Charles IV (r. 1788-1808), Godoy's favoritism erodes royal prestige. Leadership becomes contested as France revolutionizes.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: Bourbon legitimacy rests on dynastic right consolidated through the War of Spanish Succession (1700-1714). The Crown commands allegiance through patronage, reform success, and Catholic identity. Legitimacy weakens late century as Godoy's regime discredits the court.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: The reformist program demonstrates sustained political will under Charles III; colonial reorganization, economic liberalization, and educational expansion proceed. Under Charles IV, will fragments; court faction undermines coherent policy. The French alliance pulls Spain into ruinous wars.

External Relations & Posture: Alliance with France (Family Compacts) structures foreign policy. Rivalry with Britain shapes colonial defense. Spain fights Britain repeatedly (1739-1748, 1762-1763, 1779-1783, 1796-1808), with mixed results. The French Revolution strains the alliance; war with France (1793-1795) precedes renewed French alignment.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: Enlightenment optimism permeates the ilustrado elite; belief in progress through reform lifts the educated minority. Popular sentiment remains localized, religious, suspicious of foreign influence. The 1766 riots reveal the fragility of reform legitimacy among urban commoners.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: Provincial resentment from abolished fueros persists. Ilustrado reforms alienate traditionalist clergy and commoners without creating a broad reform constituency. By 1808, court scandals, military defeats, and food scarcity exhaust popular patience with the regime.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Castilian serves as the administrative and literary language; Catalan, Basque, and Galician persist in domestic use but lack print presence. Latin declines; French becomes the prestige language among elites. Literacy expands slowly; perhaps 25-30% of males can read by century's end.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: The royal postal system improves; regular courier routes connect major cities. The Gaceta de Madrid (official gazette from 1697) and Mercurio Historico y Politico transmit news weekly. Periodicals reach provincial subscribers within days. Speed remains slow by later standards but adequate for the administrative state.

Record, Storage & Persistence: Royal archives centralize under Bourbon administration; the Archivo General de Simancas and Archivo de Indias systematize colonial records. University libraries and private collections grow. The Inquisitorial archives document censorship activity. Persistence improves through standardized record-keeping.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: The Inquisition retains censorship authority; the Index prohibits heterodox works. Royal licensing (licencia) adds a second filter. Enlightened periodicals like El Pensador (1762-1767) and El Censor (1781-1787) probe limits, discussing social criticism within acceptable bounds. Discourse norms permit economic and agrarian reform discussion but forbid challenges to Church doctrine or royal authority. The band widens under Charles III, contracts after 1789 as revolutionary fear spreads.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: The reading public expands through tertulias, cafes, and Economic Societies. Newspapers and journals circulate among subscribers and in reading rooms. Amplification operates through oral retransmission; the literate read to the illiterate. Attention concentrates among urban elites; rural penetration remains limited.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: Official publications maintain high reliability; the Gaceta de Madrid reports court news accurately. Underground pamphlets and foreign gazettes introduce competing narratives. Noise increases as the French Revolution generates conflicting accounts. Verification depends on reputation and official sourcing.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Catholic teaching provides the moral foundation; charity, hierarchy, and obedience structure the ethical framework. Enlightened reformers introduce utilitarian language of public utility without displacing religious foundations. Popular justice remains oriented toward local custom and patron-client reciprocity.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: The Nueva Recopilacion (1567, updated 1775) codifies Castilian law. Bourbon reforms attempt legal rationalization; the Novisima Recopilacion (1805) consolidates statutes. Colonial law (Leyes de Indias) regulates American territories. Regulatory activity intensifies; decrees on grain trade, guild reform, and Church property multiply.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: Royal courts (audiencias, chancillerias) adjudicate civil and criminal cases. The Inquisition handles heresy and morals offenses with declining frequency. Justice remains slow; case backlogs persist. Sanction ranges from fines and exile to imprisonment; executions decline. Ecclesiastical courts retain jurisdiction over clergy.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Subjects hold traditional rights (fueros) where these survive; Bourbon centralization erodes regional protections. Property rights strengthen for the propertied; the landless lack legal protection against eviction. Compliance burden falls unevenly; guild regulations and licensing requirements constrain urban crafts.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: Noble privilege provides de facto immunity; elite offenders escape justice through connections and sanctuary. The Inquisition's decline reduces religious persecution but leaves institutional impunity unaddressed. Unredressed grievance accumulates among landless laborers and subordinate regions.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: Spanish Enlightenment (Ilustracion) imports French and Italian ideas within limits. Feijoo's Teatro Critico Universal (1726-1740) popularizes empiricism and skepticism toward superstition. Natural history, political economy, and agricultural science constitute active research fronts. The paradigm emphasizes useful knowledge over metaphysical speculation.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Royal factories (tapestries, porcelain, armaments) introduce foreign techniques. The Royal Botanical Garden (1755) and Mining School (1777) train specialists. Catalan textile producers adopt spinning innovations. Applied method advances in surveying, cartography, and civil engineering for road construction.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: University reform attempts modernization; the expulsion of Jesuits (1767) disrupts secondary education but opens institutional space for reform. Primary schools expand under municipal authority. The Colegios Mayores lose their aristocratic monopoly. Literacy and numeracy spread among urban middling groups but the rural majority remains excluded.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: Scholasticism declines in universities; the new science displaces Aristotelian natural philosophy. Inquisitorial censorship retards reception of some European advances but does not halt the transition. The knowledge stock grows; transmission improves through academies and periodicals.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: Imperial memory persists; the Habsburg past figures as golden age now declined. Catholic identity remains central; Spain understands itself as defender of the faith. The Black Legend (foreign anti-Spanish propaganda) shapes defensive cultural posture. Regional identities (Catalan, Basque) survive but lack print expression.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: The Bourbon dynasty legitimates through administrative competence and reform: efficient government, economic improvement, enlightened progress. The language of public utility (utilidad publica) permeates official discourse. Catholic legitimation continues alongside rationalist modernization.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: Neoclassicism displaces Baroque extravagance in official architecture; the Prado, Botanical Garden, and Puerta de Alcala exemplify Bourbon Madrid. Goya spans the period, from tapestry cartoons to royal portraits. Printed books adopt cleaner typography; the Royal Printing Press (Imprenta Real) sets standards. Material culture becomes plainer, more functional among elites.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: Baroque religious intensity fades; Enlightenment taste finds excess distasteful. Religious ceremony continues but loses affective power among educated elites. The Counter-Reformation synthesis exhausts itself; no new cultural synthesis replaces it before the revolutionary crisis.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: Catholic cosmology frames existence; Providence governs history. Among ilustrados, deism and rationalism erode providential certainty without open rejection. The educated hold faith alongside skepticism; the popular majority retains traditional piety. Fatalism coexists with reform optimism.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: Mass attendance, confession, and feast-day observance structure the calendar. Pilgrimages continue; popular devotions to saints and the Virgin persist. Elite participation becomes more formal, less fervent. The gap between official religion and popular piety widens.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: The Church remains wealthy and institutionally powerful; bishops wield significant influence. Bourbon regalism asserts Crown authority over ecclesiastical appointments and revenues. The Jesuits' expulsion (1767) removes the most intellectually active order. Doctrinal orthodoxy persists but enforcement softens. The Inquisition declines; its last execution occurs in 1781.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: Catholicism remains unchallenged domestically; Protestantism does not penetrate. Colonial missions continue in America. The cosmology's reach contracts among educated elites who absorb Enlightenment skepticism through foreign publications and travel.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: Ilustrado critique of superstition, miracles, and clerical excess introduces disenchantment among the educated minority. The sacred does not disappear but loses explanatory power in elite worldviews. Popular religion remains vital but increasingly diverges from elite sensibility. The spiritual need persists without full re-anchoring; the gap between enlightened and popular spirituality widens as a standing tension unresolved by century's end.

docs.title: 1898 CE – 1923 CE — Crisis of Restoration and Mass Politics
docs.text: The binding constraint is the exhaustion of the turno pacifico system as mass politics, labor mobilization, and regional nationalism outpace the oligarchic mechanisms of electoral management, while the printed press proliferates beyond elite control and amplifies every crisis from colonial disaster to military humiliation in Morocco.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: The meseta's centripetal pull toward Madrid persists, but rail integration accelerates after 1900, shrinking journey times between periphery and center; Barcelona-Madrid rail runs in under twelve hours, enabling daily newspaper distribution to provincial capitals within twenty-four hours of printing.

Climate Regime & Volatility: Mediterranean drought cycles recur, stressing dryland wheat cultivation in Castile and Andalusia; the 1905 and 1919 droughts reduce harvests and sharpen rural discontent, pushing migrants toward Barcelona and Bilbao.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: Morocco's Rif terrain proves lethal to conscript columns; the Annual disaster of 1921 kills over eight thousand soldiers in terrain utterly unsuited to Spanish logistical capacity, exposing the army's operational fragility.

Resource & Energy Endowment: Coal imports rise as domestic Asturian seams prove insufficient for industrial expansion; hydroelectric development accelerates after 1910, powering Catalan textiles and Basque metallurgy without solving the coal deficit.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Barcelona's Eixample district concentrates industrial effluent; Nervion River pollution around Bilbao intensifies as iron and steel output climbs; urban sanitation lags behind demographic growth, contributing to tuberculosis persistence.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: The 1918 influenza pandemic kills over 250,000 Spaniards; mortality peaks in autumn 1918, overwhelming inadequate public health infrastructure and exposing the state's inability to protect the population.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: Rural dietary monotony persists; urban workers consume more calories but face adulterated foodstuffs; conscript rejection rates for physical unfitness remain high, signaling generational undernutrition.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Public hospitals expand modestly under Restoration budgets; Catholic charitable nursing remains the primary care structure outside major cities; trained physicians concentrate in Barcelona, Madrid, and provincial capitals.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: Fertility remains high in rural areas but urban birth rates begin declining as working-class women enter textile factories; age at marriage rises slightly in industrial zones.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Population grows from 18.6 million in 1900 to 21.4 million by 1920; emigration to the Americas absorbs roughly 1.5 million between 1900 and 1914, relieving rural pressure but draining Galicia and Asturias of working-age males.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: War deaths in Cuba (1895–1898) and Morocco (1909–1921) create widows and orphans whose support falls to inadequate state pensions and Church charity; the 1918 pandemic leaves orphan cohorts straining extended family resources.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: Andalusian jornaleros live at subsistence margins; bread riots recur in southern towns during drought years; the 1917 general strike partly responds to wartime inflation outpacing wage gains.

Energy Capture & Conversion: Hydroelectric capacity quintuples between 1900 and 1920, shifting industry toward the Pyrenean watersheds and Basque rivers; coal dependency on British imports makes Spain vulnerable to wartime shipping disruptions.

Labor Organization & Coercion: The CNT (anarcho-syndicalist) organizes Catalan workers after 1910; the UGT (socialist) dominates Basque and Asturian unions; pistolerismo—armed conflict between employers' hired gunmen and union militants—kills hundreds in Barcelona between 1919 and 1923.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Catalan textile output doubles during World War I neutral profiteering; Basque iron exports surge to Allied demand; the postwar recession collapses export markets and triggers factory closures.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: State treasury depletes after 1898; Morocco campaigns drain budgets without colonial returns; gold reserves remain thin, limiting monetary intervention against inflation.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: Wartime neutrality opens Atlantic shipping to Spanish exports; the postwar tariff regime protects Catalan textiles but raises consumer prices; Madrid wholesale markets integrate through improved rail.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: The peseta depreciates against gold; Banco de Espana issues fiduciary currency without adequate reserves; commercial credit tightens in the 1921 recession, bankrupting marginal enterprises.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: Consumption taxes fall heaviest on the poor; direct taxation remains weak; land tax evasion by latifundistas is endemic; state revenue barely covers civil administration plus the Morocco garrison.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Landed oligarchy retains Andalusian latifundia; Catalan industrialists accumulate wartime fortunes; land reform proposals die in Cortes committee; urban workers' real wages erode through inflation.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Industrial effluent flows untreated into rivers; urban garbage collection remains rudimentary; Barcelona's old quarter breeds disease vectors amid overcrowding.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Primogeniture persists in land transmission; urban nuclear families become normative among working classes; remittances from American emigrants sustain rural households.

Association & Mutual Aid: Mutual benefit societies multiply among urban workers; Catholic Agrarian Syndicates organize conservative peasants after 1906; the ateneos (popular cultural associations) spread literacy and radical ideas.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: Football clubs proliferate (FC Barcelona 1899, Athletic Bilbao 1898) as working-class spectacle; bullfighting remains the national entertainment; cafes and casinos serve as political meeting spaces.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: The turno system concentrates power in two rotating parties managed by caciques who deliver rural votes through patronage and coercion; industrial bourgeoisie and urban professionals demand entry; workers and regionalists remain excluded.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: Caciquismo corrupts electoral returns; the 1907 electoral reform introduces nominal safeguards but rural manipulation continues; civil service remains underpaid and venal; the Morocco command structure fractures between Africanist officers and metropolitan generals.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: The army exceeds 100,000 but is poorly equipped; officer corps inflates to one officer per six men; juntas de defensa (officer syndicates) form in 1917 to demand pay increases, challenging civilian control; Civil Guard polices rural order with exemplary brutality.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: The Tragic Week of 1909 burns eighty religious buildings in Barcelona; CNT general strikes paralyze Barcelona repeatedly after 1917; pistolerismo assassinates union leaders and employers alike; the Annual disaster discredits the military command and threatens the throne.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: Canovas's assassination (1897) leaves no equivalent statesman; Antonio Maura attempts reform but falls to the Tragic Week backlash; Dato oscillates; Alfonso XIII intervenes erratically, undermining constitutional distance.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: Republican sentiment grows in urban centers; Catalan nationalism gains mass adherence after the Solidaritat Catalana coalition of 1906; Basque nationalism consolidates around the PNV; working-class loyalty shifts to unions and parties, not the crown.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: The turno paralyzes reform; the 1917 crisis sees simultaneous military, parliamentary, and labor challenges that the system survives only by mutual antagonism among challengers; no coalition can form a governing majority.

External Relations & Posture: Neutrality in World War I reflects weakness, not choice; Morocco absorbs military attention without strategic return; the League of Nations seat (1920) provides rhetorical prestige but no leverage.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: The 1898 Disaster generates desencanto—national disillusion—captured by Generation of 98 writers; regenerationist mood demands modernization but fragments into incompatible programs; Catalan sentiment hardens after Tragic Week repression.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: Electoral abstention rises in urban districts where caciquismo cannot reach; anarchist abstencionismo rejects parliamentary participation; the Annual disaster exhausts public patience with both the military and the monarchy.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Castilian literacy reaches roughly 65 percent by 1920; Catalan-language literacy spreads through the Renaixenca cultural movement; oral communication remains primary in rural Andalusia.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Telegraph links all provincial capitals; telephone service reaches major cities by 1910; daily newspapers print in Madrid by midnight and reach Barcelona newsstands by morning.

Record, Storage & Persistence: Civil registry expands; the Archivo Historico Nacional organizes colonial records; newspaper morgues accumulate clippings that journalists weaponize against political opponents.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: Press freedom nominally prevails but suspensions occur during crises; the Morocco campaigns trigger censorship of casualty figures; anarchist papers face seizure; Church papers attack anticlerical journalism.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: Mass circulation dailies—ABC, El Sol, La Vanguardia—reach tens of thousands; illustrated magazines (Blanco y Negro) shape bourgeois taste; socialist and anarchist papers circulate through union networks.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: Partisan press prints rumor as fact; the Annual disaster's true casualty count emerges only through leaked military reports; cacique-controlled provincial papers suppress local scandals.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Catholic social teaching contends with anarchist direct-action ethics and socialist class solidarity; the Tragic Week's church-burning reveals deep anticlericalism among Barcelona workers.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: The 1889 Civil Code remains in force; labor legislation lags behind industrial conditions; the 1919 eight-hour-day decree represents the first major concession to organized labor.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: Military tribunals claim jurisdiction over crimes affecting public order; the Montjuic executions after 1909 and pistolerismo impunity erode judicial credibility; cacique influence corrupts rural courts.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Constitutional rights suspend repeatedly under states of exception; press seizures and preemptive arrests become routine in Barcelona; union organizers risk assassination without legal recourse.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: Officers responsible for the Annual disaster avoid court-martial until Alfonso XIII blocks the Picasso report; industrialists hiring pistoleros escape prosecution; Church property enjoys effective immunity.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: The Institucion Libre de Ensenanza propagates positivism and Krausist ethics; Ramon y Cajal wins the 1906 Nobel Prize in Medicine, symbolizing Spanish scientific capacity; regenerationist thought seeks European models.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Engineering schools expand; hydroelectric and mining technology transfers from Germany and Britain; military doctrine stagnates, contributing to Morocco failures.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: Primary schooling remains underfunded; illiteracy persists in Andalusia and Galicia; secondary and university education serve bourgeois reproduction; technical schools produce insufficient engineers.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: Traditional agricultural methods persist in the meseta while Catalan industry adopts modern machinery; clerical control of rural schools perpetuates outdated pedagogies.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: The 1898 Disaster shatters imperial self-image; Generation of 98 writers—Unamuno, Baroja, Azorin—interrogate Spanish essence; Castilian identity competes with rising Catalan and Basque particularism.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: Regenerationism promises modernization without revolution; Catalan nationalism constructs an alternative civic identity around language and industry; anarchism offers millennial rupture.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: Modernisme transforms Barcelona's architecture (Gaudi, Domenech); Madrid Noucentisme reacts with classicism; Picasso and Miro emerge from Catalan bohemia before emigrating to Paris.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: The Romantic españolada—bullfighting, flamenco—calcifies into tourist cliche even as regionalists reject it; official patriotism rings hollow after 1898.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: Catholic orthodoxy faces positivist challenge among urban intellectuals; Unamuno's tragic sense of life expresses spiritual crisis without resolving it; rural piety persists unreflectively.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: Marian devotions intensify among conservative Catholics; anticlerical workers boycott baptisms and church marriages; Holy Week processions mark social boundaries between devout and secular.

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: The Church rebuilds after disentailment through religious orders (Jesuits return 1868); Catholic lay associations organize conservative politics; episcopal pronouncements denounce liberalism and socialism.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: Protestantism remains marginal; freemasonry attracts liberal professionals; spiritualism and theosophy circulate among bohemian intellectuals; popular religiosity incorporates pre-Christian survivals.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: Urban working-class anticlericalism burns churches but does not fill the void; anarchist millenarianism offers secular salvation; bourgeois skepticism coexists with ritual conformity.

docs.title: 1598 CE – 1700 CE — Habsburg Decline and Baroque Culture
docs.text: The binding constraint is fiscal exhaustion from continuous warfare, compounded by demographic collapse from plague and expulsion, draining the capacity to project power while print turns inward to a brilliant but anxious Baroque culture that anatomizes decline even as it adorns it.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: The peninsula remains peripheral to northern European dynamism; the meseta is depopulating, coastal cities struggle, and distances to European theaters of war impose crushing logistics. The Pyrenean barrier seals the land route; Atlantic routes to Flanders require naval protection Spain can no longer guarantee.

Climate Regime & Volatility: The century experiences the Little Ice Age's intensification; harsh winters, erratic rainfall, and drought stress agriculture. The 1640s and 1690s see severe dearths; climate volatility compounds demographic and fiscal crises.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: Plague returns catastrophically in 1647–1652, killing perhaps a quarter of Castile's remaining population; Valencia and Andalusia are devastated. Earthquakes strike (1680 Malaga). Barbary raids continue to harass coasts; the Ottoman threat recedes but is not eliminated.

Resource & Energy Endowment: American silver flows decline as New World mines deplete and colonial economies retain more bullion. Merino wool remains an export but faces competition. Timber for ships is exhausted; Spain imports masts from the Baltic. Energy capture does not advance.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Depopulation reduces urban loads; the physical sink is not stressed. Abandoned villages dot the meseta, the landscape absorbing the decay of structures. No industrial pollution emerges to test capacity.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: The 1647–1652 plague is the century's catastrophe, erasing demographic gains and hollowing cities. Typhus, smallpox, and dysentery accompany war and dearth. Mortality spikes repeatedly; life expectancy may fall below 30 in crisis years.

Nutrition & Physiological Vitality: Harvest failures and depopulation disrupt provisioning; malnutrition spreads. The diet of grain, oil, and legumes becomes precarious; the poor resort to foraged foods and charity. Physiological vitality declines across the century.

Care, Healing & Recovery Capacity: Hospital capacity is overwhelmed by plague; Church institutions strain but persist. Medical knowledge does not advance; bleeding, purging, and prayer remain standard. Recovery from crisis is slow; demographic replacement takes generations.

Reproductive Biology & Pairing Dynamics: High mortality disrupts family formation; widowhood is common, remarriage frequent among those who survive. Clerical celibacy removes a stable fraction. Fertility does not compensate for mortality spikes.

Demographic Renewal & Density: Castile's population collapses from perhaps 6.5 million (1600) to under 5 million (1650), recovering only slightly by 1700. Density falls; villages are abandoned. Emigration to the Americas continues, draining young men. The demographic foundation of power erodes.

Attrition & Dependency Overhang: War widows, orphans, and plague survivors swell the dependent population. Church charity and confraternities are stretched; begging proliferates. The productive base shrinks relative to the dependent load, deepening poverty.

docs.title: D03. Economic Domain
docs.text:
Subsistence & Provisioning Floor: Grain yields decline with depopulation and climate stress; imports from the Baltic and Sicily fill gaps but drain bullion. The provisioning floor is precarious; dearth and high prices recur. The commons subsist but with diminishing margin.

Energy Capture & Conversion: No transformation in energy; muscle, wind, and water remain the portfolio. Per-capita work capacity stagnates. Spain falls behind the Dutch and English in harnessing wind and water for industrial purposes.

Labor Organization & Coercion: Guild restrictions ossify; labor mobility is limited. Expulsion of the moriscos (1609–1614) removes some 300,000 productive workers, devastating Valencia's agriculture and Granada's silk industry. The labor force contracts; coerced labor in the Americas props up colonial extraction.

Production & Surplus Capacity: Manufacturing declines; textile production cannot compete with imports. Agricultural surplus shrinks with population and yields. The surplus available for taxation and war diminishes through the century.

Storage, Reserves & Buffering: Treasury reserves are negative; debt accumulates. Bankruptcies continue (1607, 1627, 1647, 1653, 1680). Juros consume revenue; debt service crowds out investment. Granaries cannot buffer repeated failures; emergency imports require credit Spain lacks.

Exchange, Trade & Logistics: Seville's monopoly decays; trade shifts to Cadiz. Colonial silver flows shrink and are diverted by contraband. Dutch and English penetrate Caribbean trade. Internal commerce stagnates; roads deteriorate. External dependence on foreign manufactures persists without the bullion to pay.

Value Storage, Credit & Deferred Exchange: Vellon (copper) coinage inflates repeatedly; debasement and deflation cycles destabilize prices. Credit depends on Genoese and Portuguese converso bankers; access tightens after Inquisition persecution. Value storage is insecure.

Surplus Extraction & Redistribution: The Crown attempts to extract more from a shrinking base; millones (excise taxes) rise, voted reluctantly by Cortes. Catalonia and Portugal revolt (1640) against Castilian fiscal pressure. Surplus extraction reaches its ceiling and breaks the union.

Wealth Distribution & Asset Defense: Grandee estates consolidate as smaller holders fail; Church lands grow through donation and purchase. Mayorazgo locks wealth in unproductive hands. The productive middle collapses; upward mobility contracts. Wealth polarizes and stagnates.

Byproducts & Waste Routing: Material waste diminishes with declining production. Financial waste is catastrophic: decades of war spending yield nothing but exhaustion; malinvestment in military overreach is the era's defining economic residue.

docs.title: D04. Social Domain
docs.text:
Kinship, Family & Inheritance: Mayorazgo persists, concentrating estates; younger sons enter Church or seek colonial fortune. Marriage patterns shift with mortality; complex households form around survivors. Lineage remains paramount for status, but families shrink.

Association & Mutual Aid: Confraternities and parishes remain the safety net; their resources are strained by repeated crises. Guilds defend privileges but cannot adapt. Mutual aid contracts with the social base; the fabric frays but does not tear.

Leisure, Play & Sociability: The corrales (theaters) flourish; Lope de Vega, Tirso de Molina, Calderon draw crowds. Bullfights, processions, and feast days continue. The tavern remains the sociability node. Print enters through pliegos sueltos (broadsheets) and comedias in cheap editions.

Stratification, Status & Group Structure: Status rigidity intensifies; limpieza de sangre statutes are enforced obsessively. Converso families face renewed persecution; moriscos are expelled entirely (1609–1614). Grandees dominate court; hidalgos cling to honor without substance. The commons bear the weight.

Administrative Capacity & Institutional Integrity: The valido (royal favorite) system concentrates power (Lerma, Olivares, Nithard, Valenzuela); councils persist but are bypassed. Corruption spreads; offices are sold. Olivares attempts reform (Union of Arms) but fails. Administrative capacity declines; the apparatus ossifies and is captured by faction.

Coercive Apparatus & Means of Force: The tercios lose their edge; defeats at Rocroi (1643), Lens (1648), and the Dunes (1658) mark decline. The navy cannot protect trade; Atlantic convoys are vulnerable. Fortifications hold but cannot project power. By century's end, Spain is a second-rate military power.

Discharge, Disorder & Decay: Catalonia revolts (1640–1659), submitting only after French abandonment. Portugal secedes permanently (1640–1668). Naples and Sicily rebel (1647–1648). Banditry persists; urban crime rises with poverty. The apparatus cannot contain all threats; it holds Castile but loses the periphery.

docs.title: D05. Emotional Domain
docs.text:
Leadership & Personal Authority: Philip III (1598–1621) delegates to Lerma; Philip IV (1621–1665) relies on Olivares, then lesser validos. Carlos II (1665–1700) is physically and mentally incapacitated, a symbol of dynastic exhaustion. Personal authority is diffused or absent; faction fills the vacuum.

Legitimacy as Lived Allegiance: Allegiance to Crown persists but is tested by defeat and fiscal pressure. Peripheral revolts reflect eroded legitimacy outside Castile. The dynasty's physical decay in Carlos II undermines the symbolic order; legitimacy survives but is hollowed.

Political Will & Collective Resolve: Olivares' drive for reform (1621–1643) represents concentrated will, but it breaks against resistance and failure. After his fall, will dissipates into factional maneuvering. Collective resolve for empire gives way to exhausted acceptance of diminished status.

External Relations & Posture: Spain fights continuously: the Thirty Years' War, war with France, Dutch independence, Portuguese restoration war, the Fronde intervention. Each front drains resources. By the Peace of the Pyrenees (1659) and the Treaty of Lisbon (1668), hegemony is ceded; Spain becomes a defensive power seeking to preserve remnants.

Public Sentiment & Behavioral Temper: The mood darkens through the century; desengano (disillusionment) becomes the keynote. Providential confidence yields to fatalism. Satire (Quevedo) and lament (arbitristas) voice the sense of decline. Trust in institutions erodes; honor becomes defensive posture.

Disaffection, Apathy & Spent Will: By century's end, apathy pervades. The succession crisis (Carlos II without heir) paralyzes decision. Disaffection is not revolutionary but resigned; the will to act is spent. The emotional residue is exhaustion awaiting an external resolution—which comes with the Bourbon succession.

docs.title: D06. Informational Domain
docs.text:
Communication Accessibility: Castilian consolidates as the language of print and administration; regional languages persist in speech but lose ground in publication. Literacy may hold or decline slightly with demographic collapse; the reading public contracts with population.

Channels & Transmission Velocity: Print continues in Madrid, Seville, Barcelona, but output declines. Gaceta de Madrid (from 1661) provides official news; relaciones circulate. Transmission velocity does not improve; the channel contracts with the market.

Record, Storage & Persistence: Archives persist; Simancas continues to store state papers. Church records maintain demographic information. Libraries suffer neglect but are not destroyed. Print ensures persistence of Golden Age texts even as new production slows.

Framing, Censorship & Discourse Norms: Inquisition censorship continues but is less vigorous; the Index is updated (1612, 1632, 1640, 1667) but enforcement is routine rather than zealous. Self-censorship is internalized. Discourse norms do not liberalize; heterodoxy remains suppressed.

Reception, Attention & Amplification: Baroque theater reaches the widest audience; devotional and satirical print circulates. Attention concentrates on spectacle and morality. Arbitrista tracts diagnose decline but reach limited audiences; their analyses do not translate into policy.

Signal Integrity & Noise Load: Official narratives claim victories and minimize defeats; the gap between propaganda and reality is visible. Noise increases as trust declines; rumor fills the void. Verification capacity is limited; the informed know the truth but cannot speak it openly.

docs.title: D07. Moral Domain
docs.text:
Moral Foundations & Sense of Justice: Catholic morality persists; honor remains the paramount value, though its performative hollowing advances. The gap between professed virtue and corrupt practice widens; desengano literature anatomizes this hypocrisy.

Law, Codification & Regulatory Evolution: Legal pluralism continues; royal pragmatics accumulate without systematic reform. The Recopilacion of Castilian law (1567) remains the baseline. No significant codification occurs; regulation adds layers without rationalization.

Adjudication, Liability & Sanction: Courts remain overburdened and corrupt; justice is slow and costly. Inquisition activity peaks early-century (converso persecution, quietism cases late-century) then declines. Sanction remains brutal; torture and execution continue.

Rights, Protections & Compliance Burden: Fueros are suppressed in Catalonia after the revolt but restored incompletely. The commons enjoy few rights; compliance with fiscal demands is the primary burden. Nobility and clergy retain exemptions, widening the gap.

Impunity & Unredressed Wrong: Grandees and validos enjoy effective impunity; Olivares falls but is not punished. The powerful abuse office; redress for the commons is rare. The gap between justice owed and delivered grows, accumulating as cynicism.

docs.title: D08. Intellectual Domain
docs.text:
Inquiry, Theory & Paradigm: Scholasticism persists in universities, ossifying into formalism. The scientific revolution happens elsewhere; Spain imports its results selectively and late. Natural inquiry is subordinated to theology; the paradigm does not shift.

Applied Knowledge & Technical Method: Military and navigational technique stagnates; Spain cannot match Dutch shipbuilding or French fortification. Mining and metallurgy do not advance. The technique in use is inherited, not innovated.

Education, Knowledge Stock & Skill Distribution: Universities decline; enrollment falls, quality erodes. Primary education remains Church-run and limited. Literacy may contract with population. The knowledge stock is maintained in print but not expanded; skill distribution narrows.

Obsolescence & Knowledge Decay: Censorship freezes inquiry; new European thought is blocked. The knowledge frontier moves definitively north. Spain retains classical and theological learning but falls behind in natural philosophy. Obsolescence accumulates as a gap that will take centuries to close.

docs.title: D09. Cultural Domain
docs.text:
Mythos, Memory & Foundational Identity: The Reconquista and Catholic mission remain foundational, but their triumphalism is shadowed by present failure. Memory of imperial greatness contrasts with visible decline; identity becomes defensive, nostalgic, self-critical.

Legitimating Narrative & Ideology: Divine right and Catholic mission still legitimize the order, but their plausibility erodes. Arbitrista critique proposes reforms; literature anatomizes moral decay. The narrative persists but is questioned internally.

Artistic Expression & Material Culture: The Baroque flourishes: Velazquez's paintings, Murillo's devotional art, Calderon's autos sacramentales, Quevedo's satire, Gracian's aphorisms. Architecture turns ornate (Churrigueresque emerges late-century). Material culture displays wealth where it remains but cannot mask underlying poverty. Print disseminates comedias and verse in cheap editions.

Form Exhaustion & Meaning Decay: Baroque extravagance masks and reveals exhaustion simultaneously. Honor becomes performance; religious forms elaborate into spectacle. By century's end, the forms are magnificent but the substance is hollowed. Desengano is the cultural mood: unmasking the vanity beneath appearance.

docs.title: D10. Spiritual Domain
docs.text:
Cosmology & Existential Outlook: Catholic cosmology holds, but its tone darkens. Life is a dream (Calderon), vanity of vanities; memento mori pervades. Providence still orders the world, but its designs are inscrutable, and suffering is the human lot.

Ritual, Devotion & Sacred Practice: Baroque piety intensifies ritual: elaborate processions, saint cults, relics, votive offerings. The auto-da-fe continues as public spectacle. Devotional life is fervent, sometimes hysterical (possessed nuns, mystic excess).

Religious Institutions & Doctrinal Authority: The Church remains powerful, wealthy, and orthodox. The Inquisition operates but with diminished intensity. Doctrinal disputes (quietism, Jansenist influence) are suppressed. Institutional authority is stable but complacent.

Spiritual Diffusion, Syncretism & Displacement: Catholicism is consolidated in the peninsula with moriscos expelled; no heterodoxy survives openly. In the Americas, syncretism proceeds beneath official orthodoxy. No new spiritual movements emerge; the faith is maintained, not renewed.

Disenchantment & Sacred Discharge: Disenchantment is not visible as secularization but as internalized doubt beneath fervent observance. The gap between spectacle and interiority widens. The sacred remains officially charged, but desengano hints at emptiness beneath the forms—a proto-disenchantment that will surface in the Enlightenment century to come.

docs.title: 1500 CE – 1598 CE — Habsburg Zenith and Counter-Reformation Print
docs.text: The binding constraint is the tension between an unprecedented imperial reach financed by American silver and the determination to preserve Catholic orthodoxy through censorship, channeling print into Counter-Reformation service while stunting the critical public sphere that print elsewhere enabled.

docs.title: D01. Physical Domain
docs.text:
Geography & Spatial Friction: The Iberian Peninsula sits at Europe's southwestern extremity, dominated by the central meseta ringed by peripheral coastal plains and the Pyrenean barrier sealing the land route to France. Within Habsburg dominions, distances stretch from Castile to the Low Countries, Naples, and the Americas, imposing logistical friction that print cannot overcome; couriers and ships remain the transmission substrate, with printed dispatches and books moving along the same routes as bullion and troops.

Climate Regime & Volatility: The Mediterranean-continental climate delivers hot dry summers and cold winters on the meseta, with Atlantic moisture reaching the northwest; periodic droughts stress grain yields, and the 1590s see harvest failures that compound fiscal exhaustion.

Hazard Regime & Exposure: Earthquakes strike the south sporadically; coastal cities face Barbary raids; epidemic plague returns cyclically, devastating Seville in 1597–1602. Exposure to Ottoman naval threat shapes Mediterranean defenses and drains treasure.

Resource & Energy Endowment: Merino wool from the Mesta transhumance and American silver constitute the export base; timber for shipbuilding is overcut; Almaden mercury enables silver amalgamation in the New World. Energy remains human and animal muscle, wind for mills and ships.

Waste Absorption & Sink Capacity: Urban centers like Seville, Madrid, and Barcelona concentrate effluent and refuse; the landscape absorbs deforestation for ship timber; silver mining leaves tailings in the Americas, but Iberia itself sees limited industrial pollution. The physical sink remains ample relative to pre-industrial loads.

docs.title: D02. Biological Domain
docs.text:
Pathogen Load & Mortality Baseline: Plague recurs; the late-century epidemic wave (1596–1602) kills hundreds of thousands. Typhus accompanies armies. Infant mortality runs high; life expectancy perhaps 30–35 years. Disease is the persistent reaper, with urban crowding amplifying transmission.
